The Court, composed of Judges Gediminas Sagatys (President), Stéphane Pisani, and Juha Lavapuro, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar, deliberated in private on 19 June 2025 and delivered the judgment on 10 July 2025. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore: the 2012 termination of the applicant’s secondment contract on suspicion of FETÖ/PDY affiliation; his administrative annulment action; the domestic decisions of 8 November 2017, 20 June 2018, and 2 November 2018; the applicant’s complaint that those decisions lacked adequate reasoning; his additional unspecified Convention complaint; and the lodging of his ECtHR application on 26 April 2019. These facts frame the Court’s assessment of whether the domestic proceedings complied with Convention standards, particularly regarding reasoned judicial decisions.

In *N.T. v. Cyprus* (Application no. 28150/22), the applicant, a Cypriot national born in 1992, complained that the Cypriot authorities failed to effectively investigate and prosecute her rape allegation, in breach of positive obligations under Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention, and that she suffered gender-based discrimination contrary to Article 14 read with Articles 3 and 8.

The alleged rape occurred on 1 January 2011, when the applicant was 18 and A.T. was 20. She reported it to police on 10 April 2021. She stated that after a night out with her friend C.S., A.T. and his friend G.H., A.T. insisted they enter his father’s warehouse. She initially resisted but went inside to use the bathroom. A.T. took her upstairs, grabbed and tried to undress her, forced her onto boxes, and raped her orally and vaginally despite her resistance. She said she froze, later scratched and bit him, and asked him to stop; he continued and bit her neck. Afterwards she had bruises and bite marks, which C.S. later saw. She told a male friend, D.N., and two psychologists about the rape. She decided to report after a Facebook conversation with S.N., who said A.T. had also raped another classmate.

Police opened an investigation immediately. They took statements from the applicant, C.S., D.N., S.N., G.H., and a psychologist. C.S. corroborated seeing the applicant’s bruised neck and strange behaviour, and described a separate 2010 incident in which A.T. tried to force her to perform oral sex. G.H. claimed he heard nothing unusual and that the applicant did not seem upset. A.T. refused to answer police questions. The police recommended prosecution, and in May 2021 an indictment for rape was filed; the case was referred to the Assize Court, where A.T. pleaded not guilty and was released on bail.

The applicant later gave two supplementary statements. In the first, she disclosed affectionate Facebook messages to A.T., including a 2011 message saying she loved him, and said she initially blamed herself, believed she had given him the wrong message, and wanted to protect him. In the second, she revealed that on 1 January 2010 she had had consensual sex with A.T. in the same warehouse, with C.S. and G.H. downstairs, and had orally told police but asked that it not be recorded. Prosecutors then reassessed her credibility, citing inconsistencies, ongoing texts until 2013, affectionate language, and her statements that she may have implied consent. On 1 December 2021 the Deputy Attorney General discontinued the prosecution by *nolle prosequi*, citing doubts about credibility, possible subjective belief in consent, and low prospects of conviction. The applicant sought reasons and the case file; her request for the file was refused. A.T. publicly announced the withdrawal. The applicant complained to the ECtHR that the authorities’ failure to continue the prosecution and their reliance on victim-blaming assumptions violated Articles 3 and 8, and discriminated against her as a woman under Article 14.

In *Zvonar v. Ukraine* (no. 20532/16), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning the applicant’s loss of land purchased from local authorities. In February 2009, Zvonar began renting a 0.42 ha plot near the Drahobrat ski resort, Yasinia, from local authorities. He built a cable transportation system and used the land for tourism. On 17 November 2010 and 11 January 2011, the Rakhiv District State Administration (“Rakhiv DSA”) decided to allow him to buy the land, describing it as outside urban settlements and for non-agricultural use. On 14 January 2011, the applicant signed a sale and purchase contract and paid UAH 460,056 (about EUR 43,850). He later obtained ownership certificates for subdivided plots, designating the land for “construction and maintenance of recreational facilities.”

In July 2012, at the local prosecutor’s request, the State Agricultural Inspectorate inspected the allocation. It concluded that under Article 122 § 3 of the Land Code, the Rakhiv DSA had no power to dispose of the land: local State administrations could only dispose of land outside urban settlements designated for agricultural or water-management use, or for local community infrastructure. Based on this, the prosecutor sued the applicant, seeking annulment of the DSA decisions and invalidation of the sale contract and title. The prosecutor acted in the interests of the Zakarpattia Region State Administration (“Zakarpattia RSA”), alleged to be the competent authority, and the Yasinia village council, supposed to receive the profits. Both authorities objected, saying the Rakhiv DSA had acted lawfully.

On 18 December 2013, the Rakhiv Local Court allowed the prosecutor’s claims, finding the Rakhiv DSA had acted ultra vires. It ordered reclamation under Article 387 of the Civil Code, which permits recovery of property that left an owner’s possession without a proper legal basis, even from a bona fide owner. On 20 May 2014, the Court of Appeal quashed that judgment, holding that the Zakarpattia RSA’s objection effectively approved the sale under Article 241 of the Civil Code, so an ultra vires deed later approved could be valid. The Higher Specialised Civil and Criminal Court (“HSCCC”) quashed this and remitted the case, stating that recreational land could only be disposed of by the Cabinet of Ministers. On 17 March 2015, the Court of Appeal upheld the Local Court’s conclusion but reasoned that, because the land was for recreational purposes, neither the Rakhiv DSA nor the Zakarpattia RSA could dispose of it; the transfer was therefore unlawful. On 7 October 2015, the HSCCC dismissed the applicant’s cassation appeal.

In domestic proceedings, the applicant argued that invalidating the sale would damage the State financially because it would have to reimburse the purchase price, but he did not expressly raise the restitution rules applicable to invalid contracts. The ECtHR gave notice of his complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The key issue was whether the applicant’s deprivation of land, following the prosecutor’s action and the courts’ finding that the local authority exceeded its powers, violated his right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions, including whether the interference was lawful, proportionate, and balanced against his status as a bona fide purchaser who had paid for and developed the land.

**Zvonar v. Ukraine (Application no. 20532/16)** concerns Mr Yurii Yuriiovych Zvonar, a Ukrainian national born in 1959, who complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights that he had been deprived of land he had purchased from local authorities.

In February 2009, the applicant began renting a 0.42-hectare plot from local authorities near the Drahobrat ski resort, near the village of Yasinia. He apparently built a cable transportation system on the land and used it for tourism. On 17 November 2010 and 11 January 2011, the Rakhiv District State Administration (“the Rakhiv DSA”) adopted decisions allowing him to purchase the land as a private owner. The decisions stated that the land was outside urban settlements and designated for non-agricultural use. On 14 January 2011, the applicant signed a sale and purchase contract with the Rakhiv DSA and paid UAH 460,056 (approximately EUR 43,850 at the time). He later obtained ownership certificates for the land, divided into several plots, which described the land as intended for the “construction and maintenance of recreational facilities.”

In July 2012, following a request from the local prosecutor, the State Agricultural Inspectorate of the Zakarpattia Region inspected the land allocation. It concluded, citing Article 122 § 3 of the Land Code, that the Rakhiv DSA had lacked authority to dispose of the land. According to the Inspectorate, local State administrations could dispose only of land outside urban settlements designated for agricultural use, water management, or local community infrastructure, such as schools or hospitals. Based on that conclusion, the prosecutor sued the applicant, seeking to set aside the Rakhiv DSA decisions and invalidate the sale contract and the applicant’s title. The prosecutor acted in the interests of the Zakarpattia Region State Administration (“the Zakarpattia RSA”), which was allegedly empowered to dispose of the land, and the Yasinia village council, which was supposedly entitled to the proceeds. Both authorities objected to the prosecutor’s claims, arguing that the Rakhiv DSA had acted within its powers and that the sale had been lawful.

On 18 December 2013, the Rakhiv Local Court allowed the prosecutor’s claims in full. It found that the Rakhiv DSA had acted ultra vires and that the land could be reclaimed from the applicant under Article 387 of the Civil Code, which allows recovery of property that left an owner’s possession “without a proper legal basis,” even from a bona fide owner. On 20 May 2014, the Zakarpattia Region Court of Appeal quashed that judgment. It held that, by objecting to the claim, the Zakarpattia RSA had essentially approved the sale, so under Article 241 of the Civil Code the ultra vires act could be deemed valid. The Higher Specialised Civil and Criminal Court (“the HSCCC”) quashed that judgment and remitted the case, holding that land designated for recreational purposes could only be disposed of by the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine.

On 17 March 2015, the Court of Appeal upheld the Local Court’s conclusion but changed the reasoning: because the land was for recreational purposes, only the Cabinet of Ministers could dispose of it, so the transfer to the applicant was unlawful. On 7 October 2015, the HSCCC dismissed the applicant’s cassation appeal.

In the domestic proceedings, the applicant argued that invalidating the sale would harm the State because it would have to reimburse him the purchase price. However, he did not expressly raise the issue of restitution rules for invalid contracts, under which the parties must be restored to their prior positions. He lodged his Convention application on 1 April 2016, alleging a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 regarding deprivation of his property.

In *Černý and Others v. the Czech Republic*, five Czech criminal defence lawyers applied to the European Court of Human Rights. The Court gave notice to the Government of complaints under Articles 6 §1, 8 and 13 of the Convention; other complaints were declared inadmissible. The applicants’ core complaint was that privileged lawyer-client communications with their client Z. were seized from his electronic devices, extracted, placed in a criminal case file, and disclosed to prosecutors and co-defendants.

The applicants represented Z. in two parallel criminal proceedings: one concerning membership of a criminal group, false accusations, bribery and related offences, and another concerning tax evasion. On 2 December 2016, during a search of Z.’s home ordered in the first proceedings, police seized his smartphone and tablet. These devices contained correspondence between Z. and his defence lawyers, including the applicants, draft court submissions, notes on legal strategy in both cases, witness-questioning preparations, and other legally privileged material.

In Sakellaris and Others v. Greece (Application no. 43594/16), four Greek nationals—Konstantinos Sakellaris (born 1962), Dimitrios Diskos (born 1967), Stefanos Lazaridis (born 1977), and Vasilios Tzouvaras (born 1974)—lodged an application against Greece with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention. The application was introduced on 20 July 2016. The applicants were represented by Mr G. Papastergiou, a lawyer practising in Veroia. The Greek Government was given notice of the application. The case was examined by the Third Section sitting as a Committee, composed of Judges Diana Kovatcheva, Canòlic Mingorance Cairat, and Vasilka Sancin, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The Court deliberated in private on 2 October 2025 and adopted its judgment on 23 October 2025. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The key facts relate to the non-enforcement of a final domestic judgment obtained by the applicants. According to the appended table, the judgment was delivered by the Supreme Administrative Court, Judgment no. 4917/2012, and became final on 18 December 2012. That domestic judgment was in the applicants’ favour. However, the Greek authorities did not enforce it. The table records the start date of the non-enforcement period as 18 December 2012, the date on which the judgment became final. The end date is stated as “pending,” meaning that the judgment remained unenforced at the time the table was prepared. The total length of non-enforcement is recorded as more than 12 years, 6 months, and 23 days. The provided excerpt does not describe the underlying subject matter of the domestic judgment, the nature of the applicants’ original claims before the Supreme Administrative Court, or the specific reasons why the judgment was not executed.

The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights about two matters. First, they alleged the non-enforcement of the domestic judgment in their favour. Second, they alleged the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law by which they could secure enforcement of that judgment or obtain redress for the continuing failure to execute it. In substance, the case is not about the original administrative dispute, but about the Greek State’s failure to comply with a final and binding judicial decision and the absence of an adequate domestic mechanism to challenge that failure.

The essential facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore: the Supreme Administrative Court’s final judgment of 18 December 2012 in the applicants’ favour; the authorities’ failure to enforce it; the continuing and pending nature of that non-enforcement; the lengthy period of non-enforcement, recorded as more than 12 years, 6 months, and 23 days; and the applicants’ claim that no effective domestic remedy was available. The procedural details identify the applicants, their representative, the respondent Government, the application date, and the Court’s composition. The provided judgment excerpt records the facts and complaints but does not set out the Court’s legal analysis, the specific Convention Articles invoked, or the final outcome on the merits.

In *Radelić v. Croatia* (Application no. 12432/22), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint concerning the confiscation of proceeds of crime acquired by a company but ordered from the individual perpetrator after the company had ceased to exist.

The applicant, Dražen Radelić, was the sole shareholder and director of Radelić d.o.o. The company was declared bankrupt on 12 November 2010, the bankruptcy concluded on 12 December 2010, and on 4 March 2011 it was struck off the commercial register, thereby ceasing to exist.

In 2011, the Split Municipal State Attorney’s Office indicted the applicant for business fraud and forgery of documents. It was alleged that between 27 August 2003 and 26 February 2004 he presented thirty-six foreign bank cheques to a bank, falsely claiming they were payment for services rendered abroad, intending to obtain significant pecuniary gain for the company. In 2014, the Split Municipal Court convicted him of forgery, imposed a suspended prison sentence, and acquitted him of business fraud. On appeal, the County Court upheld the forgery conviction but quashed the acquittal on business fraud and remitted that charge for retrial.

In 2017, the Municipal Court convicted the applicant of business fraud and sentenced him to one year’s imprisonment, suspended for four years. It also ordered the confiscation of HRK 854,743.39 (approximately EUR 113,440) from him personally as proceeds of crime, payable into the State budget within six months. If he failed to pay, the suspended sentence could be revoked. The court reasoned that the company had been struck off and had no legal successor, so the proceeds had to be confiscated from the accused as the sole founder, shareholder, and authorised representative who had disposed of the company’s funds.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the money had been paid into the company’s account, not to him personally; that the company had paid taxes and used the funds for its operations; and that he had not benefited. In September 2017, the Split County Court dismissed his appeals. It held that the confiscation was lawful because the amount had been kept for the company through his criminal actions, the company no longer existed, and, by analogy with section 252(5) of the Commercial Companies Act, he could be liable to creditors unable to satisfy claims against the company.

The Split County State Attorney’s Office later proposed that a request for the protection of legality be filed, arguing that confiscation from the applicant personally was contrary to law. It noted that the indictment alleged gain for the company, not for him; there was no evidence he received the proceeds; the company had been liquidated; and no injured party had made a civil claim. It also cited Supreme Court case-law that proceeds of crime cannot be confiscated from a perpetrator if the gain was acquired for a company. The Principal State Attorney never filed the request.

In November 2017, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint relying on the constitutional right of ownership. In October 2021, the Constitutional Court dismissed it, finding no breach of his ownership rights. Enforcement attempts continued: the Municipal Court invited payment in 2017 and 2021, and in January 2023 the State Attorney’s Office sought enforcement through FINA against his bank accounts. The order apparently remained unenforced due to insufficient funds.

The key alleged violation was therefore the personal confiscation order imposed on the applicant for proceeds acquired by a now-defunct company, despite the fact that he was not accused of obtaining the gain for himself. The relevant law included Article 77 of the Penal Code, which permits confiscation from a perpetrator or transferee, and Article 247, under which business fraud involves intent to obtain gain for a legal entity represented by the perpetrator or another legal entity. The case thus concerns whether ordering an individual to pay the equivalent of company proceeds after the company ceased to exist was lawful and compatible with property rights.

In *Zakaidze v. Georgia* (Application no. 42199/22, judgment of 4 November 2025), the applicant, Besik Zakaidze, complained under Articles 2, 6 and 8 of the Convention that Georgia’s criminal proceedings against three private individuals who verbally and physically assaulted him were ineffective and failed to protect him or allow him meaningful participation.

On 9 February 2021, an altercation arose after the applicant asked a neighbour to repay borrowed money. Three neighbours then beat him. Emergency services reported difficulty speaking and swallowing, pain and deformation of his lower jaw, and nausea. Hospital diagnosis included fractures to his lower jaw, excoriations on his nose, intracranial trauma and concussion. He underwent two jaw surgeries and was discharged on 16 February 2021 in a stable condition.

A criminal investigation began the same day under Article 126 § 11(b) of the Criminal Code, covering violence committed by a group. The applicant was interviewed in hospital; the three neighbours were questioned and all admitted verbally and physically assaulting him. None was remanded in custody. Various investigative steps followed, including an on-site inspection and witness questioning. On 9 March 2021 the applicant complained about investigative delay and asked about charges; the prosecutor replied that the investigation was ongoing and charging depended on further measures. A forensic examination was ordered on 10 March 2021. On 1 July 2021, the expert concluded that the abrasions and scratches were individually minor, while the jaw fractures and concussion amounted to less severe bodily injuries causing long-term harm, consistent with 9 February 2021. On 8 July 2021, the prosecution reclassified the charge from group violence to intentionally causing less serious harm to health under Article 118 § 3.

The applicant was granted victim status on 21 April 2021. However, the relevant document contained a pre-typed statement that he did not wish to review the case file or receive information about the case’s progress, which he signed. He later complained that the investigator had misled him, pressured him to give a less severe version of the assault, and ignored his complaints. These complaints went unanswered. After reclassification, he was again granted victim status on 8 July 2021.

On 22 July 2021, the Mtskheta District Court held a hearing with the prosecutor and three defendants participating online. All three pleaded guilty. The applicant was not informed of the hearing and did not attend. The judge proceeded under simplified proceedings without oral examination of evidence and convicted all three, imposing suspended three-year prison sentences and ordering them not to approach or communicate with the applicant. The applicant complained that he had not been heard and that the sentences were disproportionate. He requested access to the case file but was refused.

The prosecution appealed for a stricter penalty. The applicant wrote to the Tbilisi Court of Appeal, complaining that the first-instance proceedings occurred in his absence and that he had never been notified. On 3 November 2021, the appeal court increased the suspended sentences to four years and added 200 hours of community service. The applicant was present, but no evidence was examined because the appeal was limited to sanction. The court cited the defendants’ guilty pleas, lack of criminal record, cooperation, family and financial circumstances, and non-contact order. On 30 May 2022, the Supreme Court rejected the prosecution’s cassation appeal, noting the applicant could pursue separate compensation.

The applicant’s later civil compensation claim was dismissed on 21 February 2023 for failure to pay court fees, because the exemption did not cover non-pecuniary damage; this was upheld on appeal on 26 June 2023. The key alleged violations therefore concerned the effectiveness of the investigation, the lenient and reclassified charges, the suspended sentences, and the applicant’s exclusion from key proceedings.

The case of *Sakellaris and Others v. Greece* (Application no. 43594/16) concerns four applicants—Konstantinos Sakellaris (born 1962), Dimitrios Diskos (born 1967), Stefanos Lazaridis (born 1977), and Vasilios Tzouvaras (born 1974)—who lodged an application against Greece with the European Court of Human Rights on 20 July 2016 under Article 34 of the Convention. They were represented by Mr G. Papastergiou, a lawyer practising in Veroia. The Greek Government was given notice of the application.

The applicants complained of the non-enforcement of a domestic judgment given in their favour and of the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law in respect of that non-enforcement. The domestic judgment at issue was Judgment no. 4917/2012 of the Supreme Administrative Court, which became final on 18 December 2012. According to the appended table, the period of non-enforcement began on that date. The table records the end date of the non-enforcement period as “pending” and states that the total length of non-enforcement exceeded 12 years, 6 months and 23 days. Thus, by the time the case was examined, the final judgment in the applicants’ favour had still not been enforced.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore as follows. First, the applicants obtained a final and binding judgment from the Supreme Administrative Court in their favour on 18 December 2012. Second, the Greek authorities did not take the necessary steps to execute that judgment. Third, the non-enforcement continued for a prolonged period, exceeding twelve years and six months, and remained pending at the time of the proceedings. Fourth, the applicants asserted that no effective domestic remedy existed through which they could compel enforcement of the judgment or obtain adequate redress for its non-execution.

The applicants’ complaint therefore combined two related allegations: the prolonged non-execution of a final domestic judicial decision in their favour, and the absence of an effective remedy at the domestic level to address that failure. The facts set out in the application and the appended table focus on the date the domestic judgment became final, the start date of the non-enforcement, the continuing nature of the non-enforcement, and its substantial length.

Procedurally, the application was introduced on 20 July 2016. The Court, sitting as a Committee of the Third Section composed of Diana Kovatcheva (President), Canòlic Mingorance Cairat, and Vasilka Sancin (judges), with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar, deliberated in private on 2 October 2025 and adopted the judgment on 23 October 2025. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. The facts section of the judgment refers to the appended table for the applicants’ details and the information relevant to the application.

In essence, the case concerns an alleged failure by Greece to enforce a final administrative court judgment in the applicants’ favour, which remained unenforced for more than twelve years, and the alleged lack of any effective remedy in Greek law for that continuing non-enforcement. These are the central facts relevant to the applicants’ alleged Convention violations.

**Ibrahimi and Others v. Albania** (Applications nos. 81057/17 and 4 others) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered on 14 January 2025. The five applications concerned proceedings before Albanian courts in which the applicants’ constitutional complaints against Supreme Court decisions were rejected by the Constitutional Court as lodged out of time. The central alleged violation was that the Constitutional Court calculated the four-month time-limit from the date the Supreme Court adopted its decision, rather than from the date the applicants were actually served with or effectively learned of that decision. This, the applicants argued, restricted their right of access to the Constitutional Court and, in one case, other fair-trial rights.

The common pattern was that the Supreme Court decided each case, but the decision was served on the applicants much later. The applicants then filed constitutional complaints within four months of service or notification. Nonetheless, the Constitutional Court declared the complaints inadmissible because more than four months had passed since the Supreme Court’s adoption of the decision. In four applications, the Constitutional Court also held that a stamp showing that a party had requested service was not decisive proof of the date of first service, and that the burden was on the party to prove it had not been served earlier.

In **Ibrahimi v. Albania** (no. 81057/17), the applicant had been convicted of murder and sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment. The Supreme Court adopted its decision on 25 June 2015. A letter notifying him of the decision was served by prison authorities on 12 May 2017. He lodged a constitutional complaint on 5 June 2017, complaining that he had not been informed of the Supreme Court hearing and had been denied legal assistance. The Constitutional Court declared it inadmissible on 16 June 2017 as out of time. His case also raised alleged violations of his right to participate in person in the criminal proceedings and to defend himself through legal assistance of his own choosing before the Supreme Court.

In **Selimi v. Albania** (no. 57542/18), a property dispute, the Supreme Court adopted its decision on 25 June 2015; it was served on the applicants on 18 October 2017. They lodged a constitutional complaint on 13 February 2018, which was rejected as out of time on 30 May 2018.

In **Nika v. Albania** (no. 32939/21), the applicant challenged her dismissal as a forestry inspector. The Supreme Court decided on 27 May 2020, and the decision was served on 14 January 2021. She filed a constitutional complaint on 18 January 2021, but it was rejected on 26 February 2021 as out of time.

In **Dedaj v. Albania** (no. 54121/21), the applicant challenged his dismissal from work. The Supreme Court decided on 27 July 2020, and service occurred on 1 April 2021. He lodged a constitutional complaint on 9 June 2021; it was declared inadmissible on 26 July 2021.

In **Industri Ndërtim (IN) SH.P.K. v. Albania** (no. 7386/22), a company involved in civil contractual proceedings, the Supreme Court adopted its decision on 17 February 2021. It was served on the company on 4 June 2021. The company filed a constitutional complaint on 29 September 2021, which the Constitutional Court rejected as out of time on 29 October 2021. The application also concerned the company’s right to participate in proceedings before the Tirana District Court.

The Court gave notice of the complaints concerning access to the Constitutional Court and the additional fair-trial complaints in the Ibrahimi and Industri Ndërtim cases, while declaring the remainder inadmissible. The third party Res Publica was granted leave to intervene.

In *Marzouki and Others v. Bulgaria* (Application no. 48636/19), a Fifth Section Committee of the European Court of Human Rights considered an application lodged on 5 September 2019 by three applicants: Mohamed Nabil Marzouki, a Tunisian national; his daughter Mariam, a Bulgarian national born in 2010; and Yana Dimitrova Yankova, a Bulgarian national born in 1976 and the child’s mother. The first applicant had permanent residence in Bulgaria, where he lived with the second and third applicants. The case concerns his removal from Bulgaria and his separation from them.

In early 2018 the first applicant travelled to Serbia. On 1 February 2018, when he tried to return to Bulgaria, he was refused entry and given a standard refusal form. Two boxes were checked: one indicating that an alert had been issued for refusing entry, and another stating that he was considered a threat to public order, internal security, public health or international relations. He sought judicial review. In those proceedings the border police explained that they had acted under a decision of the State Agency for National Security (SANS), also dated 1 February 2018, which imposed a five-year entry ban because he allegedly posed a national security threat. The Sofia Region Administrative Court upheld the refusal on 29 October 2018, reasoning that the border police were bound by the SANS decision.

A copy of the SANS decision was served on the first applicant’s representative only on 31 July 2018, after the representative learned of it during the judicial-review proceedings and requested it. The SANS decision did not contain specific reasons justifying the conclusion that the first applicant threatened national security. Instead, it referred to a classified document called a “Proposal.” That Proposal was later declassified and submitted by the Government.

After receiving the SANS decision, the representative applied for judicial review of it. However, the Supreme Administrative Court, in a final decision of 6 March 2019, declared the application time-barred. It held that the fourteen-day time-limit for challenging the decision had begun on 1 February 2018, when the applicant had allegedly been “orally informed” of it. This finding apparently referred to the standard refusal form given to him at the border. The Supreme Administrative Court considered that he had been validly informed in that manner under Article 61 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Procedure, as then worded, which permitted oral notification of administrative decisions.

Before the European Court, the applicants complained that the first applicant’s removal from Bulgaria was unjustified and disrupted their family life together, contrary to Article 8 of the Convention. They further complained under Article 13, in conjunction with Article 8, that there were no effective domestic remedies available to challenge the measures. The key facts relevant to those allegations are that the first applicant had permanent residence and family ties in Bulgaria; that he was excluded and banned for five years on undisclosed national-security grounds; that the underlying decision was not adequately reasoned; that he received a copy only months later; and that his attempt to challenge it was rejected as out of time based on an alleged oral notification at the border, thereby preventing substantive review of the national-security ban and its impact on his family life.

**Case Name:** *Karović and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina*  
**Applications nos.:** 43201/22, 555/23, 5241/23 and 23976/23  
**Court:** European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section  
**Judgment date:** 24 June 2025 (final 24 September 2025)

The case concerns the non-enforcement of final domestic decisions in favour of four Bosnian nationals—Zlatan Karović, Tarik Kršlak, Vanja Bradarić and Osman Šabanović—against Sarajevo Canton, one of the ten cantons of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the failure to enforce domestic decisions in their favour. The Court gave notice of those non-enforcement complaints and declared the remainder of the applications inadmissible.

The underlying judgments were delivered by the Sarajevo Municipal Court on 5 and 19 February 2015, 24 February 2017 and 23 April 2018. They ordered Sarajevo Canton to pay the applicants various sums for unpaid work-related benefits, together with default interest at the statutory rate and legal costs. Writs of execution were issued by the same court on 5 May 2016, 5 July 2017, 13 June 2018 and 19 February 2021. Despite these final and enforceable decisions, the sums were not paid.

One applicant, Osman Šabanović, obtained a decision from the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina on 12 January 2022. That court found a violation of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to non-enforcement, ordered Sarajevo Canton to take the necessary steps to secure enforcement of the decision in his favour, and awarded him 300 convertible marks (BAM) in compensation for non-pecuniary damage.

On 13 January 2022, Sarajevo Canton adopted an enforcement plan for all domestic decisions against it, published in the Official Gazette of Sarajevo Canton no. 4/22. The plan provided that those who renounced their claims for default interest and legal costs would be paid their principal claims without delay. For those who did not agree, including the applicants, it provided that the decisions would be enforced in chronological order within five years—by the end of 2026—and that up to 0.8% of the total budget would be designated for that purpose. It also stated that Sarajevo Canton reserved the right not to adhere to the plan if it were allocated fewer funds in the future.

On 6 April 2022, the Constitutional Court rejected the case of another applicant, Mr Karović, on the ground that the Sarajevo Canton enforcement plan was acceptable. However, according to the available information, the decisions concerning the applicants have still not been enforced. As of 31 December 2024, the applicants held the following places in the chronological order of unenforced decisions against Sarajevo Canton: Mr Šabanović was 1,017th; Ms Bradarić was 2,299th; Mr Karović was 3,092nd; and Mr Kršlak was 5,797th.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore that the applicants hold final domestic judgments ordering a public authority, Sarajevo Canton, to pay work-related benefits, interest and costs; execution writs were issued; enforcement has not occurred; and the cantonal enforcement plan imposes conditions and a lengthy timetable that continue to delay payment. The Constitutional Court found a violation for one applicant but later accepted the plan in another case. The applicants complain before the ECtHR that the continued non-enforcement breaches their right to execution of final judgments and their property rights.

In *K.V. Mediterranean Tours Limited v. Türkiye* (Application no. 41120/17, ECtHR Second Section, judgment of 10 June 2025), a Cypriot company complains about proceedings before the Immovable Property Commission (“IPC”) in northern Cyprus. The applicant company owned a building complex in the fenced-up area of Famagusta (Varosha). Its shareholders and directors are Greek Cypriot, and the company abandoned the property after the 1974 Turkish military operation.

On 23 July 2010 the company applied to the IPC seeking compensation for loss of use, restitution, non-pecuniary damages, statutory interest and costs. When the “TRNC” authorities did not respond, it applied for a default judgment on 1 November 2010. Between December 2010 and June 2012, ten hearings were repeatedly adjourned at the request of the “TRNC” Attorney-General’s Office because a property report had not been provided. In October 2012 the applicant complained of delay. The authorities then indicated that the property appeared to be registered in the name of a religious organisation, the Abdullah Paşa Foundation, managed by the Evkaf Administration. In November 2012 the IPC admitted the Evkaf Administration as a third party because it might be affected by the claim.

The applicant challenged that admission and the adjournments/delays before the “TRNC” Administrative Court. In November 2015, that court held that the Evkaf Administration could not be admitted because its participation would make restitution impossible. It also held that it lacked jurisdiction over complaints about IPC adjournments and delays. Both sides appealed. In November 2016, the High Administrative Court held that it had exclusive jurisdiction over all IPC-related matters, but that adjournment and delay issues were not subject to judicial review. Relying on a 2005 Famagusta District Court judgment that the Evkaf Administration was the current registered owner, it ordered that Evkaf be admitted as a party.

The “TRNC” authorities filed submissions in December 2019. In January 2020, and again at hearings in February, June and October 2020, the applicant and its representative refused to attend the IPC. On 22 February 2024 the representative attended and agreed to forward any compensation proposals, but later stated that settlement could be reached before the European Court. The IPC proceedings remain pending.

The relevant framework is Law no. 67/2005. It allows property claims before the IPC. Applicants must prove title as of 20 July 1974, forced abandonment, and the absence of competing claims. The defendant is the Ministry/Attorney-General. The IPC must invite anyone holding a property or use right to participate as an interested party. Remedies include restitution, exchange or compensation, with restitution subject to conditions such as national security, public order, public interest and military areas. In the 2000s, the Evkaf Administration and Department of Religious Affairs obtained a 2005 declaration that listed Varosha properties belonged to the Abdullah Paşa foundation. A 2019 High Administrative Court decision later stated that the IPC could consider only 1974 title deeds and could not alter land-registry records or find fraud, and that Evkaf’s participation did not affect claimants who proved pre-1974 title. In 2023, the High Administrative Court reviewed an IPC decision for diligence and good faith but rejected a length complaint. Statistics show 7,800 IPC applications by October 2024, with 1,869 finalised and substantial compensation awarded.

The applicant alleged that the IPC proceedings were ineffective, excessively delayed, and affected by the Evkaf intervention in the Famagusta fenced-up area. It also complained that the High Administrative Court was not impartial as the appellate authority for IPC cases. The ECtHR examined complaints under Articles 6, 13 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning fair and impartial proceedings, an effective remedy, discrimination, and protection of property.

Gullotti v. Italy (Application no. 64753/14) concerns an Italian national, Giuseppe Gullotti, convicted of mafia-type offences including participation in Cosa Nostra, murder, extortion and weapons offences. Arrested in 1998, he was detained under the special prison regime in section 41 bis of the Prison Administration Act. That regime imposed restrictions such as limited family visits, no non-family visits, no telephone use, limits on money and parcels, exclusion from prison representative elections, and a maximum of two hours outdoors daily. Although section 41 bis allows correspondence monitoring, concrete limitations require a judicial order under section 18 ter.

According to available documents, the applicant’s correspondence was monitored between 5 July 2012 and 27 May 2013. From at least 4 December 2012, the Reggio Emilia sentence supervision judge limited his correspondence to relatives admitted for family visits. On 7 January 2013 the prison governor requested renewal. On 8 January 2013, relying on the applicant’s dossier, the Reggio Emilia judge renewed the limitation for three months, until 7 April 2013. The judge reasoned that the applicant retained a prominent role in Cosa Nostra despite detention since 1998, relying on investigative sources and statements by cooperating prisoners, and noting a favourable opinion from the District Anti-Mafia Prosecution Office.

The applicant appealed under sections 14 ter and 18 ter(6) of the Prison Administration Act. On 12 March 2013 the Bologna sentence supervision court upheld the order, repeating that the sources indicated he remained a member of the criminal organisation and had not distanced himself from it. On 21 March 2014 the Court of Cassation declared his further appeal inadmissible, holding that the limitation was justified.

While appeal proceedings against the 8 January order were pending, the Reggio Emilia judge renewed the correspondence limitation three more times, each for three months, by orders of 8 April, 9 July and 7 October 2013. The April and October orders relied on the same reasoning as the January order. Separately, on 30 October 2013 the Minister of Justice renewed the section 41 bis regime for two years, citing anti-mafia information that the applicant was a mafia-clan leader in the Barcellona Pozzo di Gotto area with strong links to other clans, and wiretapped conversations from 2003 showing members could not communicate with him in person or by mail.

On 21 November 2013 the Bologna sentence supervision court allowed an appeal against the 8 April order. It found the reasoning inadequate because it broadly referred to investigative sources without detailing their content, and failed to consider favourable material: a 2009 Turin decision granting early release, Parma and Cuneo prison reports from 2013 referring to good conduct and training, and only minor disciplinary matters. The applicant then asked that the 9 July and 7 October orders be declared unlawful on the same grounds, but on 22 January 2014 the Bologna court rejected the request as inadmissible because the Prison Administration Act did not provide for it. Meanwhile, on 31 December 2013, after noting the 21 November decision, the Reggio Emilia judge refused the governor’s request of 4 December 2013 to renew the correspondence limitation further.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained under Article 8 about the limitation of his correspondence during detention and under Article 13 about the effectiveness of an appeal against the renewing decisions, particularly the order of 8 January 2013. The Court gave notice of those complaints and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

K.V. Mediterranean Tours Ltd v. Türkiye (App. no. 41120/17), ECtHR Second Section, judgment of 10 June 2025, concerns a Cypriot company owning a building complex in the fenced-up area of Famagusta, northern Cyprus. The company, whose shareholders and directors are Greek Cypriots, abandoned the property after the 1974 Turkish military operation.

On 23 July 2010 the applicant applied to the Immovable Property Commission (IPC), seeking compensation for loss of use, statutory interest, restitution, non-pecuniary damages and costs. When the “TRNC” authorities did not reply, it sought a default judgment on 1 November 2010. Between December 2010 and June 2012, the Attorney General repeatedly requested adjournments because a property report had not been provided; these requests were granted each time. In October 2012 the applicant complained of delays. The authorities then indicated that the property appeared to be registered in the name of a religious organisation, the Abdullah Paşa Foundation, managed by the Evkaf Administration. In November 2012 the IPC admitted Evkaf as a third party because it might be affected by the claim.

The applicant challenged this before the “TRNC” Administrative Court, also complaining of unjustified adjournments and delays. In November 2015 the Administrative Court ruled that Evkaf could not be a third party because this would make restitution impossible, but held that it lacked jurisdiction over the delay complaint. On appeal, the High Administrative Court held in November 2016 that it had exclusive jurisdiction over all IPC matters, but that adjournments and delays were not subject to judicial review. It also held that Evkaf should be admitted, relying on a 2005 Famagusta District Court judgment that Evkaf was the current registered owner of the property.

The “TRNC” authorities filed submissions with the IPC in December 2019. In January 2020 the applicant and its representative refused to attend IPC hearings; they also missed hearings in February, June and October 2020. In February 2024 the representative attended and discussed possible compensation proposals, but stated that settlement could be reached during the ECtHR proceedings. The IPC proceedings remain pending.

The applicant alleged lack of effectiveness of the IPC proceedings, violation of the right to a fair and impartial tribunal, discrimination under Articles 6, 13 and 14, and breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The central alleged violations concern the excessive length of IPC proceedings, the practice in the Famagusta fenced-up area regarding intervention by the Evkaf/Islamic Foundation, and the alleged lack of impartiality of the High Administrative Court as appellate authority for IPC cases. The Government submitted a unilateral declaration in January 2020, which the Court refused to accept in March 2021.

Relevant framework: IPC Law no. 67/2005 allows property claims; the burden is on the applicant to prove pre-20 July 1974 registration and abandonment; the defendant is the Ministry/Attorney-General; persons holding property rights may be invited as interested parties. Section 8 permits restitution, exchange or compensation. In a related 2019 case, the High Administrative Court said the IPC could only consider 1974 title deeds and could not alter land-registry records; Evkaf’s participation did not affect claimants proving pre-1974 title. In 2023, it reviewed IPC diligence in another case but rejected an excessive-length claim. As of October 2024, 7,800 IPC applications had been lodged and 1,869 finalised.

In *Karović and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Applications nos. 43201/22, 555/23, 5241/23 and 23976/23), the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) examined four applications lodged against Bosnia and Herzegovina under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants—Zlatan Karović, Tarik Kršlak, Vanja Bradarić and Osman Šabanović—are nationals of Bosnia and Herzegovina residing in Sarajevo or Ilidža. Their applications were lodged between 11 August 2022 and 2 June 2023. The Court gave notice to the Government only of complaints concerning non-enforcement of domestic decisions under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1; the remainder was declared inadmissible.

The underlying facts concern final domestic judgments in the applicants’ favour against Sarajevo Canton, one of the ten cantons of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Between 2015 and 2018, the Sarajevo Municipal Court delivered judgments on 5 and 19 February 2015, 24 February 2017, and 23 April 2018, ordering Sarajevo Canton to pay the applicants various sums for unpaid work-related benefits, together with default interest at the statutory rate and legal costs. The corresponding writs of execution were issued by the same court on 19 February 2021, 5 May 2016, 5 July 2017 and 13 June 2018.

Despite these final and enforceable decisions, enforcement was not carried out. One applicant, Mr Šabanović, obtained a Constitutional Court decision on 12 January 2022 finding violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Constitutional Court ordered Sarajevo Canton to take the necessary steps to secure enforcement of the decision in his favour and awarded him 300 convertible marks (BAM) in compensation for non-pecuniary damage.

On 13 January 2022, Sarajevo Canton adopted an enforcement plan covering all domestic decisions against it, published in the Official Gazette of Sarajevo Canton no. 4/22. The plan provided that creditors who renounced their claims for default interest and legal costs would receive their principal claims without delay. For creditors who did not accept that arrangement—including the present applicants—the plan stated that decisions would be enforced in chronological order within five years, by the end of 2026, with up to 0.8% of the total budget allocated for that purpose. It also stated that Sarajevo Canton reserved the right not to adhere to the plan if it received fewer funds in future.

On 6 April 2022, the Constitutional Court rejected Mr Karović’s case, considering the Sarajevo Canton enforcement plan acceptable. However, according to the available information, the decisions in favour of all four applicants remained unenforced. As of 31 December 2024, their positions in the chronological queue of pending decisions against Sarajevo Canton were: Mr Šabanović, 1,017; Ms Bradarić, 2,299; Mr Karović, 3,092; and Mr Kršlak, 5,797.

The alleged violations therefore arise from the continued failure of the respondent State to enforce final domestic decisions awarding the applicants unpaid work-related benefits, interest and costs. The applicants complain that this non-enforcement breached their right to a fair hearing under Article 6 § 1 and their right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The key factual issue is whether the Sarajevo Canton enforcement plan, its chronological payment schedule extending to 2026, and the applicants’ high queue positions sufficiently justify the prolonged non-enforcement of binding judgments in their favour.

The European Court of Human Rights case **Urusbiev and Others v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia** (Applications nos. 33519/15 and 4 others) concerns the applicants’ deprivation of liberty and detention in allegedly inadequate material conditions in the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transnistria” (“MRT”). The applicants complained principally under **Article 3** (inhuman or degrading treatment, inadequate detention conditions and lack of medical assistance) and **Article 5 § 1** (unlawful deprivation of liberty). Certain applicants also raised issues under **Article 8** (private and family life), **Article 10** (freedom of expression), **Article 2 of Protocol No. 4** (freedom of movement), and relied on **Articles 6, 13 and 14** of the Convention. The case was lodged against both the Republic of Moldova and Russia, with the Court referring to its earlier case-law on the MRT, including *Mozer* and *Lypovchenko and Halabudenco*.

The key facts, drawn from the appended table, are as follows:

1. **Ruslan Urusbiev**, a stateless man residing in Dubăsari, was involved in a criminal case after firing a weapon in a bar in the “MRT” on 2 January 2001. He absconded. On 17 September 2014 he was apprehended in Dubăsari, a town controlled by the “MRT”. On 19 November 2014 the “MRT Tiraspol City Court” convicted him and sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment; the “MRT Supreme Court” upheld this on 23 December 2014. His main complaint was unlawful detention from 17 September 2014, ordered by an unlawful de facto court, contrary to Article 5 § 1.

2. **Serghei Ilcenco** and **Nicolae Ilcenco**, a father and son who are journalists, had their house searched on 18 March 2015 on charges of incitement to extremism and subversion of the “MRT Government”. Serghei was arrested and detained in Tiraspol police station, then transferred on 24 March 2015 to Tiraspol prison no. 3, where he remained until release on 17 July 2015. Their professional belongings were seized. While detained, Serghei continued publishing articles with his lawyer’s help; prison authorities then searched his cell and removed his pens and paper. He complained of inhuman detention conditions and lack of medical assistance (Article 3), unlawful four-month detention ordered by an unlawful de facto court (Article 5 § 1), and hindrance of his right to apply to the Court (Article 34). Nicolae’s entry recorded no separate main complaints.

3. **Serghei Vardiaşvili**, originally from Georgia and also a Moldovan citizen, was arrested on 9 June 2015 over the alleged expiry of his short-term “MRT” residence permit. He was held for three days in Dubăsari police station. On 11 June 2015 he was released and taken to the “Dubăsari border post”, expelled from the “MRT”, and banned from returning for six months. He alleged inhuman detention conditions and unlawful three-day detention ordered by an unlawful de facto authority.

4. **Rauşan Ahmetşin**, a stateless man from Tiraspol, was convicted on 13 March 2015 by a de facto “MRT first-instance court” of embezzlement and taken into custody from the courtroom. He was held in Tiraspol police station, then Tiraspol prison no. 3, and later Hlinaia prison no. 1. On 28 April 2015 the “MRT Supreme Court” upheld the conviction and reduced his sentence to three and a half years. On 1 December 2015 the Supreme Court of Moldova declared the “MRT” judgments null and void. He complained of inhuman conditions and lack of medical assistance, and of unlawful detention of three and a half years ordered by an unlawful de facto court.

5. **Petru Mustea**, a Moldovan from Ofatinti, was ordered detained on 23 March 2017 by the “Tiraspol City Court” for an undetermined period on theft charges; detention was extended on 18 May 2017. He was held in Tiraspol police station and then Tiraspol prison no. 3. He was released on 2 June 2017 after the “MRT Supreme Court” found pre-trial detention unnecessary. He complained of inhuman conditions and lack of medical assistance, and of unlawful detention of almost three months ordered by an unlawful de facto court.

In essence, the case concerns a series of detentions and criminal proceedings carried out by de facto “MRT” authorities, with the applicants alleging that these detentions were unlawful under Article 5 and that their conditions of detention breached Article 3.

**CASE OF MARZOUKI AND OTHERS v. BULGARIA** (Application no. 48636/19) is a European Court of Human Rights case, Fifth Section, concerning the exclusion of a foreign national from Bulgaria and the resulting separation from his family. The applicants are Mohamed Nabil Marzouki (born 1981, Tunisian national), his daughter Mariam Mohamed Nabil Marzouki (born 2010, Bulgarian national), and Yana Dimitrova Yankova (born 1976, Bulgarian national), the child’s mother. The first applicant had permanent residence in Bulgaria and lived there with the second and third applicants.

In early 2018, the first applicant travelled to Serbia. On 1 February 2018, when he attempted to return to Bulgaria, he was refused entry and given a standard refusal form. Two grounds were checked: that an alert had been issued for the purpose of refusing entry, and that he was considered a threat to public order, internal security, public health or international relations.

The first applicant sought judicial review of the refusal. In those proceedings, the border police explained that they had acted on a decision of the State Agency for National Security (“SANS”) dated 1 February 2018, which imposed a five-year entry ban on the ground that he posed a national security threat. The Sofia Region Administrative Court upheld the refusal on 29 October 2018, finding that the border police had been bound to refuse entry once the SANS decision had been issued.

The SANS decision was served on the first applicant’s legal representative on 31 July 2018, after the representative requested a copy upon learning of it during the judicial review proceedings. The decision did not contain specific reasoning justifying the conclusion that the applicant posed a national security threat. Instead, it referred to a classified document named “Proposal.” That Proposal was later declassified and submitted by the Government.

After receiving a copy of the SANS decision, the first applicant’s representative applied for judicial review. However, the Supreme Administrative Court declared the application time-barred in a final decision of 6 March 2019. It found that the fourteen-day time-limit for contesting the decision had begun on 1 February 2018, when the applicant had been “orally informed” of it. This finding apparently referred to the standard refusal form given to him at the border. According to the Supreme Administrative Court, the applicant had been validly informed in that manner under Article 61 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Procedure, as worded at the time, which allowed oral notification of an administrative decision to the interested parties. As a result, the first applicant was unable to obtain a substantive judicial review of the SANS entry ban.

The applicants complained before the European Court of Human Rights that the first applicant’s removal from Bulgaria was unjustified and disrupted their family life together. They also complained under Article 13 of the Convention, in conjunction with Article 8, that there were no effective domestic remedies available.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore: the first applicant’s permanent residence and established family life in Bulgaria with his Bulgarian daughter and her mother; his refusal of entry at the border on 1 February 2018; the underlying SANS decision imposing a five-year entry ban on national security grounds; the lack of specific reasoning in that decision due to reliance on a classified “Proposal”; the delayed service of the SANS decision on his representative; and the domestic courts’ conclusion that his judicial challenge was time-barred because the time-limit had started when he was allegedly orally informed at the border. These facts underpin the Article 8 complaint concerning disproportionate interference with family life and the Article 13 complaint concerning the absence of an effective remedy to challenge the exclusion and entry ban.

The applicant, K.V. Mediterranean Tours Limited, is a Cypriot company that owns a building complex in the fenced-up area of Famagusta, in northern Cyprus. Its shareholders and directors are of Greek Cypriot origin. The company abandoned the property after the 1974 Turkish military operation in Cyprus.

On 23 July 2010 the company applied to the Immovable Property Commission (“IPC”) seeking compensation for loss of use of its property, statutory interest, restitution, compensation for non-pecuniary damage, and legal costs. When the authorities of the “Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus” (“TRNC”) did not reply, the company applied for a default judgment on 1 November 2010. Between 7 December 2010 and 25 June 2012, ten hearings on the default application were adjourned at the request of the “TRNC” Office of the Attorney General, which said a necessary property report had not been prepared. On 23 October 2012 the applicant complained about delays.

At a hearing, the Attorney General’s office indicated that the property appeared to be registered in the name of a religious organisation, the Abdullah Paşa Foundation, managed by the Evkaf Administration. On 23 November 2012 the IPC admitted the Evkaf Administration as a third party because it might be affected by the claim. The applicant challenged that decision and the delays before the “TRNC” Administrative Court. On 6 November 2015 the Administrative Court held that the Evkaf Administration could not be admitted as a third party because this would make restitution impossible. It also held that it lacked jurisdiction to rule on complaints about adjournments and delays before the IPC.

On appeal, the “TRNC” High Administrative Court ruled on 29 November 2016 that it had exclusive jurisdiction over all matters relating to IPC proceedings, but that adjournments and delays were not subject to judicial review. Relying on a 27 December 2005 judgment of the “TRNC” Famagusta District Court, it found that the Evkaf Administration was the current registered owner of the property and should therefore be admitted as a party.

On 11 December 2019 the “TRNC” authorities filed submissions with the IPC. From 9 January 2020 the applicant company and its representative refused to attend IPC hearings. Further hearings were scheduled in 2020, but they did not attend. On 22 February 2024 the applicant’s representative attended a hearing and agreed to consider compensation proposals, but later stated that settlement could be reached during the proceedings before the European Court of Human Rights. The IPC proceedings remain pending.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights on 25 May 2017. It alleged a lack of effectiveness of the IPC proceedings, a violation of its right to a fair and impartial tribunal, and discrimination under Articles 6, 13 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The key alleged violations concerned: (1) the excessive length of proceedings before the IPC; (2) the practice applied to the Famagusta fenced-up area, particularly the intervention of the Islamic Foundation/Evkaf Administration in the proceedings; and (3) the alleged lack of impartiality of the High Administrative Court as the higher judicial authority for IPC cases.

Under Law no. 67/2005, the IPC may decide on restitution, exchange, or compensation. The applicant bears the burden of proving ownership as of 20 July 1974. The defendant is the Ministry and/or the “TRNC” Attorney-General. Persons holding property rights may be invited to participate as interested parties. The case arises from the broader property issues following the 1974 Turkish military operation in northern Cyprus.

The case of *Heinz and Haiderer v. Austria* concerns two applications lodged against Austria with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Fourth Section, sitting as a Committee composed of Anne Louise Bormann (President), Sebastian Răduleţu and András Jakab, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar, delivered judgment on 3 April 2025. The Austrian Government were given notice of the applications. Both applicants complained of the excessive length of civil proceedings.

The first application, no. 33010/22, was introduced on 4 July 2022 by Robert Carsten Heinz, born in 1965. He was represented by Karl Schelling, Dornbirn. The domestic civil proceedings began on 21 September 2012 and ended on 4 January 2022. The total length was 9 years, 3 months and 15 days, spanning four levels of jurisdiction. Thus, by the time the domestic proceedings concluded, Mr Heinz had been involved in civil litigation for almost a decade, with the case passing through multiple judicial instances before final resolution.

The second application, no. 31668/23, was introduced on 31 July 2023 by Wilhelm Haiderer, born in 1969. He was represented by Stefan Gloß, St. Pölten. The domestic civil proceedings started on 8 July 2014 and remained pending at the time of the information in the appended table. The total length was recorded as more than 10 years, 6 months and 21 days, across three levels of jurisdiction. Therefore, Mr Haiderer’s civil case had already lasted over a decade and had not yet ended when the application was lodged.

The key alleged violation in both applications was the excessive length of civil proceedings. Although the provided excerpt does not set out the Court’s legal reasoning or final conclusion, the applicants’ complaints are directed at the duration of the domestic civil proceedings. The central facts relevant to that complaint are the start dates, end dates or pending status, total durations, and the number of jurisdictional levels involved. Mr Heinz’s proceedings lasted 9 years and 3 months across four levels; Mr Haiderer’s proceedings had lasted more than 10 years and 6 months across three levels and were still pending.

The Court deliberated in private on 13 March 2025 and adopted the judgment on 3 April 2025. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. The case is therefore one of two Austrian applicants alleging that the civil courts failed to determine their cases within a reasonable time. The essential facts are limited to the procedural chronology listed in the appended table, which forms the basis for assessing whether the length of the domestic civil proceedings breached the Convention’s fair-trial guarantee, specifically the reasonable-time requirement. No additional factual circumstances, such as the subject matter of the underlying civil disputes or reasons for delay, are included in the provided text.

In **N.T. v. Cyprus** (Application no. 28150/22), the applicant, a Cypriot woman born in 1992, complained that Cyprus failed to comply with its positive obligations under **Articles 3 and 8** of the European Convention on Human Rights to effectively investigate and prosecute her rape allegation. She also alleged **gender-based discrimination** under **Article 14 read with Articles 3 and 8**, arguing that the authorities’ handling of her case reflected stereotypical and victim-blaming attitudes.

On **10 April 2021**, N.T. reported to police that A.T. had raped her on **1 January 2011**, when she was 18 and he was 20. She stated that after a night out, A.T. insisted that she, her friend C.S., and his friend G.H. enter a warehouse. N.T. went inside to use the bathroom. A.T. led her upstairs, grabbed her, tried to undress her, forced her onto boxes, and raped her orally and vaginally. She resisted by moving, scratching, and biting him, and asked him to stop. He bit her neck, leaving bruises, and left her naked on the floor. C.S. later saw bruises and a broken fingernail and noticed N.T. was upset and acting strangely. N.T. did not report immediately; she suffered nightmares and emotional instability, saw psychologists in 2014 and 2016, and reported only after learning through Facebook in 2021 that A.T. had allegedly raped another classmate.

The police investigated promptly. They took statements from C.S., who corroborated elements of N.T.’s account, including the warehouse, locked door, noises, bruises, and A.T.’s prior aggressive sexual behaviour toward her; from D.N., whom N.T. had told about the rape; from psychologists; and from S.N., who provided the Facebook information. G.H. said he heard nothing and that N.T. did not seem upset. A.T. refused to answer police questions. The police found sufficient evidence, and in **May 2021** an indictment for rape was filed; the case was referred to the Assize Court, where A.T. pleaded not guilty.

After the indictment, N.T. gave two supplementary statements. The first disclosed Facebook messages exchanged with A.T. after the incident, including a December 2011 message in which she greeted him on his name day and said she loved him. She explained that she had blamed herself, believed she had given him the wrong impression that consent was implied because she liked him, and had wanted to protect him. The second revealed that she had had consensual sex with A.T. in the same warehouse in **January 2010** and had initially mentioned it orally but asked police not to record it.

Prosecutors reassessed the case. In **December 2021**, the Deputy Attorney General discontinued the prosecution by *nolle prosequi*, citing inconsistencies, doubts about N.T.’s credibility, the possibility that A.T. reasonably believed she consented, low prospects of conviction, and the defendant’s rights. N.T. was informed by phone; her requests for written reasons and the case file were refused.

Before the ECtHR, N.T. alleged that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation and prosecution of rape, contrary to **Articles 3 and 8**, and discriminated against her as a woman, contrary to **Article 14**. The case centres on whether the discontinuation and credibility assessment relied on victim-blaming stereotypes, misconceptions about rape trauma and delayed disclosure, and her prior relationship with A.T., rather than on a proper evidentiary investigation.

**Case Name:** *Karović and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina*  
**Court:** European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section  
**Judgment:** Strasbourg, 24 June 2025; final 24 September 2025  
**Applications:** nos. 43201/22, 555/23, 5241/23, 23976/23  

The case concerns four Bosnian nationals—Zlatan Karović, Tarik Kršlak, Vanja Bradarić, and Osman Šabanović—who complained that Bosnia and Herzegovina failed to enforce final domestic decisions in their favour against Sarajevo Canton. They invoked Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair trial) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The applications were lodged between August 2022 and June 2023. All applicants resided in Sarajevo or Ilidža.

The domestic judgments were delivered by the Sarajevo Municipal Court on 5 and 19 February 2015, 24 February 2017, and 23 April 2018. They ordered Sarajevo Canton to pay the applicants various sums for unpaid work-related benefits, together with default interest at the statutory rate and legal costs. Writs of execution were issued by the same court on 19 February 2021, 5 May 2016, 5 July 2017, and 13 June 2018 respectively. Despite these final decisions, the sums were not paid.

The applicants also sought relief before the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On 12 January 2022, that court found a violation of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 in Šabanović’s case. It ordered Sarajevo Canton to take the necessary steps to secure enforcement of the decision in his favour and awarded him 300 convertible marks (BAM) in compensation for non-pecuniary damage. On 6 April 2022, however, the Constitutional Court rejected Karović’s case, accepting the Sarajevo Canton enforcement plan as adequate.

The key domestic enforcement measure was adopted on 13 January 2022, when Sarajevo Canton introduced an enforcement plan for all domestic decisions against it (Official Gazette of Sarajevo Canton no. 4/22). Under the plan, claimants who renounced their claims for default interest and legal costs would be paid their principal claims without delay. Those who refused, including the applicants, would have their decisions enforced in chronological order over five years—by the end of 2026. Up to 0.8% of the total budget was to be allocated for this purpose. The plan also allowed Sarajevo Canton to reserve the right not to adhere to it if fewer funds were allocated in future.

The applicants did not accept the proposed renunciation. According to available information, their decisions remained unenforced. As of 31 December 2024, their places in the chronological order of unenforced decisions against Sarajevo Canton were: Šabanović 1,017; Bradarić 2,299; Karović 3,092; and Kršlak 5,797. Thus, all four still faced significant delay and uncertainty about payment.

In the ECtHR proceedings, the Court gave notice to the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina of the complaints concerning non-enforcement under Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1; the remainder of the applications was declared inadmissible. The parties submitted observations. The central factual issue relevant to the alleged violations was whether the continued non-enforcement of final domestic judgments, combined with the Canton’s five-year chronological plan and the applicants’ distant positions in that queue, breached their right of access to court and property rights. The Court’s judgment was adopted on 3 June 2025 and delivered on 24 June 2025, becoming final on 24 September 2025.

Constantinou and Others v. Cyprus concerns five applications (nos. 77396/14, 45039/20, 45089/20, 45101/20 and 45899/20) lodged by 450 Cypriot nationals against Cyprus. The applicants complain about State deductions from public-sector salaries and pensions during Cyprus’s economic crisis. The European Court of Human Rights gave notice of complaints under Article 6 § 1 (applications nos. 45039/20, 45089/20, 45101/20 and 45899/20), Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (all applications), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 (application no. 77396/14); the remaining complaints were declared inadmissible.

The first set of facts concerns Law no. 112(I)/2011. Enacted on 31 August 2011 and effective from 1 September 2011, it imposed a tiered “extraordinary contribution” deducted monthly from the gross salaries and pensions of officials, employees and pensioners in the civil service and wider public sector. Deductions began at salaries over €1,500 and ranged from 1.5% to 3.5%. Initially valid for 24 months, the law was extended to 31 December 2016. A similar contribution was later imposed on private-sector workers from January 2012. The applicants challenged the law before the Supreme Court, arguing that their salaries were property protected by Article 23 of the Constitution and that the deductions violated Articles 23, 24 and 28 of the Constitution and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. In Charalambous and Others (11 June 2014), the Supreme Court dismissed the challenges 9–3. The majority held that the law was not a tax, that salary was a proprietary right but did not guarantee a particular amount, and that the relatively small deductions did not affect the core of the right. It found the measure justified by the severe financial crisis and public interest. Dissenting judges considered the deductions an unconstitutional deprivation or restriction because fiscal consolidation was not among the permissible grounds in Article 23 § 3.

The second set of facts concerns Law no. 168(I)/2012. Enacted on 6 December 2012 and effective from 1 December 2012, it reduced the emoluments and pensions of public and wider public-sector officials, employees and pensioners. Deductions initially ranged from 0% to 12.5%, later rising to as much as 17.5%, with no expiry date; they were discontinued on 1 January 2023. The applicants challenged the reductions in the Administrative Court. In 2018 and 2019, the first-instance court found the reductions unconstitutional under Article 23, because the public-interest justification relied on by the State was not among the exceptions in Article 23 § 3. On appeal, the Supreme Court in Avgousti and Others (10 April 2020) reversed 9–4. The majority held that salaries and pensions were property rights but did not guarantee a specific amount; the reductions were temporary, income-related, effective and did not affect the core or living standards, and were justified by the economic crisis. Dissenting judges argued that Article 23 afforded stricter protection than Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, that public interest was not a permissible ground, and that the reductions amounted to unconstitutional restrictions without compensation.

Before the ECtHR, the key alleged violations are that the deductions interfered with the applicants’ property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1; that the domestic proceedings failed to comply with Article 6 § 1; and that the measures were discriminatory under Article 1 of Protocol No. 12. The central factual backdrop is Cyprus’s severe economic crisis, the State’s fiscal consolidation measures, and the conflicting domestic court decisions on whether public-interest salary and pension cuts were constitutional.

The case of **Pápics and Others v. Hungary** (Applications nos. 13727/20 and 15 others) concerns 16 Hungarian applicants serving life imprisonment without release on parole. The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section, Committee) delivered judgment on 4 March 2025. The central alleged violation is Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits inhuman and degrading punishment. The applicants complain that their whole-life sentences, combined with the fact that mandatory pardon proceedings can take place only after they have served forty years, constitute inhuman and degrading punishment.

The applications were lodged under Article 34 of the Convention. The Hungarian Government was represented by Z. Tallódi. The Court gave notice of the Article 3 complaint in application no. 49294/20 and of all remaining applications to the Government, and declared the remainder of application no. 49249/20 inadmissible. Judge P. Paczolay, the judge elected in respect of Hungary, withdrew from sitting in the case.

The applicants are Hungarian nationals born between 1966 and 1990, residing in Szeged, Budapest, Tiszalök, and Szekszárd. Most were represented by Evelyn Frank; Róbert Magyar was represented by Csilla Csugányné Lakatos.

The key facts are that each applicant was convicted by final judgment in Hungary and sentenced to life imprisonment without release on parole. The final convictions occurred between 2007 and 2023. The offences included aggravated murder, murder, robbery, incitement to murder, abuse of firearms, causing bodily harm, and other crimes. Several applicants were sentenced as recidivists or multiple recidivists. The sentences were imposed by various Hungarian courts of appeal or high courts.
