Specific examples from the appended table include: Ferenc Pápics (b. 1968), sentenced by the Pécs Court of Appeal on 10 February 2009 for aggravated murder; József Ottlakán (b. 1973), sentenced as a recidivist by the Szeged Court of Appeal on 10 May 2023 for murder, robbery, and other crimes; Zoltán Sipőcz (b. 1978), sentenced by the Győr Court of Appeal on 17 February 2009 for aggravated murder; János Navratil (b. 1980), sentenced as a multiple recidivist by the Szeged Court of Appeal on 27 February 2014 for murder and robbery; József Áldott (b. 1977), sentenced by the Győr Court of Appeal on 2 October 2007 for aggravated murder and abuse of firearms; Róbert Magyar (b. 1970), sentenced by the Debrecen Court of Appeal on 13 March 2012 for incitement to murder and other crimes; Tibor János Mészáros (b. 1975), sentenced by the Szeged Court of Appeal on 29 April 2015 for murder, robbery, and other crimes; Lajos Tétényi (b. 1990), sentenced as a multiple recidivist by the Győr Court of Appeal on 10 October 2019 for murder; Zoltán Maczák (b. 1976), sentenced by the Szeged Court of Appeal on 29 June 2015 for aggravated murder; Krisztián Kovács (b. 1984), sentenced as a multiple recidivist by the Pécs Court of Appeal on 30 May 2018 for murder and other crimes; Attila Rézműves (b. 1967), sentenced by the Budapest High Court on 18 March 2016 for aggravated murder, upheld on appeal on 14 September 2016; Mihály Balog (b. 1966), sentenced as a multiple recidivist by the Budapest Court of Appeal on 10 December 2020 for robbery and other crimes; János Dániel Nagy (b. 1974), sentenced as a multiple recidivist by the Győr Court of Appeal on 24 May 2017 for murder; István Szűcs (b. 1980), sentenced by the Szeged High Court on 22 September 2011 for multiple aggravated murders; József Sándor (b. 1973), sentenced as a recidivist by the Budapest Court of Appeal on 4 July 2017 for aggravated multiple murder; and Gábor Horváth (b. 1982), sentenced as a multiple recidivist by the Győr Court of Appeal on 1 February 2022 for aggravated murder, robbery, and causing bodily harm.

The common fact relevant to the alleged Article 3 violation is that none of the applicants has access to ordinary parole. Instead, mandatory pardon proceedings can occur only after forty years of imprisonment. The applicants argue that this regime leaves them without a realistic prospect of release and therefore amounts to inhuman and degrading punishment.

In *Gullotti v. Italy* (Application no. 64753/14), the European Court of Human Rights considered complaints concerning the limitation of a prisoner’s correspondence and the effectiveness of remedies against decisions renewing that limitation. The applicant, Giuseppe Gullotti, an Italian national born in 1960 and detained in Parma Prison, had been convicted of mafia-type offences, including participation in a mafia-type organisation, murder, extortion, unlawful possession of weapons, and breach of preventive measures. Arrested in 1998, he was imprisoned under the special regime in section 41 bis of the Prison Administration Act. That regime imposed severe restrictions, including limits on visits, a telephone ban, limits on receiving money and parcels, and monitoring of incoming and outgoing correspondence subject to a judicial order under section 18 ter.

The applicant’s correspondence was monitored at least between 5 July 2012 and 27 May 2013. From at least 4 December 2012, the Reggio Emilia sentence supervision judge limited his correspondence to relatives admitted for family visits. On 7 January 2013 the prison governor requested a renewal. On 8 January 2013 the Reggio Emilia sentence supervision judge renewed the limitation for three months, until 7 April 2013. The judge relied on the applicant’s alleged continuing prominent role in Cosa Nostra despite detention since 1998, citing investigative sources, statements by cooperating prisoners, and a favourable opinion from the District Anti-Mafia Prosecution Office.

The applicant appealed. On 12 March 2013 the Bologna sentence supervision court upheld the order, reiterating that he remained a member of the criminal organisation and had not distanced himself from it. On 21 March 2014 the Court of Cassation declared his appeal on points of law inadmissible, finding the limitation justified.

While those appeal proceedings were pending, the Reggio Emilia sentence supervision judge renewed the limitation three more times, on 8 April, 9 July, and 7 October 2013, each for three months. The 8 April and 7 October orders were based on the same reasoning as the 8 January order. Separately, on 30 October 2013, the Minister of Justice renewed the section 41 bis regime for two years, relying on anti-mafia information that the applicant was a mafia-clan leader in the Barcellona Pozzo di Gotto area with strong criminal connections, and citing 2003 wiretapped conversations referring to the impossibility of communicating with him in person or by mail.

On 21 November 2013, the Bologna sentence supervision court granted an appeal against the 8 April 2013 order, finding its reasoning inadequate. It noted that the order vaguely referred to investigative sources without detailing their content, and failed to consider relevant contrary information, including a 2009 Turin decision granting early release and positive prison reports from Parma and Cuneo in 2013. The applicant then asked that the 9 July and 7 October 2013 orders be declared unlawful as based on the same grounds, but on 22 January 2014 the Bologna court declared that request inadmissible as not provided for by law. Meanwhile, on 31 December 2013, after the Bologna decision, the Reggio Emilia judge rejected a further request to renew the correspondence limitation.

The legal framework allowed correspondence restrictions or monitoring under section 18 ter by reasoned order for up to six months, renewable for periods of up to three months, to prevent crimes, maintain prison security, and protect investigations. Appeals lay under section 14 ter, with subsequent review by the Court of Cassation.

The applicant lodged his application on 20 September 2014. The Court gave notice to the Italian Government of complaints under Article 8 (right to respect for correspondence) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) concerning the judicial order of 8 January 2013; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The case thus concerns the limitation of the applicant’s correspondence during detention and whether the appeal against decisions renewing that limitation was effective.

# Summary of Vainik and Others v. Estonia

## Case Overview

The case of *Vainik and Others v. Estonia* (Applications nos. 17982/21 and 3 others) concerns a total ban on smoking in Estonian prisons, which the applicants—all prisoners at Viru Prison when the ban took effect—allege violated their rights under Articles 3 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

## Key Facts

**The Smoking Ban Implementation**

On 6 October 2016, the Minister of Justice amended Regulation no. 72 on Internal Prison Rules, prohibiting detainees from possessing smokable tobacco products and items used to assemble or smoke them. This ban, codified in section 641(31), entered into force on 1 October 2017. Separately, on 24 April 2017, Viru Prison's governor amended the prison's house rules to completely ban smoking on its premises, also effective 1 October 2017. The total ban followed successive restrictions that had gradually reduced the number of cigarettes prisoners could take during outdoor walks—from five cigarettes to three, then two, and finally one cigarette per day immediately before the complete prohibition.

**The Applicants**

The four applicants were all detained at Viru Prison and known smokers when the ban took effect. The first applicant had smoked for over thirty years and reported suffering depression, sleeping problems, and loss of appetite following the ban. The second applicant, serving a life sentence since 1996, was diagnosed with nicotine addiction in 2015. The third applicant, a thirty-year smoker, experienced fatigue, headaches, weakness, sleeplessness, and appetite loss. The fourth applicant claimed severe nicotine addiction and withdrawal symptoms.

**Legal Proceedings**

Each applicant challenged the ban through administrative complaints and court proceedings. The Tartu Administrative Court initially declared section 641(31) unconstitutional in June 2019, triggering constitutional review. However, in judgment no. 5-19-40 of 17 December 2019, the Supreme Court of Estonia declared the ban constitutional. The Supreme Court found the ban served legitimate aims including protecting non-smokers' health, preventing fire hazards, and preventing cigarettes' use as illegal currency in prisons. It determined that less restrictive measures—such as designated smoking areas or cell separation—could not achieve these aims as effectively. The Supreme Court acknowledged nicotine addiction and withdrawal symptoms but considered the interference proportionate, noting that smoking reduction had been gradual and that counselling and treatment were available.

Following the Supreme Court's judgment, the Tartu Court of Appeal upheld the smoking ban in March 2021, and the Supreme Court refused further appeals in May 2021.

**The First Applicant's Procedural Issue**

The first applicant faced additional obstacles. After his case was remitted for reconsideration, the Tartu Administrative Court denied his application for exemption from the State fee in April 2020, finding his claim lacked prospects of success. Because he failed to pay the fee, his claim was ultimately not examined on the merits.

## Alleged Violations

The applicants complained that the total smoking ban subjected them to degrading treatment (Article 3) and violated their right to respect for private life (Article 8). The Court communicated only the complaint concerning the total smoking ban to the Government. The case was referred to the Grand Chamber on 23 March 2026.

Pápics and Others v. Hungary (Applications nos. 13727/20 and 15 others) is a European Court of Human Rights case decided by the Second Section, sitting as a Committee, on 4 March 2025. The case concerns 16 Hungarian applicants who are serving life imprisonment without the possibility of release on parole. Their central complaint is under Article 3 of the Convention, alleging that their sentences constitute inhuman and degrading punishment. The key alleged defect is that under the Hungarian system, mandatory pardon proceedings can take place only after the applicant has served forty years of the life sentence. The applicants argue that this makes their punishment effectively irreducible for at least forty years and leaves them without any realistic prospect of release, causing severe mental suffering and hopelessness.

The applicants were convicted by final judgments of various Hungarian courts for serious crimes. The appended table shows convictions including aggravated murder, murder, robbery, abuse of firearms, incitement to murder, and other offences. Several applicants were sentenced as recidivists or multiple recidivists. The applicants’ years of birth range from 1966 to 1990, and most resided in Szeged or Budapest, with others in Tiszalök and Szekszárd. The impugned judgments were delivered by courts including the Pécs, Szeged, Győr, Debrecen, and Budapest Courts of Appeal, as well as the Budapest and Szeged High Courts. Most applicants are represented by Evelyn Frank; Róbert Magyar is represented by Csilla Csugányné Lakatos. The applications were lodged with the Court between 2 March 2020 and 4 August 2022.

The factual focus relevant to the alleged Article 3 violation is not the applicants’ guilt or the particular circumstances of their offences, but the nature of the penalty imposed. Each applicant received a final sentence of life imprisonment without release on parole. Under the challenged Hungarian framework, the only possible release mechanism is a mandatory pardon procedure, which cannot begin until forty years of the sentence have been served. The applicants therefore contend that the statutory regime makes their punishment irreducible for an excessively long period and thus incompatible with Article 3.

Procedurally, the Court gave notice of the Article 3 complaint in application no. 49294/20 and of all remaining applications to the Hungarian Government, represented by Z. Tallódi of the Ministry of Justice. The remainder of application no. 49249/20 was declared inadmissible, as stated in the text. The Hungarian judge elected in respect of Hungary, Mr P. Paczolay, withdrew from sitting. The Committee was composed of Anja Seibert-Fohr (President), Davor Derenčinović, and Gediminas Sagatys. It deliberated in private on 4 February 2025 and adopted the judgment on 4 March 2025. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. In essence, the case concerns whether Hungary’s regime of life imprisonment without parole, combined with a forty-year wait before any pardon review, violates the prohibition of inhuman and degrading punishment under Article 3.

The case *Radelić v. Croatia* (Application no. 12432/22, judgment of 13 May 2025) concerns the confiscation of proceeds of crime from an individual although the proceeds had been acquired by his company, which later ceased to exist.

The applicant, Dražen Radelić, was the sole shareholder and director of a limited liability company, Radelić d.o.o. Bankruptcy proceedings against the company were opened in November 2010, concluded in December 2010, and the company was struck off the commercial register in March 2011, ceasing to exist.

In March 2011 the applicant was indicted for business fraud and forgery of documents. The prosecution alleged that between August 2003 and February 2004 he had presented thirty-six foreign-bank cheques to a bank for cashing, falsely claiming they were payment for services rendered abroad, intending to obtain significant pecuniary gain for the company. In 2014 he was convicted of forgery and acquitted of business fraud. On appeal, the acquittal was quashed and a retrial was ordered. In April 2017 he was convicted of business fraud and sentenced to one year’s imprisonment, suspended for four years. The court also ordered confiscation from him personally of HRK 854,743.39 (approximately EUR 113,440) as proceeds of crime, payable into the State budget within six months; failure to pay could lead to revocation of the suspended sentence.

The trial court reasoned that the company had been struck off and had no legal successor, and that the applicant, as sole founder, shareholder and representative, should therefore pay the amount. The applicant appealed, arguing that the money had been paid into the company’s account, not to him personally; that the company had paid taxes and used the funds for its operations; that he had not personally benefited; and that there was no legal basis to confiscate the proceeds from him. The County Court dismissed the appeal. It accepted that the amount had been kept for the company, but held that because the company no longer existed and had no successor, confiscation from the applicant was justified, relying by analogy on section 252(5) of the Commercial Companies Act concerning management-board liability to creditors.

The Split County State Attorney’s Office later proposed a request for protection of legality, arguing that the confiscation was unlawful. It stressed that the applicant had been charged with obtaining gain for the company, not for himself; that no evidence showed the proceeds were transferred to him personally; and that if the company had been liquidated, the court should have ordered compensation to victims rather than confiscation, especially where no civil claim had been made. The Principal State Attorney did not lodge the request.

The applicant’s constitutional complaint alleged a breach of the right of ownership. In October 2021 the Constitutional Court dismissed it, finding no breach. Enforcement attempts followed: he was invited to pay in 2017 and 2021; after non-payment, in 2023 the State Attorney’s Office asked FINA to collect the amount from his bank accounts. The order remained unenforced due to insufficient funds.

The key alleged violation before the European Court of Human Rights concerns whether confiscating proceeds of crime from the individual applicant—although the unlawful gain was acquired for, and allegedly retained by, a now-defunct company—was compatible with Convention rights, particularly the right of property and the principle of legality in criminal matters.

In *Mediakompaniya Slovo, TOV and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 22347/14), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) examined an Article 10 complaint concerning domestic court orders requiring the applicants to retract statements published in a newspaper. The applicants were Mediakompaniya Slovo, a publishing company; Mr Vasylenko, its director and editor-in-chief of the newspaper *Subbota Plus*; and Ms Vasylenko, the newspaper’s editorial director.

On 21 March 2013, *Subbota Plus* published an article by Mr Vasylenko titled “Drained profitability of [V.]”. V. was a large municipal water-supply company. The article suggested corrupt practices at V. and contained numerous allegations: embezzlement and squandering of tens of millions of State funds; contracts with intermediary companies at inflated prices; private enterprises receiving State money; an interest-free loan of 16 million hryvnias to a private person; fraud in renovation works; use of second-hand parts; unlawful sale of pipes; management corruption; and that V. was near bankruptcy because of corruption, irresponsibility, lack of professionalism and moral bankruptcy. Some information was attributed to documents provided by workers and to employee statements.

In April 2013, V. sued all three applicants, seeking retraction of the statements and compensation for non-pecuniary damage. The applicants argued that the statements were value judgments not susceptible of proof, that the information was not negative, and that it was unclear from the article that the allegations referred to V.

On 17 June 2013, the Zhovtnevyi District Court of Zaporizhzhya found against the applicants. It examined each disputed statement and held that they were statements of fact, not value judgments. It further found that the applicants had not proved those statements were true. The court ordered them to retract the information and to publish the operative part of the judgment in the next issue of *Subbota Plus*. It also prohibited them from disseminating the information contained in the statements “by any possible means (on the television or in printed media, on the radio, on the internet, in interviews, in conversations with any person, or by any other means).” The court awarded V. 1 Ukrainian hryvnia (UAH) in non-pecuniary damages and UAH 458 (approximately EUR 42) in court fees, relying in particular on Article 278 of the Civil Code as in force at the material time.

The applicants appealed, but their appeals were rejected. The final domestic decision was given by the Higher Specialized Court on 9 September 2013. According to the Government, the writs of execution in respect of the court decisions against the applicants were never submitted to the Bailiffs Service for execution.

The application was lodged with the European Court on 7 March 2014. The applicants complained under Article 10 of the Convention that the domestic courts had ordered them to retract statements published in the newspaper. Procedurally, the Court later noted that Ms Vasylenko died on 28 June 2020, and on 29 March 2023 Mr Vasylenko informed the Court that Mediakompaniya Slovo did not wish to pursue the application.

The key facts relevant to the alleged Article 10 violation are therefore the publication of corruption allegations against a public utility, the domestic courts’ classification of those allegations as unproved statements of fact rather than value judgments, and the resulting retraction order, publication requirement, and broad prohibition on further dissemination.

The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) judgment in *Ibrahimi and Others v. Albania* (14 January 2025) concerns five applications: *Ibrahimi* (no. 81057/17), *Selimi* (no. 57542/18), *Nika* (no. 32939/21), *Dedaj* (no. 54121/21), and *Industri Ndërtim (IN) SHP.K.* (no. 7386/22). The central alleged violation is that the Albanian Constitutional Court dismissed each applicant’s constitutional complaint as lodged out of time by calculating the four-month time-limit from the date the Supreme Court adopted its decision, rather than from the date the applicants were served with or effectively learned of that decision. This, the applicants argued, restricted their right of access to the Constitutional Court.

The underlying domestic proceedings differed. In *Ibrahimi*, the applicant was convicted of murder and sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment. The Supreme Court adopted its decision on 25 June 2015. A letter notifying him of that decision was served by prison authorities on 12 May 2017. On 5 June 2017, he lodged a constitutional complaint alleging violations of his right to be informed of the Supreme Court hearing and his right to legal assistance. On 16 June 2017, the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible as out of time, counting from the Supreme Court’s adoption date.

In *Selimi*, a property dispute, the Supreme Court adopted its decision on 25 June 2015; it was served on the applicants on 18 October 2017. They lodged a constitutional complaint on 13 February 2018. On 30 May 2018, the Constitutional Court declared it inadmissible as out of time, again counting from the adoption date.

In *Nika*, the applicant challenged her dismissal as a forestry inspector. The Supreme Court adopted its decision on 27 May 2020. It was served on her on 14 January 2021. She lodged a constitutional complaint on 18 January 2021. On 26 February 2021, the Constitutional Court declared it inadmissible as out of time from the adoption date.

In *Dedaj*, the applicant challenged his dismissal from work. The Supreme Court adopted its decision on 27 July 2020. It was served on him on 1 April 2021. He lodged a constitutional complaint on 9 June 2021. On 26 July 2021, the Constitutional Court declared it inadmissible as out of time from the adoption date.

In *Industri Ndërtim*, the applicant company was involved in civil proceedings concerning contractual obligations. The Supreme Court adopted its decision on 17 February 2021. It was served on the company on 4 June 2021. The company lodged a constitutional complaint on 29 September 2021. On 29 October 2021, the Constitutional Court declared it inadmissible as out of time from the adoption date.

In four of the applications, the Constitutional Court reasoned that when a party requested service of a decision, the issuing court stamped it, but that stamp was not decisive proof of the date of first service. The burden was on the party to prove it had not been served earlier. The applicants therefore lost access to constitutional review despite lodging complaints soon after actual notification.

The ECtHR also gave notice of additional complaints: in *Ibrahimi*, the applicant’s right to participate in person in the criminal proceedings and to defend himself through legal assistance of his own choosing at the Supreme Court hearing; and in *Industri Ndërtim*, the applicant company’s right to participate in proceedings before the Tirana District Court. The third party *Res Publica* was granted leave to intervene. The key factual issue remains the Albanian Constitutional Court’s rigid time-limit calculation from the Supreme Court’s adoption date, which allegedly deprived applicants of effective access to the Constitutional Court.

In *Vainik and Others v. Estonia*, four applicants—Denis Lvov, Rene Vainik, Nikolai Šmeljov and Dmitri Tsajun—were prisoners in Viru Prison when Estonia imposed a total ban on smoking in prisons. They complained under Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention that the ban violated their rights, alleging degrading treatment and unjustified interference with private life. The European Court of Human Rights gave notice only of the complaint concerning the total smoking ban; the remainder of the applications was declared inadmissible.

The ban had two main sources. On 6 October 2016, the Minister of Justice amended the Internal Prison Rules by adding section 641(31), which prohibited prisoners from possessing smokable tobacco products and items that could be used to assemble or smoke them. It entered into force on 1 October 2017. On 24 April 2017, the governor of Viru Prison amended the prison’s house rules to ban smoking completely on its premises, also effective from 1 October 2017. Before the total ban, smoking had been permitted only in designated places. Between 2016 and 2017, the number of cigarettes prisoners could take during their daily outdoor walk was gradually reduced from five to three, then two, and finally one.

All applicants were known smokers when the ban took effect. The first applicant had smoked for over thirty years and claimed that, after the ban, he suffered depression, sleeping problems and loss of appetite. He challenged the ban before the Tartu Administrative Court in January 2018, seeking annulment and compensation. Although the Supreme Court initially remitted his case, the administrative court later refused to examine it because he did not pay the State fee after his exemption request was rejected. His claim was therefore never determined on the merits.

The second applicant had been serving a life sentence since 1996 and had been diagnosed with nicotine addiction in 2015. He argued that smokers developed nicotine addiction and could suffer withdrawal symptoms. His action for annulment was suspended pending constitutional review and later dismissed in February 2020 on the basis of the Supreme Court’s judgment in case no. 5-19-40. His appeals failed.

The third and fourth applicants were also smokers in Viru Prison. The third claimed thirty years of smoking and, after the ban, fatigue, headaches, weakness, sleeplessness and loss of appetite. The fourth claimed heavy nicotine addiction and severe withdrawal symptoms. After their complaints were dismissed by prison authorities and the Ministry of Justice, they challenged the rules before the Tartu Administrative Court in late 2017. On 12 June 2019, that court declared section 641(31) unconstitutional, set it aside, annulled Viru Prison’s smoking ban and ordered the prison to reconsider whether they could smoke. This triggered constitutional review proceedings.

On 17 December 2019, the Supreme Court in judgment no. 5-19-40 declared the Internal Prison Rules ban constitutional. It found that the ban pursued legitimate aims: protecting non-smokers’ health, ensuring prison security and order, preventing fire risks, and preventing cigarettes from being used as illegal currency. It accepted that the ban interfered with property rights and free self-realisation but held it proportionate. Less restrictive measures, such as separate cells, smoking rooms or outdoor smoking, were considered less effective. Withdrawal symptoms were unlikely to be severe because smoking had been reduced gradually, and counselling and treatment were available. The Supreme Court held that the ban did not amount to degrading treatment. Subsequently, the Tartu Court of Appeal upheld Viru Prison’s house-rule ban in March 2021, and further appeals were refused.

The core alleged violations concerned whether the complete prohibition on possessing and smoking tobacco in prison, applied to addicted prisoner-smokers, amounted to degrading treatment under Article 3 or an unjustified interference with private life under Article 8.

Case of Vainik and Others v. Estonia (Applications nos. 3184/21, 17982/21, 43852/21 and 44600/21) concerns a total ban on smoking in Estonian prisons. The applicants—Denis Lvov, Rene Vainik, Nikolai Šmeljov and Dmitri Tsajun—were prisoners in Viru Prison when the ban entered into force on 1 October 2017. They alleged that the ban violated their rights under Articles 3 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The European Court of Human Rights gave notice only of the complaint concerning the total smoking ban and declared the remainder of the applications inadmissible.

The ban had two main sources. On 6 October 2016, the Minister of Justice amended the Internal Prison Rules by adding section 641(31), which prohibited detainees from possessing smokable tobacco products and items used to assemble or smoke them. On 24 April 2017, the governor of Viru Prison amended the prison’s house rules to completely ban smoking on its premises. Both measures took effect on 1 October 2017.

Before the total ban, indoor smoking in prisons had already been prohibited since 2010, and tobacco was kept in lockers. Smoking was only allowed in designated outdoor areas. The number of cigarettes prisoners could take with them during outdoor walks was gradually reduced: from five until May 2016, to three, then two, and finally one cigarette per day shortly before the total ban.

All applicants were smokers. The first applicant, Lvov, had smoked for over thirty years and alleged that the ban caused depression, sleeping problems and loss of appetite. The second applicant, Vainik, was serving a life sentence and had been diagnosed with nicotine addiction in 2015; he argued that smokers could suffer withdrawal symptoms of varying intensity. The third applicant, Šmeljov, stated he had smoked for thirty years and suffered fatigue, headaches, weakness, sleeplessness and loss of appetite. The fourth applicant, Tsajun, claimed heavy nicotine addiction and severe withdrawal symptoms.

The applicants challenged the ban through prison complaints, complaints to the Ministry of Justice, and actions before the Tartu Administrative Court. The first applicant’s claim was ultimately refused because he did not pay the State fee after the administrative court, while accepting he lacked funds, found his claim lacked prospects of success. The second applicant’s complaint was dismissed after constitutional review proceedings. The third and fourth applicants initially succeeded: on 12 June 2019, the Tartu Administrative Court declared section 641(31) unconstitutional, set it aside, annulled the Viru Prison smoking ban and ordered reconsideration.

However, in judgment no. 5-19-40 of 17 December 2019, the Supreme Court of Estonia declared section 641(31) constitutional. It accepted that the ban interfered with property rights and the right to free self-realisation, but found legitimate aims: protecting non-smokers’ health, preventing fire risk, stopping cigarettes from being used as illegal currency, maintaining prison security and order, and ensuring efficient use of resources. It stated that protecting smokers’ own health or forcing them to quit was not a legitimate aim. Less restrictive measures were considered less effective. The Supreme Court also found withdrawal symptoms unlikely to be severe because of the gradual reduction and the availability of counselling and treatment, and held that the ban was not degrading treatment.

After that judgment, the Tartu Court of Appeal upheld the Viru Prison house-rule ban on 18 March 2021, and the Supreme Court refused further appeals. The applicants’ Convention complaints therefore centre on whether the total smoking ban, including the prohibition on possessing tobacco, subjected them to degrading treatment and an unjustified interference with private life.

**Case: Constantinou and Others v. Cyprus (Applications nos. 77396/14, 45039/20, 45089/20, 45101/20 and 45899/20)**

The case concerns State interference with the salaries and pensions of Cypriot civil-service officials, employees and pensioners during Cyprus’s economic crisis. It was brought by 450 Cypriot nationals. The applicants alleged violations mainly under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (fair hearing), Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), and, in application no. 77396/14, Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 (non-discrimination).

The relevant facts concern two sets of austerity measures.

First, Law no. 112(I)/2011 introduced an “extraordinary contribution” deducted monthly from the gross salaries and pensions of officials, employees and pensioners in the civil service and wider public sector. Deductions began at salaries over EUR 1,500 per month and ranged from 1.5% to 3.5%, depending on income scale. The law entered into force on 1 September 2011 for 24 months but was extended to 31 December 2016. The Government accordingly deducted the contribution from the applicants’ gross salaries.

The applicants challenged the law before the Cypriot Supreme Court, arguing that the deductions were unconstitutional and contrary to Articles 23, 24 and 28 of the Constitution and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. They claimed their salary was a proprietary right protected by Article 23, and that none of the conditions in Article 23 § 3 permitting restrictions on property had been met.

In *Charalambous and Others v. the Republic of Cyprus* (11 June 2014), the Supreme Court, by nine votes to three, dismissed the challenges. The majority held that the law was not a tax; that salary was a property right, but the right did not extend to a salary of a particular amount; and that the relatively small deductions of 1.5%–3.5% did not affect the core of the right or amount to deprivation. It found the measures justified by the economic crisis under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 24 of the Constitution. The dissenting judges considered the deductions an unconstitutional deprivation because public-interest grounds were not among the exceptions in Article 23 § 3.

Second, Law no. 168(I)/2012 reduced the emoluments and pensions of public-sector and broader public-sector officials, employees and pensioners. Deductions were monthly, deposited into the State fixed fund, and initially ranged from 0% for low incomes to 12.5% for high incomes, later reaching up to 17.5%. The law had no expiry date but was amended several times and the reductions were discontinued from 1 January 2023. The Government deducted these amounts from the applicants’ income and pensions.

The applicants challenged Law no. 168(I)/2012 in domestic proceedings (2012–2016), again arguing that the reductions breached Article 23 of the Constitution and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Administrative Court initially found the reductions unconstitutional because public-interest grounds did not fall within Article 23 § 3. However, on appeal, in *Republic of Cyprus v. Avgousti and Others* (10 April 2020), the Supreme Court, by nine votes to four, reversed that finding and declared the reductions constitutional. The majority held that salaries and pensions were property rights but did not guarantee a particular amount; the reductions were temporary, income-related, proportionate, and did not endanger living standards or affect the core of the right. Dissenting judges maintained that Article 23 provided stricter protection and required compensation for material restrictions.

The ECtHR therefore had to examine whether these salary and pension deductions amounted to unjustified interferences with property rights, whether the domestic proceedings complied with Article 6 § 1, and whether the measures discriminated contrary to Article 1 of Protocol No. 12.

The case *Urusbiev and Others v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* (ECHR, Fifth Section, 23 October 2025) joined five applications concerning detention in the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transnistria” (“MRT”). The applicants alleged that MRT de facto authorities unlawfully deprived them of liberty and held them in inadequate material conditions, often without proper medical assistance. Their complaints mainly arose under Articles 3 and 5 of the Convention; some also relied on Articles 8, 10, 6, 13 and 14, and Article 2 of Protocol No. 4.

**Application no. 33519/15 (Urusbiev):** The applicant, stateless and resident in Dubăsari, allegedly fired a weapon in an MRT bar on 2 January 2001. Criminal proceedings were initiated, but he absconded. On 17 September 2014 he was apprehended in MRT-controlled Dubăsari. On 19 November 2014 the “MRT Tiraspol City Court” convicted him and sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment; the “MRT Supreme Court” upheld this on 23 December 2014. He complained under Article 5 § 1 that his detention from 17 September 2014 was unlawful because it was ordered by an unlawful de facto court.

**Application no. 40836/15 (Ilcenco and Ilcenco):** A father and son, both journalists in Tiraspol. On 18 March 2015 their home was searched on charges of instigating extremism and subverting the “MRT Government.” The father was arrested and held in Tiraspol police station, then transferred on 24 March 2015 to Tiraspol prison no. 3 until 17 July 2015. Professional belongings were seized. While detained, he continued publishing articles with his lawyer’s help; after publication, authorities searched his cell and removed his pens and paper. He alleged Article 3 violations (inhuman detention conditions and lack of medical assistance), Article 5 § 1 (unlawful four-month detention by an unlawful de facto court), and Article 34 hindrance of his right to apply to the Court. The son had no separate main complaints.

**Application no. 558/16 (Vardiaşvili):** Arrested on 9 June 2015 for alleged expiry of a short-term “MRT” residence permit and held three days in Dubăsari police station. On 11 June 2015 he was released, taken to the “Dubăsari border post,” expelled from the MRT, and banned from returning for six months. He complained of inhuman detention conditions under Article 3 and unlawful three-day detention under Article 5 § 1.

**Application no. 862/16 (Ahmetşin):** On 13 March 2015 convicted by a de facto MRT first-instance court of embezzlement and taken into custody. He was held in Tiraspol police station, then Tiraspol prison no. 3. On 28 April 2015 the “MRT Supreme Court” upheld the conviction and reduced his sentence to three and a half years. On 18 May 2015 he was transferred to Hlinaia prison no. 1. On 1 December 2015 Moldova’s Supreme Court declared the MRT judgments null and void. He complained of Article 3 conditions and lack of medical assistance, and Article 5 § 1 unlawful detention for three and a half years.

**Application no. 83954/17 (Mustea):** On 23 March 2017 the “Tiraspol City Court” ordered his detention for an undetermined period on theft charges; on 18 May 2017 it was extended three months. He was held in Tiraspol police station and then Tiraspol prison no. 3. He was released on 2 June 2017 after the “MRT Supreme Court” found pre-trial detention unnecessary. He complained under Articles 3 and 5 § 1.

The common thread is that all applicants were detained under orders or judgments of the unrecognised MRT authorities, in MRT detention facilities, and alleged unlawful detention, poor conditions, and inadequate medical care.

In *Mediakompaniya Slovo, TOV and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 22347/14), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered a judgment on 10 July 2025. The applicants were Mediakompaniya Slovo, a publishing company; Mr Vasylenko, its director and editor-in-chief of the newspaper *Subbota Plus*; and Ms Vasylenko, the newspaper’s editorial director. The application, lodged on 7 March 2014, concerns their complaint under Article 10 of the Convention that Ukrainian courts ordered them to retract statements published in *Subbota Plus*.

The case centres on an article written by Mr Vasylenko and published on 21 March 2013, titled “Drained profitability of [V.]”. V. was a large municipal water-supply company. The article alleged serious corruption and mismanagement at V. It stated, among other things, that there had been embezzlement and squandering of tens of millions of hryvnias of State money; that funds were withdrawn through contracts with intermediary companies and inflated purchases; that private enterprises “pocketed” State money; that V. gave a 16 million hryvnia interest-free loan to a private person; that fraud occurred during renovation works; that pipes were unlawfully sold rather than installed; that employees who raised problems were fired or demoted; and that oversight officials failed to check anything. The article also referred to “right” suppliers, “watchmen”, and the likelihood that equipment would be bought from favoured suppliers “not without a sweetener”. It concluded that V. was on the verge of bankruptcy because of corruption, irresponsibility, lack of professionalism, and moral bankruptcy of its management.

In April 2013, V. sued all three applicants, seeking retraction of the statements and compensation for non-pecuniary damage. The applicants argued that the statements were value judgments not susceptible of proof, that the information was not negative, and that it was not clear from the article that the information referred to V.

On 17 June 2013, the Zhovtnevyi District Court of Zaporizhzhya found against the applicants. It examined each disputed statement and held that they were statements of fact, not value judgments. It further found that the applicants had not proved that the statements were true. The court ordered them to retract the information and to publish the operative part of the judgment in the next issue of *Subbota Plus*. It also prohibited them from disseminating the information contained in those statements “by any possible means (on the television or in printed media, on the radio, on the internet, in interviews, in conversations with any person, or by any other means).” The applicants were ordered to pay V. 1 Ukrainian hryvnia in non-pecuniary damages and UAH 458 in court fees. The court relied in particular on Article 278 of the Civil Code as in force at the material time. The applicants’ appeals were rejected, with a final decision by the Higher Specialized Court on 9 September 2013.

According to the Government, the writs of execution were never submitted to the Bailiffs Service. Ms Vasylenko died on 28 June 2020. On 29 March 2023, Mr Vasylenko informed the Court that Mediakompaniya Slovo did not wish to pursue the application.

The key Article 10 issue is whether the domestic orders—requiring retraction, publication of the judgment, and a sweeping ban on further dissemination—amounted to a disproportionate interference with the applicants’ freedom of expression, particularly in the context of public-interest allegations of corruption at a municipal utility.

In *Radelić v. Croatia*, the applicant, Dražen Radelić, was the sole shareholder and director of Radelić d.o.o. The company went bankrupt in November 2010, the bankruptcy was concluded in December 2010, and in March 2011 the company was struck off the register and ceased to exist.

In March 2011 the Croatian State Attorney’s Office indicted the applicant for business fraud and forgery of documents. It alleged that between August 2003 and February 2004 he presented thirty-six foreign bank cheques for cashing, falsely claiming they were payment for services rendered abroad, intending to obtain significant pecuniary gain for the company.

In 2014 the Split Municipal Court convicted him of forgery and imposed a suspended sentence, while acquitting him of business fraud. On appeal, the acquittal was quashed and a retrial was ordered. In 2017 the Municipal Court convicted him of business fraud and imposed a one-year suspended sentence. Critically, it also ordered confiscation of HRK 854,743.39—about EUR 113,440—as proceeds of crime from the applicant personally. He was ordered to pay that amount into the State budget within six months; failure could result in revocation of the suspended sentence. The court reasoned that the company had been struck off and had no legal successor, and that the applicant, as sole founder, shareholder, and authorized representative, should therefore pay the confiscated amount under Article 77 of the Penal Code.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the money had been paid into the company’s account, not to him personally; that the company had paid taxes and used the funds for its operations; and that he had not personally benefited. The Split County Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the confiscation. It held that the illegal gain had been acquired for the company through the applicant’s criminal acts, but because the company no longer existed and had no successor, confiscation from the applicant was justified by analogy with section 252(5) of the Commercial Companies Act, concerning a management board member’s liability to creditors for gross breach of duty.

The Split County State Attorney’s Office later proposed that a request for protection of legality be lodged, arguing that confiscation from the applicant personally was unlawful: the indictment alleged gain for the company, no evidence showed the gain was transferred to the applicant, and if the company had been liquidated the court should have ordered compensation to victims, though no injured party or civil claim existed. The Principal State Attorney did not lodge the request.

The applicant’s constitutional complaint was dismissed in 2021; the Constitutional Court found no breach of his right of ownership. Enforcement efforts later failed because his bank accounts lacked sufficient funds.

The European Court of Human Rights gave notice only of the complaint concerning the confiscation of proceeds of crime. The key issue was whether confiscating proceeds from the applicant personally—even though the proceeds were allegedly acquired by and for the company, which had ceased to exist—was compatible with the Convention, particularly his property rights and the lawfulness of the measure. Relevant facts included that he was not found to have personally acquired or retained the proceeds, that domestic Supreme Court case-law suggested proceeds could not be confiscated from a perpetrator when acquired for a company, and that the State Attorney’s Office itself considered the confiscation unlawful.

A.R., a British national born in 1978 and a qualified teacher working as a taxi driver, was charged in March 2010 with raping a 17-year-old female passenger. The allegation was that he drove her to a secluded location and forcibly had sex with her without consent. He denied any sexual contact, and there was no forensic evidence linking him to the complainant. On 21 January 2011 he was acquitted at trial.

The alleged violations arise from two enhanced criminal record certificates (“ECRCs”) issued in 2011 and 2012. In March 2011, an ECRC was issued for his application for a college lecturer post. Although A.R. had no convictions or cautions, the ECRC disclosed, under police “other relevant information,” that he had been charged with rape, acquitted, and included a summary of the complainant’s account and his denial. In March 2012, a second ECRC for a private hire driver licence contained the same information.

A.R. objected, arguing that disclosure was highly prejudicial because there was no conviction, that the jury had rejected the complainant’s evidence, and that he would have to defend himself in every future job application. His internal appeals failed. The police reviewing officer considered the information relevant and sufficient, relying on the fact that the CPS had authorised a rape charge, the medical evidence, the complainant’s distress, and the absence of an apparent motive to lie. She reasoned that the allegation was more likely true than false and that the acquittal did not prove innocence. Disclosure was justified as necessary to protect vulnerable persons, especially given his proposed roles as a lecturer and taxi driver.

A.R. sought judicial review under Articles 6 § 2 and 8 of the Convention. The High Court accepted that Article 8 was engaged but found the disclosure reasonable, proportionate, and necessary to protect young and vulnerable persons. It found no breach of Article 6 § 2. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal, holding that the ECRC did not undermine the acquittal and that there was no procedural link to the criminal trial; the Article 8 balance had been correctly struck. The Supreme Court granted permission only on Article 8 and dismissed the appeal in July 2018. It held that disclosure interfered with private life but was proportionate. The police were not required to conduct a “mini-trial” or reassess the trial evidence. Although the reviewing officer’s “more likely than not” approach was flawed, the chief officer could rely on the information as “not lacking substance” and possibly true, given its seriousness, relevance, and recency. The Supreme Court nevertheless raised concerns about how employers use ECRCs and the risk of unfair stigmatisation of acquitted persons.

The ECtHR application concerns whether the 2011 and 2012 disclosures violated A.R.’s rights under Article 8, by interfering with private life, and Article 6 § 2, by undermining the presumption of innocence following acquittal.

Georgios Papadopoulos v. Cyprus (Application no. 21454/21) concerns the repeated annulment of the applicant’s declaration as an elected member of the Cypriot Parliament for the Limassol constituency. In the 22 May 2016 parliamentary elections, Cyprus used an open-list proportional representation system. Papadopoulos and Ms E.T. were candidates for the Solidarity Movement in Limassol. Ms E.T., then Solidarity president and an MEP, was declared elected for Solidarity’s one Limassol seat on 23 May 2016. On 27 May 2016, before the parliamentary term began, she informed the Chief Returning Officer that she would not take the seat, preferring to remain an MEP. Domestic law only provided for filling seats that became vacant after the parliamentary term started; it did not address a seat declined before the term began.

The CRO then applied section 35(1) of the Elections Law by analogy and, on 31 May 2016, declared Papadopoulos, the runner-up, elected. He affirmed in Parliament on 2 June 2016. Following an electoral petition by an unsuccessful candidate and a voter, the Electoral Court annulled his election on 31 May 2017. It found that Ms E.T. never acquired parliamentary status because she had not affirmed under Article 69 of the Constitution; the seat had not been “vacated” but was “not taken.” Section 35(1) therefore did not apply, and in the absence of clear legislation the CRO had acted impermissibly.

Parliament amended section 35(1) in June 2017 to cover “not taken” seats. On 5 July 2017 the CRO again declared Papadopoulos elected; he affirmed on 7 July. A new petition followed. On 30 April 2018 the Electoral Court, by six votes to five, annulled his election for a second time and declared the 2017 amendment unconstitutional. The majority held that the Constitution addressed only “vacated” seats, not “not taken” seats; that the seat had never lawfully belonged to Solidarity; and that the runner-up could not claim it. It also found that retroactively conferring such a right violated non-retroactivity and popular sovereignty. The minority considered that Parliament had validly filled a legislative gap consistent with proportional representation.

In October 2019 Parliament amended Articles 66 and 71 of the Constitution and section 35 of the Elections Law to include “renounced,” “not taken,” and “vacated” seats. On 29 October 2019 the Returning Officer declared Papadopoulos an MP for a third time, and he affirmed on 1 November. A further petition led the Electoral Court, on 29 October 2020, by ten votes to one, to annul his election again. The court invoked the basic structure doctrine, holding that the amendments could not retroactively overturn final Electoral Court decisions or undermine popular sovereignty, separation of powers, non-retroactivity, and equality. It found that targeted legislation had appointed a specific person as MP, depriving other candidates of by-elections and voters of their effective vote. The dissenting judge disagreed, finding the amendments valid and compatible with Cyprus’s party-based proportional system.

Papadopoulos applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 21 April 2021. The factual core of the alleged violations is that, although he was declared elected three times as the runner-up for the seat declined by Ms E.T., each declaration was annulled by the Electoral Court on constitutional and statutory grounds. The domestic courts consistently found that the seat was never “vacated” during the parliamentary term but was “not taken” before it, and that later retroactive constitutional and legislative amendments could not validly transfer it to him. The applicant argued that the amendments aligned with the proportional party-list system and the 2016 election result. The ECtHR is therefore called upon to assess whether the repeated annulments and the domestic legal framework violated his Convention rights, principally the right to free elections and to stand as a candidate under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1, and potentially related fair-trial or legal-certainty guarantees. The case turns on the tension between finality of electoral decisions, parliamentary sovereignty, retroactive remedial legislation, and popular sovereignty in filling parliamentary seats.

**Summary of *Georgios Papadopoulos v. Cyprus* (Application no. 21454/21)**

The case concerns the repeated annulment of the applicant’s declaration as an elected Member of Parliament (MP) in Cyprus following the 2016 parliamentary elections.

**Background and Initial Election**

In the May 2016 elections, the applicant was a candidate for the Solidarity Movement in the Limassol constituency. Ms E.T., then president of Solidarity and a Member of the European Parliament (MEP), was declared elected as the party’s representative for Limassol. However, on 27 May 2016, Ms E.T. informed the Chief Returning Officer (CRO) that she would not take the seat in order to retain her MEP position. Cypriot law at the time only provided for filling seats vacated *after* the parliamentary term began, not seats not taken *before* the term commenced.

**First Declaration and Annulment**

On 31 May 2016, the CRO applied section 35(1) of the Elections Law by analogy and declared the applicant, the runner-up, elected. After the applicant affirmed his duties in Parliament, two individuals filed an electoral petition. On 31 May 2017, the Electoral Court annulled the applicant’s election, unanimously holding that section 35(1) only regulated seats vacated during the parliamentary term. Since Ms E.T. had never been affirmed and her seat was “not taken” rather than “vacated,” the CRO’s analogical application was impermissible in the absence of clear legislation.

**Second Declaration and Annulment**

Parliament amended section 35(1) in June 2017 to cover “not taken” seats, and on 5 July 2017 the CRO declared the applicant elected once more. The applicant took up his duties. A new electoral petition followed. On 30 April 2018, the Electoral Court, by a 6-5 majority, annulled the election for the second time and declared the 2017 amendment unconstitutional. It held that Article 66 of the Constitution addressed only “vacated” seats, not “not taken” ones. The seat had never lawfully belonged to Solidarity, and the retroactive amendment violated the principle of non-retroactivity by conferring rights retrospectively on the applicant.

**Third Declaration and Annulment**

In October 2019, Parliament amended Articles 66 and 71 of the Constitution and section 35 of the Elections Law to expressly include “renounced” and “not taken” seats. On 29 October 2019, the Returning Officer declared the applicant elected a third time. Another petition followed.

On 29 October 2020, the Electoral Court, by a 10-1 majority, annulled the election again. The court invoked the “basic structure doctrine,” holding that while constitutional amendments were generally permissible, they could not undermine the Constitution’s fundamental principles. The court found that the Twelfth Amendment and the 2019 Law violated the principle of non-retroactivity, the finality of prior Electoral Court decisions, and popular sovereignty by targeting a specific individual and applying to a seat already adjudicated as never lawfully held by Solidarity. The court concluded that had the amendments applied only to future cases, they would have been acceptable, but their retroactive effect unlawfully appointed a particular person as MP.

**Core Alleged Violation**

The applicant, a Cypriot national, lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 21 April 2021, complaining about the Electoral Court’s repeated decisions to annul his declaration as an elected MP, raising issues under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (right to free elections).

The case *A.R. v. the United Kingdom* (Application no. 6033/19) concerns police disclosures in 2011 and 2012, through enhanced criminal record certificates (“ECRCs”), of information that the applicant had been charged with rape and subsequently acquitted. The applicant, a British national born in 1978 with teaching qualifications, was working as a taxi driver. In March 2010 he was charged with raping a 17-year-old passenger who alleged that he drove her to a secluded location and forcibly had sex with her without consent while she was intoxicated. He denied any sexual contact. There was no forensic evidence linking him to her, and he was acquitted on 21 January 2011.

In March 2011, an ECRC was issued for his application for a college lecturer post. Although he had no convictions or cautions, the certificate disclosed the rape charge and acquittal as “other relevant information” under section 113B of the Police Act 1997. It described the allegation, his arrest and denial, the CPS decision to charge, and the not guilty verdict. The applicant objected, arguing that disclosure of an allegation after jury acquittal was grossly prejudicial and would prevent fair consideration for employment. The police upheld disclosure. A reviewing officer reasoned that CPS authorisation of the charge indicated a realistic prospect of conviction and that, on balance, the allegation was more likely true than false; an acquittal did not prove innocence because the criminal standard was higher than that for CRB disclosure. She relied on medical evidence, the complainant’s distress, lack of motive to lie, and inconsistencies not central to the allegation. She concluded disclosure was reasonable and proportionate to protect vulnerable females. In March 2012, a second ECRC for a private hire driver licence repeated the same information and conclusion, authorised by a senior officer who saw a risk to children and vulnerable adults.

The applicant challenged the decisions by judicial review, invoking Article 6 § 2 (presumption of innocence) and Article 8 (private life). The High Court rejected the claim in 2013, finding Article 8 engaged but disclosure reasonable and proportionate, and no Article 6 breach. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal in 2016, holding that the ECRC cast no aspersion on the acquittal, did not suggest guilt, and was a public-protection measure; the police did not have to conduct a mini-trial. The Supreme Court granted permission only on Article 8 and dismissed the appeal in 2018. It accepted that disclosure interfered with Article 8 but found it proportionate. Lord Carnwath held that police should not attempt to replicate the trial or decide likely guilt; the reviewing officer had erred if she assessed whether the allegation was more likely true than false, but the information was serious, relevant to the posts, and recent, and the judge had struck the balance correctly. He nevertheless expressed concern about how employers use ECRCs and the risk that disclosure of an acquittal could be read as implying guilt.

Before the European Court, the applicant’s alleged violations therefore concern: (1) Article 6 § 2, because disclosing the charge and circumstances after acquittal allegedly undermined the presumption of innocence; and (2) Article 8, because the disclosure of non-conviction information interfered with his private life and damaged his employment prospects.

In *Tverdokhlebova v. Ukraine* (Application no. 15830/16), judgment of 16 January 2025, the applicant is a Ukrainian national born in 1965 who lives in Kyiv. Her application concerns the deprivation of her title to a 0.18-hectare plot of land after a prosecutor brought proceedings to return the land to the State, and the alleged unfairness of those proceedings because she was not informed of them. She relied on Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In 2011, the Brovary District State Administration allocated a 1.8-hectare plot to D. for individual farming. D. later divided it into plots of 1.62 ha and 0.18 ha and changed the purpose to “gardening”. In November 2013, the applicant bought the smaller plot from D. The sales contract stated the price was UAH 147,600, equal to USD 18,000 on the signing date, received in USD by D.

In June 2014, a local prosecutor sued in the local court, seeking invalidation of the decision allocating the disputed land to D., D.’s title, the sale contract between D. and the applicant, and the applicant’s title. The prosecutor argued that the land was located within Bohdanivka village and therefore could not have been disposed of by the Brovary District State Administration. The local court rejected the claims. On appeal, however, the Kyiv Region Court of Appeal granted them by judgment of 14 May 2015. It relied on separate proceedings concerning the original larger plot, involving different parties, in which a forensic technical expert assessment had established that the land lay within Bohdanivka village boundaries. The appellate court invalidated the applicant’s title and restored the land to the village’s ownership.

The applicant alleged that she had not been informed of either the first-instance or appellate proceedings. She said that all summonses were sent to an allegedly non-existent address at 6 Krasovskyy Street, Brovary, while she actually lived in Kyiv. She learned of the proceedings only in May 2015, after the appellate judgment, when her representative reviewed the case file. In her cassation appeal, she argued that the failure to notify her was a gross procedural violation. She noted that the 2013 sales contract, which the prosecutor had and relied on, indicated her Kyiv address. The letters and summonses in the file had been sent to the wrong address, and registered letters had been returned as undelivered. She also argued that the lower courts had misapplied land legislation and disregarded evidence. D. also filed a cassation appeal. On 16 September 2015, the Higher Specialized Court for Civil and Criminal Cases upheld the appellate findings, stating that the facts had been comprehensively established, domestic law correctly applied, and the remaining cassation arguments not borne out by the file.

Later, the applicant sued D. to recover the purchase money. On 10 December 2019, the Brovary Local Court allowed her claim under Article 216 of the Civil Code, awarding UAH 426,393.20 (USD 18,000 at the then exchange rate) plus UAH 4,037 for notary fees and land tax. This was upheld on appeal on 4 June 2020 and became final. Enforcement proceedings began against D. in July 2022; the applicant alleged non-enforcement but provided no details or challenges to bailiffs’ actions. In 2021 she received permission to prepare technical documentation for a 0.18-hectare plot for individual farming in Bohdanivka, but it is unclear whether she obtained title.

The key alleged violations are therefore: under Article 6, unfairness because the courts allegedly failed to notify her, preventing her participation in proceedings that invalidated her title; and under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, deprivation of her property/title through the prosecutor’s action and resulting court decisions. The provided excerpt does not include the Court’s final assessment.

**Case Summary: A.R.E. v. Greece (Application no. 15783/21)**

The applicant, A.R.E., is a Turkish national born in 1992. In November 2016, she was placed in pre-trial detention in Türkiye for alleged membership of the FETÖ/PDY organisation, remaining in custody for 28 months. On 12 March 2019, she was sentenced to six years and three months’ imprisonment but released the same day pending appeal, subject to a ban on leaving the country.

On 4 May 2019, at around 5:30 a.m., the applicant crossed the Evros River from Türkiye into Greece with two other Turkish nationals seeking international protection. Shortly after, she contacted her brother via WhatsApp, sharing live location data, photographs, and videos expressing fear of being unlawfully returned to Türkiye. At 10:55 a.m., she emailed UNHCR Greece, stating that she and two others had fled persecution and feared “inhuman behaviours and push back by Greek Security Forces.”

A lawyer, N.O., travelled to Nea Vyssa, where he saw the applicant and her companions in the town square. He took a photograph of them. Shortly afterwards, police arrived and arrested the three. The applicant alleged that the police refused to let the lawyer enter the vehicle but allowed him to follow in his car. She was taken to the Orestiada border guard station in Neo Cheimonio, where she reiterated her asylum request. She claimed she was held unofficially until 7 p.m., then transferred with 31 other migrants in a lorry to the Evros River. There, masked men in camouflage ordered them out; some who refused were beaten. The group was forced onto small inflatable boats and sent back to Türkiye. Turkish gendarmerie arrested them. The applicant was detained in Edirne Prison, then Gebze Prison, where she remained until October 2021.

On 18 June 2019, the Greek Council for Refugees filed a criminal complaint alleging abuse of power, unlawful detention, life-endangerment, grievous bodily harm, torture and other offences. On 13 December 2019, the Orestiada public prosecutor dismissed the complaint for lack of evidence. On appeal, the Thrace Court of Appeal ordered further investigation. Witnesses included lawyer N.O. and journalist Z.K., who corroborated key elements: N.O. testified he witnessed the applicant’s arrest; Z.K. confirmed the applicant’s live location and fear of pushback. On 23 September 2020, the prosecutor again dismissed the case, finding no evidence to substantiate the allegations and relying on police testimony denying any pushback.

The Government denied all allegations, citing inconsistencies, lack of original evidence, the brother’s failure to testify, and a National Transparency Authority report finding no evidence of pushbacks. They also pointed to three Turkish nationals arrested on 4 May 2019 by the Didymoteicho border guard station who applied for asylum, disputing the applicant’s account.

The applicant relied on Articles 2, 3, 5 and 13 of the Convention, alleging that her pushback exposed her to a real risk of ill-treatment and that Greece failed to conduct an effective investigation.

Case A.R.E. v. Greece (Application no. 15783/21) concerns an alleged “pushback” by Greek authorities of a Turkish national to Türkiye, raising issues under Articles 2, 3, 5 and 13 ECHR.

The applicant, a Turkish national born in 1992, had been accused of belonging to FETÖ/PDY. In November 2016 she was placed in pre-trial detention for 28 months. On 12 March 2019 she was sentenced to six years and three months’ imprisonment, released pending appeal, and prohibited from leaving Türkiye. On 4 May 2019 she crossed the Evros River into Greece with two other Turkish nationals seeking international protection. Near Nea Vyssa, from about 5:30 a.m., she contacted her brother in Greece via WhatsApp live location, sent photographs and videos, and emailed UNHCR, saying she feared unlawful removal and danger if returned to Türkiye. A lawyer, N.O., contacted her and went to Nea Vyssa. Around 2:40 p.m., police arrested the three while they waited for the lawyer; at the police station they requested asylum. They were allegedly taken to the Orestiada border guard station in Neo Cheimonio and held unofficially until 7 p.m.

The alleged pushback then began. They were transported by van to an unknown station, where belongings, phones, money and shoes were confiscated. A larger lorry took them and 28 others—31 people in total, including Syrians, Afghans, Pakistanis and Kurds—to the Evros River. Masked men in camouflage uniforms forced them out; some who resisted were beaten. At about 11 p.m. they were placed in a small inflatable boat and returned to Türkiye in several crossings. Turkish gendarmerie arrested most of the group; the applicant and two companions hid in reeds but were found and arrested on 5 May 2019. She was held in Edirne Prison, then Gebze Prison. She submitted that her brother stopped seeing her live location at 6:52 p.m. on 4 May; he and the lawyer searched police stations without success. A Turkish court decision later stated she had fled to Greece and was sent back.

On 18 June 2019 the Greek Council for Refugees filed a criminal complaint alleging abuse of power, unlawful detention, life endangerment, grievous bodily harm, torture and offences against human dignity. The Orestiada prosecutor dismissed it in December 2019 for lack of evidence. On appeal, the Thrace Court of Appeal prosecutor ordered further investigation; statements were taken from lawyer N.O. and journalist Z.K. N.O. said he saw the applicant in Nea Vyssa and witnessed her alleged arrest; Z.K. said he tracked her location and spoke with her and others. In September 2020 the prosecutor again dismissed the case, finding no evidence of pushback, no arrest matching the applicant, and relying on police testimony.

The Government denied all allegations, citing inconsistencies, lack of originals/metadata, absence of the brother’s testimony, and no proof she entered Greece or was pushed back. The applicant relied on WhatsApp live-location data, photos/videos, UNHCR emails, witness statements and Turkish court documents. The alleged violations concern exposure to serious harm and detention in Türkiye through summary removal without examining her asylum claim, unlawful detention in Greece, and failure to provide an effective investigation/remedy.

Constantinou and Others v. Cyprus concerns five applications brought by 450 Cypriot nationals against Cyprus. The applicants were public-sector officials, employees, or pensioners whose salaries and/or pensions were reduced by legislation adopted during Cyprus’s financial crisis. The communicated complaints concern Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing) in four later applications, Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) in all applications, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 (non-discrimination) in application no. 77396/14.

Two main laws were at issue. First, Law no. 112(I)/2011, passed on 31 August 2011, imposed an “extraordinary contribution” deducted monthly from the gross salaries and pensions of civil-service and wider public-sector officials, employees, and pensioners. Deductions were tiered: no deduction below EUR 1,500; 1.5% on EUR 1,501–2,500; 2.5% on EUR 2,501–3,500; 3% on EUR 3,501–4,500; and 3.5% above EUR 4,500. It began on 1 September 2011 for 24 months but was extended to 31 December 2016, with minor amendments; the rate never exceeded 3.5%. A comparable private-sector contribution was introduced in January 2012.

Second, Law no. 168(I)/2012, passed on 6 December 2012, reduced public-sector emoluments and pensions. Deductions ranged initially from 0% for low incomes/pensions to 12.5% for high incomes/pensions, later amended up to 17.5%. It applied from 1 December 2012, had no expiry date, and the reductions ended for everyone on 1 January 2023.

The applicants challenged the deductions before domestic courts. In relation to Law no. 112(I)/2011, they argued before the Supreme Court that the deductions violated, inter alia, Articles 23 (property), 24 (taxation), and 28 (equality) of the Constitution, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. In Charalambous and Others v. Republic of Cyprus (11 June 2014), the Supreme Court dismissed the challenges 9–3. The majority accepted that salaries were a proprietary right, but held that the right did not extend to a salary of a particular amount. It found the relatively small 1.5–3.5% deductions did not affect the core of the right, did not amount to deprivation, and were justified under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 24. The dissenting judges considered the deductions unconstitutional under Article 23 because public-interest grounds were not among the permissible exceptions in Article 23 § 3, and because the deductions effectively deprived applicants of property without compensation. They also found unequal targeting of public officials.

As to Law no. 168(I)/2012, the Administrative Court in 2018 and 2019 found the salary and pension reductions unconstitutional under Article 23, reasoning that consolidating public finances was not a permissible Article 23 § 3 ground and that material curtailments required compensation. On 10 April 2020, however, the Supreme Court in Avgousti and Others v. Republic of Cyprus reversed 9–4, declaring the reductions constitutional. The majority held that salaries and pensions were property, but did not guarantee a particular amount; the reductions were limited, effective, proportionate, and did not affect the core of the right or living standards. Dissenting judges maintained that Article 23 provided stronger protection than Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, that public-interest justifications were insufficient, and that the reductions required compensation. The ECtHR must now assess whether these measures and domestic rulings violated the applicants’ Convention rights.
