**Case: Radchenko v. Ukraine (Application no. 21217/17), European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), judgment 11 September 2025.** The applicant, a Ukrainian national born in 1977, alleged violations of Articles 10 and 13 of the Convention. The case concerns the prolonged non-enforcement of a domestic court judgment ordering the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources of Ukraine to provide him with public environmental information.

The applicant’s request was prompted by several environmental incidents in the Kyiv Region in June 2015: massive fires at a petroleum storage depot on 8 June, a plastic goods warehouse on 12 June, and peat burning from 9 June. On 17 June 2015, relying on the Law on Access to Public Information and the Law on Protection of Environment, he asked the Ministry for: (i) air pollution levels by district and dangerous gases; (ii) measures to combat pollution and improve air quality; (iii) the Ministry’s own measures against technogenic catastrophes; and (iv) the names and addresses of the owners of the depot and warehouse, their responsibility, and compensation for damage.

The Ministry, acting through the State Ecologic Inspectorate, replied but, as later court judgments established, provided none of the requested information. The reply referred to a general ban on inspections, a special request to inspect the P. company, and soil and water tests. The applicant sued. On 17 September 2015, the Kyiv Circuit Administrative Court granted his claim. It found the Ministry’s reply contained none of the requested information and gave no explanation for the refusal. It held that the Ministry had broad environmental duties, that the requested information was public, and that environmental danger information had to be communicated within 48 hours. It ordered a full reply within that time-limit.

On 26 October 2015, the Ministry sent another letter, providing information about air-quality monitoring bodies, links to data on the Kyiv Regional Sanitary and Epidemic Service website, and a 2015–16 plan concerning the petroleum depot fire. The applicant considered this incomplete and sought enforcement and judicial control. On 25 November 2015, the Kyiv Circuit Administrative Court acknowledged the Ministry’s omissions. It found that air-quality measurements were scattered and irregular, and that ecological information was not systematically gathered or publicized, causing a “systemic violation of the citizens’ right to information about the environment,” partly due to legislative inconsistencies. The court stated that those systemic problems could not be resolved through an individual court judgment and issued a separate ruling addressed to the Ministry, the Cabinet of Ministers, the National Security and Defence Council, and a parliamentary committee.

The applicant then initiated enforcement proceedings in respect of the 17 September 2015 judgment. The Ministry sent further replies. A letter of 21 September 2018 stated that a governmental commission created on 9 June 2015 had conducted laboratory air monitoring, disseminated daily information, taken measures, and found no excess pollution, but that the Ministry did not possess part of the requested information concerning air pollution levels. The enforcement proceedings were terminated and reopened multiple times. Courts essentially held that the Ministry could not be exempted from fully enforcing the judgment, despite claiming unavailability of certain information. In October 2019, the enforcement proceedings were definitively terminated for impossibility of enforcement “without the debtor’s participation.” A bailiff complained to the police about possible wilful non-enforcement, but no criminal proceedings were instituted for lack of elements of an offence. The applicant’s challenge failed.

In October 2016, the applicant also complained to the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights. The Commissioner found that the Ministry did not possess comparative air pollution data, that only “existing” information is public, and requested the Cabinet to ensure the Ministry complied with its environmental obligations.

The alleged violations therefore concern the failure to enforce a final judgment ordering the provision of public environmental information and the alleged absence of an effective remedy, under Articles 10 and 13.

**Summary of *Radchenko v. Ukraine* (Application no. 21217/17)**

In *Radchenko v. Ukraine*, a Ukrainian national, Mr Oleksiy Volodymyrovych Radchenko (born 1977), complained under Articles 10 and 13 of the Convention about the prolonged non-enforcement of a domestic court judgment ordering the provision of public information to him.

On 17 June 2015 the applicant requested information from Ukraine’s Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources. His request was prompted by environmental incidents in the Kyiv Region: major fires at a petroleum storage depot on 8 June 2015, a plastic goods warehouse on 12 June 2015, and peat burning from 9 June 2015. He asked for: (i) air pollution levels by district and dangerous gases present; (ii) measures taken to combat pollution and improve air quality; (iii) measures by the Ministry itself against technogenic catastrophes; and (iv) names and addresses of the owners of the depot and warehouse, their responsibility for the incidents, and compensation for damage. He relied on the Law on Access to Public Information and the Law on Protection of the Environment.

The Ministry, through the State Ecologic Inspectorate, replied on 25 June 2015. Later court judgments indicated that the reply referred to a legislative ban on inspections, a request for an exceptional inspection, soil and water tests, and crisis monitoring. The applicant considered the reply incomplete and sued.

On 17 September 2015 the Kyiv Circuit Administrative Court granted his claim. It found that the Ministry’s reply contained none of the requested information and gave no explanation why it could not be provided. It held that the information was public, that environmental danger information had to be communicated within forty-eight hours, and ordered a full reply within that time-limit.

The Ministry sent another letter on 26 October 2015, providing links to online data and a plan concerning the petroleum depot fire. The applicant again considered this incomplete. On 25 November 2015 the court acknowledged the Ministry’s omissions and found the reply still insufficient. More broadly, it found that air quality measurements were scattered and irregular and that ecological information was not systematically gathered or publicised, causing a “systemic violation” of citizens’ right to environmental information, partly due to inconsistent legislation. The court stated that these systemic problems could not be resolved by an individual enforcement judgment and issued a separate ruling addressed to several State authorities.

The applicant then initiated enforcement proceedings for the 17 September 2015 judgment. The Ministry sent further replies. A letter of 21 September 2018 stated that a governmental commission had been created, tests had been conducted, air pollution information was disseminated daily, measures had been taken, and pollution limits had not been exceeded—but that the Ministry lacked some requested air pollution data. Enforcement proceedings were terminated and reopened multiple times. Courts held that the Ministry could not be exempted from full enforcement because the judgment was clear and contained no exceptions. In October 2019 enforcement was definitively terminated as impossible “without the debtor’s participation.” A bailiff complained to police about possible wilful non-enforcement, but no criminal proceedings were instituted. The applicant’s challenge failed.

In October 2016 the applicant complained to the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights. The Commissioner found that the Ministry did not possess the comparative air pollution information, that only “existing” information was public, and that nothing could be done. The Commissioner asked the Cabinet of Ministers to ensure the Ministry complied with its environmental and air-quality obligations.

The application was lodged on 10 March 2017. The applicant relied on Articles 10 and 13, alleging prolonged non-enforcement of the domestic judgment ordering provision of public information. The Court gave notice of those complaints to the Government and declared the remainder inadmissible.

**Case: Lubarda and Milanov v. Serbia**  
**Applications nos. 6570/19 and 43604/19**  
**European Court of Human Rights, Third Section — Judgment of 29 April 2025**

The case concerns two applicants, Zoran Lubarda and Slađan Milanov, who were convicted in Serbian minor-offence proceedings for road-traffic offences. They complained under Article 6 of the Convention that the proceedings were unfair because they were not given an opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses—police officers—whose evidence formed the basis of their convictions.

The first applicant was convicted in 2017 of failing to comply with a traffic-light signal. He was fined €120, banned from driving for three months, and received penalty points. The second applicant was convicted in 2015 of driving while intoxicated (“in a state of complete intoxication”). He was fined €850, banned from driving for eight months, and received penalty points. Although these were minor-offence proceedings, both offences were potentially punishable by imprisonment. Under the Serbian Minor Offences Act, if the fines were not paid, they could be converted into effective prison sentences of up to 15 days for the first applicant and up to 60 days for the second applicant. This brought the proceedings within the criminal limb of Article 6.

At the scene, both applicants signed reports drawn up by police officers. Later, however, they disputed the contents of those reports in court. Their convictions were based on those reports and on evidence given by the police officers. The officers’ evidence was taken in court, but not during the main hearings in the applicants’ cases. Neither the applicants nor their lawyers were summoned to the examination of those witnesses, even though both had explicitly requested to be present and to cross-examine them. In the first applicant’s case, the request was refused on grounds of efficiency and economy of proceedings. In the second applicant’s case, the court held that cross-examination would not have led to a different determination of facts because the officer’s evidence was consistent with the report the applicant had signed.

Both applicants appealed. Their convictions were upheld by the Appeals Court and subsequently by the Constitutional Court. The final domestic decisions were notified to the applicants on 1 August 2018 in Lubarda’s case and 26 February 2019 in Milanov’s case. They lodged applications with the European Court on 22 January 2019 and 2 August 2019, respectively, represented by counsel.

Before the European Court, they relied on Article 6 of the Convention, alleging that the minor-offence proceedings against them had not been fair. Specifically, they complained that they had not been given an opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses on whose statements their convictions had been based.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore: (1) the convictions rested significantly on police reports and police witness evidence; (2) the applicants disputed the contents of the reports they had signed; (3) the police witnesses were examined without the applicants or their lawyers being summoned, despite explicit requests; and (4) the domestic courts refused or discounted cross-examination either for reasons of procedural efficiency or because the evidence was considered consistent with the signed reports.

**Summary of *Radchenko v. Ukraine* (Application no. 21217/17)**

The case of *Radchenko v. Ukraine* concerns the prolonged non-enforcement of a domestic court judgment ordering the provision of public information, in violation of Articles 10 (freedom of expression) and 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant, Mr Oleksiy Radchenko, submitted a request for public information to the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources of Ukraine on 17 June 2015. His request was prompted by several environmental incidents in the Kyiv Region, including massive fires at a petroleum storage depot (8 June 2015), a plastic goods warehouse (12 June 2015), and the burning of peat. He sought specific data: (i) air pollution levels by district and pollutant; (ii) measures taken to combat pollution and improve air quality; (iii) the Ministry's own actions to combat technogenic catastrophes; and (iv) the names and addresses of the legal entities owning the depot and warehouse, their level of responsibility, and how they were compensating for damage.

The Ministry's reply on 25 June 2016 did not contain the requested information. It stated that legislative bans prevented inspections of legal entities and mentioned that soil and water tests had been conducted. The applicant sued, and on 17 September 2015, the Kyiv Circuit Administrative Court ruled in his favour. The court found the Ministry's reply addressed none of his questions, with no explanation for the failure to provide the data. It established that the information was "public" under the Law on Access to Public Information and related to environmental protection, requiring communication within 48 hours. The court ordered a full reply within that time-limit.

The Ministry's subsequent letter of 26 October 2015 was again deemed incomplete by the applicant. A further court judgment on 25 November 2015 acknowledged the Ministry's failure to fully execute the first judgment. Critically, this court found systemic deficiencies: air quality measurements were scattered and irregular, and ecological information was not systematically gathered or made public. The court stated these issues could not be resolved by enforcing an individual judgment and issued a separate ruling to multiple state authorities to address the systemic problems.

The applicant initiated enforcement proceedings. The Ministry sent several more replies. A key letter of 21 September 2018 stated the Ministry did not possess part of the requested information, specifically the air pollution levels. The enforcement proceedings were repeatedly terminated and reopened, with courts consistently holding that the Ministry could not be exempted from fully enforcing the judgment. In October 2019, the proceedings were definitively terminated due to the impossibility of enforcement "without the debtor's participation." A bailiff's complaint to police regarding wilful non-enforcement led to no criminal proceedings.

The applicant also complained to the Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, who confirmed the Ministry did not possess the comparative air pollution data, explaining that only "existing" documented information was considered public.

The case before the European Court of Human Rights centred on this failure to enforce the final domestic judgment, which had clearly identified the specific information to be provided.

text:
**Case: Lubarda and Milanov v. Serbia**  
**Applications nos. 6570/19 and 43604/19 – European Court of Human Rights, Third Section – Judgment of 29 April 2025**

The case concerns two applicants, Zoran Lubarda and Slađan Milanov, who were convicted in separate minor-offence proceedings in Serbia for road-traffic offences. Lubarda was convicted in 2017 of failing to comply with a traffic-light signal. Milanov was convicted in 2015 of driving while in a state of complete intoxication. Lubarda was fined €120, banned from driving for three months, and had penalty points added to his licence. Milanov was fined €850, banned from driving for eight months, and also received penalty points. Although the proceedings were classified as minor-offence proceedings, both offences were potentially punishable by imprisonment. Under the Minor Offences Act, if the fines were not paid, they could be converted into effective prison sentences of up to 15 days for Lubarda and up to 60 days for Milanov.

The alleged violation arose from the manner in which the convictions were established. At the scene, both applicants signed reports drawn up by police officers, but they later disputed the contents of those reports in court. Their convictions were based on those police reports and on evidence given by the police officers. The officers’ evidence was taken in court, but not during the main hearings in the applicants’ cases. Neither the applicants nor their lawyers were summoned to the examination of those witnesses, even though they had explicitly requested to be present and to cross-examine them.

In Lubarda’s case, the request to cross-examine was refused on the grounds of efficiency and economy of proceedings. In Milanov’s case, the court held that cross-examination would not have led to a different determination of facts because the officer’s evidence was consistent with the report Milanov had signed. Both applicants appealed, but their convictions were upheld by the Appeals Court and subsequently by the Constitutional Court. The final domestic decisions were notified to Lubarda on 1 August 2018 and to Milanov on 26 February 2019. They lodged applications with the European Court of Human Rights on 22 January 2019 and 2 August 2019, respectively.

Before the European Court, the applicants complained under Article 6 of the Convention that the minor-offence proceedings against them had been unfair. Specifically, they argued that they had not been given an opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses on whose statements their convictions had been based. The Court gave notice of the applications to the Serbian Government, received the parties’ observations, and rejected the Government’s objection to examination by a Committee. The Court deliberated on 25 March 2025 and delivered judgment on 29 April 2025.

The key facts relevant to the alleged Article 6 violation are therefore that the convictions rested substantially on police reports and police witness evidence; the applicants disputed that evidence; they expressly requested to cross-examine the officers; neither they nor their lawyers were summoned; and the domestic courts refused or dismissed those requests for reasons of procedural economy or because the evidence was considered consistent with the signed reports. Because the unpaid fines could be converted into imprisonment, the proceedings carried a sufficiently serious potential penalty to engage the criminal fair-trial guarantees under Article 6. The case thus concerns whether reliance on untested witness evidence, without any opportunity for cross-examination, rendered the minor-offence proceedings unfair.

In *Pápics and Others v. Hungary* (Applications nos. 13727/20 and 15 others), the European Court of Human Rights’ Second Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 4 March 2025. The case concerns 16 Hungarian nationals who were sentenced by final judgments of Hungarian courts to life imprisonment without the possibility of release on parole. Their convictions, handed down between 2007 and 2023, concerned serious offences including aggravated murder, murder, robbery, abuse of firearms, incitement to murder and other crimes. Several applicants were sentenced as recidivists or multiple recidivists.

The applicants lodged their applications with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention between March 2020 and August 2022. Most were represented by Evelyn Frank; Róbert Magyar was represented by Csilla Csugányné Lakatos. The Hungarian Government was represented by its Agent, Z. Tallódi. Judge P. Paczolay, the judge elected in respect of Hungary, withdrew from sitting in the case.

The central alleged violation is Article 3 ECHR, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. The applicants complain not simply about their convictions but about the nature and effect of the sentences imposed on them. Under the Hungarian regime, they are serving life imprisonment without any possibility of release on parole. Release may only be considered through mandatory pardon proceedings, and those proceedings cannot take place until the applicant has served forty years of the life sentence. The applicants argue that this combination—a whole-life sentence with no parole and only a distant, mandatory pardon process after forty years—amounts to inhuman and degrading punishment contrary to Article 3.

The appended table sets out the individual facts relevant to the complaint. The applicants’ birth years range from 1966 to 1990. They reside in various Hungarian cities, including Szeged, Budapest, Tiszalök and Szekszárd. The impugned final judgments include: Ferenc Pápics (aggravated murder, 2009); József Ottlakán (murder, robbery and other crimes as a recidivist, 2023); Zoltán Sipőcz (aggravated murder, 2009); János Navratil (murder and robbery as a multiple recidivist, 2014); József Áldott (aggravated murder and abuse of firearms, 2007); Róbert Magyar (incitement to murder and other crimes, 2012); Tibor János Mészáros (murder, robbery and other crimes, 2015); Lajos Tétényi (murder as a multiple recidivist, 2019); Zoltán Maczák (aggravated murder, 2015); Krisztián Kovács (murder and other crimes as a multiple recidivist, 2018); Attila Rézműves (aggravated murder, 2016, upheld on appeal); Mihály Balog (robbery and other crimes as a multiple recidivist, 2020); János Dániel Nagy (murder as a multiple recidivist, 2017); István Szűcs (multiple aggravated murders, 2011); József Sándor (aggravated multiple murder as a recidivist, 2017); and Gábor Horváth (aggravated murder, robbery and causing bodily harm as a multiple recidivist, 2022).

The Court gave notice of the Article 3 complaint in application no. 49294/20 and of all remaining applications to the Hungarian Government and declared the remainder of application no. 49249/20 inadmissible. The case therefore focuses on whether Hungary’s whole-life sentence regime, with mandatory pardon only after forty years, violates Article 3 of the Convention.

**Vervele v. Greece** (Application no. 34012/20, Third Section, judgment 26 August 2025) concerns the alleged excessive length of civil proceedings in Greece and the effectiveness of the domestic remedy for that delay. The applicant, Ms Nikoletta Vervele, a Greek national born in 1945, worked as a cleaner at Ippokrateio General Hospital of Athens from 1984. On 22 June 2001 she brought a civil action against the hospital, claiming EUR 75,739.72 in salary supplements and allowances allegedly owed for the period 1 June 1994 to 31 December 2000 under an indefinite employment contract.

A prior related action was already pending. On 23 June 1994, the applicant had sued the same hospital for salary supplements and allowances for 1 January 1986 to 31 May 1994. In judgment no. 882/2000, the Athens Court of First Instance partly allowed that claim and awarded her EUR 15,298. The hospital appealed, and the appeal was heard on 15 January 2002. In the meantime, in the 2001 action, the Athens Court of First Instance by decision no. 871/2002 of 15 April 2002 adjourned the case under Article 249 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It considered it necessary to wait for a final judgment in the earlier action in order to avoid conflicting judgments. That earlier action was only concluded on 24 February 2011, when the Athens Court of Appeal delivered judgment no. 826/2011 dismissing the hospital’s appeal and confirming the first-instance award.

The applicant made repeated requests for a hearing in the 2001 action—on 5 April 2004, 7 June 2007, 19 May 2009 and 23 August 2010. The action was eventually heard on 24 May 2012. On 7 June 2012, by decision no. 1091/2012, the Athens Court of First Instance adjourned again because decision no. 871/2002 and the hospital’s observations were missing from the case file. On 14 December 2012 the applicant requested a new hearing date. The next hearing took place on 18 February 2015. By judgment no. 942/2015, delivered on 20 April 2015, the first-instance court partly upheld her action. It ordered the hospital to pay EUR 21,250.66 plus statutory interest for 1999–2000, but found that claims concerning 1994–1998 had become time-barred under the two-year limitation period in Article 48 § 3 of Legislative Decree no. 496/1974.

The applicant appealed on 18 May 2015. The appeal was presented on 25 September 2015, and a hearing was scheduled for 19 April 2016, but it was adjourned because of a lawyers’ strike and rescheduled for 5 December 2017. By decision no. 5366/2018, delivered on 1 November 2018 and finalised at the applicant’s expense on 6 December 2018, the Athens Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance judgment and partly upheld the action, ordering the hospital to pay EUR 55,757 plus statutory interest.

The applicant then lodged an appeal on points of law on 28 November 2018, presented it on 14 December 2018, and the case was heard on 21 May 2019. By judgment no. 246/2020, delivered on 27 February 2020, the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal. The judgment became final on 10 March 2020, and an official copy became available on 9 April 2020.

The civil proceedings therefore lasted from 22 June 2001 until final cassation in 2020—approximately 18 years and 8 months. The key alleged violations were: (i) unreasonable length of proceedings under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, given the prolonged adjournment pending the earlier action, repeated delays in fixing hearings, further adjournments, the lawyers’ strike, and delays at appeal and cassation; and (ii) lack of an effective domestic remedy under Article 13, notwithstanding Greece’s Law no. 4239/2014 on just satisfaction for excessive length. The applicant lodged her application with the European Court of Human Rights on 3 August 2020. The Court gave notice only of the Article 6 § 1 length complaint and the Article 13 complaint; the remainder was declared inadmissible.

text:
In *Lubarda and Milanov v. Serbia* (Applications nos. 6570/19 and 43604/19), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered judgment on 29 April 2025. The case concerned two applicants’ complaints under Article 6 of the Convention that they had not been given an opportunity to cross-examine witnesses in minor-offence proceedings against them for road-traffic offences in Serbia.

The first applicant, Zoran Lubarda, was convicted in 2017 of failing to comply with a traffic light signal. He was fined €120, banned from driving for three months, and given penalty points. The second applicant, Slađan Milanov, was convicted in 2015 of driving while intoxicated (“in a state of complete intoxication”). He was fined €850, banned from driving for eight months, and given penalty points. Although these were minor-offence proceedings, both offences were potentially punishable by imprisonment. Under the Minor Offences Act, if the fines were not paid, they could be converted into effective prison sentences of up to 15 days for Lubarda and up to 60 days for Milanov.

At the scene of the incidents, both applicants signed reports drawn up by police officers. They later disputed the contents of those reports in court. Their convictions were based on those reports and on evidence given by the police officers. According to the applicants, the police officers’ evidence was taken in court but not during the main hearings in their cases. Neither the applicants nor their lawyers were summoned to the examination of those witnesses, even though they had explicitly requested to be present and to cross-examine them.

The domestic courts refused those requests. In Lubarda’s case, the request was refused on the grounds of efficiency and economy of proceedings. In Milanov’s case, the court held that cross-examination would not have led to a different determination of facts because the police officer’s evidence was consistent with the report Milanov had signed.

Both applicants appealed against their convictions, but the convictions were upheld by the Appeals Court and subsequently by the Constitutional Court. The final domestic decisions were notified to the applicants on 1 August 2018 in Lubarda’s case and 26 February 2019 in Milanov’s case. They lodged applications with the European Court of Human Rights on 22 January 2019 and 2 August 2019, respectively.

Before the Strasbourg Court, the applicants relied on Article 6 of the Convention, complaining that the minor-offence proceedings against them had not been fair because they had not been given the opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses on whose statements their convictions had been based. The case therefore raised the question whether reliance on police reports and police witness evidence that the defence could not test, combined with the refusal of the applicants’ explicit requests to cross-examine those witnesses, was compatible with the fair-trial guarantees of Article 6. The Court gave notice of the applications to the Serbian Government and rejected the Government’s objection to examination of the applications by a Committee.

In **Marzouki and Others v. Bulgaria** (Application no. 48636/19), judgment of 27 February 2025, the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints brought by three applicants: Mohamed Nabil Marzouki, a Tunisian national born in 1981; Mariam Mohamed Nabil Marzouki, his daughter, born in 2010 and a Bulgarian national; and Yana Dimitrova Yankova, the child’s mother, born in 1976 and also Bulgarian. The first applicant had permanent residence in Bulgaria. The case concerns his removal from Bulgaria and his separation from the second and third applicants, allegedly disrupting their family life.

In early 2018, the first applicant travelled to Serbia. On 1 February 2018, when he returned, Bulgarian border authorities refused him entry and gave him a standard refusal form. Two grounds were checked: that an alert had been issued for the purpose of refusing entry, and that he was considered a threat to public order, internal security, public health or international relations.

Through a legal representative, the first applicant sought judicial review of the refusal. In those proceedings, the border police explained that they had acted on a decision of the State Agency for National Security (SANS) dated 1 February 2018. That SANS decision imposed a five-year entry ban on the ground that the applicant posed a national security threat. The Sofia Region Administrative Court upheld the refusal of entry on 29 October 2018, finding that the border police had been bound to act after the SANS decision.

The SANS decision was served on the applicant’s representative only on 31 July 2018, after the representative requested a copy upon learning of it during the refusal proceedings. The decision contained no specific reasoning to justify the conclusion that the applicant threatened national security. Instead, it referred to a classified document called a “Proposal.” That Proposal was later declassified and submitted by the Government in the Strasbourg proceedings.

After receiving a copy of the SANS decision, the representative applied for judicial review of it. However, the Supreme Administrative Court declared the application time-barred in a final decision of 6 March 2019. It held that the fourteen-day time-limit had started to run on 1 February 2018, when the applicant had allegedly been “orally informed” of the decision. That finding apparently referred to the standard refusal form given to him at the border. According to the Supreme Administrative Court, the applicant had been validly informed of the SANS decision in that manner under Article 61 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Procedure, as worded at the time, which allowed oral notification of administrative decisions to interested parties.

Before the European Court, the applicants complained that the first applicant’s removal from Bulgaria was unjustified and had disrupted their family life together. They further complained under Article 13, read in conjunction with Article 8, that there were no effective domestic remedies for those alleged violations. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations therefore include the first applicant’s permanent residence and family ties in Bulgaria, the five-year entry ban based on an unreasoned national-security decision, the reliance on classified material, the delayed service of the SANS decision, and the domestic courts’ treatment of the judicial-review application as time-barred because of the alleged oral notification at the border. These facts are central to the alleged breaches of Article 8 and Article 13.

**Case: Vervele v. Greece (Application no. 34012/20), ECtHR Third Section, judgment 26 August 2025 (final 26 November 2025).**

The applicant, Ms Nikoletta Vervele, a Greek national born in 1945 living in Athens, worked as a cleaner at Ippokrateio General Hospital of Athens from 1984. Her complaints before the European Court concerned the excessive length of civil proceedings she brought for unpaid salary supplements and allowances, and the effectiveness of the domestic remedy for obtaining just satisfaction for that delay. The Court gave notice of her complaints under Article 6 § 1 (length of proceedings) and Article 13 (effective remedy); the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The underlying dispute began on 22 June 2001, when the applicant sued the hospital for EUR 75,739.72 in salary supplements and allowances allegedly owed from 1 June 1994 to 31 December 2000. A prior action concerning the period 1986–1994 had been partly successful in 2000, but an appeal was pending. In 2002, the Athens Court of First Instance adjourned the 2001 action under Article 249 of the Code of Civil Procedure, considering it necessary to wait for a final judgment in the earlier case to avoid conflicting judgments. That earlier case was only concluded by the Athens Court of Appeal on 24 February 2011.

The applicant repeatedly sought hearing dates—on 5 April 2004, 7 June 2007, 19 May 2009 and 23 August 2010—but her action was not heard until 24 May 2012. On 7 June 2012, the first-instance court adjourned again because decision no. 871/2002 and the hospital’s observations were missing from the file. After a further request on 14 December 2012, a new hearing took place on 18 February 2015. By judgment of 20 April 2015, the court partly upheld the claim, awarding EUR 21,250.66 plus interest for 1999–2000, but found that the 1994–1998 claim was time-barred under the two-year limitation period in Legislative Decree no. 496/1974.

The applicant appealed on 18 May 2015. The appeal was scheduled for 19 April 2016 but was adjourned due to a lawyers’ strike and eventually heard on 5 December 2017. On 1 November 2018, the Athens Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance judgment and awarded EUR 55,757 plus statutory interest; the judgment was finalised on 6 December 2018. The applicant then appealed on points of law on 28 November 2018. The Court of Cassation heard the case on 21 May 2019 and dismissed the appeal by judgment of 27 February 2020. That judgment became final on 10 March 2020, and an official copy was made available on 9 April 2020.

Overall, the proceedings lasted roughly 18 years and 9 months from the initial action to the final cassation judgment. Key delay factors included the long adjournment pending the earlier case, repeated postponements in setting hearings, a further adjournment due to missing documents, and a lawyers’ strike. The delay also had substantive consequences, because part of the applicant’s claim was held to be time-barred.

The case also concerned Law no. 4239/2014, Greece’s compensatory remedy for excessive length of proceedings. The Court had previously found in Xynos v. Greece that this remedy was effective for Article 35 § 1 and Article 13 purposes, though it lacked preventive effect. The Government submitted domestic case-law showing that claims under that law sometimes led to awards ranging from EUR 500 to EUR 5,000, but many claims were dismissed or only partially allowed. CEPEJ and EU Justice Scoreboard data showed Greece remained among the slower Council of Europe states in civil and commercial cases, with high disposition times. The Court was thus called upon to assess whether the length of the applicant’s proceedings was reasonable and whether the domestic remedy was effective in her circumstances.

In *Radchenko v. Ukraine* (Application no. 21217/17), the applicant, a Ukrainian national, complained under Articles 10 and 13 of the Convention about the prolonged non-enforcement of a domestic court judgment ordering the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources of Ukraine (“the Ministry”) to provide him with public environmental information. The application was lodged on 10 March 2017.

The facts arose from environmental incidents in the Kyiv Region in June 2015: large fires at a petroleum storage depot and a plastic goods warehouse on 8 and 12 June, and peat burning from 9 June. On 17 June 2015, the applicant requested information from the Ministry under the Law on Access to Public Information and the Law on Protection of Environment. He sought: (i) air pollution levels by district and dangerous gases; (ii) measures being taken to combat pollution and improve air quality; (iii) measures taken by the Ministry itself to combat technogenic catastrophes; and (iv) the names and addresses of the entities owning the depot and warehouse, their responsibility for the incidents, and how they were compensating damage.

The Ministry, through the State Ecological Inspectorate, replied in June 2015. According to later judgments, it said inspections of legal entities were generally banned, that a special request had been made to inspect the P. company (apparently the depot owner), and that soil and water tests and crisis monitoring had been ordered. The applicant considered the reply non-responsive and sued.

On 17 September 2015, the Kyiv Circuit Administrative Court granted his claim. It found the Ministry’s reply contained none of the requested information, gave no explanation why the information could not be provided, and confirmed that the requested environmental information was public and had to be supplied within 48 hours. The court ordered a full reply within that time.

On 26 October 2015, the Ministry sent another reply with links to online data and a plan concerning the petroleum depot fire, but the applicant still found it incomplete. In November 2015, the administrative court acknowledged the Ministry’s omissions. It found the reply did not fully answer the request and identified systemic deficiencies: air quality measurements were scattered and irregular, and ecological information was not systematically gathered or properly published, causing a systemic violation of citizens’ right to environmental information, partly due to inconsistent legislation. The court also found the Ministry did not possess the requested information and that the problem could not be resolved by enforcing an individual judgment. It issued a separate ruling to several State authorities.

The applicant then pursued enforcement proceedings. The Ministry sent further replies, including a 21 September 2018 letter stating that a governmental commission had conducted testing, that air pollution information had been disseminated daily via media, that measures had been taken, and that no excess pollution had been established, but also that the Ministry lacked part of the requested air pollution information. Enforcement proceedings were repeatedly terminated and reopened. Courts generally held that the Ministry could not be exempted from full enforcement because the judgment was clear and contained no exceptions. In October 2019, enforcement was definitively terminated as impossible “without the debtor’s participation.” A bailiff’s complaint to police about wilful non-enforcement led to no criminal proceedings for lack of elements of an offence, and the applicant’s challenges failed.

In October 2016, the Ombudsman advised that the Ministry did not possess comparative air pollution information and that only “existing” information was public; nothing could be done, though the Cabinet was asked to ensure compliance with environmental information duties.

The applicant thus alleged that Ukraine violated Article 10 by failing to enforce the judgment granting access to public information, and Article 13 by providing no effective remedy for that non-enforcement.

**Vervele v. Greece** (Application no. 34012/20) is a European Court of Human Rights case concerning the length of civil proceedings and the effectiveness of the domestic remedy for excessive length. The applicant, Nikoletta Vervele, a Greek national born in 1945, worked as a cleaner at Ippokrateio General Hospital of Athens from 1984.

On 22 June 2001, she brought an action against the hospital claiming EUR 75,739.72 in unpaid salary supplements and allowances for the period 1 June 1994 to 31 December 2000 under an indefinite employment contract. A related earlier action, lodged on 23 June 1994 concerning 1986 to May 1994, had been partly allowed in 2000, awarding her EUR 15,298; the hospital appealed.

In April 2002, the Athens Court of First Instance adjourned the 2001 action pending final judgment in the earlier related case, seeking to avoid conflicting judgments. That earlier case was only finally concluded on 24 February 2011, when the Athens Court of Appeal dismissed the hospital’s appeal. Meanwhile, the applicant repeatedly requested hearing dates in 2004, 2007, 2009 and 2010. Her 2001 action was eventually heard on 24 May 2012. It was then adjourned again on 7 June 2012 because certain documents were missing from the file. After another request in December 2012, the hearing took place on 18 February 2015.

By judgment no. 942/2015, delivered on 20 April 2015, the Athens Court of First Instance partly upheld her claim. It ordered the hospital to pay EUR 21,250.66 plus statutory interest for 1999–2000, but found that her claims for 1994–1998 were time-barred under the two-year limitation period in Legislative Decree no. 496/1974.

The applicant appealed on 18 May 2015. A hearing was scheduled for 19 April 2016 but was adjourned because of a lawyers’ strike and rescheduled for 5 December 2017. By decision no. 5366/2018, delivered on 1 November 2018, the Athens Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance judgment and partly upheld the action, ordering the hospital to pay EUR 55,757 plus interest. The applicant then appealed on points of law on 28 November 2018. The Court of Cassation heard the case on 21 May 2019 and, by judgment no. 246/2020, delivered on 27 February 2020, dismissed the appeal. The judgment became final on 10 March 2020, and an official copy was made available on 9 April 2020.

The civil proceedings therefore lasted from 22 June 2001 until at least 27 February 2020—nearly 19 years—with significant delays and adjournments, including a long suspension pending the related case and a lawyers’ strike.

The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the excessive length of the proceedings and under Article 13 about the lack of an effective domestic remedy for excessive length. The Court gave notice of those complaints and declared the remainder inadmissible.

Relevant to the Article 13 complaint, Greece had enacted Law no. 4239/2014, in force from 20 February 2014, allowing claims for just satisfaction for unjustifiably long civil, criminal and Court of Auditors proceedings. Claims must be lodged separately at each level within six months of the final decision, signed by a lawyer, and accompanied by a fee, though legal aid may be available. The competent judge considers party conduct, complexity, authorities’ conduct and what was at stake. In *Xynos v. Greece* (2014), the Court found this compensatory remedy effective for Articles 35 § 1 and 13, while regretting the absence of a preventive remedy. Pilot judgments such as *Glykantzi v. Greece* had earlier identified excessive length as a structural problem.

The key issues were whether the almost 19-year duration violated Article 6 § 1 and whether Law no. 4239/2014 provided an effective remedy under Article 13 in the circumstances.

B.A. v. Iceland (Application no. 17006/20) concerns the alleged failure of Icelandic authorities to conduct an effective investigation into complaints of domestic violence and sexual assault, and alleged gender-based discrimination in handling such cases. The applicant complained under Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention, alone and in conjunction with Article 14.

The applicant, an Icelandic national born in 1975 living in Reykjavík, lodged a police complaint in December 2017 against her former cohabitant, F.Þ., alleging physical, psychological and sexual violence during their relationship between 2011 and 2014. She claimed that F.Þ. repeatedly humiliated and criticised her, isolated her from her family and controlled her life. The psychological abuse allegedly intensified during her pregnancy and escalated into physical and sexual violence.

She described four alleged incidents of sexual violence: during her pregnancy while hospitalised, F.Þ. allegedly coerced her into sexually stimulating him; he raped her during a visit to a rehabilitation clinic where she was staying; he raped her in the hallway of their home; and he raped her while she was sleeping, causing bruising. She also alleged two instances of physical violence: a brief chokehold and a headbutt.

During the police investigation, the applicant was assisted by a legal representative. She stated she had never sought immediate medical attention after the incidents. F.Þ. was first questioned on 19 September 2018. He denied all wrongdoing and denied physical, psychological or sexual violence. He attributed relationship difficulties to the applicant’s excessive alcohol consumption. He admitted sexual intercourse at the rehabilitation clinic but denied rape. He denied psychological violence but admitted controlling behaviour when urging her to stop drinking or refrain from working under the influence.

Eleven witnesses were questioned. Several observed changes in the applicant after cohabitation began, including reduced contact and communication. Some described humiliation or anger by F.Þ., though not directed at the applicant. One witness heard the applicant scream and found her trembling and scared after an incident involving F.Þ., which the applicant described as a chokehold. There were no direct witnesses to the alleged physical or sexual violence; most accounts were based on disclosures made after the relationship ended.

The case file included a Stígamót certificate from December 2017 stating the applicant had attended since April 2015 and reported severe mental, physical and sexual violence by F.Þ. It also contained psychiatric records from 2012 and 2017 noting depression and anxiety, and a psychologist’s statement from February 2019 diagnosing post-traumatic stress disorder following an alleged sexual offence.

On 11 June 2019, police discontinued the investigation. Regarding sexual violence, given F.Þ.’s denial and the evidence, there was insufficient support and further investigation was unlikely to improve the evidentiary position. Regarding physical violence, Article 218b of the General Penal Code was not enacted until 2016, so the conduct could only be considered under Article 217; the statute of limitations had expired.

On 25 September 2019, the State Prosecutor upheld the decision. It found Article 218b could not apply retroactively. Physical violence before 2016 was punishable under Article 217 with a two-year limitation period, which had expired. For sexual violence, the evidence, including witness testimony and expert documentation of distress, did not sufficiently support the applicant’s testimony to overcome F.Þ.’s denial and was not “sufficient or likely” to secure a conviction. Further investigation would not change the evidentiary position. Later, when asked whether the conduct could constitute gross defamation under Article 233b, the State Prosecutor replied that its review had not been confined to the police’s classification.

The applicant alleges an ineffective investigation into domestic violence and sexual assault and gender-based discrimination, relying on Articles 3, 8 and 14.

In *Panopoulou and Others v. Greece* (Application no. 28983/20), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered judgment on 23 October 2025. The case originated in an application against Greece lodged on 6 July 2020 by 13 applicants under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants were represented by Mr A. Papakonstantinou, a lawyer practising in Athens. Their details are set out in an appended table, listing 13 applicants with birth years ranging from 1935 to 1991 and including members of the Panopoulou and Antypas families.

The applicants complained of the non-enforcement of a domestic judgment and of the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law in that regard. The relevant domestic judgment was delivered by the Athens Administrative Court of First Instance, Judgment no. 14300/2005, and became final on 30 November 2005. According to the appended table, the non-enforcement period began on 22 August 2006. As of the proceedings, enforcement remained pending: the end date of non-enforcement is recorded as “pending.” The total length of non-enforcement is stated as more than 18 years, 5 months, and 21 days.

The key factual basis of the alleged violation is therefore that the applicants obtained a final and binding domestic judgment against the Greek State, but that judgment was not executed. The judgment apparently imposed obligations on the State, although the provided extract does not describe the subject matter of the judgment or the specific relief granted. What is clear is that the applicants were unable to secure enforcement of the final judgment for over 18 years. They further alleged that Greek law did not provide them with any effective domestic remedy to challenge or compel that non-enforcement.
