In *B.A. v. Iceland* (Application no. 17006/20, judgment 26 August 2025), the applicant, an Icelandic national born in 1975, complained under Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention, both alone and in conjunction with Article 14, that the Icelandic authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into her allegations of domestic violence and sexual assault and discriminated against her on gender grounds in handling such cases.

In December 2017, B.A. lodged a police complaint against her former cohabitant, F.Þ., alleging physical, psychological, and sexual violence during their relationship between 2011 and 2014. She claimed F.Þ. humiliated and criticised her, isolated her from family, and controlled her life. The abuse allegedly intensified during her pregnancy and escalated into physical and sexual violence. She described four sexual-violence incidents: being coerced into sexually stimulating F.Þ. while hospitalised during pregnancy; being raped at a rehabilitation clinic; being raped in the hallway of their home; and being raped while sleeping, which left bruising. She also alleged two physical incidents—a brief chokehold and a headbutt. She stated she never sought immediate medical attention after any incident.

During the police investigation, F.Þ. was questioned in September 2018. He denied all wrongdoing and attributed relationship difficulties to the applicant’s excessive alcohol consumption. He admitted sexual intercourse at the rehabilitation clinic but denied rape. While denying psychological violence, he admitted controlling behaviour when urging her to stop drinking or avoid work while intoxicated. Eleven witnesses were questioned. Several observed changes in the applicant after cohabitation began, including reduced contact with others. Some described F.Þ. humiliating her or displaying anger. One witness heard the applicant scream and found her trembling and scared after an alleged chokehold. No one directly witnessed the physical or sexual violence; most accounts were based on disclosures after the relationship ended. The file contained a Stígamót certificate from December 2017 stating she had attended since April 2015 and reported severe mental, physical, and sexual violence by F.Þ.; psychiatric records from 2012 and 2017 documenting depression and anxiety; and a psychologist’s February 2019 statement diagnosing PTSD following an alleged sexual offence.

In June 2019, police discontinued the investigation. As to sexual violence, they found insufficient evidence given F.Þ.’s denial and concluded further investigation would not improve the evidentiary position. As to physical violence, Article 218b of the General Penal Code—the domestic-violence provision—had not been enacted until 2016, so the conduct could only be considered under Article 217; the two-year limitation period had expired. In September 2019, the State Prosecutor upheld this decision, finding Article 218b could not apply retroactively, the Article 217 offence was time-barred, and the sexual-violence evidence—including witness testimony and expert documentation of distress—was not sufficiently strong to overcome F.Þ.’s denial or likely to secure a conviction. Further investigative measures were deemed unlikely to change the position. The applicant’s lawyer later raised whether the conduct could constitute gross defamation of a closely related person under Article 233b; the State Prosecutor replied that its review had not been limited to the police’s classification.

The alleged violations therefore centred on the authorities’ alleged failure to effectively investigate domestic violence and sexual assault and on gender-based discrimination in the handling of such cases, contrary to Articles 3, 8, and 14.

**Case: Zafferani and Others v. San Marino**  
**ECtHR, Fifth Section, judgment of 9 January 2025; final 9 April 2025**  
Applications nos. 38127/22 and six others, lodged on 1 August 2022 by seven San Marino nationals. The Court gave notice of complaints under **Article 6 § 1** and **Article 1 of Protocol No. 1**; the remainder were inadmissible.

Between 2006 and 2008, the applicants were temporarily employed as officers in the Uniformed Unit of the Fortress Guard, a San Marino military body. They claimed that under Law no. 132/1987, as amended by Law no. 99/1997, their enrolment should have become permanent after a successful one-year probationary period, and that the same laws governed career advancement. Their employment was repeatedly extended until **18 January 2016**, when Parliament acknowledged their permanent recruitment under **Article 63(1) of Law no. 189/2015**, assigning them “Scale 5.”

Between **28 January and 2 February 2016**, the applicants asked the Public Administration Personnel Management Office (“PAPMO”) to reconstruct their careers, affecting salary and entitlements. The acknowledgments of receipt indicated that the deadline for concluding proceedings began then and that remedies lay before the administrative courts. No immediate reply followed.

On **25 July 2016**, while those requests/proceedings were pending, **Delegated Decree no. 88/2016** entered into force. Its Article 1 provided that, for persons recruited under Article 63 of Law no. 189/2015, economic benefits from retrospective career adjustment would run only from **1 February 2016**, without arrears and without payment of statutory withholding taxes on the unpaid sums. PAPMO then reconstructed the applicants’ careers under that decree. Each applicant allegedly lost around **EUR 25,000 or more**.

In 2018, the applicants asked the Minister of Foreign and Political Affairs and the Director General of Civil Service to intervene so they could obtain arrears under ordinary rules. On **7 November 2018**, officials confirmed that the PAPMO calculation complied with Law no. 88/2016 and noted that the applicants had not been employed under the ordinary procedure in Law no. 132/1987 as amended.

On **20 March 2019**, the applicants applied to the Judge of First Instance (“CoL”) in administrative jurisdiction, seeking annulment of the 7 November 2018 decision. They argued that the career reconstruction under Law no. 88/2016 was unlawful and that the law was unconstitutional, violating Articles 4 (equality) and 9 (equitable remuneration) of the Declaration of Citizens’ Rights. They requested a referral to the Constitutional Court. On **9 December 2019**, the CoL refused the referral as manifestly ill-founded, finding it legitimate to apply different conditions to persons recruited through extraordinary procedures.

The applicants then sought the CoL’s abstention, alleging prejudgment. On **17 July 2020**, the Judge for Extraordinary Remedies dismissed that challenge. However, in an obiter observation, the JER noted that the impugned provision should be examined in light of Convention principles and that the applicants had suffered a **legislative interference in pending proceedings** begun in January/February 2016, before the July 2016 decree.

On **4 November 2020**, the CoL dismissed the claim, holding that Law no. 88/2016 clarified Article 63(1) of Law no. 189/2015, was a lex specialis, and prevailed over ordinary rules. It also found that the applicants, recruited without a public competition, were differently situated from publicly selected officers. On appeal, the applicants reiterated constitutional complaints and added **Article 6 § 1** and **Article 1 of Protocol No. 1**, but later withdrew the constitutional request. On **30 March 2022**, the Judge of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment and ordered costs.

The key alleged violations are therefore that the 2016 legislative decree retroactively changed the legal basis of the applicants’ pending career-reconstruction claims, interfering with fair proceedings under **Article 6 § 1**, and deprived them of salary arrears/economic entitlements amounting to possessions under **Article 1 of Protocol No. 1**.

In *Jóhannes Baldursson and Birkir Kristinsson v. Iceland*, the applicants were Icelandic nationals convicted of financial crimes following the 2008 financial crisis. The first applicant was an executive at Glitnir bank; the second was an employee in Glitnir’s Private Banking department and owner of BK-44 ehf. After Glitnir’s collapse, Iceland’s Special Prosecutor investigated a 2007 loan by Glitnir to BK-44 to purchase 150 million Glitnir shares then owned by Glitnir itself.

The second applicant was interviewed three times. On 1 December 2011 he was questioned as a suspect with counsel. On 21 December 2011 he was questioned as a witness without counsel, warned of his duty to testify truthfully and of his privilege against self-incrimination. On 18 June 2012 he was again questioned as a suspect with counsel. He argued that no important new evidence justified changing him back from witness to suspect, and that the only new material consisted of recorded phone calls with co-accused E.S. The District Court and Supreme Court rejected his request to dismiss the case, though the Supreme Court excluded his second interview from evidence. This underpins his alleged violation concerning unlawful reopening of proceedings and *ne bis in idem*.

In June 2013, both applicants and two co-accused were indicted. The charges included fraud by abuse of position for granting a large loan to BK-44 without committee approval or sufficient security; fraud concerning a verbal put option that shifted the entire market risk of Glitnir shares back to Glitnir; and market manipulation. The second applicant was also charged with aiding and abetting, concealment, money laundering and accounting violations. The District Court convicted all accused; the applicants received five-year sentences. The Supreme Court upheld the convictions but reduced the first applicant’s sentence to three years and the second’s to four years, while narrowing the first applicant’s market-manipulation conviction.

The key facts relevant to the alleged impartiality violation concern the Supreme Court panel that decided the case: Justices M.S., G.B., H.I.J., Ó.B.Þ. and Þ.Ö. In December 2016, media disclosures revealed financial interests of Supreme Court justices. Justice M.S. had inherited Glitnir shares, sold them in 2003 and 2007, and from January 2007 had an asset-management contract with Glitnir. In early 2008 he placed ISK 61,450,000 in asset management, partly in equity funds and savings, and lost ISK 7,607,000 by the end of 2008. Justice Ó.B.Þ. acquired Glitnir shares in July 2007 by inheritance and sold them in December 2007 for ISK 11,532,528. Justice G.B. had owned shares in Kaupþing and Landsbanki, but not Glitnir. The Committee on Judicial Functions initially considered equity-fund assets not reportable; some shareholdings were reported retroactively.

The applicants requested information on these interests and argued that the justices’ links to Glitnir and other banks raised justifiable doubts about the Supreme Court’s impartiality under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. Domestic law required disqualification where circumstances could justifiably raise questions about impartiality, and judges were obliged to report certain shareholdings. The alleged violations therefore centre on the second applicant’s claim of unlawful reopening/*ne bis in idem* and both applicants’ complaint of lack of impartiality of the Supreme Court.

Chonin and Others v. Bulgaria (Application no. 30116/23) is a European Court of Human Rights case brought by ten Bulgarian nationals, two of whom also hold Belgian and German nationality. The applicants lodged their application on 20 July 2023. The Third Section Committee gave notice to the Bulgarian Government only of the complaints concerning the lengthy duration of a restitution procedure under the Restitution of Title to Forests and Forestry Land Act (“the Forests Restitution Act”); the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. Belgium and Germany did not intervene.

The applicants are heirs of Ms F., together inheriting approximately four-fifths of her estate. Ms F. had owned an afforested island in the Danube and mainland forests, all of which were nationalised in 1948. After the Forests Restitution Act was adopted in 1997, the applicants initiated restitution proceedings. The earlier stages of those proceedings were described in Popov and Chonin v. Bulgaria (no. 36094/08, 17 February 2015), brought by one of the current applicants.

On 12 December 2000, the competent land commission, later renamed the Agriculture Department, recognised the heirs’ right to compensation in lieu of restitution for 93.38 hectares of forestry land. Restitution in kind was impossible because Ms F.’s former land lay in a frontier zone and was classified as exclusive State property. Under the Forests Restitution Act, compensation could only be provided through equivalent State-owned land. The authorities therefore spent years trying to identify suitable substitute plots. In 2007, a court judgment identified one such plot and ordered its transfer to the applicants, but the judgment was ultimately unenforceable because the land formed part of a national park.

After the Popov and Chonin judgment, further developments occurred. In a series of decisions issued in 2013 and 2018, the Agriculture Departments in Montana and Berkovitsa allocated forestry land totalling about 59 hectares to the applicants. These decisions were served on Mr Chonin, acting as representative of all the applicants, in 2018. He challenged the decisions, arguing that the quality of the allocated forests was inferior to that of Ms F.’s original forests. The decisions were nevertheless upheld by final court judgments given in 2023 and 2024.

An additional plot of about 5.3 hectares has been identified, but the process of officially allocating it to the applicants remains ongoing. The competent authorities are still working to locate further plots to compensate the applicants for the remaining approximately 29 hectares of forestry land. Thus, of the original compensation entitlement of about 93.38 hectares, roughly 59 hectares have been allocated, about 5.3 hectares are identified but not yet allocated, and about 29 hectares remain unresolved.

The key alleged violation before the Court is the excessive length of the restitution proceedings, essentially the reasonable-time guarantee in civil proceedings. The process began after the 1997 Act and the 2000 compensation decision, yet by the time of the 2025 judgment full equivalent land compensation had still not been completed. Although some land was allocated in 2013 and 2018, significant portions remained outstanding, and the dispute over the quality of the substituted forests was finalised only in 2023 and 2024. The facts relevant to the alleged violation therefore concern the prolonged administrative and judicial efforts to identify and transfer substitute State-owned forestry land, the 2007 unenforceable judgment, the partial allocations, the applicants’ challenge to the inferior quality of the substituted forests, and the continuing failure to complete compensation for the full area recognised in 2000. The Court’s review was limited to the length complaint; the other complaints were declared inadmissible.

The case concerns Georgios Papadopoulos, a Cypriot national, and the repeated annulment of his election as a Member of Parliament for Limassol. In the May 2016 parliamentary elections, he stood for the Solidarity party. Solidarity won one seat in Limassol. Ms E.T., Solidarity’s president and an MEP, was declared elected as the party’s top preference candidate. On 27 May 2016, before the parliamentary term began, she informed the Chief Returning Officer (CRO) that she would not take the seat, preferring to remain an MEP. At the time, Cypriot law only provided for filling a seat vacated after the parliamentary term had begun; it did not regulate a seat “not taken” before the term began. The CRO applied section 35(1) of the Elections Law by analogy and declared Papadopoulos, the runner-up, elected. He affirmed in Parliament on 2 June 2016.

Two voters/candidates challenged this. On 31 May 2017, the Electoral Court unanimously annulled his election and declaration. It held that Ms E.T. had never acquired parliamentary status because she never made the Article 69 affirmation; her seat had therefore never been “vacated” under section 35(1). Article 66 of the Constitution did not cover a seat not taken before the term began, and the CRO had unlawfully applied the law by analogy.

In June 2017, Parliament amended section 35(1) to include a “not taken” parliamentary seat. On 5 July 2017, the CRO again declared Papadopoulos elected; he affirmed on 7 July 2017. A new petition followed. On 30 April 2018, the Electoral Court, by six to five, annulled his election for a second time and declared the 2017 amendment unconstitutional. The majority reasoned that the Constitution only recognised a “vacated” seat, not a “not taken” one; parliamentary status began only upon affirmation. Since Ms E.T. never affirmed and renounced the seat before the term, the seat never lawfully belonged to Solidarity and could not be assigned to its runner-up. Retroactively granting the applicant the seat violated non-retroactivity and popular sovereignty. The minority considered the amendment a legitimate filling of a legislative gap consistent with proportional representation.

In October 2019, Parliament amended Articles 66 and 71 of the Constitution and the Elections Law to cover “renounced”, “not taken” and “vacated” seats. On 29 October 2019, the Returning Officer declared Papadopoulos elected a third time; he affirmed on 1 November 2019. A further petition was filed. On 29 October 2020, the Electoral Court, by ten to one, annulled the election and declaration again. It held that the 2019 constitutional and statutory amendments were unconstitutional and unlawful because they retroactively applied to the 2016 election, violated the finality/res judicata of earlier decisions, and breached non-retroactivity. It invoked the basic structure doctrine, holding that Parliament could not amend the fundamental principle of popular sovereignty by legislating a specific person into Parliament after the people’s electoral choice had been judicially resolved. Applying the amendments to the applicant would also violate equality and deprive other candidates and voters of by-elections. The dissent disagreed, finding the amendments compatible with the Constitution and proportional representation.

The applicant lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 21 April 2021. The case therefore concerns whether the three successive annulments of his parliamentary election—based on the absence of a valid legal basis at the time and later retroactive constitutional/statutory amendments—interfered with his Convention rights, particularly in relation to his right to stand for election and the free expression of the people in choosing the legislature.

The case of *Panopoulou and Others v. Greece* (Application no. 28983/20) concerns an application lodged against Greece with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention. The application was introduced on 6 July 2020 by thirteen applicants, represented by Mr A. Papakonstantinou, a lawyer practising in Athens. The Greek Government were given notice of the application. Following communication of the case, the parties attempted but failed to reach a friendly settlement. The Third Section of the Court, sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 23 October 2025.

The applicants’ details are set out in the appended table. They appear to be members of the Panopoulou and Antypas families, born between 1935 and 1991. The listed applicants include Nikoleta Panopoulou, Alexandra Gkioka, Dimitrios Gkiokas, Kalliopi Panopoulou, Magdalini Panopoulou, Alexandra Panopoulou, Kalliopi Panopoulou, Gavriela Panopoulou, Ioanna Panopoulou, Vasilios Antypas, Ioannis Antypas, and Gerasimos Antypas. The application is brought by thirteen applicants in total.

The key domestic proceeding was a judgment of the Athens Administrative Court of First Instance, Judgment no. 14300/2005, dated 30 November 2005. That judgment became final. According to the appended table, the period of non-enforcement began on 22 August 2006. The end date of the non-enforcement period is recorded as “pending.” The total length of non-enforcement is therefore stated as more than 18 years, 5 months, and 21 days.

The applicants complained before the European Court of Human Rights about the non-enforcement of that domestic judgment. They also complained of the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law in that regard. In substance, the alleged violations concern the continued failure of the Greek authorities to give effect to a final domestic court decision and the absence of an adequate domestic mechanism to challenge or remedy that non-enforcement. The case therefore centres on a prolonged period during which a final administrative judgment remained unexecuted, with no effective domestic redress available to the applicants.

The available judgment excerpt records the procedural steps and factual details relevant to those complaints. It does not, in the extract provided, set out the Court’s legal reasoning or final conclusion on the merits. The essential facts relevant to the alleged violations are the existence of a final domestic judgment dated 30 November 2005, the commencement of non-enforcement on 22 August 2006, the continuation of that non-enforcement for over eighteen years and five months at the time recorded, and the applicants’ related complaint that Greek law provided no effective remedy for that situation. The case thus focuses on the prolonged non-execution of a final administrative judgment and the alleged lack of effective domestic remedies for that non-enforcement.

**Petrosyan v. Armenia** (Application no. 51448/15, European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, 9 January 2025) concerns the death of the applicant’s son, H. Movsisyan, in detention and the ensuing investigations. The applicant, Heghine Petrosyan, an Armenian national, is the deceased’s mother. The application raised issues under Articles 2 and 13 of the Convention.

In June 2011, H. Movsisyan, aged 18, was conscripted into the Armenian army despite health complaints, then assigned to a military unit of the Nagorno-Karabakh armed forces. From the start he showed severe maladjustment: he refused duties and uniforms. On 27 June 2011 he left his unit; after being returned, he cut his left forearm with a razor blade during a conversation with Lieutenant Colonel H.S. He was hospitalized. A military-medical examination on 25 July 2011 diagnosed “organic psychopathic-like disorder [and] non-adaptive decompensation with attempted suicide.” On 2 August 2011 he was found unfit for peacetime military service and discharged on 28 September 2011.

Despite this, criminal proceedings for evasion of military service and later self-mutilation continued. Charges were brought in 2011, and the case was sent to the Syunik Regional Court. In January 2012 his detention was authorized; he was arrested in July 2012 and transferred to Shushi Detention Centre in Nagorno-Karabakh on 10 September 2012. On 20 November 2012 he was convicted and sentenced to three years’ imprisonment.

On 28 November 2012, H. Movsisyan was found hanged in his cell by a bedsheet from the window bars. The official version was suicide. An autopsy concluded death by mechanical asphyxiation due to hanging; apart from a ligature mark and minor scratches, no significant injuries were found. Guards stated they observed him hanging during routine checks. Cellmates described him as withdrawn, complaining of unlawful conviction, sometimes refusing food, but he had been playing cards earlier that evening. No suicide note was found. The authorities concluded there had been no ill-treatment, threats, or incitement by guards or detainees.

The “NKR” Prosecutor’s Office opened a criminal case for alleged incitement to suicide, terminated in March 2013, attributing the death to his psychiatric disorder and conviction. Armenia’s Special Investigative Service then opened an official-negligence case, combined it with the suicide case, and terminated it in December 2013, finding no crime by officials, prosecutors, judges, or medical experts. The applicant was never granted victim status, was denied copies of decisions and case-file access, and her appeals were dismissed; courts refused to compel production of the full investigative file. Meanwhile, the General Prosecutor appealed the son’s conviction. In April 2013 the Court of Appeal acquitted him, holding that he should not have been prosecuted because he had been discharged as unfit for service. The Court of Cassation later terminated proceedings because of his death.

The applicant alleged that the authorities failed to protect her son’s life in detention despite knowing his psychiatric vulnerability and suicide risk, and that the investigation into his death was ineffective and inaccessible to the family. She further complained under Article 13 that she had no effective remedy, including no meaningful opportunity to participate or obtain case material. The case thus concerns the State’s positive obligations to protect detainees’ lives and to conduct an independent, adequate, and participatory investigation into a death in custody.

In *Kyrian v. the Czech Republic*, the applicant is a Czech national and the biological father of a child born in December 2013 from an extramarital relationship. Because the mother was married, her husband was presumed to be the child’s legal father, and the child lived with his legal parents. The applicant established biological paternity by DNA test in 2015.

Until February 2016, he saw his son two to four times monthly when the mother brought him. In April 2016 he sought contact under Article 927 of the Civil Code. The District Court provisionally granted contact every Wednesday afternoon and every second Sunday in summer, upheld on appeal. The appellate court noted an emotional bond and the child’s right to know his biological father. However, conflicts arose between the applicant and the mother/legal father, leading to supervised visits and worsening child psychology. In September 2017, the applicant sought more contact; the mother sought prohibition, citing verbal abuse and the child’s refusal/anxiety. The legal father alleged physical assault. After further proceedings, mediation in 2018 produced an agreement, but later visits were missed due to the child’s refusal and an incident requiring police. Supervised visits in October 2018 also involved conflict.

An October 2018 psychologist report said the child was strongly attached to his legal parents, found unfamiliar people stressful, and should not be forced into unwanted visits. In December 2018 the legal parents sought to prohibit contact. In 2020 the courts set no contact regime, finding no positive emotional bond and no harm from lack of contact. An expert found the child, who had developmental delays, was caught in a relationship triangle, mirrored the legal parents’ attitude, and was attached to his legal father; no contact was in his best interests at least until the legal parents’ marital crisis resolved. The courts also found the applicant pressured the child and legal parents, exacerbating conflict. The Constitutional Court dismissed his appeal in 2022.

In April 2021 the applicant again sought weekly contact. Hearings showed the child was anxious; the guardian ad litem recommended dismissal. A March 2022 expert report said previous visits and witnessed conflicts were traumatic and likely caused the child’s negative attitude. Given developmental delays, the expert did not recommend contact, though it might be possible later if the applicant respected the child’s needs and a positive bond developed. The applicant then sought at least written communication via the guardian and regular information about the child’s development. The legal parents refused, saying contact would distress the child and the applicant’s lingering near the kindergarten or home bordered on stalking. The guardian ad litem said all requests were contrary to the child’s best interests.

On 24 March 2022 the District Court dismissed the claim but warned the legal parents to respect the applicant’s biological parenthood. It found contact was not in the child’s best interests due to the applicant’s coercive tactics, the child’s strong bond with the legal parents, and his unchanged negative attitude. Information about the child was a matter of parental responsibility; the legal parents opposed it, and it was not shown to be in the child’s best interests. The Regional Court upheld this on 12 September 202

**Case: Kyrian v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 15956/23)**

The case concerns an Article 8 complaint by David Kyrian, a Czech national, that the domestic courts refused to grant him contact rights with his biological son and declined to order that he receive information about the child’s development.

The applicant is the biological father of a child born in December 2013 from an extramarital relationship with the mother. Because the mother was married at the time, her husband was presumed to be the child’s legal father, and the child lived with the mother and legal father. The applicant established his biological paternity through a DNA test taken on his own initiative in 2015.

Until February 2016, the applicant saw his son two to four times per month when the mother brought the child to visit him. In April 2016, he sought contact rights under Article 927 of the Civil Code. In May 2016, the District Court granted provisional contact, later upheld on appeal in November 2016. The courts found a positive relationship had developed and acknowledged the child’s right to know his biological father and have regular personal contact with him.

However, conflicts repeatedly arose between the applicant and the mother, and later with the legal father. Visits became irregular and sometimes required supervision. The child’s psychological condition worsened; the mother sought to prohibit contact, alleging verbal abuse and the child’s anxiety and refusal to see the applicant. The legal father alleged a physical assault by the applicant. After mediation in April 2018, contact resumed and a July 2018 court-approved agreement provided for Wednesday afternoons and alternate Sundays in summer. Yet several visits failed because the child refused, and an incident led to police involvement. Supervised visits in October 2018 also produced conflicts.

A psychologist reported in October 2018 that the child was strongly attached to the mother and legal father, found imposed contact stressful, and should not be forced into unwanted visits. In December 2018, the legal parents sought a prohibition on contact. In 2020, the District Court and Regional Court ruled that no contact regime should be set. They found no positive emotional bond between the child and the applicant and no indication that lack of contact would harm the child. An expert concluded the child, who had developmental delays, was caught in a relationship triangle and mirrored the legal parents’ attitude; the child was very attached to the legal father. The expert considered no contact to be in the child’s best interests at that time, at least until the legal parents’ marital crisis resolved. The courts also found the applicant had pressured the child and legal parents, exacerbating conflict and burdening the child.

In April 2021, the applicant began new proceedings seeking Wednesday contact. In March 2022, an expert again recommended no contact, finding prior visits and witnessed conflicts traumatic and the child’s attitude negative; future contact was not ruled out if the applicant became more respectful and a positive bond developed. The child’s psychologist confirmed anxiety attacks. At a March 2022 hearing, the applicant also requested written communication via the guardian ad litem and regular information about the child. The legal parents refused, and the guardian ad litem opposed all requests. The District Court dismissed the claim in March 2022, finding contact contrary to the child’s best interests, though it warned the legal parents to respect the applicant’s biological parenthood. The Regional Court upheld that decision in September 2022, and the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal in January 2023.

The applicant alleged that these refusals violated his right to respect for family and private life under Article 8, arguing that he could not be entirely excluded from his son’s life absent important reasons grounded in the child’s best interests.

The case of *Lubarda and Milanov v. Serbia* (Applications nos. 6570/19 and 43604/19) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights, Third Section. The judgment was delivered on 29 April 2025. The applicants are two Serbian nationals, Zoran Lubarda and Slađan Milanov. Their applications alleged violations of Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically the right to a fair trial, in minor-offence proceedings concerning road-traffic offences.

The first applicant, Lubarda, was convicted in 2017 of failing to comply with a traffic light signal. He was fined EUR 120, banned from driving for three months, and received penalty points. The second applicant, Milanov, was convicted in 2015 of driving while intoxicated, described as being in a state of complete intoxication. He was fined EUR 850, banned from driving for eight months, and also received penalty points. Although the cases were dealt with as minor offences, both offences were potentially punishable by imprisonment. Under Serbia’s Minor Offences Act, if the fines were not paid, they could be converted into effective prison sentences — up to 15 days for Lubarda and up to 60 days for Milanov. This factor was relevant to whether Article 6’s criminal-fair-trial guarantees applied.

In both cases, police officers drew up reports at the scene of the incidents. The applicants signed those reports but later disputed their contents in court. Their convictions were based on the police reports and on evidence given by the police officers. However, the police officers’ evidence was taken in court but not during the main hearings in the applicants’ cases. Neither applicant nor their lawyers were summoned to the examination of those witnesses, even though both had explicitly requested to be present and to cross-examine them. In Lubarda’s case, the request was refused on grounds of efficiency and economy of proceedings. In Milanov’s case, the court held that cross-examination would not have led to a different determination of facts because the officer’s witness evidence was consistent with the report Milanov had signed.

Both applicants appealed against their convictions. The Appeals Court upheld the convictions, and the Constitutional Court subsequently also upheld them. The final domestic decisions were notified to Lubarda on 1 August 2018 and to Milanov on 26 February 2019. They then lodged applications with the European Court of Human Rights, relying on Article 6 of the Convention. They complained that the minor-offence proceedings against them had not been fair because they were not given an opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses whose statements formed the basis of their convictions. The Government was given notice of the applications and submitted observations, and the Court rejected the Government’s objection to examination by a Committee. The central alleged violation was therefore the lack of cross-examination of police witnesses in proceedings that carried potential imprisonment, contrary to the applicants’ fair-trial rights under Article 6.

In *I.C. v. the Republic of Moldova*, the applicant is a Moldovan woman born in 1974 with a moderate intellectual disability. Abandoned at birth, she had no known relatives and had lived in State care her entire life. In 2011 the Soroca District Court deprived her of legal capacity owing to her intellectual disability, and no subsequent guardian appears to have been appointed. At the relevant time, she had spent twenty-four years in a State neuropsychiatric asylum.

In 2013 a couple, L.P. and I.P., approached the asylum asking for a person who could be a “bride” for G.B., an employee on their farm. They first requested that the applicant stay with them for a month, then sought her permanent placement. In March 2013 the Ministry supported termination of her asylum placement for integration into the P. family, and the asylum director issued an order releasing her. The applicant lived on the farm from 15 January 2013 to 23 October 2018.

The applicant alleged that she worked every day from about 4 a.m. until dark, feeding livestock, cleaning stalls, carrying milk, and disposing of rubbish. She was paid only occasionally and in small amounts. She alleged that I.P. began raping and sexually abusing her, using psychological control and exploiting her intellectual disability, lack of family, and lack of any alternative place to live. She said she could not refuse. I.P. allegedly threatened to kill her dogs and told her the police would not intervene because his son was in the police. L.P. allegedly beat, insulted, and threatened her, and sometimes chased her away; the applicant occasionally stayed in abandoned train cars before being found and returned.

On 23 October 2018 the applicant fled and called a disability hotline, reporting forced labour, sexual abuse by I.P., and abuse and threats by L.P. An NGO contacted the police, and on 25 October 2018 the applicant lodged a formal criminal complaint. She described sexual acts by I.P., said she had refused but was persuaded, feared L.P. finding out, and had nowhere to go. A multidisciplinary meeting assessed her situation as high risk and removed her temporarily from the family.

A criminal investigation for rape and sexual violence began on 29 October 2018. The applicant was granted victim status and repeated her allegations, adding that I.P. had threatened to kill her dog. Medical examinations found a sexually transmitted disease but no signs of violence. The Labour Inspectorate found no formal labour relations. Psychiatric and psychological reports described moderate intellectual disability, high suggestibility, limited ability to understand or resist, and dependency on caregivers. A later independent forensic psychological report found trauma and PTSD symptoms.

In February 2019 I.P. was charged with rape and sexual abuse. In March 2019 the applicant requested additional investigation of human trafficking and sexual harassment. In September 2019 I.P. and L.P. were charged with human trafficking involving two or more perpetrators, based on forcing the applicant to work without pay through threats and violence. In December 2019 the prosecutor charged I.P. with human trafficking, treating the sexual relations as non-commercial sexual exploitation and essentially dropping separate rape and sexual abuse charges. The applicant’s objections and appeals were rejected, and the case was sent for trial.

The applicant complains under Articles 3, 4, and 8, alone and with Article 14, and under Articles 6 and 13, that Moldova failed to protect her from ill-treatment and human trafficking and failed to effectively investigate her allegations. Key facts include her known disability and institutional background, State-approved deinstitutionalisation into an unmonitored farm placement, alleged unpaid labour and sexual abuse, threats and dependency, and the later investigation’s reclassification or dropping of core abuse charges.
