He challenged the decisions, arguing that the quality of the allocated forests was inferior to that of Ms F.’s original forests. The decisions were nevertheless upheld in final court judgments given in 2023 and 2024.

An additional plot of about 5.3 hectares has been identified, but the process of officially allocating it to the applicants remains ongoing. The competent authorities are still working to locate further plots to compensate the applicants for the remaining approximately 29 hectares of forestry land. Thus, more than two decades after the initial compensation decision, the restitution process remains incomplete. The central alleged violation concerns the prolonged duration of those restitution proceedings.

In *Petrosyan v. Armenia*, the applicant, Heghine Petrosyan, is the mother of H. Movsisyan, who died in custody on 28 November 2012 while detained in Shushi Detention Centre in the unrecognised “Nagorno-Karabakh Republic” (“NKR”). The case concerns his death and the ensuing investigation, raising issues under Articles 2 and 13 of the Convention.

In June 2011, H. Movsisyan, aged 18, was conscripted into the Armenian army and assigned to a military unit of the Nagorno-Karabakh armed forces. Although he reportedly had health problems, he was found fit for combatant service. From the outset he had difficulty adapting, refused duties, and on 27 June 2011 left his unit; after being returned, he cut his left forearm with a razor blade during a conversation with the battalion commander. He was diagnosed with an “organic psychopathic-like disorder [and] non-adaptive decompensation with attempted suicide.” In August 2011 the Central Military Commission found him unfit for peacetime military service, fit only for non-combatant wartime service, and he was discharged in September 2011.

Meanwhile, criminal proceedings had been brought against him for evasion of military service, later changed to self-mutilation to evade service. In January 2012 the court authorised his detention, and in July 2012 he was arrested. In September 2012 he was transferred to Shushi Detention Centre. On 20 November 2012 he was convicted and sentenced to three years’ imprisonment.

Seven days later, during the night of 27-28 November 2012, he was found hanged by a bedsheet from the window bars of his cell. The official version was suicide. An autopsy concluded mechanical asphyxiation by hanging, with no alcohol detected. A later forensic report noted a scratch on his right forearm inflicted before death. Guards claimed they checked cells every ten to fifteen minutes; cellmates said they were asleep and woke only when the guard shouted. The “NKR” prosecutor’s office opened a case concerning alleged incitement to suicide. In March 2013 it terminated the proceedings, finding no threats, ill-treatment, psychological pressure or violence by detention staff or inmates. It attributed the suicide to his psychiatric disorder and recent conviction.

Separately, Armenia’s Special Investigative Service opened a case concerning official negligence, later combined with the NKR case. In December 2013 that investigation was also terminated for absence of crime, finding no negligence by investigators, prosecutors, the judge, or medical experts. In parallel, the General Prosecutor appealed H. Movsisyan’s conviction; the Court of Appeal acquitted him in April 2013, finding he had been unfit for service and unlawfully prosecuted. The Court of Cassation later terminated proceedings because of his death.

The applicant’s alleged violations focus on the state’s failure to protect her son’s life and to conduct an effective investigation. Key facts are that he died in state custody while known to have a psychiatric disorder and a prior suicide attempt. The authorities allegedly failed to monitor suicide risk or provide adequate psychological or medical care. The investigation relied heavily on detention staff and cellmates, and the applicant argued it failed to clarify crucial issues: how the hanging occurred within minutes, whether adequate first aid was given, the origin of the forearm injury, the link to his earlier suicide attempt, and possible liability of officials and experts. She was denied victim status and access to the case file, and courts refused to compel production of the full evidence, limiting her ability to challenge the termination. The case thus concerns whether Armenia complied with its positive obligation to protect a detainee’s life and conducted an effective, accessible investigation, and whether the applicant had an effective remedy.

In **I.C. v. the Republic of Moldova** (ECtHR, Fifth Section, 27 February 2025), the applicant is a Moldovan woman with moderate intellectual disability. She was abandoned at birth, had no known relatives, and had spent her entire life in State care. In 2011 she was deprived of legal capacity; no guardian appears to have been appointed. At the relevant time, she had lived for 24 years in a State neuropsychiatric asylum.

In January 2013, a couple, L.P. and I.P., approached the asylum asking for a woman who could be a “bride” for G.B., an employee on their farm. The applicant initially went for a one-month “holiday,” then the couple sought her permanent placement. The Ministry approved her deinstitutionalisation and integration into the P. family, and the asylum issued an order terminating her placement in March 2013. In February 2014, her identity and disability documents were handed to L.P.

From January 2013 to October 2018, the applicant lived and worked on the P. family farm. She alleged that she worked every day from about 4 a.m. until dark, feeding livestock, cleaning stalls, carrying milk, and disposing of rubbish, but was paid only a few times, around EUR 5–15. She further alleged that I.P. raped and sexually abused her over several years. She stated that she could not refuse, and that I.P. threatened to kill her dogs and told her the police would not intervene because his son was in the police. She also alleged physical and psychological abuse and threats by L.P., and said she escaped repeatedly but had nowhere to go and was sometimes found and returned.

In October 2018, the applicant ran away and called a disability hotline, complaining of unpaid work, sexual abuse, and threats. An NGO contacted the police. She lodged a criminal complaint, initially in ambivalent terms, but later gave detailed statements describing repeated oral and vaginal sex, crying and refusal, threats to kill her dog, and dependency on the perpetrators. A medical report found a sexually transmitted disease but no signs of violence. Psychological reports described moderate/mild intellectual disability, IQ 50, high suggestibility, limited autonomy, and dependency. A later forensic report found trauma and vulnerability, noting that she perceived the perpetrators as parental figures.

A criminal investigation began in October 2018 for rape and sexual violence. In February 2019, I.P. was charged with rape and sexual abuse. The applicant later asked the prosecutor to investigate human trafficking and sexual harassment. Additional trafficking cases were opened and joined. In September 2019, I.P. and L.P. were charged with human trafficking involving two or more perpetrators, based on taking the applicant to the farm and forcing her to work without pay through threats and violence, exploiting her disability. In December 2019, however, the prosecutor essentially dropped the rape and sexual abuse charges, reclassifying the sexual relations as “non-commercial sexual exploitation” within the trafficking charge. The applicant’s challenges were rejected, and the case was sent to trial. The Labour Inspectorate found no formal labour relationship.

Witness G.B. initially stated he had seen I.P. having sex with the applicant, that she resisted and had been threatened, and that she was unpaid; he later recanted, allegedly under pressure. The defendants denied the allegations. Before the ECtHR, the applicant complains that Moldova failed to protect her from ill-treatment and human trafficking and to effectively investigate her allegations, relying on Articles 3, 4 and 8, alone and with Article 14, and on Articles 6 and 13.

In *Hora v. the United Kingdom* (Application no. 1048/20, Second Section, judgment 23 September 2025), the applicant, Michael Christopher Hora, a British national born in 1966 and detained at HMP Bure, complained under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 that he was ineligible to vote in the UK general election of 12 December 2019. The Court gave notice only of that complaint and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

Key facts: On 10 October 2007, Hora was convicted of two counts of rape and one count of sexual assault committed in the victim’s home. His defence that the sexual relations were consensual was rejected. He had a previous 2000 rape conviction and had been sentenced in 2001 to seven years’ imprisonment, reduced on appeal. After the 2007 conviction, he received an indeterminate sentence of imprisonment for public protection with a minimum term of four years, less 296 days spent on remand. The minimum term expired in 2011, but he remained in detention because the Parole Board had not recommended his release. At the 2019 general election, therefore, he was still serving an indeterminate sentence in custody.

Under section 3 of the Representation of the People Act 1983, a convicted person detained in a penal institution pursuant to sentence is legally incapable of voting at parliamentary or local elections. Exceptions exist for prisoners held for contempt, default, such as fine default, or on remand. Hora did not fall within any exception, so he was ineligible to vote in the 2019 election.

He did not bring domestic proceedings. UK courts can make a declaration that primary legislation is incompatible with Convention rights but cannot disapply statutory provisions. A domestic court had already declared section 3 incompatible in *Smith v. Scott* (2007), and Hora saw no value in seeking another such declaration.

The broader background concerned the UK’s delay in implementing *Hirst v. the United Kingdom (no. 2)* (2005), where the Court found the blanket prisoner voting ban violated Article 3 of Protocol No. 1. Later consultations and proposals considered limited enfranchisement—for example, allowing prisoners sentenced to less than four years, or 12 months or less, to vote—but Parliament repeatedly opposed change. In 2017 the government announced only administrative measures: clarifying at sentencing that prisoners lose the vote, and allowing certain prisoners on temporary licence or home detention curfew to vote. The custodial ban remained. Scotland later allowed prisoners serving 12 months or less to vote in Scottish Parliament and local elections; a Welsh proposal to extend local-election voting to some prisoners was not pursued.

In *R (Chester) v. Secretary of State for Justice* (2013), the Supreme Court declined to make a further declaration of incompatibility, noting that incompatibility had already been recognised and that Parliament was considering the issue. It also suggested that disenfranchisement of serious offenders could be compatible with the Convention.

The alleged violation therefore concerns the automatic, blanket disenfranchisement of convicted prisoners in custody—without individual assessment of offence seriousness, sentence length or the applicant’s circumstances—and its application to Hora in the 2019 general election.

This case concerns seven San Marino nationals who served as officers in the Uniformed Unit of the Fortress Guard, originally on temporary contracts between 2006 and 2008. They claimed their enrolment should have become permanent after a successful one-year probationary period under Law no. 132/1987, as amended by Law no. 99/1997, which also governed career advancement. Their employment was repeatedly extended until 18 January 2016, when Parliament acknowledged their permanent recruitment under Article 63(1) of Law no. 189/2015 and assigned them a “Scale 5” career category.

Between late January and early February 2016, the applicants asked the Public Administration Personnel Management Office (“PAPMO”) to reconstruct their careers, which would affect salary and entitlements. The acknowledgments of receipt indicated that those dates started the deadline for concluding the proceedings and that remedies lay under Law no. 68/1989. No immediate reply followed. On 25 July 2016, while their requests were pending, the legislature adopted Delegated Decree no. 88/2016. Its Article 1 provided that, for persons recruited under Article 63 of Law no. 189/2015, the economic effects of retrospective career reconstruction could only run from 1 February 2016, without payment of arrears and without payment of the statutory withholding taxes normally due under Article 54 of Law no. 41/1972.

PAPMO then carried out the applicants’ career reconstruction in line with Law no. 88/2016. Each applicant allegedly suffered losses of around EUR 25,000 or more. In 2018, they asked the Minister of Foreign and Political Affairs and the Director General of Civil Service to intervene so that arrears could be paid under ordinary provisions. On 7 November 2018, the authorities confirmed that the reconstruction complied with Law no. 88/2016 and noted that the applicants had not been employed under the ordinary procedure in Law no. 132/1987, as amended by Law no. 99/1997.

On 20 March 2019, the applicants applied to the Judge of First Instance, exercising administrative jurisdiction, seeking annulment of the 7 November 2018 decision. They argued that Law no. 88/2016 was unconstitutional because it conflicted with Articles 4 (equality) and 9 (equitable remuneration) of the Declaration of the Citizens’ Rights, and asked for referral to the Constitutional Court. On 9 December 2019, the Judge of First Instance refused the referral as manifestly ill-founded, finding it legitimate to apply different conditions to persons employed through extraordinary procedures.

The applicants then challenged the judge’s continued involvement. On 17 July 2020, the Judge for Extraordinary Remedies dismissed that challenge but noted, in an obiter dictum, that the impugned provision had to be examined in light of Convention principles. He observed that the applicants had suffered a legislative interference in pending proceedings begun in January/February 2016, before the July 2016 decree. The case was returned to the Judge of First Instance.

On 4 November 2020, the Judge of First Instance dismissed the claim. He found that Law no. 88/2016 clarified Article 63(1) of Law no. 189/2015, was a lex specialis, and prevailed over ordinary rules. The applicants had benefited from permanent recruitment without any public competition, unlike officers recruited through public selection, so their different remuneration was not unreasonable, and no violation of Article 9 of the Declaration was established. On appeal, the applicants reiterated their constitutional challenge and added Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, though they later withdrew the constitutional request. On 30 March 2022, the Judge of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment, emphasising that the applicants had been recruited through an ad hoc process rather than a public competition, and ordered them to pay costs.

The Strasbourg Court gave notice of the complaints under Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and declared the remainder inadmissible. The central alleged violations concern the legislative intervention in pending career-reconstruction proceedings and the resulting loss of salary arrears and entitlements.

**Tsatani v. Greece** (Application no. 42514/16) concerns disciplinary proceedings brought against Ms Georgia Tsatani, a Greek prosecutor at the Athens Court of Appeal. Her complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention was that she had not been heard by an impartial tribunal. Specifically, she alleged that V.T., then President of the Court of Cassation (“CC”), had conducted the preliminary disciplinary investigation against her, had herself dealt with the applicant’s recusal request directed at her, and had subsequently brought disciplinary proceedings against the applicant.

On 23 March 2016, V.T. informed the applicant that she had opened a preliminary disciplinary investigation. V.T. acted on letters from the Cypriot Minister of Justice and Attorney-General, both dated 24 February 2016, expressing concern about the applicant’s decision to close criminal investigations into a media-covered fraud case involving Greek and Cypriot individuals. V.T. sent the applicant witness statements, documents and reports, and invited her written defence.

The applicant objected that the Prosecutor of the CC had exclusive competence, complained that the deputy Minister of Justice had referred to the confidential disciplinary proceedings in Parliament on 29 March 2016, and argued that V.T. had failed to specify the alleged disciplinary acts or hear her orally. V.T. then provided a more detailed statement and a fresh time-limit.

On 4 April 2016, the applicant submitted her written defence and a recusal request against V.T. She argued that V.T. could not be impartial because of her previous role as interim Prime Minister, her ongoing relations with the deputy Minister of Justice, her relations with the Cypriot officials who had written about the case, alleged leaking of confidential information, prejudicial questioning of witnesses, and an incomplete copy of the file.

On 12 April 2016, V.T. referred the preliminary investigation to a Vice-President of the CC. In that referral, V.T. described the recusal request as an abuse of process and unfounded, and explained that she had acted under Article 99 § 9 of Law no. 1756/1988, which allowed her either to conduct the investigation herself or assign it to another judge. On 18 April 2016, V.T. issued a press release stating that the recusal request was ill-founded and an abuse of process, while explaining that she had delegated the investigation to protect the credibility of the judiciary.

On 5 May 2016, the Vice-President concluded the preliminary investigation and proposed that V.T. bring a disciplinary action. She declared the applicant’s recusal request inadmissible for lack of standing, noting that V.T. had already dismissed it as an abuse of process.

On 24 June 2016, V.T. brought a disciplinary action and referred the applicant to the seven-member disciplinary council of the CC. V.T. maintained that the recusal request was inadmissible because it had not been lodged with the Prosecutor of the CC under the Code of Criminal Procedure; it could only be treated as an invitation to withdraw. On 10 October 2016, the seven-member council found the applicant guilty of serious negligence damaging the prestige of the judiciary and imposed sixty days’ salary deprivation. It held the recusal request inadmissible and found that V.T. had lawfully delegated the investigation. The nine-member disciplinary council dismissed her appeal on 16 March 2017, finding the recusal request inadmissible and, in any event, unfounded. It considered V.T.’s relations official and found no bias. A request to reopen was rejected on 22 March 2021.

The applicant’s Article 6 § 1 complaint therefore centred on the same official, V.T., having combined the roles of investigator, decision-maker on the recusal request against herself, and the person who ultimately initiated disciplinary proceedings.

In **N.T. v. Cyprus**, the applicant complained that Cyprus failed to fulfil its positive obligations under Articles 3 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights to effectively investigate and prosecute her rape allegation. She also alleged gender-based discrimination contrary to Article 14 read together with Articles 3 and 8.

The key facts concern an alleged rape on 1 January 2011. The applicant, then 18, reported to police on 10 April 2021 that A.T., then 20, had raped her. They knew each other from school, and she had been attracted to him. After a night out, A.T. led the applicant and friends to a warehouse. The applicant alleged that A.T. forced her upstairs, tried to undress her, forced her onto boxes, and raped her orally and vaginally despite resistance, including scratching and biting him. He bit her neck forcefully. She said she felt humiliated and used. Her friend C.S., who had been downstairs, later saw bruises and bite marks on the applicant’s neck and a broken fingernail; the applicant was upset but did not disclose the rape. She later told a male friend and psychologists, and in 2021 decided to report after learning that A.T. had allegedly raped another classmate.

Police investigated promptly. They took statements from the applicant, C.S., D.N., psychologists, S.N., and A.T.’s friend G.H. C.S. corroborated seeing the applicant’s injuries, her strange behaviour, and A.T. locking the warehouse door; she also described a separate attempted sexual assault by A.T. on her in 2010. D.N. confirmed the applicant had earlier disclosed the rape. G.H. claimed he heard no screams or unusual noises and that the applicant did not seem upset. Police photographed the area, but the warehouse had been demolished years earlier. In May 2021 police found sufficient evidence and A.T. was indicted for rape; the case was sent to the Assize Court. A.T. pleaded not guilty and was released on bail.

After the indictment, the applicant gave supplementary statements. In the first, she disclosed 2011 Facebook messages in which she told A.T. she loved him. She said she had blamed herself, believed she may have given the wrong impression that consent was implied, and had wanted to protect him. In the second, she revealed she had had consensual sex with A.T. in the same warehouse on 1 January 2010, with C.S. and G.H. downstairs; she said this was different from the 2011 rape and had been omitted earlier as she thought it unrelated.

Prosecutors reviewed the case and noted inconsistencies, late disclosures, and the possibility that A.T. reasonably believed she consented. In October 2021 the applicant met prosecutors and was later treated for anxiety disorder. On 1 December 2021 the Deputy Attorney General discontinued the prosecution by entering a nolle prosequi, citing credibility doubts, inconsistencies, possible mistaken belief in consent, low chance of success, and public interest. The applicant requested reasons and the case file; she received only limited explanation and was refused the file.

The alleged violations therefore centre on whether the Cypriot authorities effectively investigated and prosecuted the rape; whether the discontinuation relied on victim-blaming stereotypes, rape myths, and a failure to gather or assess corroborating evidence; and whether this amounted to gender discrimination. The case context also includes GREVIO’s criticisms of Cyprus concerning patriarchal attitudes, overreliance on victim statements, lack of training, and risks of secondary victimisation.

In *Kyrian v. the Czech Republic*, the applicant, a Czech national born in 1982, is the biological father of a child born in December 2013 from an extramarital relationship with the child’s mother. Because the mother was married at the time, her husband became the child’s legal father by presumption. The applicant’s biological paternity was confirmed by a DNA test he arranged in 2015. He initially saw the child two to four times per month until February 2016.

In April 2016 the applicant sought contact rights under Article 927 of the Civil Code. A May 2016 judgment granted him Wednesday afternoon and alternate Sunday summer contact, upheld on appeal in November 2016. The Regional Court noted an emotional bond and the child’s right to know his biological father. However, visits became conflictual, requiring supervised visits, and the child’s psychological condition worsened. In 2017 the applicant sought more contact, while the mother sought a contact prohibition. After that decision was quashed, mediation in April 2018 led to an approved agreement maintaining similar contact. Later visits were missed due to the child’s refusal and an incident involving police.

An October 2018 psychologist report found the child strongly attached to his mother and legal father, stressed by unfamiliar people, and that imposed contact might cause difficulties and should not be forced. In December 2018 the legal parents sought a prohibition. In 2020 the courts ruled that no contact regime should be set, finding no positive emotional bond and no harm from lack of contact. An expert described the child as developmentally delayed, caught in a relationship triangle, attached to his legal father, and mirroring the legal parents’ attitude. The expert recommended no contact at least until the legal parents’ marital crisis resolved. The applicant’s pressure was found to exacerbate conflict. A constitutional appeal was dismissed in October 2022.

In April 2021 the applicant again sought Wednesday contact. At a 2021 hearing, the legal parents described the child as anxious, and the guardian ad litem advised dismissal. A March 2022 expert report concluded that previous visits and witnessed conflicts were traumatic and had likely created a negative attitude toward the applicant. Given the child’s developmental delays, forcing contact was inappropriate; no contact was recommended, though future contact might be possible if the applicant respected the child’s needs and a positive bond developed. The child’s psychologist confirmed anxiety.

At a March 2022 hearing, the applicant requested at least written communication via the guardian and regular information about the child’s development. The legal parents refused, claiming any contact would distress the child and that the applicant’s lingering near the kindergarten or home bordered on stalking. The guardian opposed all requests.

In March 2022 the District Court dismissed the claim but warned the legal parents about non-cooperation and respect for the applicant’s biological parenthood. It held that contact was not in the child’s best interests under Article 927: both sides had failed to respect the child’s needs, the applicant’s coercive tactics prevented de-escalation, and the child remained strongly attached to his legal parents with an unchanged negative attitude toward the applicant. As to information, the court treated it as a matter of parental responsibility, opposed by the legal parents, with no best-interests reason to order it. The Regional Court upheld this in September 2022, reasoning that information could only be granted within contact rights under Article 927 and that no even partially positive bond existed. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal in January 2023 as manifestly ill-founded.

Subsequent developments included the legal parents’ divorce in 2022, the mother later resuming a relationship with the applicant, and occasional indirect contact. In 2024 custody proceedings, the child said he feared the applicant; he was placed with his legal father, and the mother’s contact application was dismissed because she would not meet without the applicant. The applicant alleged that the refusal of contact and information violated Article 8 of the Convention.

In *A.J. and L.E. v. Spain* (Applications nos. 40312/23 and 40388/23), two Spanish nationals lodged complaints against Spain under Articles 3 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. They alleged that the Spanish authorities failed to conduct an effective criminal investigation into their complaints of sexual assault by chemical submission, and that crucial evidence in police custody was lost or manipulated.

The alleged facts concerned the night of 7–8 December 2016, when the applicants went to a bar in Pamplona and met two men, D.C.M. and R.G.S. The applicants claimed that after drinking alcohol with the men they had no recollection of events until waking the next morning in one man’s residence, undressed and with the physical sensation of having had sexual intercourse. They alleged they had been drugged and rendered unable to consent. On 11 December 2016 A.J. attended a health centre. The medical report noted no genital lesions but activated the protocol for suspected sexual assault involving chemical submission and notified the police. L.E. did not seek immediate medical attention.

The National Police UFAM unit investigated. On 27 December 2016 police arrested the two men, and on 29 December the court questioned them. Both admitted sexual intercourse but claimed it was consensual. Restraining orders were imposed. Formal proceedings opened in January 2017. During the investigation, it emerged that R.G.S. was the brother-in-law of a UFAM police officer assigned to the case. Several pieces of potentially crucial evidence also disappeared or were compromised while in police custody: the full forensic report on R.G.S.’s mobile phone vanished after being sent from Madrid to Pamplona in April 2017; bar video surveillance footage was partially lost or altered; and a hard drive containing forensic data from both suspects’ phones, including backups, was wiped and overwritten.

In November 2018 the investigating court declined to prosecute. It found the applicants’ accounts credible but held that there was insufficient evidence of non-consensual acts. No timely toxicological evidence supported chemical submission, physical discomfort could not be definitively linked to the alleged events, and forensic examination showed no injuries typically associated with violent sexual assault. In October 2021 the court concluded the proceedings without charges. It noted that hair analysis found no chemical submission substances but that both applicants had prescription medication that could have increased alcohol’s effects. Taxi drivers, bar staff, and a friend had observed nothing clearly unusual. The court acknowledged the investigation had been “notably affected” by irregularities and missing digital evidence, but still found insufficient substantive evidence. The Audiencia Provincial upheld the closure in June 2022 and provisional dismissal in September 2022. The Constitutional Court declared the amparo appeal inadmissible in July 2023 on procedural grounds.

Separate investigations were opened into the alleged police misconduct, including digital evidence deletion, video manipulation, and hard-drive erasure. These were discontinued or closed for lack of evidence of intentional wrongdoing, and an internal disciplinary file remained suspended. The ECtHR’s key focus was therefore whether Spain breached its procedural obligations under Articles 3 and 8 by failing to effectively investigate the alleged chemically facilitated sexual assault and by losing or mishandling critical evidence.

The case of *Ayala Flores v. Italy* concerns the alleged violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from the enforcement of a demolition order against the applicant’s home.

The applicant, a Peruvian national born in 1957, lived in Procida, Italy. In the early 1990s, she and her husband built a small 30 sq. m dwelling on land owned by her husband and made it their home. The construction was erected without a building permit. The site was subject to significant planning and environmental restrictions: it was in a highly seismic zone, subject to landscape protection, and fell within an area of “specific environmental interest” with an absolute ban on construction.

In August 1996, the municipality of Procida found that the premises had been built without authorisation. In September 1996, it ordered the applicant to restore the site to its original condition. In 1998, the municipality issued a demolition order. Criminal proceedings followed in 1999, charging the applicant and her husband with unauthorised construction under Law no. 47 of 1985 and with breaking seals placed on the property after earlier modifications. In May 2002, the Naples District Court convicted them, imposed a suspended five-month prison sentence and a fine, and ordered demolition of the construction. On appeal in July 2003, the Naples Court of Appeal declared some offences time-barred but upheld the convictions for unauthorised construction and violation of seals, reduced the sentence, and lifted the seizure only to allow demolition. The judgment became final in October 2003.

In December 2004, the applicant applied for a building amnesty under Decree-Law no. 269 of 2003 and paid the required fees. The application was never answered. Her husband died in 2009, and she continued living in the dwelling.

Enforcement resumed in 2016. The public prosecutor asked the municipality whether demolition had been carried out or whether public-interest reasons prevented it. The municipality served an eviction notice, and the prosecutor ordered the applicant to demolish the dwelling within ninety days or have it demolished at her expense. The applicant asked the municipality to recognise a public interest in preserving the structure. In March 2016, she filed a review of the enforcement order (*incidente di esecuzione*), seeking annulment, revocation, or a stay of the demolition order.

Her initial appeal did not raise Article 8. She later submitted written arguments stating that the building was her only home, that she had lived there for more than fifteen years after conviction, and that she had financial difficulties. Relying on Article 8 and *Ivanova and Cherkezov v. Bulgaria*, she argued that demolition would be disproportionate. The Government disputed this.

In November 2018, the Naples Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal, characterising the demolition order as a mandatory restorative measure required to restore lawful land use and building compliance. It did not address her Article 8 submissions. In 2020, the Court of Cassation rejected her further appeal as inadmissible, partly for failing to satisfy the self-sufficiency requirement. It nonetheless reasoned that her Article 8 complaint was generic, that she had not shown individual circumstances outweighing the public interest, that she could not have a legitimate expectation to remain after fifteen years because she always knew the building was unauthorised, and that she had not proved necessity.

After the case was communicated to the Court, the applicant sought public housing in 2021. Government inspections in 2020, 2022, and 2024 reported that the construction appeared uninhabited, unfit for use, and altered by unauthorised fence, gate, and shutters. The applicant submitted statements, a surveyor’s opinion, a residence certificate since 2001, pension and income documents, and photographs showing water damage and the exterior. By April 2025, the house had not been demolished.

**Case summary: Hora v. the United Kingdom (App. no. 1048/20)**

In *Hora v. the United Kingdom*, the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) considered an application by Michael Christopher Hora, a British national detained at HMP Bure, Norwich. The case concerns his ineligibility to vote in the United Kingdom general election of 12 December 2019 while serving a prison sentence. He complained under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention (right to free elections). The Court gave notice only of the complaint concerning his ineligibility to vote in that election; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The key facts are that Hora was convicted on 10 October 2007 of two counts of rape and one count of sexual assault committed in the victim’s home. His defence that the sexual relations were consensual was rejected by the jury. He had a previous conviction for rape in similar circumstances in 2000, for which he had been sentenced in 2001 to seven years’ imprisonment, reduced on appeal. Following the 2007 conviction, he received an indeterminate sentence of imprisonment for public protection with a minimum term of four years, less 296 days spent on remand. The minimum term expired in 2011, but he remained in detention because the Parole Board had not recommended his release. At the time of the 2019 general election, he was therefore still a convicted prisoner in custody.

Under section 3 of the Representation of the People Act 1983, a convicted person detained in a penal institution pursuant to sentence is legally incapable of voting at any parliamentary or local election. Limited exceptions exist, such as imprisonment for contempt, default, or being on remand. Hora did not fall within any exception and was thus ineligible to vote in the 2019 election.

Hora brought no domestic proceedings. Although UK courts may consider the Convention compatibility of primary legislation, they cannot disapply statutory provisions. A domestic court had already declared section 3 incompatible with a Convention right in *Smith v. Scott* (2007). Hora considered that seeking another declaration of incompatibility would be futile. In *R (Chester) v. Secretary of State for Justice* (2013), the UK Supreme Court had also declined to make a further declaration, noting that the matter was for Parliament and that a lifelong ban for serious offenders might be compatible with the Convention under *Scoppola v. Italy (no. 3)*.

The broader factual context is the long-running political dispute over prisoner voting following *Hirst v. the United Kingdom (no. 2)* (2005). The Committee of Ministers repeatedly urged the UK to implement that judgment. The UK government consulted and proposed limited enfranchisement, including for prisoners sentenced to less than four years, and a draft bill was published. A Joint Committee later recommended allowing prisoners serving 12 months or less to vote and permitting pre-release registration. However, Parliament repeatedly opposed relaxing the ban. The government eventually introduced administrative changes, including clarifying at sentencing that prisoners lose the right to vote and allowing certain prisoners on temporary licence or home detention curfew to vote. These did not remove the blanket ban on detained prisoners. Scotland later allowed prisoners sentenced to 12 months or less to vote in Scottish Parliament and local elections; a proposed Welsh change was abandoned during the Covid-19 pandemic.

The alleged violation is therefore that section 3 imposed an automatic blanket ban on voting for all convicted prisoners in custody, regardless of the nature or gravity of the offence, sentence length, or individual circumstances. Hora, still detained after his minimum term, was unable to vote in the 2019 general election, and he claimed this breached Article 3 of Protocol No. 1.

**I.C. v. the Republic of Moldova** concerns an intellectually disabled Moldovan woman who alleged that the State failed to protect her from labour exploitation, sexual abuse and human trafficking, and failed to investigate her allegations effectively. She relied on Articles 3, 4 and 8 of the Convention, alone and with Article 14, and on Articles 6 and 13.

The applicant was born in 1974, abandoned at birth, and had no known relatives. She had spent her entire life in State care. In 2011 the Soroca District Court deprived her of legal capacity based on a medical report assessing severe intellectual disability; no subsequent guardian was reported. At the material time she had lived for 24 years in a neuropsychiatric asylum.

In 2013 a couple, L.P. and I.P., approached the asylum seeking a suitable “bride” for G.B., an employee on their farm. L.P. initially requested that the applicant stay with them “on holiday” for a month. The applicant signed a note agreeing. The couple then sought her permanent placement. In March 2013 the Ministry supported terminating asylum services to integrate her into the P. family, and the asylum issued an order releasing her for that purpose. In February 2014 the asylum handed her identity, disability and medical documents to L.P. No formal guardianship or employment arrangement appears to have been established.

From January 2013 to October 2018 the applicant lived and worked on the P. family farm. She alleged that she worked from 4 a.m. until dark, feeding livestock, cleaning stalls and premises, carrying milk and disposing of rubbish. She was paid only a few small sums, around EUR 5–15. She alleged that I.P. repeatedly raped and sexually abused her, exploiting her intellectual disability and lack of anywhere to go. When she protested, he allegedly threatened to kill her dogs and said the police would not intervene because his son was in the police. She escaped several times, sometimes staying in abandoned train wagons, but I.P. found her and brought her back.

In October 2018 the applicant ran away and called a disability hotline run by an NGO. The NGO contacted the police. She lodged a formal criminal complaint alleging sexual abuse by I.P. Her police statements contained conflicting elements: she described some acts as “voluntary” or pleasurable, but also said she refused, was afraid, could not refuse, and that I.P. used nice words, threats and psychological pressure. A multidisciplinary meeting assessed her as high risk and temporarily placed her in an asylum. A criminal investigation into rape and sexual violence began; she received victim status.

Medical reports showed a sexually transmitted disease but no physical violence signs. A psychiatric report found moderate intellectual disability, IQ 50, high suggestibility, limited capacity to understand or resist, and a tendency to develop dependency on third parties, including the perpetrator. An independent psychological report later found trauma/PTSD, avoidance, hypervigilance and a need for a specialised shelter. The Labour Inspectorate could not establish a formal labour relationship, stating that this was for a court to determine.

In February 2019 the prosecutor charged I.P. with rape and sexual abuse. Later, I.P. and L.P. were charged with human trafficking involving two or more perpetrators for unpaid farm work obtained through threats, violence and the applicant’s vulnerability. In December 2019 the prosecutor essentially dropped the rape and sexual abuse charges, reclassifying the sexual relations as “non-commercial sexual exploitation” within the trafficking charge. The applicant’s requests to investigate rape, sexual abuse and harassment were rejected on appeal. The case was sent to trial, and the investigating judge declined jurisdiction over her complaint. The defendants denied the allegations, and witness accounts, including G.B.’s, were contradictory.

**Case: Mediakompaniya Slovo, TOV and Others v. Ukraine**  
**Application no. 22347/14 – ECHR Fifth Section, judgment of 10 July 2025**

The application was lodged on 7 March 2014 by three applicants: Mediakompaniya Slovo, TOV, a company publishing the newspaper *Subbota Plus*; Mr Vasylenko, the company’s director and the newspaper’s editor-in-chief; and Ms Vasylenko, the newspaper’s editorial director. The case concerned their complaint under Article 10 of the Convention that Ukrainian courts had ordered them to retract statements published in the newspaper, thereby allegedly violating their right to freedom of expression.

The key facts arose from an article written by Mr Vasylenko and published on 21 March 2013 in *Subbota Plus*, entitled “Drained profitability of [V.]”. The article concerned V., a large municipal water-supply company. It suggested corrupt practices at V. and contained numerous allegations, including that financial reports had not been published since a certain director took over; that documents showed embezzlement and squandering of tens of millions of State funds; that from summer 2012 funds were withdrawn “like an avalanche”; that contracts were made with intermediary companies at inflated prices; that private enterprises “pocketed” State money; that V. had given a 16 million hryvnia interest-free loan to a private person; that fraud occurred during renovation works; that second-hand parts were used and pipes unlawfully sold; that employees who complained were fired or demoted; that officials responsible for checking State budget expenditures did nothing; and that V.’s management was marked by corruption, irresponsibility, lack of professionalism and “moral bankruptcy”, leaving V. on the verge of bankruptcy. The article purported to rely on documents and statements from V. employees.

In April 2013, V. instituted proceedings against all three applicants, seeking retraction of the statements and compensation for non-pecuniary damage. The applicants argued before the domestic courts that the statements were value judgments not susceptible of proof, that the information was not negative, and that it had not been clear from the article that the statements referred to V.

On 17 June 2013, the Zhovtnevyi District Court of Zaporizhzhya found against the applicants. It examined each disputed statement and concluded that they were statements of fact, not value judgments. It further found that the applicants had failed to prove that those statements were true. The court ordered the applicants to retract the information and to publish the operative part of the judgment in the next issue of *Subbota Plus*. It also prohibited them from disseminating the information contained in those statements “by any possible means”, including television, printed media, radio, the internet, interviews, conversations with any person, or by any other means. The applicants were ordered to pay V. 1 Ukrainian hryvnia in non-pecuniary damages and UAH 458 in court fees. The court relied in particular on Article 278 of the Civil Code as in force at the material time.

The applicants’ appeals were rejected, with the final decision given by the Higher Specialized Court on 9 September 2013. According to the Government, the writs of execution in respect of the court decisions were never submitted to the Bailiffs Service for execution. Ms Vasylenko died on 28 June 2020. On 29 March 2023, Mr Vasylenko informed the Court that Mediakompaniya Slovo did not wish to pursue the application.

The central alleged violation was therefore under Article 10: the domestic courts’ orders requiring the applicants to retract allegedly factual but unproven statements and imposing a broad prohibition on any further dissemination of that information, which the applicants claimed unjustifiably restricted their freedom of expression.

In *A.J. and L.E. v. Spain*, two Spanish nationals complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention that Spain failed to conduct an effective criminal investigation into their alleged sexual assault by chemical submission, and that crucial evidence held in police custody was lost or manipulated.

On the night of 7–8 December 2016, the applicants went to a bar in Pamplona. They met two men, D.C.M. and R.G.S., and drank alcohol. The applicants alleged they had no recollection of events from their time at the bar until the following morning, when they awoke undressed in the residence of one of the men with the physical sensation of having had sexual intercourse. They claimed they had been subjected to chemical submission—administered substances that rendered them unconscious and incapable of consenting. On 11 December 2016, A.J. attended a health centre. The medical report noted no genital lesions but activated the protocol for suspected sexual assault involving chemical submission and notified police. L.E. did not seek immediate medical attention.

The National Police Family and Women’s Unit (UFAM) investigated. On 27 December 2016, police arrested D.C.M. and R.G.S. On 29 December, the investigating court questioned them; both admitted sexual intercourse but claimed it was consensual. Restraining orders were imposed. The case was transferred and formal criminal proceedings opened in January 2017. During the investigation, it emerged that R.G.S. was the brother-in-law of a UFAM police officer involved in the case.

Several crucial evidence items disappeared or were compromised in police custody. The full forensic report from R.G.S.’s mobile telephone, prepared in Madrid and sent to Pamplona on 11 April 2017, disappeared. Bar video surveillance footage was partially lost and altered, with missing or manipulated segments. The hard drive storing forensic data from both suspects’ mobile phones was wiped and overwritten, losing all contents and backups.

In November 2018, the investigating court declined to prosecute. It found the applicants’ accounts credible and without ulterior motive, but concluded there was insufficient evidence of non-consensual acts. No timely toxicological evidence supported chemical submission; physical discomfort could not be definitively linked to the alleged events; and forensic examination showed no typical injuries of violent assault. Vulgar messages exchanged by suspects after the event were not probative. The threshold of reasonable suspicion was not met. Separate proceedings were opened regarding possible misconduct and evidence tampering.

In October 2021, the court concluded proceedings without charges. Hair analysis found no substances consistent with chemical submission but showed prescription medications that could increase alcohol’s effects. Taxi drivers, bar staff, friends, bank records, residence searches, WhatsApp messages, and police reports on lost video were considered. The court accepted the applicants were credible and that intercourse occurred, but found the evidence did not prove beyond reasonable doubt that the suspects administered substances or knew the applicants lacked consciousness. Witnesses described no rapid intoxication typical of GHB or scopolamine; the barman and taxi driver saw nothing unusual. The court acknowledged the investigation was “notably affected” by irregularities and lost digital evidence, but held this did not compensate for the lack of substantive evidence. Appeals were dismissed in 2022, and an amparo appeal was declared inadmissible on procedural grounds.

Three separate investigations examined alleged police misconduct: handling of digital forensic evidence, including by the officer related to the suspect; manipulation or disappearance of bar video; and erasure of the hard drive. These were largely discontinued or closed for insufficient evidence of intentional criminal conduct. A disciplinary file remained suspended.

The applicants’ Convention complaints therefore concerned the alleged ineffectiveness of the criminal investigation into sexual assault and the loss or manipulation of crucial police-held evidence, including a conflict of interest.

In *Petrosyan v Armenia* (App no. 51448/15, ECtHR, 9 January 2025), the applicant, Heghine Petrosyan, is the mother of H. Movsisyan. She complained under Articles 2 and 13 about her son’s death in custody and the ensuing investigation.

In June 2011 Movsisyan was conscripted into the Armenian army and assigned to a Nagorno-Karabakh armed forces unit despite reported health problems. From the outset he failed to adapt, refused duties, and on 27 June 2011 absconded. When returned, during an interview with Lt Col H.S., he cut his left forearm with a razor. He was diagnosed with an organic psychopathic-like disorder and non-adaptive decompensation with attempted suicide. On 2 August 2011 the Central Military Commission found him unfit for peacetime service and fit only for non-combatant wartime service; he was discharged on 28 September 2011.

Nevertheless, criminal proceedings for evasion had begun in July 2011. Charges were later replaced by charges of self-mutilation to evade military service. The indictment was sent to the Syunik Regional Court in December 2011. In January 2012 the court authorised his detention, stayed the case, and ordered a search. He was arrested in July 2012, held in Nubarashen, and transferred in September 2012 to Shushi Detention Centre in the unrecognised “NKR”. On 20 November 2012 he was convicted and sentenced to three years. On 28 November 2012 he was found dead in his cell, hanging from window bars by a bedsheet.

The official version was suicide. An autopsy found mechanical asphyxiation due to hanging; no alcohol; and no visible injuries apart from a ligature mark and a scratch on his right forearm. The “NKR” authorities opened a criminal case for alleged incitement to suicide. After questioning guards and cellmates, the investigation concluded that he had not been threatened or ill-treated by staff or detainees and that he had killed himself because of his psychiatric disorder and recent conviction. The case was terminated in March 2013 for absence of a crime.
