The case of *Panopoulou and Others v. Greece* (Application no. 28983/20) is an application against Greece lodged with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention on 6 July 2020. The applicants are 13 individuals. They are represented by Mr A. Papakonstantinou, a lawyer practising in Athens. The Greek Government were given notice of the application. After the case was communicated, the parties attempted but failed to reach a friendly settlement. The Third Section of the Court, sitting as a Committee composed of Diana Kovatcheva, Canòlic Mingorance Cairat and Vasilka Sancin, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar, deliberated in private on 2 October 2025 and delivered judgment on 23 October 2025. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The factual foundation of the complaint is a domestic judgment given by the Athens Administrative Court of First Instance, Judgment no. 14300/2005, dated 30 November 2005. The applicants did not complain about the content or fairness of that judgment as such. Instead, they complained that the judgment was not enforced. According to the appended table, the non-enforcement period began on 22 August 2006. The end date is recorded as pending, meaning that enforcement had still not occurred at the time the table was prepared. The total length of non-enforcement is stated as more than 18 years, 5 months and 21 days. That prolonged failure to execute a final domestic judicial decision is the central factual element relevant to the alleged violations.

The applicants’ details and information relevant to the application are set out in the appended table. They include members of the Panopoulou and Antypas families, with birth years ranging from 1935 to 1991; several entries are identified as households. The table does not set out the underlying substantive dispute or identify the authority responsible for enforcement. It does, however, establish the chronology: a final administrative-court judgment in 2005, the start of non-enforcement in August 2006, and an unresolved enforcement situation lasting more than eighteen years by the time of the proceedings. That chronology is key because the complaint is not about a single delay but about a continuing failure to give effect to a final judgment.

Before the Court, the applicants complained of the non-enforcement of a domestic judgment and of the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law in that regard.

The case of *Monteiro and Trinta Santos v. Portugal* (Applications nos. 40620/22 and 44221/22) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered on 6 March 2025. It originated in two applications lodged against Portugal under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Both applicants complained under Article 3 that the conditions of their detention at Coimbra Prison were inadequate. The second applicant, in application no. 44221/22, additionally complained under Article 13 that there was no effective domestic remedy for those conditions. The Portuguese Government were given notice of the applications. The applicants were represented by Mr R. Mendes Martins, a lawyer practising in Lisbon, and Mr V. Carreto, a lawyer practising in Torres Vedras.

The first applicant, António Augusto Monteiro, born in 1986, introduced application no. 40620/22 on 12 August 2022. He was detained at Coimbra Prison from 27 December 2021 to 3 December 2022, a period of 11 months and 7 days, and then again from 30 June 2023, still pending at the time of the appended table, for more than 1 year and 6 months. During both periods he was held in a cell with two inmates, with 3.10 m² per inmate and one toilet. He alleged overcrowding, lack of privacy when using the toilet, lack of fresh air, inadequate temperature, passive smoking, poor quality food, infestation of the cell with insects or rodents, and a mouldy or dirty cell. The table indicates that the same grievances applied to both detention periods.

The second applicant, Hugo David Trinta Santos, born in 1984, introduced application no. 44221/22 on 6 September 2022. He was detained at Coimbra Prison from 15 July 2022, still pending, for more than 1 year and 6 months. He was also held in a cell with two inmates, but with only 2.25 m² per inmate and one toilet. His specific grievances were overcrowding, inadequate temperature, lack of requisite medical assistance, a mouldy or dirty cell, lack of fresh air, and lack or insufficient quantity of food. He further alleged, under Article 13, that no effective domestic remedy was available in respect of these detention conditions.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the prolonged periods of detention and the very limited cell space per inmate—3.10 m² for Monteiro and 2.25 m² for Trinta Santos—in shared cells with only one toilet. The applicants rely on a combination of overcrowding, lack of privacy, poor hygiene, infestation, inadequate ventilation and temperature, passive smoking, insufficient or poor food, and, for Trinta Santos, lack of medical assistance. These conditions form the basis of their Article 3 complaint that they were subjected to inhuman or degrading treatment. Trinta Santos’s additional Article 13 complaint concerns the alleged absence of an effective domestic remedy to challenge those conditions. The judgment was adopted on 6 February 2025 and delivered on 6 March 2025

In *Aslan and Others v. Türkiye* (Applications nos. 12531/21 and 8 others), the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) delivered judgment on 13 November 2025. The case originated in nine applications against Türkiye lodged under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants’ central complaint was that their pre-trial detention had been excessively long and had been ordered or extended without relevant and sufficient reasons. In applications nos. 18927/21 and 16303/23, the applicants also raised other Convention complaints, but the judgment’s appended table focuses on the detention-related facts.

The applicants were Dilan Aslan, Mehmet Bozkurt, Ayşegül Çağatay Gökçe, Sadun Kaya, Şeyhmus Çeri, Mensur Akar, Helin Yapıcı, İrfan Yıldız, and Mücahit Doğan. Their detention periods varied widely, from about seven months to nearly nine years.

Dilan Aslan (b. 1991) was detained from 16 March 2020 to 27 October 2020, a total of 7 months and 12 days, by the Denizli 2nd and 3rd Assize Courts. The grounds cited were strong suspicion, the nature of the offence, the fact that it was a “catalogue offence” under Article 100 § 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the severity of the potential sentence, risk of absconding, and risk of tampering with evidence.

Mehmet Bozkurt (b. 1975) was detained from 5 July 2015 to 5 June 2020—4 years, 11 months, and 1 day—by the Ağrı Assize Court. The grounds included the nature of the offence, strong suspicion, the severity of the offences and potential sentence, and the offence being listed in Article 100 § 3.

Ayşegül Çağatay Gökçe (b. 1991) was detained from 25 June 2011 to 31 March 2020—8 years, 9 months, and 7 days—by Istanbul magistrate and assize courts. The grounds cited were the nature of the offence, catalogue offence status, minimum and maximum prescribed sentences, risk of absconding, and risk of tampering with evidence.

Sadun Kaya (b. 1968) was detained from 2 July 2018 to 16 September 2022—4 years, 2 months, and 15 days—by the Kocaeli 1st and 2nd Assize Courts. The stated grounds were the severity of potential sentences, the scope of the case, and the fact that evidence such as expert reports had not yet been collected.

Şeyhmus Çeri (b. 1997) was detained from 17 August 2016 to 10 October 2018—2 years, 1 month, and 24 days—by the Şanlıurfa Assize Court. Grounds were strong suspicion, nature of the offence, and severity of the potential sentence.

Mensur Akar (b. 1995) was detained from 18 April 2016 to 3 January 2019, and again from 20 December 2019 to 27 October 2022—a total of 6 years, 6 months, and 23 days—by the Hakkari Assize Court. Grounds included strong suspicion, nature of the offences, catalogue offence status, and severity of the offence.

Helin Yapıcı (b. 1994) was detained from 23 March 2016 to 6 April 2021—5 years and 15 days—by the Diyarbakır Assize Court. Grounds were strong suspicion, nature of the offence, catalogue offence status, and severity of the potential sentence.

İrfan Yıldız (b. 1980) was detained from 16 February 2017 to 27 March 2019, and from 25 December 2019 to 25 June 2020—2 years, 1 month, and 12 days plus 6 months and 1 day—by Istanbul magistrate and assize courts. Grounds included his contacts, the state of evidence, insufficiency of alternative judicial supervision measures, catalogue offence status, severity of the potential sentence, the fact that ISIS had resorted to terror acts on New Year’s Eve and special days, and that detention was more appropriate.

Mücahit Doğan (b. 1983) was detained from 31 December 2021 to 27 December 2022—11 months and 28 days—by Küçükçekmece magistrates and criminal courts. Grounds were strong suspicion, nature of the offence, catalogue offence status, severity of the potential sentence, risk of absconding, and risk of tampering with evidence.

The key issue for the Court was whether these often lengthy detentions, particularly where courts repeatedly relied on statutory catalogue offences and the severity of potential sentences, were supported by relevant and sufficient reasons.

**Case Summary: Hora v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 1048/20)**

The applicant, Michael Christopher Hora, is a British national born in 1966 and detained at HMP Bure, Norwich. In October 2007 he was convicted of two counts of rape and one count of sexual assault committed against a victim in her home. His defence that the sexual relations were consensual was rejected. He had a previous rape conviction in 2000, for which he received a seven-year prison sentence later reduced on appeal. Following the 2007 conviction, the court imposed an indeterminate sentence of imprisonment for public protection with a minimum term of four years, less time on remand. That minimum term expired in 2011, but Hora remained in detention because the Parole Board had not recommended his release.

A UK general election was held on 12 December 2019. Under section 3 of the Representation of the People Act 1983, convicted prisoners detained in a penal institution pursuant to their sentence are legally incapable of voting in parliamentary or local elections. Limited exceptions apply, including to prisoners detained for contempt of court, default in paying a fine, or on remand. Hora fell within the general disqualification and was therefore ineligible to vote in the 2019 election. He complained under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights, which guarantees the right to free elections. His application was lodged on 6 January 2020. The Court gave notice to the UK Government of the complaint concerning his ineligibility to vote and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

Hora did not bring domestic proceedings. Although UK courts may consider whether primary legislation is Convention-compatible, they cannot disapply statutory provisions. A domestic court had already made a declaration that section 3 of the 1983 Act was incompatible with a Convention right in Smith v. Scott (2007). Hora considered that seeking another such declaration would be futile.

The case arises against long-running political and legal controversy over prisoner voting. In Hirst v. the United Kingdom (no. 2) (2005), the European Court of Human Rights found that the UK’s blanket ban on prisoner voting violated Article 3 of Protocol No. 1. Subsequent UK consultations and proposals considered limited enfranchisement. In 2010 the Government proposed replacing the blanket ban with a rule disenfranchising prisoners sentenced to four years or more. In 2011 the House of Commons passed a non-binding motion supporting the existing position that no prisoner could vote except those imprisoned for contempt, default, or on remand. A 2012 draft bill and a 2013 Joint Committee report recommended allowing prisoners serving 12 months or less to vote and permitting pre-release registration, but no legislation followed. In 2017 the Government instead proposed administrative changes: clarifying at sentencing that prisoners lose the vote, and allowing prisoners on temporary licence or home detention curfew to vote, while maintaining the bar on prisoners in custody.

Domestic courts in R (Chester) v. Secretary of State for Justice (2013) declined to make a further declaration of incompatibility, with the Supreme Court finding no individual violation for serious offenders and stressing that reform was for Parliament. The Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers repeatedly urged the UK to implement Hirst, but the UK cited parliamentary opposition. Scotland later allowed prisoners sentenced to 12 months or less to vote in Scottish Parliament and local elections; a similar Welsh proposal was not pursued. The central alleged violation is that Hora, while detained in prison on polling day, was automatically disenfranchised under section 3 despite the nature of his sentence and individual circumstances.

In *Ayala Flores v. Italy*, the European Court of Human Rights examined whether enforcing a criminal demolition order against the applicant’s home violated her right to respect for her home under Article 8 of the Convention. The applicant, a Peruvian national born in 1957 living in Procida (Naples), had in the early 1990s erected a small dwelling with her husband on his land without a building permit. The property was in a highly seismic zone and subject to landscape/environmental constraints and an absolute ban on construction. The couple made it their home.

In 1996 the municipality found the construction unauthorised and ordered restoration within sixty days. In 1998 it issued a demolition order. In 1999 the applicant and her husband were prosecuted for unauthorised construction and for twice breaking police seals after further altering the building. In May 2002 the Naples District Court convicted them, imposed suspended sentences, and ordered demolition. On appeal in 2003, some offences were time-barred, but the convictions for unauthorised construction and violating seals were upheld; the sentence was reduced and the seizure lifted to allow demolition. The judgment became final in October 2003. In 2004 the applicant applied for a building amnesty and paid fees, but received no response. Her husband died in 2009, and she continued living in the dwelling.

In 2016 the public prosecutor responsible for enforcing the demolition order asked the municipality whether demolition had occurred or whether public-interest reasons prevented it. The municipality served an eviction notice, and the prosecutor ordered the applicant to demolish within ninety days or have it done at her expense. The applicant asked the municipality to recognise a public interest in keeping the structure, then filed an application for review of enforcement (*incidente di esecuzione*), seeking annulment, revocation or a stay of demolition. Initially she did not invoke Article 8; in additional submissions she claimed the dwelling was her only home, she had lived there over fifteen years since conviction, and she had financial difficulties, relying on Article 8 and *Ivanova and Cherkezov v. Bulgaria*.

In November 2018/2019 the Naples Court of Appeal dismissed her application, treating the demolition order as a mainly restorative, mandatory consequence of unauthorised construction, and did not address her Article 8 submissions. In 2020 the Court of Cassation rejected her appeal as inadmissible, partly because she had not attached the additional submissions and thus failed the self-sufficiency requirement. It also reasoned that Article 8 does not confer an absolute right to a home; she could not have a legitimate expectation to remain in a building she knew was unauthorised; her Article 8 complaint was generic; and she had not shown individual circumstances outweighing the public interest in restoring the site.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained under Article 8 about the proportionality of enforcing the demolition order and, specifically, the lack of domestic review of its impact on her right to a home. The Court communicated only that complaint; the remainder was declared inadmissible.

After communication, the government submitted inspection reports (2020, 2022, 2024) describing the construction as apparently uninhabited or unfit, with unauthorised fence and shutters. The applicant submitted evidence of residence since 2001, a pension of about EUR 551.59 monthly, annual income of EUR 4,943, no other home, and photos of the interior and exterior. As of April 2025, the house had not been demolished. Italian law required demolition upon conviction, but Cassation case-law recognised that enforcement judges should conduct a proportionality review under Article 8 when the individual specifically raises personal circumstances.

**A.R. v. the United Kingdom** (Application no. 6033/19) concerns the police disclosure, through enhanced criminal record certificates (“ECRCs”), of information that the applicant had been charged with rape and later acquitted, together with details of the alleged offence. The applicant, a British national born in 1978, was a qualified teacher but worked as a taxi driver. In March 2010 he was charged with raping a 17-year-old female passenger. He denied any sexual contact; there was no forensic evidence linking him to her. On 21 January 2011 he was acquitted by a jury.

In March 2011, an ECRC was issued for his application for a college lecturer post. Under section 113B of the Police Act 1997, an ECRC contained convictions and cautions plus “other relevant information” disclosed at the chief police officer’s discretion, sometimes called “soft intelligence.” The applicant had no convictions or cautions. The ECRC nevertheless stated that police had received an allegation that an intoxicated 17-year-old taxi passenger had been taken to a secluded location and forcibly raped; that the applicant was identified, arrested, denied sex and claimed he rejected her advances; and that he was charged, appeared before the Crown Court on 21 January 2011, was found not guilty, and the case was discharged.

The applicant objected on 20 April 2011, arguing that there was no conviction, the jury had rejected the complainant’s evidence, and disclosure was grossly prejudicial and would prevent fair consideration for employment. His appeal was rejected. A reviewing officer, Inspector K., considered disclosure relevant because the lecturer role could allow him to befriend vulnerable females. She reasoned that the Crown Prosecution Service’s decision to charge indicated a realistic prospect of conviction, that the allegation was more likely true than false on the balance of probabilities, and that acquittal did not prove innocence because the criminal standard was higher. She referred to medical evidence, the complainant’s distress, lack of motive to lie, and explained inconsistencies by intoxication. She concluded that disclosure was reasonable and proportionate because the alleged offence was serious, relatively recent, and relevant to safeguarding vulnerable people, and that the risk outweighed the impact on the applicant’s Article 8 rights.

In March 2012, a further ECRC was issued for a private hire driver licence. It contained the same information. The same reviewing officer reached the same conclusion, and a senior officer authorised disclosure, noting the risk to children and vulnerable adults.

The applicant sought judicial review, relying on Article 6 § 2 (presumption of innocence) and Article 8 (private life). The High Court rejected the claim on 5 September 2013. It found Article 8 engaged, but held disclosure reasonable, proportionate, and no more than necessary. Although the reviewing officer had wrongly treated the charging decision as showing likely truth, the judge found the police were entitled to conclude the information was “not lacking in substance” and “might be true.” The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 10 June 2016, finding no undermining of the acquittal and no Article 8 breach. The Supreme Court granted permission only on Article 8 and dismissed the appeal on 30 July 2018. Lord Carnwath held that police were not required to conduct a “mini-trial” or decide guilt after acquittal. While the reviewing officer had erred in assessing whether the allegation was more likely true than not, the judge had correctly applied a lower “might be true” test. Disclosure was proportionate given the seriousness, recent occurrence, relevance to the same employment, and protection of vulnerable persons. A postscript noted concerns about how employers treat ECRCs and the stigmatisation of acquitted persons.

The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 21 January 2019. His name was not disclosed. The key alleged violations concern whether the disclosure of his rape charge and acquittal in employment vetting breached the presumption of innocence under Article 6 § 2 and the right to respect for private life under Article 8.

Federici v. France (Application no. 52302/19) concerns Jean-François Federici, a French national born in 1957 and detained. He was indicted and committed for trial before the Bouches-du-Rhône Assize Court on charges of murder committed as a member of an organised group and conspiracy to commit a crime. In 2011, after failing to comply with court supervision, he absconded. In 2014 he was convicted in absentia and sentenced to thirty years’ imprisonment. Arrested in 2016, he was retried in 2017 and again sentenced to thirty years; he appealed.

The appeal hearings took place in April 2018 at the Aix-en-Provence Law Courts. Federici appeared in a glass dock under Article 318 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The dock was an open-roofed glass enclosure measuring 3.68 by 2.47 metres, with perforations (hygiaphones) for communication with defence lawyers seated adjacent, document slots, fixed microphones and a loudspeaker enabling him to hear courtroom proceedings. It had a glass door to the courtroom and a solid security door to a secure waiting area.

On 6 April 2018, Federici was questioned about his personality; he did not complain of hearing difficulties or ask to be questioned outside the dock. On 10 April, his lawyer requested that he appear in the courtroom rather than the glass dock, relying on Article 6 of the Convention, the preliminary article of the Code of Criminal Procedure and Directive (EU) 2016/343. The request cited the public’s security checks and the applicant’s hearing impairment, which sometimes made it harder to hear questions. On 11 April, the president questioned him while he remained in the dock.

On 13 April 2018, the Assize Court dismissed the request. It held that Articles 318 and D.294 required security measures for an accused’s appearance, considering the danger he posed and the need to prevent escape. It noted the charges, his exposure to life imprisonment, and that he had absconded for more than four years. It observed that despite his hearing problems he could answer questions and communicate confidentially with his lawyers, and that he could move freely in the dock. It found the measures lawful, proportionate and necessary, not infringing the presumption of innocence, dignity or defence rights. The same day, the Assize Court convicted him of double murder as a member of an organised group and sentenced him to thirty years. On 10 April 2019, the Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal on points of law, finding no indication that he had been prevented from communicating with his lawyers.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Federici alleged violations of Article 6 §§ 1, 2 and 3(b) of the Convention—fair trial, presumption of innocence, and adequate facilities for defence—arising from his appearance in the glass dock and the refusal to allow him to answer questions from the witness stand. Relevant contextual material included a Public Defender’s Office opinion recommending repeal or restricted use of secure docks, and an Inspector-General report warning that such docks could hinder confidential lawyer-client exchanges and defence rights. Domestic law provided that an accused appears free and only accompanied by guards to prevent escape, while EU Directive 2016/343 permitted physical restraints only for case-specific security, absconding or contact-prevention reasons.

**Case: A.R.E. v. Greece (App. No. 15783/21)** concerns the alleged “pushback” of a Turkish national from Greece to Türkiye in May 2019, raising issues under Articles 2, 3, 5, and 13 ECHR.

The applicant, a Turkish national born in 1992, had been accused of membership in FETÖ/PDY. She was detained for 28 months, then sentenced in March 2019 to six years and three months’ imprisonment, but released pending appeal with a ban on leaving Türkiye. On 4 May 2019, she crossed the Evros River into Greece with two other Turkish nationals seeking international protection. Near Nea Vyssa, she contacted her brother, an asylum seeker in Greece, using WhatsApp live location. She sent photos and videos stating she feared unlawful removal. She and her brother also emailed UNHCR, explaining their fear of pushback and danger if returned to Türkiye.

A lawyer, N.O., traveled to Nea Vyssa. Shortly afterward, police arrived and arrested the three Turkish nationals. The applicant alleged that police refused to let the lawyer enter the vehicle but allowed him to follow in his car. At the police station, she requested asylum for the first time; she repeated the request at the Orestiada border guard station in Neo Cheimonio. She claimed she was then held unofficially until 7 p.m., when the alleged pushback began.

She described being transferred in a green van and later in a larger lorry with 31 migrants. Their belongings—bags, shoes, mobile phones, and money—were confiscated. She had injured her leg and was forced to walk barefoot, worsening her injury. Near the Evros River, masked men in camouflage, probably police officers, made them disembark. Those who resisted, including Syrians, were allegedly beaten. When she shouted “asylum,” an officer allegedly replied in Turkish, “you will see where we will take you.” Around 11 p.m., they were placed in a small inflatable boat and returned to Türkiye in several crossings. Turkish gendarmerie arrested them. She was taken to Edirne Prison and later Gebze Prison. Her brother lost her WhatsApp location at 6:52 p.m. on 4 May 2019.

Domestically, the Greek Council for Refugees filed a complaint in June 2019 alleging abuse of power, unlawful detention, life-endangerment, bodily harm, torture, and other offences. In December 2019, the Orestiada prosecutor dismissed the complaint for lack of evidence. On appeal, further investigation heard lawyer N.O. and journalist Z.K. N.O. stated he had seen the applicant in Nea Vyssa, witnessed her arrest, and later saw the van at the Orestiada border guard station. Z.K. described communications with the applicant and her brother and the location tracking. In September 2020, the prosecutor again dismissed the case, finding no substantiating evidence, noting no arrest of a person with the same name, stating police had orders and did not conduct pushbacks, and concluding asylum would have been possible if she had been detected.

The Greek Government denied all allegations. It argued that the evidence was unverified, that photos and videos lacked metadata, that the applicant’s brother never testified, and that N.O.’s account was unreliable. The applicant maintained that she had submitted evidence, including a Turkish court decision referring to her pushback, and that she had indeed been arrested and imprisoned in Türkiye. The case therefore turned on whether the alleged pushback, detention, and risk of ill-treatment in Türkiye were established and whether Greece violated the Convention.

In *Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V. and Others v. the Netherlands*, six Dutch limited liability companies complained under Article 8 of the Convention that intercept data lawfully obtained during criminal investigations had been transmitted to competition authorities and used against them in administrative fine proceedings. They also alleged a violation of Article 13, arguing that no effective domestic remedy existed for that complaint.

The first group of applicants were companies involved in collecting waste liquids from ships in Rotterdam. In 2006, the VROM-IOD began a criminal investigation, “Toto”, into suspected forgery and environmental offences. An investigating judge authorised telephone interceptions. Some intercepted conversations indicated possible price-fixing. In 2008, an official record with transcripts was prepared, and in October 2008 the public prosecutor authorised transmission of selected transcripts and audio recordings to the Netherlands Competition Authority (NMA) under section 39f of the Judicial and Criminal Data Act (WJSG). Further transmissions occurred in 2009 and 2010, sometimes approved by handwritten notes or pre-printed forms without detailed reasoning. The NMA used the material in its competition-law investigation, inspected premises, questioned managers, and ultimately imposed fines for anti-competitive conduct, including EUR 834,000 on Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V. and joint fines of up to EUR 1,861,000 on related companies.

The applicants objected, arguing that the intercepted data were not “criminal data” under the WJSG, that they were irrelevant “by-catch”, that there was no prior judicial review of the transmissions, that the NMA itself had no power to intercept communications, and that using intercept material in administrative penalty proceedings circumvented criminal-procedure safeguards. The Rotterdam Regional Court initially accepted part of these arguments, finding no identifiable weighing of interests by the prosecutor and excluding the transcripts as evidence. However, the Supreme Administrative Court for Trade and Industry later quashed that judgment. It held that the interceptions formed part of the criminal file, qualified as criminal data, and could be transmitted. It found a compelling general interest in enforcing competition law—the economic well-being of the country—and that transmission was necessary, especially because price-fixing agreements are rarely documented. It also considered that sufficient judicial review existed in civil and administrative proceedings.

The second group, the Janssen de Jong construction companies, arose from the “Cleveland” criminal investigation into bribery. Interceptions authorised by an investigating judge revealed possible bid-rigging. Police gave NMA officials confidential access to transcripts, and a prosecutor later permitted use of the data. The NMA imposed a EUR 3 million joint fine. These applicants similarly argued that the transmission was unlawful, unforeseeable, lacked prior judicial review, and that the NMA could not lawfully use intercept material. A provisional-measures judge dismissed their claims, finding the WJSG applicable, a compelling economic interest, and no Article 8 breach.

The central alleged violations were therefore whether the transmission of lawfully intercepted criminal data to competition authorities, and its use in administrative fine proceedings, was “in accordance with the law” and “necessary in a democratic society” under Article 8, and whether the applicants had an effective remedy under Article 13. The Chamber declared the applications admissible, found no violation of Article 8 by four votes to three, and no violation of Article 13. The Grand Chamber subsequently accepted referral and delivered judgment on 1 April 2025.

**Federici v. France (Application no. 52302/19)** concerns an applicant’s complaint that his appearance in a glass dock during criminal proceedings before an assize court of appeal, and the court’s refusal to let him answer questions from the witness stand, violated Article 6 §§ 1, 2 and 3(b) of the Convention (fair trial, presumption of innocence, and rights of the defence).

The applicant, Jean-François Federici, a French national born in 1957, was indicted for murder committed as a member of an organised group and for conspiracy to commit a crime. In 2011, while under court supervision, he absconded. In December 2014, the Assize Court tried him in absentia and sentenced him to thirty years’ imprisonment. He was arrested in 2016, placed in pre-trial detention, and retried. In January 2017, the Assize Court again sentenced him to thirty years’ imprisonment and ordered confiscation. He appealed.

The appeal hearings took place in April 2018 in the Aix-en-Provence Law Courts, in its standard courtroom. The applicant was assisted by two lawyers. He appeared in a glass dock pursuant to Article 318 of the French Code of Criminal Procedure. The dock was an open-roofed glass enclosure measuring 3.68 metres by 2.47 metres. It had two perforations (hygiaphones) at human height for communication with defence counsel, two slots for passing documents, fixed microphones for hearing the accused, and a loudspeaker allowing him to hear courtroom microphones. It also had a glass door to the courtroom and a solid security door to a secure waiting area.

On 6 April 2018, the applicant was heard regarding his personality. He did not complain of hearing difficulties and did not ask to be questioned outside the dock. On 10 April, his lawyer requested that he appear outside the glass dock, relying on Article 6 of the Convention, the preliminary article of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and recital 20 of Directive (EU) 2016/343. The lawyer argued that members of the public had undergone security checks and that the applicant had a hearing impairment which sometimes made it difficult for him to hear questions. On 11 April, the applicant was questioned while remaining in the dock.

In an interlocutory judgment of 13 April 2018, the Assize Court dismissed the request. It held that Articles 318 and D.294 of the Code of Criminal Procedure required courts to take security measures necessary for the accused’s appearance, considering the danger he posed and the need to protect him. It noted that Article 5 of Directive 2016/343 did not prevent physical restraints where necessary for security or to prevent absconding or contact with third parties. The court emphasised that the applicant faced life imprisonment, was in pre-trial detention, and had absconded for more than four years. It observed that, despite his hearing problems, he had been able to answer questions and communicate confidentially with his lawyers and was free to move within the dock. It concluded that the measure was lawful, proportionate, and necessary, and did not breach the presumption of innocence, human dignity, or defence rights. The same day, he was convicted of double murder as a member of an organised group and sentenced to thirty years’ imprisonment.

The applicant appealed on points of law, arguing insufficient reasoning and citing Belousov v. Russia. On 10 April 2019, the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal, finding that the Assize Court’s reasoning did not show he had been prevented from communicating with his lawyers. The case also referenced criticism of glass docks by the Public Defender’s Office and the Inspector-General of Custodial Premises, and French case-law permitting docks where free movement and confidential communication are ensured.

**Case: Ayala Flores v. Italy (Application no. 16803/21)** concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from the enforcement of a demolition order against the applicant’s home. The applicant, a Peruvian national born in 1957, lived in Procida, Italy.

In the early 1990s, the applicant and her husband built a small 30 sq. m dwelling on land owned by him in Procida and made it their home. The construction was erected without a building permit in an area subject to seismic risk, landscape constraints, and an absolute ban on building because it was classified as of specific environmental interest.

In August 1996, the municipality found that the premises had been built without authorisation. In September 1996, it ordered restoration of the site within sixty days, and in 1998 it issued a demolition order. In 1999, the applicant and her husband were prosecuted for unauthorised construction under Law no. 47 of 1985 and for breaking police seals placed on the site after further modifications. In 2002, the Naples District Court convicted them, imposed a suspended five-month prison sentence and a €300 fine, and ordered demolition of the construction. In 2003, the Naples Court of Appeal partly declared the offences time-barred but upheld convictions for unauthorised construction and violation of seals, reduced the sentence, and lifted seizure solely to allow demolition. The judgment became final in October 2003.

In December 2004, the applicant applied for a building amnesty under Decree-Law no. 269 of 2003 and paid the required fees, but the application went unanswered. Under the relevant law, building work in areas subject to landscape and environmental constraints could not benefit from amnesty. Her husband died in 2009, and she continued living in the dwelling.

In 2016, the public prosecutor began enforcing the demolition order. The municipality served an eviction notice in February 2016, and in March 2016 the prosecutor ordered the applicant to demolish the dwelling within ninety days or have it demolished at her expense. The applicant asked the municipality to recognise an overriding public interest in keeping the structure.

She then lodged an application for review of the enforcement order (*incidente di esecuzione*) before the Naples Court of Appeal, seeking annulment, revocation, or suspension of the demolition order. Her original grounds did not invoke Article 8. She later submitted additional written submissions claiming that the construction was her only home, that she had lived there for over fifteen years after conviction, and that she had financial difficulties. Citing *Ivanova and Cherkezov v. Bulgaria*, she argued that enforcement would disproportionately affect her Article 8 rights. The Government disputed that these submissions had actually been filed.

In 2018–2019, the Court of Appeal dismissed her application, treating the demolition order as a mainly restorative and mandatory measure under Cassation case-law. It did not address her Article 8 submissions. In 2020, the Court of Cassation rejected her further appeal as inadmissible, finding the Article 8 complaint lacked self-sufficiency because the additional submissions had not been attached or proven filed. It nonetheless reasoned that although loss of a home should permit proportionality review, her complaint was generic and did not show individual circumstances outweighing the public interest. It found no legitimate expectation after fifteen years because she knew the construction was unauthorised, that demolition was necessary to restore the site, and that no state of necessity was proven.

After the case was communicated, the Government submitted inspections from 2020, 2022, and 2024 indicating the construction was not inhabited and was unfit for use or suitable only as storage; later reports noted unauthorised fencing and shutters. The applicant submitted statements that she lived there and had nowhere else, a residence certificate since 2001, proof of a monthly pension of €551.59, annual household income of €4,943, and a surveyor’s report on her limited means and age. By April 2025, the dwelling had not been demolished.

The key Article 8 issue was whether enforcing the demolition order, and the domestic review of its proportionality, adequately protected the applicant’s right to respect for her home.

In *Ftiti v. Greece* (Application no. 37957/14), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint by Cherif Ftiti, a Tunisian national, concerning the effectiveness of his right of appeal under Article 2 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention. The applicant had lived in Greece since 1996 and held a residence permit; he also had two children born in Greece.

On 29 December 2009, the applicant was arrested in Rethymno on suspicion of aggravated livestock theft committed jointly and was detained pending trial. On 17 February 2010, the Chania Mixed Jury Court convicted him and sentenced him to seventeen years’ imprisonment and a €1,000 fine. The first-instance court ruled that any appeal would not have suspensive effect and ordered his deportation after completion of his sentence. It did not give reasons for refusing to suspend execution of the sentence.

The applicant lodged an appeal. On 30 January 2014, he attended a hearing before the Crete Criminal Court of Appeal, but the case was adjourned to 13 November 2014 because key prosecution witnesses were absent. On 27 October 2014, the prison director informed the prosecutor that the applicant did not wish to be transferred to court for the 13 November hearing, as his lawyer would represent him. On the day of that hearing, the applicant requested an adjournment, saying he could not contact his lawyer. On 20 January 2015, while still detained, he was notified that the appeal hearing had been rescheduled for 1 November 2015.

On 25 February 2015, the Chalkidiki Criminal Court of First Instance granted the applicant conditional release under Article 105 of the Criminal Code, finding that he had served three-fifths of his sentence after deductions for work and had demonstrated good behaviour. He was formally released on 6 March 2015, but was transferred to the Department of Illegal Migration in Triglia and placed in a detention facility for migrants. On 22 April 2015, he was deported to Tunisia and banned from entering the Schengen area. He was therefore removed from Greece before his appeal was heard.

On 26 October 2015, the Crete Mixed Jury Court of Appeal requested the prosecutor at the Chania Court of First Instance to secure the applicant’s attendance at the forthcoming hearing. That request could not be forwarded to him because he had not appointed a new representative and had provided an incomplete residential address in Tunisia. On 1 November 2015, the appeal court rejected the appeal because the applicant failed to appear. The appeal was thus dismissed as unfounded or unsupported (*ανυποστήρικτη*) on account of his absence, without a substantive examination.

The relevant domestic framework included Article 497 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which governs the suspensive effect of appeals. An appeal may lack suspensive effect where the accused has no known stable residence, may abscond, or where restrictive measures are insufficient. Under Article 497 § 9, a detained accused who is far from the court need not appear. The Court referred to its case-law in *Fırat v. Greece* and *Martzaklis and Others v. Greece*.

The alleged violation under Article 2 of Protocol No. 7 was that the applicant’s right of appeal was rendered ineffective: he was conditionally released and expelled before the appeal hearing, yet the appeal was later dismissed solely because he did not appear. The key issue was whether the Greek authorities’ conduct and the domestic procedure deprived him of a practical opportunity to have his criminal appeal examined.

**Summary of the Case**

The case of *Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V. and Others v. the Netherlands* (Application nos. 2799/16, 2800/16, 3124/16 and 3205/16) concerns four applications lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by six Dutch limited liability companies on 7 January 2016. The applicants complained that the transmission of intercept data—lawfully obtained during criminal investigations—to competition authorities violated their rights under Article 8 of the Convention and that they lacked an effective domestic remedy under Articles 8 and 13.

**First Group (Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V. et al.):** The applicants were engaged in collecting waste liquids from ships in the Rotterdam port region. In 2006, the VROM-IOD, a special investigative service, began a criminal investigation ("Toto") into the I. company for forgery and environmental offences. With authorisation from an investigating judge, telephone conversations of I. company employees were intercepted, including conversations with Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V. employees. Certain intercepted conversations contained indications of price-fixing and were identified as potentially relevant to the Netherlands Competition Authority (NMA). In October 2008, the public prosecutor authorised transmission of an official record and transcripts to the NMA under section 39f of the Judicial and Criminal Data Act (WJSG). Further transmissions occurred in October 2009, June, July, and August 2010. The NMA used this evidence to impose fines for price-fixing under section 6 of the Competition Act: EUR 834,000 on Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V. and EUR 1,861,000 jointly on the other companies.

**Second Group (Janssen de Jong Groep B.V. et al.):** The applicants were construction companies. Around 2007, a criminal investigation ("Cleveland") began into bribery of local government officials. Intercepted telephone conversations of Janssen employees, authorised under Article 126m of the Code of Criminal Procedure, contained indications of price-fixing. NMA officials were initially given confidential access to transcripts on police premises, then provided a CD of audio-recordings, and finally, in December 2008, formal transmission was authorised. The NMA imposed a EUR 3,000,000 fine on the Janssen companies for collusion on bidding figures.

**Alleged Violations:** The applicants argued that the transmission of intercept data to competition authorities was neither "in accordance with the law" nor "necessary in a democratic society," citing insufficient procedural safeguards, lack of prior judicial review, and the fact that the NMA lacked the power to intercept communications itself. They also contended that the intercept material should not have been admitted as evidence in administrative proceedings.

**Domestic Proceedings:** The Rotterdam Regional Court initially ruled in favour of the applicants, holding that the absence of an identifiable, reviewable weighing of interests by the public prosecutor meant the transcripts had to be excluded as evidence. However, the Supreme Administrative Court for Trade and Industry quashed these judgments, finding that the transmissions were lawful under the WJSG, that written reasoning at the time of transmission was not required, and that the enforcement of competition law constituted a compelling general interest—namely, the economic well-being of the country. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld the fines.

**ECtHR Proceedings:** A Chamber of the Third Section declared the applications admissible but found no violation of Article 8 (4-3) and no violation of Article 13 (unanimous). Following referral to the Grand Chamber, a hearing was held on 6 March 2024, and the Grand Chamber delivered its judgment on 1 April 2025.

**Ftiti v. Greece** (Application no. 37957/14), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, judgment of 26 August 2025, concerns the effectiveness of the applicant’s right of appeal in criminal proceedings. The applicant, Mr Cherif Ftiti, a Tunisian national born in 1973, had a Greek residence permit and had lived in Crete since 1996. He had two children born in Greece.

On 29 December 2009 the applicant was arrested in Rethymno on suspicion of aggravated theft of livestock committed jointly and was detained pending trial. On 17 February 2010 the Chania Mixed Jury Court sentenced him to seventeen years’ imprisonment and a fine of EUR 1,000. The first-instance court ruled that any appeal would not have suspensive effect and ordered his deportation from Greece upon completion of his sentence. It did not give reasons for refusing to suspend execution of the sentence.

The applicant lodged an appeal. On 30 January 2014 he attended a hearing before the Crete Criminal Court of Appeal, but the case was adjourned to 13 November 2014 because key prosecution witnesses were absent. On 27 October 2014 the director of Kassandra Prison informed the prosecutor that the applicant did not wish to be transferred to court for the 13 November hearing, since his lawyer would represent him. On the day of that hearing, the applicant sought an adjournment on the ground that he could not contact his lawyer. On 20 January 2015, while still detained, he was notified that the appeal hearing had been rescheduled for 1 November 2015.

On 25 February 2015 the Chalkidiki Criminal Court of First Instance granted the applicant conditional release under Article 105 of the Criminal Code. He had served three-fifths of his sentence after deduction of work days and had demonstrated good behaviour. He was formally released on 6 March 2015, but was transferred to the Department of Illegal Migration in Triglia and placed in a detention facility for migrants. On 22 April 2015 he was deported to Tunisia and banned from entering the Schengen area.

On 26 October 2015 the Crete Mixed Jury Appeal Court asked the prosecutor at the Chania Court of First Instance to arrange the applicant’s attendance at the forthcoming appeal hearing. That request could not be forwarded to him because he had not appointed a new representative and had provided an incomplete residential address in Tunisia. On 1 November 2015 the Crete Mixed Jury Court of Appeal rejected the appeal owing to the applicant’s failure to appear in court. The appeal was thus dismissed as unfounded for non-appearance.

The Court gave notice to the Greek Government of the complaint under Article 2 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention, concerning the effectiveness of the right of appeal. The key alleged violation is that the applicant’s appeal became ineffective because the hearing was set for a date after his conditional release and expulsion from Greece, making his attendance impossible, while the domestic court then dismissed the appeal solely because he was absent.

Relevant domestic law includes Article 497 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It provides that where a conviction entails imprisonment, the court hearing the case decides whether an appeal has suspensive effect, giving reasons and applying statutory criteria. Suspensive effect may be refused where, for example, restrictive measures are insufficient, the accused lacks a known and stable residence, or there is a risk of absconding. However, suspension must be granted if immediate imprisonment would cause disproportionate and irreparable harm to the accused or family. The provision also states that if a detained accused is far from the court, he or she shall not appear. The case therefore turns on whether Greece breached the applicant’s right to an effective appeal by deporting him before the appeal hearing and then dismissing his appeal for non-appearance.

The applicant, Mr Cherif Ftiti, a Tunisian national born in 1973, lived in Crete, Greece, from 1996 and held a Greek residence permit. He had two children born in Greece. On 27 October 2014 the director of Kassandra Prison, where the applicant was detained, wrote to the prosecutor stating that the applicant did not wish to be transferred to court for the 13 November 2014 hearing because his lawyer would represent him. On the day of that hearing, the applicant requested an adjournment, claiming he could not contact his lawyer. On 20 January 2015, while still detained, he was notified that the appeal hearing had been rescheduled for 1 November 2015.

On 25 February 2015 the Chalkidiki Criminal Court of First Instance granted him conditional release under Article 105 of the Criminal Code, as he had served three-fifths of his sentence after deductions for work and had demonstrated good behaviour. He was formally released on 6 March 2015, but was transferred to the Department of Illegal Migration in Triglia and placed in a detention facility for migrants. The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 6 May 2014. The case therefore concerns the effectiveness of that right: specifically, whether the applicant’s appeal was rendered ineffective because the hearing was scheduled after his conditional release and expulsion from Greece, and because the appeal was ultimately dismissed due to his absence from the hearing.

In *Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V. and Others v. the Netherlands*, six Dutch limited liability companies complained under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that intercept data lawfully obtained in criminal investigations had been transmitted to and used by Dutch competition authorities, and under Article 13 that they had no effective domestic remedy. Some conversations between I. company employees and Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V. indicated possible price-fixing. In 2008–2010, the public prosecutor authorized transmission of an official record, transcripts and recordings to the Netherlands Competition Authority (NMA) under the Judicial and Criminal Data Act (WJSG). **Case Summary: Malgazhdarov and Others v. Russia**  
*European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, Committee Judgment, 16 January 2025*  
*Applications nos. 4562/23 and 7 others*

The case concerns eight applications lodged against Russia under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants complained primarily of disproportionate measures taken against solo demonstrators. The Russian Government were given notice of the applications. The Court, sitting as a Committee, deliberated in private on 5 December 2024 and adopted the judgment on 16 January 2025.

The applicants were individuals who held or participated in solo demonstrations in Moscow in early 2022. Their details are set out in the appended table. Anton Aleksandrovich Malgazhdarov (born 1990), application no. 4562/23, demonstrated on 5 January 2022 in support of protests in Kazakhstan. The other applicants took part in anti-war protests: Taisiya Yevgenyevna Yazrikova (born 1987) on 26 February 2022; Varvara Vladimirovna Obrosova (born 1986) on 27 February 2022; Natalya Viktorovna Ladygina (born 1964) on 26 February 2022; Olga Gennadyevna Nikitina (born 1983) on 2 March 2022; Mikhail Aleksandrovich Salomatin (born 1981) on 5 March 2022; Polina Valeryevna Kuzavleva (born 1986) on 5 March 2022; and Anna Vladimirovna Danilina (born 1988) on 6 March 2022. All demonstrations took place in Moscow.

In each case, the applicants were subjected to administrative charges under Article 20.2 § 5 of the Russian Code of Administrative Offences (CAO). The penalties imposed were fines ranging from RUB 10,000 to RUB 20,000. For example, Malgazhdarov received a RUB 10,000 fine; Yazrikova, Obrosova, Nikitina, and Kuzavleva received RUB 20,000 fines; Salomatin received RUB 15,000; and Danilina and Ladygina received RUB 10,000. The first applicant’s case also included a “distance requirement” and the event was classified as an assembly post facto, though no equivalent detail is provided for the other applicants.

The final domestic decisions were issued by the Moscow City Court between 15 September 2022 and 25 October 2022. This indicates that the applicants exhausted domestic remedies before applying to the European Court. Their applications were lodged with the Court at various dates in January and February 2023.

The key alleged violation is that the Russian authorities imposed disproportionate administrative penalties on individuals engaged in solo demonstrations. The applicants complained specifically of “disproportionate measures against solo demonstrators.” While some applicants also raised other complaints under the Convention, the appended table and the provided facts focus on the administrative fines imposed for solo protests. The central issue before the Court was therefore whether these fines constituted an unjustified interference with the right to freedom of peaceful assembly, primarily under Article 11 of the Convention. The facts relevant to that alleged violation include the peaceful nature of the solo demonstrations, the absence of any indicated violence or disruption in the table, the administrative classification of the events, the imposition of financial penalties, and the final review by the Moscow City Court. The Court’s task was to assess whether these measures complied with Convention standards. The provided text does not include the Court’s full reasoning or final disposition, but it identifies the case as concerning Russia’s treatment of solo demonstrators and the fines imposed under CAO Article 20.2 § 5.

In *Tsatani v. Greece*, the applicant, Georgia Tsatani, was a Greek prosecutor at the Athens Court of Appeal. She complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that disciplinary proceedings against her were not conducted by an impartial tribunal. The key facts concern the role of V.T., then President of the Court of Cassation.

On 23 March 2016, V.T. opened a preliminary disciplinary investigation into Tsatani. This followed letters from the Cypriot Minister of Justice and Attorney-General expressing concern about Tsatani’s decision to close criminal investigations into a high-profile fraud case involving Greek and Cypriot individuals. V.T. collected evidence and invited Tsatani to submit a written defence. Tsatani objected that the Prosecutor of the Court of Cassation, not V.T., had exclusive competence, and complained that the Deputy Minister of Justice had referred to the confidential disciplinary proceedings in Parliament on 29 March 2016.

On 4 April 2016, Tsatani submitted her defence and a recusal request against V.T. She alleged bias because V.T., a former interim prime minister, had ongoing special relations with the Deputy Minister of Justice; had official relations with the Cypriot officials who had complained about Tsatani; had asked prejudicial questions; and had provided an incomplete copy of the file. On 12 April, V.T. referred the further preliminary investigation to a Vice-President of the Court of Cassation. In that referral, V.T. stated that Tsatani’s recusal request was an abuse of process and unfounded, but that she was delegating the investigation to safeguard the authority of her office and the judiciary. On 18 April, V.T. issued a press release repeating that the recusal request was unfounded and an abuse of process, and naming Tsatani and the pending disciplinary case.

On 5 May 2016, the Vice-President concluded the preliminary investigation and proposed that V.T. bring disciplinary action. The Vice-President declared Tsatani’s recusal request inadmissible for lack of standing, because V.T. had already dismissed it. On 24 June 2016, V.T. brought disciplinary proceedings against Tsatani before the seven-member disciplinary council of the Court of Cassation. V.T. argued that the recusal request was inadmissible because it had not been lodged with the Prosecutor of the Court of Cassation under the Code of Criminal Procedure, and that she had not “dismissed” it but had merely delegated the investigation.

By decision of 10 October 2016, the seven-member council found Tsatani guilty of serious negligence damaging the prestige of the judiciary. It found that she had terminated investigations within the exclusive competence of the Anti-Corruption Prosecutor and breached a Eurojust agreement. She was sentenced to sixty days’ salary deprivation. The council also held the recusal request inadmissible; V.T. was not bound by it and had lawfully assigned the investigation. On 16 March 2017, the nine-member disciplinary council dismissed Tsatani’s appeal, again finding the recusal request inadmissible and unfounded and that V.T. had not acted as a decision-maker on it. A reopening request was rejected in 2021.

The alleged Article 6 § 1 violation therefore arises from V.T.’s cumulative roles: she initiated and conducted the preliminary disciplinary investigation, was the subject of Tsatani’s recusal request, publicly rejected its merits, and then brought the disciplinary action against Tsatani. Tsatani argued that this deprived her of an impartial tribunal, because the person whose impartiality was challenged effectively evaluated the challenge and later prosecuted her.

**Case:** *Kashbollina and Others v. Russia* (Applications nos. 1964/22 and 4 others)  
**Court:** European Court of Human Rights, Third Section (Committee)  
**Judgment:** Strasbourg, 13 November 2025 (deliberated 23 October 2025)

The case originated in five applications lodged against Russia under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants were represented by Natalya Andreyevna Baranova, based in Moscow. The Russian Government was given notice of the applications. The applicants complained of disproportionate measures taken against them as organisers or participants of public assemblies in St Petersburg, concerning various public events that allegedly breached regional COVID-19-related restrictions. They also raised other complaints under the Convention.

The appended table provides the key facts for each applicant.

**Alena Valeriyevna Kashbollina** (born 1998) participated in the rally “Free Navalnyy” in St Petersburg on 2 February 2021. She was charged under Article 20.2.2 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences (CAO) and fined RUB 10,000. The final domestic decision was given by the St Petersburg City Court on 3 June 2021.

**Aleksandra Vadimovna Eller** (born 1990) took part in an anti-war protest in St Petersburg on 24 February 2022. She was charged under Article 20.2.2 § 1 of the CAO and sentenced to detention for five days. The St Petersburg City Court issued the final domestic decision on 22 March 2022.

**Sergey Aleksandrovich Fedorov** (born 1997) participated in an anti-war protest in St Petersburg on 27 February 2022. He was charged under Article 20.2.2 § 1 of the CAO and fined RUB 15,000. The final domestic decision was given by the St Petersburg City Court on 22 March 2022.

**Oksana Nikolayevna Shurukhina** (born 1977) also participated in an anti-war protest in St Petersburg on 27 February 2022. She was charged under Article 20.2.2 § 1 of the CAO and fined RUB 10,000. The final domestic decision was issued by the St Petersburg City Court on 5 April 2022.

**Pavel Viktorovich Arkhipov** (born 1997) took part in an anti-war protest in St Petersburg on 6 March 2022. He was charged under Article 20.2 § 2 of the CAO and fined RUB 10,000. The final domestic decision was given by the St Petersburg City Court on 24 May 2022.

The central alleged violation concerns the administrative sanctions imposed on the applicants for participating in public assemblies in St Petersburg. The applicants argued that these measures were disproportionate, particularly in the context of public events that Russian authorities treated as violating regional COVID-19-related restrictions. The complaints therefore engage the Convention’s guarantees of freedom of peaceful assembly and related rights, as well as the other Convention provisions invoked by the applicants. The Court was asked to assess whether the administrative penalties—fines and, in one case, detention—and the underlying restrictions were compatible with Russia’s Convention obligations. The provided excerpt sets out the procedural background and factual details from the appended table, but does not include the Court’s full reasoning or final findings on the merits.

**B.A. v. Iceland** (Application no. 17006/20) concerns an Icelandic woman who alleged that the Icelandic authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into her complaints of domestic violence and sexual assault, and that they discriminated against her on gender grounds. The application was lodged on 23 March 2020 under Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention, both alone and in conjunction with Article 14. The Court gave notice of the complaints concerning the ineffective investigation of domestic violence and gender-based discrimination, declaring the remainder inadmissible.

The applicant, born in 1975 and living in Reykjavík, complained to the police in December 2017 against her former cohabitant, F.Þ., alleging physical, psychological and sexual violence during their relationship between 2011 and 2014. She stated that F.Þ. repeatedly humiliated and criticised her, isolated her from family and controlled aspects of her life. The psychological abuse allegedly intensified during pregnancy and escalated into physical and sexual violence.

She described four sexual violence incidents: being coerced into sexually stimulating F.Þ. while hospitalised during pregnancy; rape at a rehabilitation clinic; rape in the hallway of their home; and rape while sleeping, which allegedly caused bruising. She also alleged two physical incidents: a brief chokehold and a headbutt.

During the police investigation, the applicant was assisted by a legal representative. She said she had never sought immediate medical attention after the incidents. F.Þ. was questioned on 19 September 2018 and denied all wrongdoing. He attributed relationship difficulties to the applicant’s alcohol consumption. He admitted sexual intercourse at the rehabilitation clinic but denied rape, and admitted being controlling when urging her to stop drinking or avoid work under its influence.

Eleven witnesses were questioned. Several observed changes in the applicant after cohabitation, including reduced contact with others. Some described humiliation or anger by F.Þ. One witness heard the applicant scream and found her trembling and scared after an incident she described as a chokehold. However, there were no direct witnesses to the alleged physical or sexual violence; most accounts were based on disclosures after the relationship ended. The case file included a Stígamót certificate from December 2017 stating she had attended since April 2015 and reported severe mental, physical and sexual violence. Psychiatric records from 2012 and 2017 noted depression and anxiety, and a psychologist in February 2019 diagnosed PTSD following an alleged sexual offence.

On 11 June 2019 the police discontinued the investigation. Regarding sexual violence, they found insufficient support for the allegations given F.Þ.’s denial and the evidence, and considered further investigation unlikely to improve the position. Regarding physical violence, Article 218b of the General Penal Code had not been enacted until 2016, so the conduct could only be considered under Article 217; the statute of limitations had expired. On 25 September 2019 the State Prosecutor upheld the decision. It held that Article 218b could not apply retroactively. The physical violence, punishable under Article 217 with a two-year limitation period, was time-barred. For sexual violence, the evidence—including witness testimony and expert documentation of distress—did not sufficiently overcome F.Þ.’s denial to be “sufficient or likely” to secure a conviction. Further investigative measures would not change the evidentiary position. Later, the applicant’s lawyer raised whether the conduct could fall under Article 233b (gross defamation of a closely related person), but the State Prosecutor replied that its review had not been confined to the police’s classification.

The applicant alleged violations of Articles 3 and 8, alone and with Article 14, focusing on the ineffective investigation and gender-based discrimination. International reports by GREVIO and CEDAW noted broader concerns about high discontinuances, low conviction rates, delays and lack of data in gender-based violence cases in Iceland.

**Case:** *Monteiro and Trinta Santos v. Portugal*  
**Applications nos.:** 40620/22 and 44221/22  
**Court:** European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section  
**Judgment:** 6 March 2025 (Committee)

The case originated in two applications against Portugal lodged under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The first applicant, António Augusto Monteiro (born 1986), introduced application no. 40620/22 on 12 August 2022. The second applicant, Hugo David Trinta Santos (born 1984), introduced application no. 44221/22 on 6 September 2022. Monteiro was represented by Mr R. Mendes Martins, a lawyer practising in Lisbon, and Trinta Santos by Mr V. Carreto, a lawyer practising in Torres Vedras. The Portuguese Government were given notice of the applications.

Both applicants complained under Article 3 of the Convention about the inadequate conditions of their detention in Coimbra Prison. In application no. 44221/22, Trinta Santos also complained under Article 13 of the lack of an effective domestic remedy in respect of the alleged Article 3 violation.

As regards Monteiro, the appended table shows that he was detained in Coimbra Prison from 27 December 2021 to 3 December 2022, a duration of 11 months and 7 days. He was again detained in the same prison from 30 June 2023 and remained there pending at the time of the application, a period of more than 1 year and 6 months. The table records that he shared a cell with two inmates, with 3.10 m² per inmate and one toilet. His specific grievances for both periods were overcrowding, lack of privacy for the toilet, lack of fresh air, inadequate temperature, passive smoking, poor quality of food, infestation of the cell with insects or rodents, and a mouldy or dirty cell.

As regards Trinta Santos, he was detained in Coimbra Prison from 15 July 2022 and remained there pending, a period of more than 1 year and 6 months. The table records that he shared a cell with two inmates, with 2.25 m² per inmate and one toilet. His specific grievances were overcrowding, inadequate temperature, lack of requisite medical assistance, a mouldy or dirty cell, lack of fresh air, and lack of or insufficient quantity of food.

The applicants’ complaints therefore centre on severe overcrowding and associated physical conditions in Coimbra Prison. Monteiro’s cell space was recorded as 3.10 m² per inmate, while Trinta Santos’s was 2.25 m² per inmate. Both cells held two inmates and had one toilet, which is directly relevant to the complaints of overcrowding and lack of privacy. Additional alleged deficiencies included poor ventilation, inadequate temperature, passive smoking, poor food, hygiene problems, pests, and, for Trinta Santos, lack of requisite medical assistance. Trinta Santos further alleged that domestic remedies were ineffective or unavailable, giving rise to his Article 13 complaint.

The Court’s judgment concerns whether these detention conditions reached the threshold of inhuman or degrading treatment under Article 3 and, in Trinta Santos’s case, whether Portugal provided an effective domestic remedy under Article 13. The appended table provides the core factual basis for the alleged violations.

**Zafferani and Others v. San Marino** (Applications nos. 38127/22 and 6 others) is a European Court of Human Rights case lodged on 1 August 2022 by seven San Marino nationals. The case concerns a legislative intervention that allegedly affected the outcome of proceedings relating to the applicants’ career reconstruction as military officers.

Between 2006 and 2008, the applicants were officers, initially temporary, in the Uniformed Unit of the Fortress Guard, a San Marino military body. They claimed that under Law no. 132/1987, as amended by Law no. 99/1997, their enrolment should have become permanent after a successful probationary year and should have entitled them to career advancement. Their employment was instead periodically extended until 18 January 2016, when Parliament acknowledged their permanent recruitment under Article 63(1) of Law no. 189/2015 and assigned them “Scale 5” career category.

Between 28 January and 2 February 2016, the applicants requested the Public Administration Personnel Management Office to reconstruct their careers, affecting salary and entitlements. The acknowledgment receipts indicated that the deadline for concluding proceedings began to run from those dates and that remedies lay under Law no. 68/1989. No immediate reply followed.

On 25 July 2016, Delegated Decree no. 88/2016 was enacted. Article 1 provided that, for persons recruited under Article 63 of Law no. 189/2015, economic benefits from retrospective career adjustment could only run from 1 February 2016. It excluded arrears and payment of statutory withholding taxes under Article 54 of Law no. 41/1972. The applicants’ career reconstruction was then carried out under that provision. Each applicant allegedly lost around EUR 25,000 or more.

In 2018, the applicants asked the Minister of Foreign and Political Affairs and the Director General of Civil Service to intervene so they could also obtain arrears under ordinary provisions. On 7 November 2018, the Director of Civil Service and Director of Human Resources confirmed the reconstruction complied with Law no. 88/2016, noting the applicants had not been employed under the ordinary procedure in Law no. 132/1987 as amended.

On 20 March 2019, the applicants applied to the Judge of First Instance in administrative jurisdiction, seeking annulment of the 7 November 2018 decision. They argued that Law no. 88/2016 was unconstitutional because it conflicted with equality and equitable remuneration principles, and asked for referral to the Constitutional Court. On 9 December 2019, the Judge refused the referral as manifestly ill-founded, finding it legitimate to apply different conditions to persons employed through extraordinary procedures.

The applicants then challenged the Judge’s participation. On 17 July 2020, the Judge for Extraordinary Remedies dismissed that challenge but noted, in an obiter dictum, that the impugned law had to be examined in light of Convention principles and that the applicants had suffered a legislative interference in pending proceedings begun in January/February 2016, before the July 2016 decree. On 4 November 2020, the Judge of First Instance dismissed the claim, holding that Law no. 88/2016 was a lex specialis and that the applicants’ permanent recruitment without public competition placed them in a different position from officers recruited by public selection.

On 4 December 2020, the applicants appealed, reiterating a constitutional challenge and adding Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 complaints, though they later withdrew the constitutional request. On 30 March 2022, the Judge of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment, emphasising that the applicants had not been recruited by public competition but through an ad hoc process, and ordered them to pay costs.

The communicated complaints concern Article 6 § 1—fairness of proceedings allegedly affected by retrospective legislative intervention—and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1—the alleged unjustified loss of remuneration and arrears from career reconstruction.

In *A.J. and L.E. v. Spain* (ECtHR, Fifth Section, judgment of 23 October 2025), two Spanish nationals allege violations of Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention arising from Spain’s handling of their sexual-assault complaints. The applications concern the alleged ineffectiveness of the criminal investigation into sexual assault by chemical submission and the loss and manipulation of crucial evidence held in police custody.

On the night of 7–8 December 2016, the applicants went to a bar in Pamplona. They met D.C.M. and R.G.S., drank alcohol with them, and alleged that they had no recollection of events until waking the next morning in one man’s residence, undressed and with the physical sensation of having had sexual intercourse. They claimed they had been subjected to chemical submission and were unable to consent. A.J. attended a health centre on 11 December 2016; no genital lesions were found, but the suspected sexual assault/chemical submission protocol was activated, leading to police notification. L.E. did not seek immediate medical attention.

The National Police UFAM unit investigated. D.C.M. and R.G.S. were arrested on 27 December 2016 and questioned on 29 December. Both admitted sexual intercourse but maintained it was consensual. Restraining orders were imposed. The case was transferred to Investigating Court No. 1, and formal proceedings opened in January 2017. A significant issue was that R.G.S. was the brother-in-law of a UFAM police officer assigned to the investigation. Several pieces of evidence then disappeared or were compromised: a full forensic report on R.G.S.’s mobile phone, sent from Madrid to Pamplona in April 2017, vanished; CCTV footage from the bar was partially lost and altered; and a hard drive containing forensic data from both suspects’ phones, including backups, was wiped and overwritten.

Domestic courts declined to prosecute and later provisionally dismissed the case. In November 2018, the investigating judge found the applicants’ accounts credible but concluded there was insufficient evidence of non-consensual acts. No timely toxicological evidence supported chemical submission; reported injuries could not be definitively linked to the alleged events; the forensic examination showed no injuries typical of violent sexual assault; and vulgar messages exchanged by the suspects after the event were not probative. In October 2021, the court concluded proceedings without charges. It reviewed hair-sample analysis, which found no chemical-submission substances but showed prescription medication in both applicants that could have intensified alcohol’s effects; taxi driver and witness testimony; bar staff evidence; bank records; searches; WhatsApp messages; police reports on lost video footage; and medical reports. The court accepted that intercourse occurred and that the applicants were credible, but found no proof beyond reasonable doubt that the suspects administered drugs or knew the applicants lacked consciousness. Witnesses had not described rapid intoxication consistent with GHB or “burundanga”; the barman and taxi driver saw nothing unusual; a friend noticed something unusual but not enough to intervene. As the suspects were unacquainted with the applicants, disinhibition would not necessarily have appeared abnormal. The court acknowledged the investigation was “notably affected” by irregularities and lost digital evidence, but found no substantive evidence to charge. Appeals were dismissed, and the amparo appeal was declared inadmissible on procedural grounds.

Separate investigations into the evidence loss—digital forensic handling, video manipulation, and hard-drive erasure—mostly ended without charges due to insufficient proof of intentional misconduct or inability to identify who accessed or deleted data. An internal police disciplinary file remained suspended. The applicants’ core complaint before the ECtHR is that Spain failed to conduct an effective investigation into alleged sexual assault by chemical submission and that crucial police-held evidence was lost or manipulated, undermining their rights under Articles 3 and 8.
