The case *Malgazhdarov and Others v Russia* (Applications nos. 4562/23 and 7 others) was decided by the Third Section of the European Court of Human Rights, sitting as a Committee, with judgment delivered on 16 January 2025. The case originated in applications lodged against Russia under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants complained principally of disproportionate measures taken against solo demonstrators. Some applicants also raised other complaints under the Convention. The Russian Government were given notice of the applications.

The facts, set out in the appended table, concerned eight individual demonstrators. All demonstrations took place in Moscow. Anton Aleksandrovich Malgazhdarov (born 1990) demonstrated on 5 January 2022 in support of protests in Kazakhstan. The remaining applicants took part in anti-war protests: Taisiya Yevgenyevna Yazrikova (1987) on 26 February 2022; Varvara Vladimirovna Obrosova (1986) on 27 February 2022; Natalya Viktorovna Ladygina (1964) on 26 February 2022; Olga Gennadyevna Nikitina (1983) on 2 March 2022; Mikhail Aleksandrovich Salomatin (1981) on 5 March 2022; Polina Valeryevna Kuzavleva (1986) on 5 March 2022; and Anna Vladimirovna Danilina (1988) on 6 March 2022. Some applicants had legal representation in Moscow: Belova for Malgazhdarov, Petrova for Nikitina, and Baranova for Kuzavleva.

In each case, the Russian authorities imposed administrative penalties under Article 20.2 § 5 of the Code of Administrative Offences (CAO). The fines varied: Malgazhdarov, Danilina and Ladygina were fined RUB 10,000; Salomatin RUB 15,000; and Yazrikova, Obrosova, Nikitina and Kuzavleva RUB 20,000. In Malgazhdarov’s case, the table additionally noted a “distance requirement” and that the event was classified as an assembly post facto. The final domestic decisions were issued by the Moscow City Court between 15 September and 25 October 2022. The applications were lodged with the European Court in January and February 2023.

The principal alleged violation concerned the disproportionate administrative measures imposed on solo demonstrators. The applicants argued, in substance, that punishing individual, peaceful protests through CAO fines interfered with their Convention rights, particularly freedom of peaceful assembly. The manner in which the authorities treated one-person demonstrations—including, in Malgazhdarov’s case, classifying the event after the fact as a regulated assembly and applying a distance requirement—was central to the complaint. The case therefore raised the question whether Russia’s administrative enforcement against solo protests complied with Convention standards, including whether the restrictions were prescribed by law, pursued a legitimate aim, and were necessary in a democratic society. Some applicants also raised additional Convention complaints, but the main factual focus remained the fines and related measures imposed for their individual demonstrations.

**Summary of *Aslan and Others v. Türkiye* (ECtHR, Second Section, 13 November 2025)**

In *Aslan and Others v. Türkiye*, the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section, sitting as a Committee) examined nine applications—no. 12531/21 and eight others—lodged against Türkiye under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants’ principal complaint was the excessive length of their pre-trial detention in the absence of relevant and sufficient reasons. In applications nos. 18927/21 and 16303/23, the applicants also raised other complaints under the Convention. The Turkish Government were given notice of the applications. The appended table sets out the individual facts.

The applicants were held in pre-trial detention by various Turkish courts over significantly differing periods. Dilan Aslan (b. 1991) was detained from 16 March 2020 to 27 October 2020—7 months and 12 days—by the Denizli 2nd and 3rd Assize Courts. The grounds cited included strong suspicion, the nature of the offence, the offence being a “catalogue offence” under Article 100 § 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the severity of the potential sentence, risk of absconding, and risk of tampering with evidence.

Mehmet Bozkurt (b. 1975) was detained from 5 July 2015 to 5 June 2020—4 years, 11 months and 1 day—by the Ağrı Assize Court. The grounds were the nature of the offence, strong suspicion, the severity of the offences and potential sentence, and catalogue-offence status.

Ayşegül Çağatay Gökçe (b. 1991) had the longest detention: from 25 June 2011 to 31 March 2020—8 years, 9 months and 7 days—before the Istanbul 11th and 12th Magistrate’s Courts and the Istanbul 29th Assize Court. The courts relied on the nature of the offence, catalogue-offence status, the minimum and maximum prescribed sentence, risk of absconding, and risk of tampering with evidence.

Sadun Kaya (b. 1968) was detained from 2 July 2018 to 16 September 2022—4 years, 2 months and 15 days—by the Kocaeli 1st and 2nd Assize Courts, based on the severity of potential sentences, the scope of the case, and the fact that some evidence, such as expert reports, had not yet been collected.

Şeyhmus Çeri (b. 1997) was detained from 17 August 2016 to 10 October 2018—2 years, 1 month and 24 days—by the Şanlıurfa Assize Court, on grounds of strong suspicion, the nature of the offence, and the severity of the potential sentence.

Mensur Akar (b. 1995) was detained in two periods: 18 April 2016 to 3 January 2019 and 20 December 2019 to 27 October 2022—a total of 6 years, 6 months and 23 days—by the Hakkari Assize Court. The grounds included strong suspicion, the nature of the offences, catalogue-offence status, and the severity of the offence.

Helin Yapıcı (b. 1994) was detained from 23 March 2016 to 6 April 2021—5 years and 15 days—by the Diyarbakır Assize Court, based on strong suspicion, the nature of the offence, catalogue-offence status, and the severity of the potential sentence.

İrfan Yıldız (b. 1980) was detained from 16 February 2017 to 27 March 2019 and from 25 December 2019 to 25 June 2020—2 years, 1 month and 12 days plus 6 months and 1 day—before the Istanbul 6th Magistrate’s Court and the Istanbul 27th Assize Court. The grounds included his contacts, the state of evidence, the insufficiency of alternative judicial supervision measures, catalogue-offence status, the severity of the potential sentence, the fact that ISIS resorted to terror acts on New Year’s Eve and special days, and the appropriateness of detention.

Finally, Mücahit Doğan (b. 1983) was detained from 31 December 2021 to 27 December 2022—11 months and 28 days—by the Küçükçekmece Magistrates’ Courts and the Küçükçekmece Criminal Court of First Instance. The grounds were strong suspicion, the nature of the offence, catalogue-offence status, the severity of the potential sentence, risk of absconding, and risk of tampering with evidence.

These facts are relevant to the alleged violations because the applicants contended that their prolonged pre-trial detention was not justified by relevant and sufficient reasons, particularly where courts repeatedly relied on statutory catalogue offences, the seriousness of offences, and abstract risks.

The case *Arvanitis and Phileleftheros Public Company Limited v. Cyprus* concerns an alleged breach of Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights—freedom of expression—arising from civil defamation proceedings in Cyprus. The first applicant, Christos Arvanitis, is a journalist and columnist; the second applicant, Phileleftheros Public Company Limited, publishes the daily newspaper *Phileleftheros*.

The facts begin in June 2007, when a lawyer, C.K., published an article in the Greek newspaper *To Vima*. He described recovering two family paintings left in the occupied areas of Cyprus after the 1974 Turkish invasion. He said he recovered the first painting by paying over thirty silver coins to unknown persons and, unable to recover the second by payment, replaced it with a forgery, inspired by the film *The Thomas Crown Affair*.

On 1 July 2007, Arvanitis published an article in *Phileleftheros* entitled “Property-Dignity, One-Nil.” The article commented on C.K.’s account, questioning how a stolen house differs from a stolen painting and criticising the payment of a “ransom” for property in the occupied territories. It suggested C.K. was negotiating with thieves, buying from a new owner, selling his dignity, and harming his compatriots. The issue sold 24,482 copies.

C.K. sued the applicants for civil defamation in 2008, claiming the article damaged his personal and professional reputation. He alleged it falsely portrayed him as prioritising material goods over national interests, negotiating with thieves, and harming Greek Cypriots pursuing property claims. The applicants relied on defences of truth and fair comment on a matter of public interest, arguing the article concerned the recovery of Greek-Cypriot property and was written in good faith based on C.K.’s own published account.

On 18 September 2014, the Nicosia District Court found for C.K., awarding EUR 12,000 plus interest. It held the article was defamatory, went beyond opinion, and personally attacked C.K., harming his professional standing as a lawyer then representing clients before the English Court of Appeal in property cases. The court found the article lacked a truth basis: C.K. had said he “recovered” rather than “bought” the paintings; he paid CYP 1,000 for a painting worth over CYP 50,000; and it was unclear whether the money went to a tavern owner or an intermediary. The applicants wrongly inferred that C.K. had bargained with thieves. The court also found Arvanitis failed to contact C.K. or verify key facts. The fair-comment defence failed because, despite the public interest in property issues, the article contained vulgar, bad-faith personal attacks and had insufficient factual basis. C.K. was not a public figure.

On 24 June 2022, the Supreme Court upheld the District Court. It agreed C.K. was a private individual, that “recovered” did not mean “purchased,” and that the article was neither true nor fair comment.

The applicants lodged an Article 34 application on 20 October 2022. The complaint under Article 10 concerns whether the civil defamation judgment and damages unjustifiably interfered with journalistic expression on a public-interest debate, and whether domestic courts properly balanced reputation against freedom of expression. The Greek Government declined to intervene; the Cypriot Government was represented. The Fifth Section delivered judgment on 3 July 2025, final on 3 October 2025.

In *Kashbullina and Others v Russia*, the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section), sitting as a Committee, examined five applications against Russia. The applications were lodged under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates between 3 December 2021 and 24 September 2022. The Russian Government were given notice. The judgment was delivered in Strasbourg on 13 November 2025, after private deliberations on 23 October 2025. It is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The applicants are Russian nationals: Alena Kashbullina, Aleksandra Eller, Sergey Fedorov, Oksana Shurukhina and Pavel Arkhipov. Four were represented by Baranova Natalya Andreyevna of Moscow; no representative is indicated for Arkhipov in the appended table. The case concerns administrative measures imposed on them as organisers or participants of public assemblies in St Petersburg. The events took place during the COVID-19 pandemic and were treated as breaching regional COVID-19-related restrictions. The applicants complained that the measures taken against them were disproportionate. They also raised other complaints under the Convention.

The key events and domestic penalties were as follows:

- **2 February 2021:** Kashbullina participated in the rally “Free Navalnyy” in St Petersburg. She was penalised under Article 20.2.2 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences (CAO) with a RUB 10,000 fine. The St Petersburg City Court gave the final domestic decision on 3 June 2021.
- **24 February 2022:** Eller participated in an anti-war protest in St Petersburg. She was penalised under Article 20.2.2 § 1 CAO with five days’ detention. The final domestic decision was given by the St Petersburg City Court on 22 March 2022.
- **27 February 2022:** Fedorov participated in an anti-war protest in St Petersburg. He was penalised under Article 20.2.2 § 1 CAO with a RUB 15,000 fine. The St Petersburg City Court gave the final domestic decision on 22 March 2022.
- **27 February 2022:** Shurukhina participated in an anti-war protest in St Petersburg. She was penalised under Article 20.2.2 § 1 CAO with a RUB 10,000 fine. The St Petersburg City Court gave the final domestic decision on 5 April 2022.
- **6 March 2022:** Arkhipov participated in an anti-war protest in St Petersburg. He was penalised under Article 20.2 § 2 CAO with a RUB 10,000 fine. The St Petersburg City Court gave the final domestic decision on 24 May 2022.

**Arvanitis and Phileleftheros Public Company Limited v. Cyprus** (Application no. 49917/22) is a European Court of Human Rights case, Fifth Section, judgment of 3 July 2025, concerning an alleged violation of Article 10 (freedom of expression). The applicants are Christos Arvanitis, a journalist and columnist, and Phileleftheros Public Company Limited, publisher of the Cypriot daily *Phileleftheros*. They complained that a civil defamation judgment against them in Cyprus breached their right to freedom of expression.

The dispute arose from an article written by Arvanitis and published by the second applicant on 1 July 2007, entitled “Property-Dignity, One-Nil.” It responded to a June 2007 article by C.K., a lawyer, in the Greek newspaper *To Vima*. C.K. had described recovering two family paintings left in occupied Cyprus after the 1974 Turkish invasion: he recovered one after paying money and the second by replacing it with a forgery, inspired by the film *The Thomas Crown Affair*. Arvanitis’s article criticised C.K.’s conduct, questioned whether he advised clients similarly, and suggested that paying a ransom, bargaining with thieves, and prioritising property over dignity harmed Greek-Cypriot property claims. The issue sold 24,482 copies.

In November 2008, C.K. sued the applicants for civil defamation. He claimed the article damaged his personal and professional reputation, falsely portraying him as prioritising material goods over national interests, harming compatriots, and negotiating with thieves. The applicants defended the article as true and as fair comment on a matter of public interest, arguing it was based on C.K.’s own published account and expressed honest opinion in a public debate about Greek-Cypriot property in the occupied areas.

On 18 September 2014, the Nicosia District Court found for C.K. and awarded EUR 12,000 plus interest. It held that the article was defamatory and went beyond opinion, directly attacking C.K.’s personality and professional standing by depicting him as someone who gave up his dignity, sold out his compatriots, and bargained with thieves. The court noted the article was published when C.K. was representing clients before the England and Wales Court of Appeal on occupied-property matters, thereby calling his reputation into question. It found the article lacked factual basis: C.K. had never said he bought a painting, only that he recovered it; paying money did not necessarily mean a purchase; and C.K. had not said he negotiated with the Turkish tavern owner or new owner. Arvanitis had failed to contact C.K. or verify the amount paid (1,000 CYP) against the painting’s value (over 50,000 CYP), or whether it amounted to a ransom. The court rejected fair comment because, although property issues were of public interest, the article contained vulgar, bad-faith personal attacks. It also found that other individuals and State bodies had paid to recover cultural goods, which was not reprehensible, and that failure to seek C.K.’s views showed lack of good faith. C.K. was not a public figure.

On appeal, the Supreme Court upheld the judgment on 24 June 2022. It agreed that C.K. was a private individual, that the article was not true, that “recovered” did not mean “bought,” and that the accusation of bargaining with thieves or buying from a new owner was unsupported. It also agreed that fair comment did not apply.

The applicants applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 20 October 2022. The Court gave notice solely of the Article 10 complaint. The key issue is whether the domestic civil defamation judgment and damages award unjustifiably interfered with the applicants’ freedom of expression.

**Summary of Mohammed v. Austria (Application no. 2283/12)**

The case of *Mohammed v. Austria* concerns a Sudanese national, Mr. Salaheldin Mohammed, who lodged an application against the Republic of Austria with the European Court of Human Rights on 11 January 2012. The applicant alleged that his forced transfer to Hungary under the Dublin Regulation would breach Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) of the European Convention on Human Rights, and that he lacked an effective remedy under Article 13 concerning his second asylum application.

The applicant arrived in Austria on 9 October 2010, having travelled through Greece and Hungary. He lodged an asylum application, but on 5 January 2011, the Federal Asylum Office determined that Hungary had jurisdiction under the Dublin II Regulation and ordered his transfer. The applicant did not appeal this decision. He subsequently went into hiding, thwarting a planned transfer attempt in May 2011.

On 21 December 2011, the applicant was detained in Vienna, and the following day, the Federal Police Authority ordered his detention pending forced transfer to Hungary. On 30 December 2011, he lodged a second asylum application, which had no suspensive effect on the transfer order. He argued that the Asylum Court’s own practice at the time acknowledged a real risk of Article 3 violations for asylum-seekers transferred to Hungary. This practice was based on a UNHCR letter of 17 October 2011, which detailed serious concerns about detention conditions in Hungary, including routine detention of asylum-seekers, ill-treatment by police, and inadequate judicial review of detention. The UNHCR also highlighted that Hungary treated Dublin returnees as second-time applicants, limiting their access to asylum proceedings and increasing the risk of refoulement to Serbia.

The applicant’s detention was upheld by the Vienna Independent Administrative Panel on 5 January 2012. On 10 January 2012, the Administrative Court dismissed his motion for suspensive effect but noted that immigration police would still need to refrain from transferring him if the situation in Hungary breached Article 3. The applicant also applied to the Federal Police Directorate to establish that his transfer would constitute a risk under the Immigration Police Act, but this was rejected on procedural grounds as no relevant proceedings were pending.

The applicant’s transfer was scheduled for 12 January 2012. However, on 11 January 2012, the European Court of Human Rights applied an interim measure under Rule 39, requesting the Austrian Government to stay the transfer until further notice.

The case raised significant issues regarding the protection of asylum-seekers under the Dublin Regulation, particularly in light of documented deficiencies in Hungary’s asylum system. The applicant argued that his transfer would expose him to a real risk of inhuman or degrading treatment and that he had no effective domestic remedy to prevent it.

The case *Arvanitis and Phileleftheros Public Company Limited v. Cyprus* concerns an alleged violation of Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants were Christos Arvanitis, a journalist and columnist, and Phileleftheros Public Company Limited, the publisher of the Cypriot daily newspaper *Phileleftheros*. They complained that a civil defamation judgment against them in Cyprus breached their right to freedom of expression.

The facts began in June 2007, when a lawyer, C.K., published an article in the Greek newspaper *To Vima*. He described recovering two family paintings left in the occupied areas of Cyprus after the 1974 Turkish invasion. He said he recovered the first painting after paying a sum of over thirty silver coins to unknown persons, and recovered the second by replacing it with a forgery after being unable to recover it in exchange for money.

On 1 July 2007, Arvanitis wrote an article in *Phileleftheros*, published by the second applicant, entitled “Property-Dignity, One-Nil.” The article commented on C.K.’s account. It questioned how paying a “ransom” for art in the occupied territories fitted with dignity and American film morality. It asked whether C.K. advised his clients in that way and suggested that paying a ransom, selling one’s dignity, “sucking up to your rapists,” and “hanging” compatriots were matters of public concern. The issue sold 24,482 copies.

In November 2008, C.K. sued the applicants for defamation in the Nicosia District Court. He claimed the article damaged his personal and professional reputation, falsely portrayed him as prioritising material goods over the national interest, and depicted him as negotiating with thieves. The applicants defended the article as true and fair comment on a matter of public interest, written in good faith. Arvanitis said he had relied on C.K.’s published account and had no obligation to seek C.K.’s opinion before commenting on an already published article.

In September 2014, the District Court found for C.K. It held the article defamatory and ordered the applicants to pay €12,000 jointly and/or severally, plus statutory interest. The court found the article went beyond opinion and directly attacked C.K.’s personality and professional standing, characterising him as having given up his dignity and sold out his compatriots by bargaining with thieves. It noted the article was published while C.K. was representing clients before the Court of Appeal of England and Wales concerning property in occupied Cyprus. The court found Arvanitis failed to contact C.K., check the amount paid (CYP 1,000), or verify the painting’s value (over CYP 50,000). C.K. had never said he bought the painting; he used “recovered” and did not say he negotiated with the Turkish tavern owner or new owner. The court found the article lacked truth and was not fair comment, as it contained vulgar, bad-faith personal attacks. It also found C.K. was not a public figure.

In June 2022, the Supreme Court upheld the judgment. It agreed C.K. was a private individual, the article was not true because C.K. never suggested he had bought the paintings, and the applicants wrongly accused him of bargaining with thieves. It held the article was not fair comment and had no basis in truth. The applicants then complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 10.

In **Federici v. France** (ECtHR, Fifth Section, Application no. 52302/19, judgment of 3 April 2025), the applicant, Jean-François Federici, complained about his appearance in a glass dock during proceedings before an assize court of appeal and that court’s refusal to allow him to answer questions from the witness stand rather than from the dock. He alleged violations of Article 6 §§ 1, 2 and 3(b) of the Convention, concerning the right to a fair trial, the presumption of innocence, and the rights of the defence.

The applicant, a French national born in 1957, was indicted for murder committed as a member of an organised group and conspiracy to commit a crime. In 2011, after failing to comply with a court supervision order, he absconded. In 2014, the Assize Court sentenced him in absentia to thirty years’ imprisonment. He was arrested in 2016, placed in pre-trial detention, and in 2017 the Assize Court again sentenced him to thirty years’ imprisonment. He appealed.

The appeal hearings took place in April 2018 in the Aix-en-Provence Law Courts. The applicant was assisted by two lawyers and appeared in a glass dock, described as an open-roofed glass enclosure measuring 3.68 metres by 2.47 metres. It had perforations for communication with defence lawyers, document slots, fixed microphones, and a loudspeaker allowing him to hear courtroom proceedings. On 6 April 2018, when questioned about his personality, he did not mention hearing difficulties or ask to be heard outside the dock.

On 10 April 2018, before his questioning, his lawyer requested that he appear in the courtroom itself rather than in the glass dock, relying on Article 6 of the Convention, the preliminary Article of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and recital 20 of Directive (EU) 2016/343. The grounds were that members of the public had undergone security checks and that the applicant had a hearing impairment that sometimes made it difficult to hear questions. On 11 April 2018, the President questioned him while he remained in the dock.

In an interlocutory judgment of 13 April 2018, the Assize Court dismissed the request. It held that Articles 318 and D.294 of the Code of Criminal Procedure required security measures based on the danger posed and the need to protect the accused. It noted that EU Directive 2016/343 did not prevent physical restraints where necessary for security or to prevent absconding or contact with third parties. The court observed that the applicant faced charges of organised-group murder and conspiracy, possible life imprisonment, and had absconded for over four years. Despite his hearing problems, the court found he could answer questions and communicate confidentially with his lawyers. It concluded that the glass dock was lawful, proportionate, and necessary, and did not infringe the presumption of innocence, dignity, or defence rights. The same day, he was convicted of double murder and sentenced to thirty years’ imprisonment.

The applicant appealed on points of law, arguing insufficient reasoning and failure to examine whether alternative security measures could have allowed him to appear at the witness stand. The Advocate General advised dismissal, and on 10 April 2019 the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal, finding that the Assize Court had ruled on the relevant grounds, exercised its discretion, and that nothing showed the applicant had been prevented from communicating with his lawyers.

Relevant context included a 2018 Public Defender’s Office opinion recommending repeal or strict limitation of secure docks, and a CGLPL report finding that glass docks could hinder lawyer-client communication, confidentiality, hearing, and defence rights.

**Beltram and Beltram Cerovšek v. Slovenia (Application no. 10017/10)** concerned two Slovenian nationals, Marijan Beltram and Anuška Beltram Cerovšek, who alleged that the length of civil proceedings in Slovenia violated their right to a trial within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The case arose from a civil action instituted on 2 October 2007 before the Ljubljana District Court against O.J. concerning defects in an apartment the applicants had purchased. On 2 April 2008 the applicants requested a hearing. Two days later, the District Court replied that their case could not be granted priority and that no hearing could be scheduled until the end of 2008.

On 6 February 2009, after the case had been pending for about fourteen months, the applicants lodged a supervisory appeal. They relied on the Court Rules, under which a first-instance decision should be issued within eighteen months in civil proceedings. On 26 February 2009 the President of the Ljubljana District Court dismissed the supervisory appeal, stating that the case was not a priority case and that, under the order of precedence for non-priority cases, a hearing would likely be scheduled in the second half of 2009.

On 5 March 2009 the applicants lodged a motion for a deadline with the Ljubljana Higher Court. That motion was dismissed on 27 March 2009, again by reference to the order of precedence and the fact that the case was not considered priority. On 25 May 2009 the applicants lodged a constitutional appeal against the dismissal of both the supervisory appeal and the motion for a deadline, alleging a violation of their right to a trial within a reasonable time. The Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal on 3 November 2009.

After the domestic remedies were exhausted, the applicants lodged their application with the European Court of Human Rights on 9 February 2010.

The domestic proceedings continued slowly. On 22 January 2010 the Ljubljana District Court held a main hearing and appointed a construction expert. On 2 March 2010 it dismissed that expert and appointed another. Two hearings were postponed between April and June 2010. On 27 September 2010 the court held a hearing, heard the expert, issued an order requiring the construction company K.Z. to provide documentation concerning the construction of the apartment, and adjourned the hearing until 8 December 2010.

On 15 October 2010 K.Z. appealed against the order, arguing that it was insufficiently precise. The hearing of 8 December 2010 was therefore postponed. On 17 February 2011 the Ljubljana Higher Court granted K.Z.’s appeal and remitted the case to the first-instance court. On 9 March 2011 the District Court indicated that a new order would be issued and adjourned the hearing. A new order was issued on 24 March 2011. After K.Z. informed the court on 14 April 2011 that the documents would be available at its office, the court on 19 April 2011 asked the expert to inspect them and supplement his opinion. The supplementary opinion was submitted on 7 October 2011.

At a hearing on 11 January 2012 the court granted the applicants’ motion to appoint a noise-exposure expert. That expert was appointed on 4 April 2012, and the opinion was received on 25 May 2012. On 24 August 2012 the court held a main hearing and allowed the construction expert’s opinion to be amended in light of the noise-pollution opinion. The supplemented construction opinion was submitted on 15 October 2012. On 15 March 2013 the District Court held a main hearing, heard the construction expert, and issued a decision largely granting the applicants’ claim. The decision was served on 17 April 2013. Both parties appealed, and the proceedings were still pending before the Ljubljana Higher Court at the time of the European Court’s judgment.

Relevant domestic law provided that civil proceedings before a first-instance court lasting more than eighteen months were considered to involve judicial delay. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation were therefore the repeated inability to obtain a timely hearing, the rejection of the applicants’ supervisory appeal, motion for a deadline and constitutional appeal, and the continuing delays caused by court scheduling, expert replacements, and K.Z.’s appeal.

In *Pyrantienė v. Lithuania* (Application no. 45092/07), the applicant, Kotrina Pyrantienė, a Lithuanian national born in 1942, complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that domestic court decisions deprived her of land she had owned for nine years without adequate compensation. The key facts concern the acquisition, loss, and compensation for a 0.5-hectare plot in the Kaunas Region.

In 1994 a local authority assigned the plot to the applicant. On 6 August 1996 the Kaunas Region Administration confirmed the sale of the land, and on 24 September 1996 she acquired it from the State for 61 single-use investment vouchers. She registered the plot in the Land Registry and used it to grow vegetables, which she sold at market. In December 2001, third parties brought a civil claim seeking restoration of ownership rights to the same plot. On 2 October 2003 the Kaunas Regional Court, acting as a court of appeal, quashed the 1996 decision as unlawful and cancelled the sale, ordering the land to be returned to the State. The court found that the authorities had no right to sell the plot because the former owners had already lodged a restitution request in 1991 for the nationalised property. The case was remitted to the first-instance court to determine restitution and compensation, since the sale agreement was null and void. On 6 February 2004 the Supreme Court refused the applicant leave to appeal on points of law as out of time.

After the State took the plot, by a decision of 16 September 2005 the Kaunas Region Administration restored the former owners’ rights and transferred the land to T.M.K. and J.R. In the remitted proceedings, an independent certified valuer assessed the plot’s market value: LTL 112,500 (about EUR 32,580) in September 2005, compared with LTL 18,000 in August 1996. Despite this evidence, on 5 October 2006 the Kaunas Regional Court, as first-instance court, awarded the applicant only LTL 1,466 (about EUR 430), the amount corresponding to the single-use investment vouchers she had paid in 1996. On 26 February 2007 the Court of Appeal upheld that decision and rejected her argument that Civil Code Article 6.147 § 2 required the highest value because she had been deprived of the property through error by State authorities. On 8 May 2007 the Supreme Court refused to accept her cassation appeal, saying it raised no important legal issues.

The applicant therefore alleged that the domestic courts had deprived her of property she had lawfully owned and used for nine years, yet awarded compensation far below its actual and market value. She relied on Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. The relevant domestic law included the Constitution’s guarantee of inviolable property and just compensation for expropriation; Civil Code provisions on nullity, restitution, and valuation, including the possibility of awarding the highest value where the restitution debtor was in bad faith or at fault; and State liability for unlawful acts of public authorities. Lithuanian case-law also provided that land subject to unresolved restitution claims was disputed and could not lawfully be transferred to third parties. These facts formed the basis of her complaint that the State’s unlawful sale and subsequent inadequate compensation breached her property rights.

**CASE OF ABBATE AND OTHERS v. ITALY**

**Summary of Key Facts Relevant to Alleged Violations**

This case originates from five applications lodged against Italy with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants—Ferdinando Emilio Abbate, Daniela Jossa, Lucio Benigni (in two separate applications), and Maria Stella Saveriano—are Italian nationals and legal professionals. They complained primarily of the non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of domestic court decisions given in their favour, raising issues under Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) of the Convention.

All applications share a common factual pattern: each applicant obtained one or more favorable judgments from Italian courts—specifically, the Latium Administrative Court, the Rome District Court, and various divisions of the Naples Court of Appeal. These decisions, issued between 2017 and 2021, ordered the relevant Italian ministries (the Ministry of Economy and Finance or the Ministry of Justice) to pay the applicants their legal fees as "avvocato antistatario"—meaning as lawyers who had represented themselves or their clients and were entitled to collect fees directly from the opposing party.

Despite obtaining these enforceable judgments, the applicants did not receive payment. The domestic decisions remained unenforced for substantial periods, leading to the present applications before the European Court.

**Application 27814/23 – Ferdinando Emilio Abbate (introduced 26/06/2023):**
This applicant obtained fourteen separate domestic decisions. Ten were judgments from the Latium Administrative Court dated 05/06/2017 and 20/07/2017. Four were enforcement orders from the Rome District Court issued in July 2019, confirming the enforceability of the earlier administrative judgments. The non-enforcement periods for these decisions ranged from approximately 3 years and 8 months to 5 years and 9 months, ending in March 2023. The debtor was the Ministry of Economy and Finance.

**Application 27974/23 – Daniela Jossa (introduced 05/07/2023):**
The applicant obtained three judgments from the Rome Court of Appeal (25/09/2017) and the Naples Court of Appeal (04/07/2018 and 06/08/2020). As of the date of application, enforcement remained pending for all three. The delays exceeded 7 years, 6 years, and 4 years respectively. The Ministry of Justice was the debtor.

**Application 33199/23 – Lucio Benigni (introduced 23/08/2023):**
This applicant obtained four judgments from the Naples Court of Appeal between January 2017 and September 2020. Enforcement remained pending for all, with delays ranging from over 4 years to more than 7 years and 9 months. The debtor was the Ministry of Justice.

**Application 33278/23 – Maria Stella Saveriano (introduced 23/08/2023):**
The applicant obtained four judgments from the Naples Court of Appeal between November 2018 and May 2019. Enforcement remained pending, with delays exceeding 5 years for each decision. The Ministry of Justice was the debtor.

**Application 35651/23 – Lucio Benigni (introduced 11/09/2023):**
This second application by Mr. Benigni concerns five additional judgments from the Naples Court of Appeal, issued between June 2017 and April 2021. Enforcement remained pending for all, with delays ranging from over 3 years and 6 months to more than 7 years and 4 months. The debtor was again the Ministry of Justice.

In summary, the key facts relevant to the alleged violations concern the prolonged failure of Italian authorities to enforce final domestic court decisions ordering the payment of legal fees to the applicants, resulting in enforcement periods ranging from approximately 3 to over 7 years.

**Summary of *Pyrantienė v. Lithuania* (Application no. 45092/07)**

The case of *Pyrantienė v. Lithuania* concerns an application brought by Ms. Kotrina Pyrantienė, a Lithuanian national born in 1942, against the Republic of Lithuania. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to property, after domestic court decisions deprived her of land she had owned for nine years without adequate compensation.

The facts of the case begin in 1994, when a local authority assigned a 0.5-hectare plot of land to the applicant. On 6 August 1996, the Kaunas Region Administration confirmed the sale of this land to her. Subsequently, on 24 September 1996, the applicant acquired the plot from the State for 61 "single-use investment vouchers" and duly registered the property in her name with the Land Registry. She then used the land for agricultural purposes, growing and selling vegetables. This situation persisted for several years.

The applicant's ownership was challenged in December 2001 when third parties filed a civil claim seeking the restoration of their ownership rights to the same plot. On 2 October 2003, the Kaunas Regional Court, acting as an appellate court, ruled in favour of the third parties. It quashed the 1996 administrative decision as unlawful and cancelled the sale of the land to the applicant, ordering its return to the State. The court's reasoning was that the State authorities had no right to sell the plot because the former owners had already lodged a request for its restitution under the post-Soviet restitution laws in 1991. The land-sale agreement with the applicant was thus declared null and void. The case was remitted to a first-instance court to determine the issues of restitution and compensation. The applicant's subsequent appeal to the Supreme Court was rejected as out of time on 6 February 2004.

Following this, the land was officially transferred to the former owners in September 2005. In the proceedings to determine the compensation owed to the applicant, an independent expert valuer assessed the property. The valuation established that the plot's market value in September 2005 was 112,500 Lithuanian litai (LTL), whereas its value in August 1996 had been LTL 18,000. Despite this expert evidence, the Kaunas Regional Court on 5 October 2006 awarded the applicant only LTL 1,466. The court justified this minimal sum by stating it corresponded to the price the applicant had originally paid in investment vouchers in 1996, rather than reflecting the property's current or even its 1996 monetary value.

The applicant's appeals were unsuccessful. On 26 February 2007, the Court of Appeal upheld the lower court's decision, rejecting her argument that the Civil Code required awarding her the highest value of the property since she had been deprived of it due to an error by State authorities. On 8 May 2007, the Supreme Court refused to accept her cassation appeal for examination, finding no important legal issues.

The core of the applicant's complaint to the European Court of Human Rights was that the compensation she received was manifestly inadequate. She had been deprived of property she had lawfully acquired and possessed for nine years, a deprivation caused by the State's own unlawful actions, yet was compensated with a sum far below its established market value, thereby violating her right to the peaceful enjoyment of her possessions.

In January 2011, the Austrian Federal Asylum Office determined that Hungary was responsible under the Dublin II Regulation, rejected the applicant’s asylum application as inadmissible, and ordered his transfer to Hungary. The applicant did not appeal that decision. He later went into hiding and thwarted an attempted detention and forced transfer in May 2011.

On 21 December 2011, the applicant was detained in Vienna. The next day, the Vienna Federal Police Authority ordered his detention with a view to forced transfer to Hungary. On 30 December 2011, he lodged a second asylum application, which did not suspend the valid transfer order. He relied on the Austrian Asylum Court’s practice and on reports concerning reception conditions and access to asylum procedures in Hungary. On 2 January 2012, he also complained against the detention order, referring to a December 2011 Asylum Court decision that had granted suspensive effect in a similar case involving transfer to Hungary. That decision relied on a UNHCR letter of 17 October 2011 regarding detention conditions in Hungary and the risk of refoulement to Serbia.

Domestic remedies failed to stop the transfer. On 5 January 2012, the Vienna Independent Administrative Panel dismissed the applicant’s complaint against detention as unfounded, finding the detention order lawful. On 10 January 2012, the Administrative Court dismissed his motion for suspensive effect. It stated that it would not decide on the lawfulness of the transfer to Hungary, but added that the immigration police would have to refrain from transferring him if the current situation in Hungary for Dublin returnees would breach Article 3 of the Convention. On 9 January 2012, the applicant also asked the Federal Police Directorate to establish that his transfer would pose a risk under section 50(1) or (2) of the Immigration Police Act. That request was rejected because such an application was only permitted in certain pending proceedings, and no such proceedings were pending. His transfer was again scheduled for 12 January 2012. On 11 January 2012, the European Court of Human Rights applied an interim measure under Rule 39, requesting Austria not to expel him until further notice.

The applicant alleged under Article 3 that his forced transfer to Hungary under the Dublin Regulation would expose him to a real risk of inhuman or degrading treatment. He also alleged under Article 13 that he lacked an effective remedy in the proceedings concerning his second asylum application that would have stayed his transfer to Hungary.

The key evidence relevant to those allegations included UNHCR and Hungarian Helsinki Committee reports describing the detention of asylum-seekers and Dublin returnees in Hungary, formalistic judicial review of detention, allegations of police ill-treatment and harassment, forced drugging with tranquilisers, inadequate reception and medical conditions, limited access to asylum proceedings, treatment of Dublin returnees as second applicants without automatic suspensive effect, and the risk of refoulement to Serbia, which Hungary wrongly treated as a safe third country. Austrian Asylum Court decisions in late 2011 had quashed some Dublin transfers to Hungary or granted suspensive effect, citing these concerns and the need for closer examination. Under Austrian law, a second asylum application after a Dublin rejection did not confer de facto protection against deportation, and appeals generally lacked suspensive effect unless the Asylum Court granted it where a real risk under Article 2 or 3 existed.

**Beltram and Beltram Cerovšek v. Slovenia** (Application no. 10017/10) is a European Court of Human Rights case concerning the alleged excessive length of civil proceedings. The applicants, Marijan Beltram and Anuška Beltram Cerovšek, Slovenian nationals born in 1977 and living in Ljubljana, lodged their application on 9 February 2010. They complained that their civil action against O.J. concerning defects in an apartment they had bought was not determined within a reasonable time, contrary to the right to a fair trial under Article 6 of the Convention. The Government were represented by their Agent, and the application was communicated to them on 22 November 2012.

The underlying civil proceedings began on 2 October 2007, when the applicants sued O.J. before the Ljubljana District Court over apartment defects. On 2 April 2008 they requested a hearing. On 4 April 2008 the District Court informed them that their case could not be granted priority and that a hearing could not be scheduled until the end of 2008. On 6 February 2009 the applicants lodged a supervisory appeal, stressing that under the Court Rules a first-instance decision should be issued within eighteen months, while their case had already been pending for fourteen months. On 26 February 2009 the President of the Ljubljana District Court dismissed the supervisory appeal, stating that the case was not a priority and that a hearing was foreseen for the second half of 2009.

On 5 March 2009 the applicants lodged a motion for a deadline with the Ljubljana Higher Court. On 27 March 2009 the Higher Court dismissed it, referring to the order of precedence for non-priority cases. On 25 May 2009 the applicants lodged a constitutional appeal alleging a violation of their right to a trial within a reasonable time. On 3 November 2009 the Constitutional Court dismissed that appeal.

Only on 22 January 2010 did the Ljubljana District Court hold a main hearing and appoint a construction expert. On 2 March 2010 it dismissed that expert and appointed another. Two hearings were postponed between April and June 2010. On 27 September 2010 the court heard the expert, ordered the construction company K.Z. to provide documentation concerning the apartment’s construction, and adjourned the hearing until 8 December 2010. On 15 October 2010 K.Z. appealed against that order, saying it was insufficiently precise. The 8 December 2010 hearing was therefore postponed. On 17 February 2011 the Ljubljana Higher Court granted K.Z.’s appeal and remitted the case to first instance. On 9 March 2011 the District Court indicated that a new order would be issued and adjourned. A new order was issued on 24 March 2011. After K.Z. informed the court on 14 April 2011 that the documents would be available at its office, the court on 19 April 2011 asked the expert to inspect them and supplement the opinion. The supplementary opinion was submitted on 7 October 2011.

On 11 January 2012 the court granted the applicants’ motion to appoint a noise-exposure expert. That expert was appointed on 4 April 2012, and the opinion was received on 25 May 2012. On 24 August 2012 a main hearing was held, and the construction expert opinion was to be amended to take account of noise pollution. The supplemented opinion was submitted on 15 October 2012. On 15 March 2013 the District Court held a hearing, heard the construction expert, and issued a decision largely granting the applicants’ claim. The decision was served on 17 April 2013. Both parties appealed, and the proceedings remained pending before the Ljubljana Higher Court.

Under the relevant domestic law, Article 50 of the Court Rules provided that civil proceedings before a first-instance court lasting more than eighteen months were considered judicial delay. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation were therefore the long duration of the proceedings, the unsuccessful domestic remedies, repeated expert appointments, postponements, and delay caused by K.Z.’s appeal and remittal.

**Summary of the Case**

The case of *MoskalENKO AND OTHERS v. Ukraine* (Application no. 1270/12 and 249 other applications) was a judgment delivered by the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) on 18 July 2013. The case originated from 250 separate applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights by Ukrainian nationals. The applicants alleged a violation of their right to a fair trial and to the protection of property, primarily under Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, due to the prolonged non-enforcement of final domestic court decisions.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are consistent across the applications. On various dates, domestic courts in Ukraine delivered decisions in favor of the applicants. These decisions, which are detailed in appended tables, granted the applicants entitlement to various pecuniary amounts or ordered certain actions to be taken in their favor. Crucially, all these decisions became final and enforceable under Ukrainian law.

The central factual issue is that, despite the final and binding nature of these judgments, the applicants were unable to obtain their enforcement in due time. The State authorities failed to comply with the court orders, leading to significant delays. For example, in the lead application (no. 1270/12), the Desnyanskyy District Court of Chernigiv issued a decision on 29 January 2010. Other decisions date back even further, such as one from the Slovyansk Court in 1997. The applications were lodged with the European Court between late 2011 and mid-2012. This chronology demonstrates a systemic problem in Ukraine where final court decisions were not being executed promptly, leaving applicants without the remedies they had been legally granted.

The case also addressed procedural matters. It was noted that two applicants, Mr. V. S. Grunskiy and Mr. P. A. Plyaka, had died, and their spouses expressed a wish to pursue the applications. The Government also informed the Court that two other applicants had died and, following no response from their addresses, the Court assumed no one wished to pursue their applications.

In summary, the key facts relevant to the alleged violations are that the Ukrainian government consistently failed to enforce final domestic court decisions that were in favor of the applicants. This failure constituted a systemic and ongoing issue, depriving numerous individuals of their lawfully awarded entitlements. The applicants had exhausted domestic remedies by obtaining final judgments, but the State's non-enforcement forced them to seek redress at the European Court of Human Rights, alleging a violation of their rights to a fair trial and peaceful enjoyment of their possessions. The case highlights a widespread administrative practice in Ukraine that was incompatible with the Convention's guarantees.

**Case Summary: Moskalenko and Others v. Ukraine (Application no. 1270/12 and 249 other applications)**

**Court:** European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section)
**Date of Judgment:** 18 July 2013

**Parties and Procedure:**
The case originated from 250 applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights by Ukrainian nationals. The applicants alleged a violation of their rights due to the State's failure to enforce final domestic court decisions. Two applicants, Mr. Grunskiy and Mr. Plyaka, died during the proceedings, and their spouses expressed a wish to pursue the applications. Two other applicants, Mr. Motuzkov and Ms. Moroz, also died; the Court received no response from their estates and subsequently struck their applications out. The Ukrainian Government was represented by their Agent, Mr. Nazar Kulchytskyy. The applications were communicated to the Government on 11 December 2012.

**Key Facts and Alleged Violations:**
The central factual basis of the case is uniform across all 250 applications. On various dates, domestic courts in Ukraine issued decisions in favour of the applicants. These decisions either entitled them to specific pecuniary amounts (such as pension arrears or social benefits) or required certain actions to be taken in their favour.

Crucially, these court decisions became final and were subject to enforcement under Ukrainian law. However, the applicants were unable to obtain their timely enforcement. The State authorities, primarily the State Bailiffs' Service and other state bodies, failed to comply with the binding and enforceable judgments. The period of non-enforcement was significant, ranging from several months to many years.

The applicants' primary complaint, therefore, was that the State's failure to enforce the final judgments in their favour constituted a violation of their rights under Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) of the Convention. The non-enforcement rendered the judicial decisions in their favour ineffective, depriving them of the expected financial or material benefits and undermining the principle of legal certainty.

**Examples from the Appended Table:**
The sheer scale of the problem is illustrated by the appended table of applications. For instance:
- **Applicant Moskalenko** (application no. 1270/12) had a final judgment from the Desnyanskyy District Court of Chernigiv dated 29 January 2010 which remained unenforced.
- **Applicant Neshcheret** (application no. 1789/12) had a decision from the Nizhyn Court dated 28 April 2010.
- **Applicant Dmytrenko** (application no. 1886/12) secured a decision from the Zhytomyr Circuit Administrative Court on 26 January 2009.
Many applicants, such as Mr. Malygin (no. 16355/12) or Ms. Papka (no. 28038/12), held multiple final judgments from as early as 2007 and 2008, all of which suffered from the same non-enforcement issue. The decisions were primarily against state-owned enterprises or the state itself, often concerning obligations under the Law on State Social Standards and social guarantees.

In its judgment, the Court (noting that some applicants had also raised “unrelated” matters, which were not the focus) concentrated on the systemic non-enforcement of final domestic decisions. The case was one of many similar cases against Ukraine, highlighting a widespread structural problem where state bodies systematically failed to obey court orders for prolonged periods, a practice the Court consistently found to violate the Convention. The applicants sought just satisfaction for the delays they had endured.

text:
**Case: Moskalenko and Others v. Ukraine (Application no. 1270/12 and 249 other applications)**

The case originated in 250 applications lodged against Ukraine with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were Ukrainian nationals whose details were set out in appended tables. The applications were communicated to the Ukrainian Government on 11 December 2012. The Government was represented by its Agent, Mr Nazar Kulchytskyy. A Fifth Section Committee delivered judgment on 18 July 2013.

Several procedural issues arose because some applicants had died. Mr Vasiliy Spiridonovich Grunskiy and Mr Petro Andriyovych Plyaka died, and their spouses, Ms Valentina Petrovna Grunskaya and Ms Valentyna Oleksandrivana Kuzmina, expressed the wish to pursue the applications on their behalf. The Government also informed the Court that Mr Viktor Mykolayovych Motuzkov and Ms Olga Mykhaylivna Moroz had died. No replies were received from their addresses after the Court warned that, absent response, it would assume that no one was entitled or wished to pursue those applications.

The central factual basis of the case concerned the non-enforcement of final domestic court decisions. On the dates listed in the appended tables, Ukrainian domestic courts delivered decisions according to which the applicants were entitled to various pecuniary amounts or to have certain actions taken in their favour. These decisions became final and enforceable. However, the applicants were unable to obtain their enforcement in due time. The table shows a large number of decisions from local and administrative courts across Ukraine, including Chernihiv, Nizhyn, Zhytomyr, Korosten, Feodosiya, Druzhkivka, Kharkiv, Lviv, Zaporizhzhya, Poltava, Kyiv and other locations. The relevant domestic decisions dated from 1997 to 2011, and many applicants held more than one final decision in their favour. For example, Mr Oleksandr Petrovych Moskalenko had a decision of the Desnyanskyy District Court of Chernihiv dated 29 January 2010; Mr Oleksandr Vasylovych Neshcheret and Mr Viktor Vasylyovych Neshcheret had a decision of the Nizhyn Court dated 28 April 2010; and Ms Oksana Ruslanivna Dmytrenko had a decision of the Zhytomyr Circuit Administrative Court dated 26 January 2009. Other applicants had decisions concerning various district, city, circuit and administrative courts.

The applicants complained primarily about the failure of the Ukrainian authorities to enforce those final and binding judgments. In Convention terms, this alleged non-enforcement engaged the right to a fair trial under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, particularly the right of access to court and the requirement that civil rights and obligations be determined within a reasonable time. It also engaged Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, protecting the peaceful enjoyment of possessions, because the final judgments gave rise to enforceable pecuniary entitlements or required specific actions in the applicants’ favour. The applicants essentially alleged that although domestic courts had recognised their rights, the State failed to ensure that those rights were realised in practice, resulting in prolonged delay and uncertainty. Some applicants also made submissions concerning factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issues, but the main case concerned the systemic or repeated failure to enforce final domestic decisions.

The case therefore belonged to a group of repetitive applications concerning Ukraine’s longstanding problem of non-enforcement of domestic judgments. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were that final and enforceable decisions existed in the applicants’ favour, that the authorities did not enforce them in due time, and that the applicants consequently suffered delay and loss of the benefit of those judgments. The Court was called upon to determine whether that situation amounted to a violation of the Convention.

**N.M.B. v. Sweden** (Application no. 68335/10) concerned an Iraqi national, born in 1973 and originally from Baghdad, who alleged that his deportation from Sweden to Iraq would violate Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. He arrived in Sweden on 12 December 2007 and applied for asylum the following day. He claimed a risk of persecution as a Christian academic and because of threats arising from his university work and his accusation against a colleague connected to the Iraqi Islamic Party (IIP).

In April 2006 the applicant began working for a university committee established to develop research methods. The committee was soon accused of cooperating with Americans. On 20 June 2006 he wrote to the Minister of Education accusing a university colleague of corruption and of counteracting the committee’s work. The colleague, said to be an IIP member, allegedly found out and threatened him, saying bad things would happen. On 27 June 2006 armed men attempted to kidnap the applicant’s daughter; her mother called the police and, after shooting, the daughter was released. On 30 June 2006 the applicant received a letter calling him and his family Christian traitors and stating they would be killed if he did not quit his job. On 8 July 2006 he reported the incidents to police, and the family moved in with relatives. Later he learned that the head of the committee had been kidnapped and killed on 16 July 2006, and that other committee members had received threatening letters. The committee’s work ended, and on 3 October 2006 the applicant fled with his family to Syria.

The applicant further claimed that on 15 January 2008 his parents in Baghdad were shot at and his father was kidnapped and tortured until he revealed the applicant’s whereabouts. In October and December 2008 he allegedly received threatening messages on a website; one from the Islamic Brigade, a militia within the IIP, warned him against returning to Iraq. He later added that in December 2009 IIP members had asked for him and written threatening messages on the wall of his old house. He also stated that he had reported to police his suspicion that high-profile members of the Ministry of Education were responsible for the kidnapping attempt against his daughter.

Domestically, the Migration Board rejected his asylum application on 17 March 2009. It accepted that he was Christian and had worked for the university committee, but did not find it likely that this work had made him suspected of cooperating with Americans. It noted that he had quit the job three years earlier, that his accusation against the former colleague was unlikely to have harmed the colleague or the IIP, and that there was no reasonable explanation for the alleged attack on his parents. It also considered that the security situation in Baghdad and Iraq had improved.

On 9 June 2010 the Migration Court upheld the Board’s decision. It found that the incidents did not amount to persecution on religious grounds, that the applicant had exaggerated his story, that his committee work had been limited and had ended long before, and that, absent political activity, his letter was unlikely to create the threat he alleged. The Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal on 3 November 2010. The applicant then claimed impediments to enforcement based on the general situation for Christians in Baghdad and attacks in November 2010 in his former residential area. On 26 January 2011 the Migration Board declined to reconsider the case.

The applicant lodged his application with the European Court on 15 November 2010. On 14 December 2010 the President of the Section applied Rule 39, indicating that the applicant should not be deported during the proceedings. The case was communicated to the Government on 22 September 2011. The key alleged violation was that deporting him to Iraq would expose him to a real risk of treatment contrary to Article 3.

**Case: Jeznik v. Slovenia (Application no. 32238/08)**  
**Court:** European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section  
**Judgment date:** 20 June 2013  

The applicant, Ms Marija Jeznik, was a Slovenian national born in 1940 and living in Vuzenica. She was represented by a Slovenian law firm. The application was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 1 July 2008 and communicated to the Slovenian Government on 27 April 2012. The case primarily concerned the alleged excessive length of civil proceedings and the absence of an effective domestic remedy, raising issues under Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention.

The facts arose from the applicant’s investments in commercial papers of the company Kompas Consulting d.d., made through Kompas Maribor D.O.O. beginning in 1994. At the end of 1994, trading in such commercial papers was prohibited by the Securities Market Act, but the applicant continued the activity until 1996. In 1996, she instituted enforcement proceedings against Kompas Maribor D.O.O. before the Maribor District Court, seeking payment for lost investments. She alleged that Kompas Maribor had failed to inform her of the legislative amendments and had continued trading commercial papers. She also complained that because Kompas Consulting d.d. was bankrupt, she could recover only a small proportion of her investments in the bankruptcy proceedings.

The domestic proceedings were lengthy. On 14 October 1996, the Maribor District Court issued a writ of execution. After an objection, the case was referred to contentious proceedings on 12 November 1996. On 4 February 1998, the District Court rejected the applicant’s request. She appealed. On 24 November 1998, the Maribor Higher Court upheld the appeal and remitted the case for re-examination. The Higher Court found that the applicant had clarified during the appeal that she was seeking compensation for damages only, which constituted a new fact requiring first-instance consideration.
