**CASE OF Á.F.L. v. ICELAND** — Summary

This case concerns an Icelandic father, Á.F.L., who was deprived of custody of his daughter after authorities allegedly failed to provide him with reasonable accommodation for his disability, in violation of Articles 8 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant was diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder, ADHD, and a mild intellectual disability. He had a history of alcohol and drug abuse but had been sober since 2012. In February 2019 he and his girlfriend had a daughter, V.F. The parents initially shared custody, but the relationship was unstable, with conflict, mental-health concerns, and reports of violence. By September 2019, after maternal care difficulties, the child protection services (CPS) arranged for the applicant to care for V.F. with support from his mother.

The CPS placed V.F. with the applicant at Mánaberg, a residential diagnostic and guidance facility. Both parents consented. After the mother left, the applicant cared for V.F. under staff supervision. Staff knew of his impairment and provided extensive guidance on parenting, routines, hygiene, and stimulation. A December 2019 psychologist report found that he needed extensive assistance and could not care for V.F. without it. Mánaberg reports noted progress but found he struggled to recognise his daughter’s needs and transfer skills between situations. A January 2020 report concluded he could care for V.F. only with targeted support, recommending a support family, autism and anxiety counselling, and regular CPS visits.

After leaving Mánaberg, the applicant and V.F. moved to his mother’s home. A support plan was implemented: CPS follow-up visits, a YLFA counsellor twice weekly for six weeks tailored to his disability, a support family, and continued counselling. The support was later increased. Despite this, reports from March to June 2020 stated that the applicant still lacked insight into V.F.’s physical, social, and emotional needs, showed little initiative, and had difficulty stimulating her development. Concerns grew about possible attachment disorder, motor delays, and self-stimulation. In May 2020 the YLFA counsellor recommended foster care.

In July 2020 the Child Protection Committee removed V.F. for two months and placed her with a foster family. Contact was limited to three hours every two weeks. An August 2020 parenting assessment found the applicant was attached and cooperative but that his autism and intellectual challenges restricted his ability to meet V.F.’s basic needs. The child improved significantly in foster care. The District Court upheld the removal.

In September 2020 the CPC decided permanent foster care was necessary and sought to deprive the applicant of custody; he refused to relinquish it. A court-appointed expert in April 2021 validated earlier findings, concluding the applicant lacked basic parenting skills and needed daily guidance; returning V.F. would be contrary to her interests. At trial, a YLFA counsellor testified that additional disability services could not compensate for the lack of care and bonding. The applicant’s experts argued he had begun ADHD medication and was entitled to targeted assistance under disability legislation, and that previous measures had not fully accounted for his condition.

In September 2021 the District Court deprived the applicant of custody under Article 29(1)(a) and (d) of the Child Protection Act. It found extensive measures had been tried, V.F.’s needs remained unmet, no realistic additional measures had been proposed, and her stability should be maintained. The Court of Appeal upheld the decision in February 2022, and the Supreme Court denied leave to appeal in March 2022.

The alleged violation centres on whether Iceland failed to provide reasonable accommodation—necessary support measures—to enable the applicant, as a disabled parent, to care for his daughter, and whether the custody deprivation was therefore discriminatory.

In *Qama v. Albania and Italy* (Application no. 4604/09), the European Court of Human Rights’ Fourth Section delivered judgment on 8 January 2013; it became final on 8 April 2013. The applicant, Flamur Qama, an Albanian national born in 1960 and living in Durrës, complained under Article 6 § 1 and Article 8 of the Convention that the Albanian and Italian authorities had failed to secure his right of contact with his child in Italy.

The applicant’s son was born on 25 August 1994. In September 1999 the applicant’s late spouse, who was suffering from a serious disease, entered Italy irregularly with the son in order to obtain medical treatment. The applicant later joined them in Italy. In August or September 2002, following disagreements with his in-laws, the applicant was expelled from Italy because he did not have a residence permit. His wife and son, whose status in Italy had not yet been regularised, remained there. The applicant’s wife died on 7 October 2002.

On 17 October 2002, the applicant’s sister-in-law, Z., brought custody proceedings before the Ancona Youth Court in Italy. On 30 December 2002, a report from the local social health centre stated that the child feared returning to live with his father because of the father’s alleged ill-treatment of the deceased mother. The report also said that the father had abandoned the child and spouse without notice when they most needed him.

On 4 June 2003, the Italian court granted Z.’s request. It entrusted Z. with custody of the child under the supervision of the Social Service of Senigallia, appointed the Mayor of Senigallia as the child’s temporary guardian, suspended the parents’ parental rights, prohibited the child’s removal from Italian territory, and assigned the International Social Service (“ISS”), an NGO, to investigate the applicant’s family situation. Importantly, the court made no provision for the applicant’s visiting or contact rights with his child.

On 25 September 2003, after trying to contact the applicant, the ISS informed the Italian court that he refused to speak to them and simply requested that the child be returned to him. Following contacts with neighbours, the ISS reported that the applicant had remarried, that his new wife was expecting a child, and that he was unemployed and living on his spouse’s income. On 22 March 2004, the Italian social services updated the court that the child’s status in Italy had been regularised and that his situation appeared to be balanced.

The alleged violations arose from this cross-border custody and contact situation. Although the Italian court suspended parental rights and placed the child with a relative in Italy, it did not establish any contact or visitation arrangements for the applicant. The applicant, who was living in Albania after his expulsion, claimed that both the Albanian and Italian authorities failed to secure his right of contact with his son, thereby breaching his right to family life under Article 8 and his fair-trial/access rights under Article 6 § 1.

The application was lodged on 23 December 2008. On 21 September 2009, it was communicated to both respondent Governments, and the Court decided to rule on admissibility and merits simultaneously under Article 29 § 1. The Albanian Government was represented initially by E. Hajro and later by L. Mandia; the Italian Government by N. Lettieri and later by P. Accardo. The provided extract ends before the Court’s merits assessment and final conclusion.

The case *M.L. v. North Macedonia* (Application no. 30206/23) concerns an Article 8 complaint about a barring order that prohibited the applicant from approaching his daughter and from visiting her home or school, and about the domestic courts’ alleged failure to reassess the need for that order every two months, as required by domestic law.

The applicant married D.B.L. in July 2013, and their daughter D. was born in December 2013. In December 2021 the applicant filed for divorce and sought custody. In March 2022 the Social Care Centre recommended that he be granted custody. After he moved out in June 2022, D. stayed with him every other week until early October 2022. On 25 October 2022 he informed the Centre that the mother had initiated criminal proceedings against him and that he had not seen D. since 2 October 2022. In January 2023 the Centre established contact rights allowing him to see D. every other weekend and on Wednesdays. The applicant complained that the mother did not comply and that D. refused contact because of the mother’s and her family’s influence. His appeal against the contact decision was dismissed in April 2023.

In parallel, criminal proceedings developed. In October 2022 the mother reported that the applicant had sent her threatening messages, and in December 2022 police filed a criminal complaint against him for threatening her. The applicant lodged counter-complaints against the mother. On 1 March 2023 the mother alleged that between October 2022 and March 2023 the applicant had physically and psychologically abused D. The same day, police interviewed D., who said she had not wanted to see the applicant since October 2022 and alleged that he had hit, threatened and insulted her. Police also interviewed D.’s teacher, the school psychologist, a pedagogical expert and the maternal grandmother; the grandmother alleged repeated abuse. Psychiatric reports noted that D. was upset, anxious, afraid and recommended that she speak to a psychologist.

On 6 March 2023 police interviewed the applicant, who denied the accusations and stated that he had not seen D. since 2 October 2022. The police filed a criminal complaint against him for bodily injury through domestic violence and violence against a child. That same day, the public prosecutor requested protective measures. A pre-trial judge issued a barring order under the Criminal Proceedings Act, prohibiting the applicant from approaching D. and the mother within 100 metres and from visiting D.’s school or the apartment where they lived. The order was to last as long as necessary, but at the latest until a final judgment in the criminal proceedings, and the court was to reassess the need for the measures every two months. The judge reasoned that the seriousness of the offences, the possible sentence, the risk of influencing the victims, and D.’s psychological and physical health justified the measures to facilitate the proceedings.

The applicant received the order on 7 March 2023 and appealed on 9 March. He argued that he could not have abused D. because he had barely seen her since October 2022. He submitted Centre documents, the contact-rights decision, his earlier complaints, and an expert report denying that threatening messages had been sent from his phone. He also argued that the barring order would further distance D. from him. On 15 March 2023 a three-judge panel dismissed the appeal, finding a reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offences and that the measures were necessary during the investigation.

Earlier, in November 2022, the civil court had ordered protective measures against both parents, including not arguing or threatening each other in D.’s presence and not involving her in their disputes; the applicant was also barred from domestic violence against the mother in D.’s presence and ordered to attend counselling. Those measures were upheld in July 2023. In May 2023 the Centre set aside its January 2023 contact decision because of the criminal measures. In September 2023 it recommended that the mother be granted custody, and in December 2023 it allowed the applicant one-hour visits twice monthly at the Centre. In March 2024 the civil court dissolved the marriage, granted custody to the mother and determined contact rights.

The European Court of Human Rights gave notice of the complaints concerning the issuing and prolonged validity of the barring order and the alleged failure to reassess it every two months, raising an issue under Article 8.

In *Chonin and Others v. Bulgaria* (Application no. 30116/23), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) examined complaints by ten Bulgarian nationals, two of whom also hold Belgian and German nationality, about the excessive length of restitution proceedings under Bulgaria’s Restitution of Title to Forests and Forestry Land Act. The application was lodged on 20 July 2023. The applicants are represented by Bulgarian lawyers. The Governments of Belgium and Germany did not intervene.

The applicants are heirs of Ms F. and collectively inherited about four-fifths of her estate. Ms F. had owned an afforested island in the Danube and mainland forests, all nationalised in 1948. After the 1997 Forests Restitution Act, the applicants initiated restitution proceedings. The earlier stages of the case were described in *Popov and Chonin v. Bulgaria* (no. 36094/08, judgment of 17 February 2015), brought by one of the current applicants.

On 12 December 2000, the competent land commission, later renamed the Agriculture Department, recognised the heirs’ right to compensation in lieu of restitution for 93.38 hectares of forestry land. Restitution in kind was impossible because the original land was located in a frontier zone and classified as exclusive State property. Under the Forests Restitution Act, compensation could only be provided through equivalent State-owned land. As a result, the authorities spent years trying to identify suitable substitute plots. In 2007, a court judgment identified one such plot and ordered its transfer to the applicants, but the judgment was ultimately deemed unenforceable because the land formed part of a national park.

After the *Popov and Chonin* judgment, further developments occurred. In decisions issued in 2013 and 2018, the Agriculture Departments in Montana and Berkovitsa allocated forestry land totalling about 59 hectares to the applicants. These decisions were served on Mr Chonin, who acted as representative of all applicants, in 2018. He challenged the decisions, arguing that the quality of the allocated forests was inferior to that of Ms F.’s original forests. Nevertheless, the decisions were upheld in final court judgments given in 2023 and 2024. An additional plot of about 5.3 hectares has been identified, but its official allocation to the applicants remains ongoing. The competent authorities are still working to locate further plots to compensate the applicants for the remaining approximately 29 hectares of forestry land.

The key alleged violation concerns the lengthy duration of the restitution procedure. Although entitlement to compensation was recognised in 2000, the applicants had received only partial substitute land decades later. By the time of the application and the subsequent domestic proceedings, full compensation had still not been achieved. The delay therefore spans more than two decades and involves repeated attempts to identify equivalent State-owned land, partial allocations, challenges to the quality of that land, and continuing unresolved allocation for a substantial remainder. The Court gave notice of the complaints concerning the lengthy duration of the restitution procedure and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The judgment was delivered on 30 September 2025, having been adopted on 9 September 2025.

**Case: Abbate and Others v. Italy**  
**Applications nos. 27814/23, 27974/23, 33199/23, 33278/23 and 35651/23**  
**European Court of Human Rights, First Section, Judgment of 16 January 2025**

The case originated in five applications against Italy lodged under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants complained primarily of the non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of final domestic decisions given in their favour. They also raised other Convention complaints. The Italian Government was given notice of the applications.

The applicants were Ferdinando Emilio Abbate, Daniela Jossa, Lucio Benigni (in two applications), and Maria Stella Saveriano. The domestic decisions at issue generally ordered the Ministry of Economy and Finance or the Ministry of Justice to pay lawyers’ legal fees, in the context of the lawyer acting as *avvocato antistatario*—that is, a lawyer entitled to collect fees directly from the opposing party.

In application no. 27814/23, introduced on 26 June 2023, Ferdinando Emilio Abbate relied on numerous judgments of the Latium Administrative Court dated 5 June 2017 and 20 July 2017, as well as Rome District Court orders of July 2019 enforcing several of those judgments. These decisions ordered the Ministry of Economy and Finance to pay legal fees. The non-enforcement periods ended between 2 and 24 March 2023. The delays ranged from approximately 3 years and 8 months to 5 years and 9 months, depending on the decision. Thus, by the time enforcement occurred, the applicant had faced lengthy delays of several years.

In application no. 27974/23, introduced on 5 July 2023, Daniela Jossa relied on three decisions: Rome Court of Appeal, 25 September 2017; Naples Court of Appeal, 4 July 2018; and Naples Court of Appeal, 6 August 2020. These ordered the Ministry of Justice to pay legal fees. Enforcement remained pending. The periods of non-enforcement had lasted more than 7 years, 1 month and 11 days; more than 6 years, 4 months and 1 day; and more than 4 years, 2 months and 30 days respectively.

In application no. 33199/23, introduced on 23 August 2023, Lucio Benigni relied on four Naples Court of Appeal decisions dated 20 January 2017, 3 December 2018, 20 December 2018, and 22 September 2020. They ordered the Ministry of Justice to pay legal fees. Enforcement was still pending, with delays exceeding 7 years, 9 months and 16 days; 5 years, 11 months and 2 days; 5 years, 10 months and 16 days; and 4 years, 1 month and 14 days.

In application no. 33278/23, introduced on 23 August 2023, Maria Stella Saveriano relied on four Naples Court of Appeal decisions dated 22 November 2018, 21 February 2019, 15 March 2019, and 22 May 2019. These also ordered the Ministry of Justice to pay legal fees. Enforcement remained pending. The delays exceeded 5 years and 11 months, 5 years and 8 months, 5 years and 7 months, and 5 years and 5 months respectively.

In application no. 35651/23, introduced on 11 September 2023, Lucio Benigni relied on five Naples Court of Appeal decisions dated 16 June 2017, 30 January 2019, 18 September 2019, 10 December 2020, and 15 April 2021. These ordered the Ministry of Justice to pay legal fees. Enforcement was still pending, with delays ranging from more than 3 years and 6 months to more than 7 years and 4 months.

The key alleged violation therefore concerns the failure or delay by Italian authorities in enforcing binding domestic decisions in the applicants’ favour. In Abbate’s case, enforcement eventually occurred in March 2023 after delays of several years. In the other applications, enforcement remained pending at the time of introduction, with delays exceeding several years. The applicants alleged that this prolonged non-enforcement breached their Convention rights, particularly fair-trial and property-protection guarantees.

**Summary of Pyrantienė v. Lithuania (Application no. 45092/07)**

The case of Pyrantienė v. Lithuania concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Ms. Kotrina Pyrantienė, a Lithuanian national, on 11 October 2007. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, claiming she did not receive adequate compensation after domestic court decisions deprived her of property she had legally owned for nine years.

The key facts are as follows: In 1994, a local authority assigned a 0.5-hectare plot of land to the applicant. On 6 August 1996, the Kaunas Region Administration confirmed the sale of this land to her. Subsequently, on 24 September 1996, she acquired the plot from the State for 61 "single-use investment vouchers" and registered it in her name with the Land Registry. The applicant used the land for growing and selling vegetables.

However, in December 2001, third parties filed a civil claim seeking the restoration of their ownership rights to the same plot, based on a request for restitution they had lodged in 1991. On 2 October 2003, the Kaunas Regional Court, acting as an appellate court, quashed the 1996 administrative decision as unlawful and cancelled the sale. The court found that the authorities had no right to sell the land because a prior claim for its restitution was pending. The land was ordered to be returned to the State, and the case was remitted for determination of compensation, as the sale agreement was declared null and void. The Supreme Court later refused the applicant leave to appeal.

Following the court's decision, the plot was transferred to the former owners in September 2005. In the subsequent proceedings to determine compensation, an independent expert valued the plot's market value at 112,500 Lithuanian litai (LTL) (approximately EUR 32,580) in September 2005, while its value in August 1996 was LTL 18,000.

Despite this expert valuation, the Kaunas Regional Court, on 5 October 2006, awarded the applicant only LTL 1,466 (approximately EUR 430). The court reasoned that this sum corresponded to the price the applicant had originally paid in investment vouchers in 1996. The Court of Appeal upheld this decision on 26 February 2007, rejecting the applicant's argument that under Article 6.147 § 2 of the Civil Code, she should be awarded the highest value of the property because she had been deprived of it due to an error by State authorities. The Supreme Court refused to accept her cassation appeal on 8 May 2007.

The applicant's central complaint to the European Court was that this compensation was manifestly inadequate, effectively depriving her of the full value of the property she had legally acquired and held for nearly a decade. The domestic courts' decisions resulted in her losing the land, which was then returned to the original owners, while she received a nominal sum that did not reflect its true market value, contrary to the principle of "just compensation" for property deprivation.

In *Brzuszczyński v. Poland* (Application no. 23789/09), the applicant, Piotr Brzuszczyński, a Polish national, complained under Article 6 of the Convention that his criminal trial was unfair. The central issue was the use against him of statements by R.N., the actual perpetrator of the murder, who died before the applicant’s trial and therefore could not be examined in court by the defence.

The underlying facts concerned the murder of E.U. on 19 May 2001 by R.N. The applicant and R.N. were arrested on 6 June 2001; R.N. had a loaded gun. R.N. was questioned four times—twice on 7 June 2001, then on 8 June and 25 July 2001. On 7 June he confessed to the murder and implicated the applicant, saying that the applicant had provided him with the gun to kill E.U. and that they planned to split the victim’s money. He repeated this account on 8 June and 25 July 2001, specifying that he had received the gun from the applicant in Kobyłka near the Zepter warehouse. During his fourth interview, however, R.N. slightly changed his statements, mentioning an unnamed man present at the killing and claiming that he himself had been kidnapped. He then broke off, saying he needed to think and would write to the prosecutor. On 31 August 2001 R.N. committed suicide in his prison cell.

On 23 May 2002 the prosecution indicted the applicant for aiding and abetting murder by providing the gun, illegal possession of the gun, and attempted extortion of ransom from E.U.’s family. The applicant denied all involvement and said he had never possessed or supplied a gun.

In the first trial, the Warsaw Regional Court reclassified the first charge to aiding and abetting armed robbery, finding no irrefutable proof that the applicant knew the gun would be used to kill. It convicted him and sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment, relying heavily on R.N.’s pre-trial statements, which it found credible. The court noted it would have been useful to hear R.N. in court but that his death made this impossible. On appeal, the Warsaw Court of Appeal quashed the judgment on 9 December 2003. It found the first-instance proceedings flawed, especially because the trial court had failed to examine all evidence and had assessed the evidence inconsistently. The appellate court stressed that reliance on R.N.’s statements required particularly thorough scrutiny since R.N. could not be heard in court, and it ordered the trial court to clarify, among other things, whether the applicant had provided the gun, whether his fingerprints were on it, and whether he had a gun permit.

On retrial, the Regional Court held 19 hearings and convicted the applicant on 27 November 2007 of aiding and abetting murder, illegal gun possession, and aiding attempted extortion, sentencing him to 15 years. The court relied on the applicant’s and co-defendant’s statements, R.N.’s statements, about 40 witnesses, documents, autopsy and firearms expert evidence. It found that the applicant and R.N. were close friends and business partners in financial difficulty; that R.N. planned to fake a car sale and kill the buyer; and that the applicant, knowing this, provided the gun and was to help hide the body and share the proceeds. The court found R.N.’s early statements credible, detailed, self-incriminating, and corroborated by other evidence, while discounting defence witnesses who changed testimony.

The applicant’s Article 6 complaint therefore focused on whether his conviction, based significantly on the untested statements of a deceased witness whom he could not cross-examine, violated his right to a fair trial, particularly his right to examine witnesses against him.

Tarasov v. Ukraine (no. 17416/03) concerned a Ukrainian national arrested on 13 January 2000 by Makiyivka police and held in police custody until 25 January 2000. He alleged that he was denied access to a lawyer and severely ill-treated to force confessions. He claimed repeated beatings, suffocation with a plastic bag and ammonia-filled gas mask, and electric shocks to his penis and right hand. Police said his rights, including to counsel and freedom from self-incrimination, were explained and that he signed waivers before confessing to car theft, robbery and other thefts.

Medical evidence was central. On 14 January 2000 hospital reports recorded abdominal trauma and lumbar bruising. Forensic examinations in 2000–2001 found discolouration on his wrist and penis allegedly consistent with electric shocks, and bruising in the lumbar/coccyx area possibly inflicted on 13 January 2000 as described. Many other scars were old, and experts found no link between those injuries and later health problems. He alleged SIZO staff failed to record injuries and police told him to say they were self-inflicted. The CPT’s 2000 report noted similar allegations and that the wrist mark and penis scar remained visible.

After confessing, Tarasov recanted on 16 January, claiming duress. On 2 March 2000, with lawyer M., he denied guilt and repeated the duress claims. At trial from March 2000 he sought to prove ill-treatment. Two witnesses, U.G. and U.A., testified they heard screams and saw him after beatings. The court refused to summon the ambulance doctor but ordered a forensic exam. The trial was delayed due to his health; in December 2001 he was brought to court on a stretcher. He claimed he could not properly participate and that his lawyer advised him to waive presence at the last hearing.

**Summary of *Rozhenko and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 2644/04 et al.)**

The case of *Rozhenko and Others v. Ukraine* was brought before the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) by 24 Ukrainian nationals against the Government of Ukraine. The applications were lodged on various dates between 2003 and 2011 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The central legal issue, as noted by the Court, was already the subject of well-established case-law, particularly referencing *Yuriy Nikolayevich Ivanov v. Ukraine* (no. 40450/04, 15 October 2009).

**Key Facts and Alleged Violations:**

The primary grievance in all 24 applications was the lengthy failure by Ukrainian authorities to enforce final domestic court decisions rendered in the applicants’ favour. The core of the alleged violation concerns the applicants' right to a fair trial under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and their right to the peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

1.  **Domestic Court Decisions:** In each case, domestic courts (including regional, district, and commercial courts) issued judgments ordering the State or state-owned entities to pay various pecuniary amounts to the applicants or to perform specific actions in their favour (e.g., provide housing, recalculate pensions). These judgments, detailed in an appended table, became final and enforceable under Ukrainian law.
2.  **Failure to Enforce:** Despite the final nature of these decisions, the applicants were unable to obtain timely enforcement. The judgments remained unexecuted for extended periods due to the State's failure to comply. This non-enforcement is the central factual basis for the applications. For instance, the domestic decisions in these cases were issued between 2001 and 2008, yet enforcement was still pending years later when the applications were lodged with the ECtHR.
3.  **Procedural History:** The applications were communicated to the Ukrainian Government, which is represented by its Agent, Mr. Nazar Kulchytskyy. On various dates, the Government submitted unilateral declarations acknowledging the non-enforcement and offering to settle the cases. The Government requested that the applications be struck out of the Court's list of cases based on these declarations. However, the Court examined the declarations and rejected the Government's request, indicating that the declarations did not provide sufficient redress or that the issues warranted a full examination.
4.  **Individual Circumstances:** The applicants are a diverse group of individuals, with dates of birth ranging from 1914 to 1975, residing in various regions of Ukraine. They were awarded sums or entitlements by courts such as the Kyiv Regional Court of Appeal, the Kirovskyy District Court of Dnipropetrovsk, the Krasnyy Luch Court, the Zhytomyr Regional Administrative Court, and others. The relevant domestic decisions span from 2001 to 2008. In two applications (nos. 17176/07 and 48229/07), the original applicants died, and the proceedings were pursued by their relatives or heirs.
5.  **Other Submissions:** The judgment notes that some applicants also made submissions concerning factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issues, but the primary and common focus of all applications remained the failure to enforce domestic judicial decisions.

In essence, the applicants alleged that the Ukrainian State's persistent failure to execute final court judgments against it or its entities violated their right to a fair and effective remedy for the determination of their civil rights and obligations (Article 6 § 1) and their right to the protection of their property (Article 1 of Protocol No. 1), as the awarded sums or entitlements constituted possessions which they could not effectively enjoy due to the non-enforcement.

**Summary of Rozhenko and Others v. Ukraine (App. No. 2644/04 et al.)**

The case of *Rozhenko and Others v. Ukraine* concerns 24 applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights by Ukrainian nationals. The applicants alleged violations arising primarily from Ukraine's lengthy failure to enforce final domestic court decisions issued in their favour. The Court, sitting as a Committee of the Fifth Section, noted that the underlying legal issue was already the subject of well-established case-law, referencing *Yuriy Nikolayevich Ivanov v. Ukraine* (no. 40450/04, 15 October 2009).

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are as follows. In each application, domestic courts delivered judgments entitling the applicants to various pecuniary amounts or to have certain actions taken in their favour. These judgments became final and enforceable. However, the applicants were unable to obtain enforcement of these decisions in due time because of the State's failure to comply with them. The delay in enforcement, attributable to the State, formed the core of the applicants' complaints.

The domestic decisions at issue span a considerable period. They were delivered by various courts across Ukraine, including the Kyiv Regional Court of Appeal (12 March 2003), the Kirovskyy District Court of Dnipropetrovsk (27 June and 25 August 2003), the Suvorovskyy District Court of Odesa (28 February 2003), the Krasnyy Luch Court (multiple decisions between 2001 and 2006), the Torez Court (23 March 2005), the Komsomolskyy District Court of Kherson (24 May 2004), the Mykolayiv Regional Court of Appeal (15 March 2006), the Zhytomyr Regional Administrative Court (5 October and 21 November 2007), the Pecherskyy District Court of Kyiv (28 February 2002), the Rivne Regional Administrative Court (28 April 2009), the Frunzenskyy District Court of Kharkiv (26 November 2007), the Dzerzhynsk Court (29 November 2005), the Lysychanskiy Court (November 2008), the Kryukivskyy District Court of Kremenchuk (23 January 2003), the Avtozavodskyy District Court of Kremenchuk (27 December 2001), the Starokostiantyniv Court (8 August 2007), the Tsentralno-Miskyy District Court of Makiyivka (26 December 2007), and the Kherson Regional Commercial Court (6 October 2006).

Two applicants, Mr. Aleksandr Pavlovich Mikhaylov (application no. 17176/07) and Ms. Klavdiya Ivanovna Kasperovich (application no. 48229/07), died during the proceedings. Their applications were pursued by their relatives or heirs. Some applicants also made submissions concerning factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issues, though these were not central to the case.

The Government submitted unilateral declarations on various dates, requesting that the applications be struck out under Article 37 § 1 (c) of the Convention. The Court examined these declarations and rejected the Government's request, meaning the cases proceeded to judgment. The Court's decision underscores the systemic problem of non-enforcement of domestic judicial decisions in Ukraine, a matter already addressed in its established case-law.

**Case of Moskalenko and Others v. Ukraine** (Application no. 1270/12 and 249 other applications) was a judgment delivered by the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) on 18 July 2013. The case concerned 250 applications lodged against Ukraine by Ukrainian nationals under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applications were joined because they raised the same core issue: the failure or prolonged delay by Ukrainian authorities in enforcing final domestic court decisions.

The key facts are set out in the appended tables. On various dates, Ukrainian domestic courts delivered decisions under which the applicants were entitled to various pecuniary amounts or to have certain actions taken in their favour. These decisions became final and enforceable. However, the applicants were unable to obtain their enforcement in due time. The domestic decisions dated from 1997 to 2011 and were issued by numerous courts across Ukraine, including district, city, circuit administrative, and appellate courts. For example, applicant Oleksandr Moskalenko had a decision from the Desnyanskyy District Court of Chernigiv dated 29 January 2010. Other applicants obtained decisions from courts in Nizhyn, Zhytomyr, Korosten, Feodosiya, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhya, Lviv, Poltava, and many other locations. In each case, despite the decisions being final and binding, the State authorities failed to execute them within a reasonable time or, in some instances, at all.

The applicants’ central complaint was therefore not about the substance of the domestic decisions, but about the State’s failure to enforce them. The Court has consistently held that execution of a final judgment is an integral part of the “trial” for the purposes of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and that prolonged non-enforcement may also interfere with the right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The applicants alleged violations of these provisions. Some applicants also made submissions concerning factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issues, but those did not form the core of the case.

Procedurally, the applications were communicated to the Government of Ukraine on 11 December 2012. The Government were represented by their Agent. Several applicants died during the proceedings. In two applications, the deceased applicants’ spouses expressed a wish to pursue the applications on their behalf. In two other cases, the Government informed the Court of the applicants’ deaths; no responses were received from persons entitled to pursue those applications, so the Court proceeded on the basis that no such persons wished to continue them.

The essential facts relevant to the alleged violations were that the applicants held final and enforceable domestic judgments awarding them money or requiring action, yet the Ukrainian authorities delayed or failed to enforce those judgments for extended periods. This left the applicants in a state of uncertainty and deprived them of the benefits they had secured through the courts. The Court examined these circumstances and found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The case is representative of the systemic problem of non-enforcement of final domestic judgments in Ukraine during the relevant period.

**Case: Aslan and Others v. Türkiye (Applications nos. 12531/21 and 8 others)**

This case is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered on 13 November 2025. It originated in nine applications lodged against Türkiye under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates between 12 February 2021 and 7 April 2023. The Turkish Government was given notice of the applications.

The central complaint was that each applicant had been held in pre-trial detention for an excessive length without relevant and sufficient reasons. In applications nos. 18927/21 and 16303/23, the applicants also raised other complaints under the Convention.

The applicants and key detention facts were as follows. Dilan Aslan (b. 1991) was detained from 16 March 2020 to 27 October 2020, a period of 7 months and 12 days, by the Denizli 2nd and 3rd Assize Courts. Mehmet Bozkurt (b. 1975) was detained from 5 July 2015 to 5 June 2020, lasting 4 years, 11 months and 1 day, by the Ağrı Assize Court. Ayşegül Çağatay Gökçe (b. 1991) was detained from 25 June 2011 to 31 March 2020, a period of 8 years, 9 months and 7 days, by Istanbul magistrate and assize courts. Sadun Kaya (b. 1968) was detained from 2 July 2018 to 16 September 2022, lasting 4 years, 2 months and 15 days, by the Kocaeli 1st and 2nd Assize Courts. Şeyhmus Çeri (b. 1997) was detained from 17 August 2016 to 10 October 2018, a period of 2 years, 1 month and 24 days, by the Şanlıurfa Assize Court. Mensur Akar (b. 1995) was detained from 18 April 2016 to 3 January 2019 and again from 20 December 2019 to 27 October 2022, totaling 6 years, 6 months and 23 days, by the Hakkari Assize Court. Helin Yapıcı (b. 1994) was detained from 23 March 2016 to 6 April 2021, a period of 5 years and 15 days, by the Diyarbakır Assize Court. İrfan Yıldız (b. 1980) was detained from 16 February 2017 to 27 March 2019 and from 25 December 2019 to 25 June 2020, periods of 2 years, 1 month and 12 days and 6 months and 1 day, by Istanbul magistrate and assize courts. Mücahit Doğan (b. 1983) was detained from 31 December 2021 to 27 December 2022, a period of 11 months and 28 days, by Küçükçekmece magistrates’ courts and the Küçükçekmece Criminal Court of First Instance.

The detention decisions relied on recurring grounds. These included strong suspicion that the applicant had committed an offence, the nature of the offence, the severity of the potential sentence, and, in most cases, the fact that the offence was among “catalogue offences” listed in Article 100 § 3 of the Turkish Code of Criminal Procedure. Authorities also cited risks of absconding and tampering with evidence. Some decisions referred to the scope of the case, outstanding evidence such as expert reports, the applicant’s contacts, the insufficiency of alternative judicial supervision measures, and—in İrfan Yıldız’s case—the alleged risk of ISIS terror acts on special days. The applicants’ essential complaint was that these reasons were not relevant and sufficient to justify detention of such length, making their continued pre-trial detention excessive. The appended table set out the specific periods, competent courts, lengths of detention and stated grounds for each applicant.

**Summary of *Tarasov v. Ukraine* (App. No. 17416/03)**

The case of *Tarasov v. Ukraine* concerns allegations of police ill-treatment and violations of the right to a fair trial. The applicant, Mr. Aleksey Gennadyevich Tarasov, a Ukrainian national born in 1965, was arrested on 13 January 2000 by officers from the Makiyivka Police Department and held in police custody until 25 January 2000.

The applicant alleged that during this period he was subjected to severe ill-treatment aimed at forcing him to confess to various crimes. He claimed he was beaten multiple times, suffocated with a plastic bag and a gas mask filled with ammonia, and subjected to electric shocks applied to his genitals and right hand. On 14 January 2000, an ambulance was called, and he was taken to a hospital where medical reports documented abdominal trauma and bruising in the lumbar region. According to the Government, the applicant was informed of his procedural rights, including the right to legal representation, and signed waivers of this right on multiple occasions between 13 and 19 January 2000, during which he confessed to theft and robbery. The applicant later retracted these confessions, claiming they were extracted under duress.

On 15 January 2000, criminal proceedings were instituted against the applicant. He was charged with car theft on 16 January and with additional charges of theft from a garage, theft of non-ferrous metals, and robbery on 18 January. During this time, he participated in on-site reconstructions of events. On 2 March 2000, the applicant requested and was granted legal representation by lawyer M. From that point, he denied all charges, stating his earlier confessions were coerced.

The applicant’s trial began on 17 March 2000. During the proceedings, he reiterated his claims of ill-treatment and sought to examine witnesses. Two witnesses testified that they had heard him screaming at the police station. The court ordered a forensic medical examination, which was conducted between 12 July and 2 August 2000. The expert found marks on the applicant's wrist, lumbar region, and penis, concluding they could be signs of healing bruises inflicted on 13 January 2000, consistent with his allegations.

The applicant's health deteriorated during the trial, suffering from severe neurological pain. On 21 December 2001, he was brought to a final court hearing on a stretcher. He was convicted on 25 December 2001 and sentenced to five years’ imprisonment. The court rejected his ill-treatment complaint as unsubstantiated, and his subsequent appeals, including a cassation appeal to the Supreme Court, were unsuccessful.

Separately, the applicant's ill-treatment complaints were repeatedly investigated by the prosecutor's office. Multiple decisions refusing to institute criminal proceedings were made between 2000 and 2005. These refusals were periodically quashed by higher prosecutors or courts due to incomplete investigations, but ultimately, the proceedings were terminated in June 2005 for lack of evidence, as police officers denied the allegations, cellmate testimonies were contradictory, and key medical documentation from his arrival at the detention facility had been destroyed.

The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 26 February 2003, alleging that he had been ill-treated by the police in violation of Article 3 and that his right to mount a defence had been violated under Article 6 of the Convention.

**Summary of Facts in *Abdi v. the United Kingdom* (Application no. 27770/08)**

The applicant, Mr. Mustafa Abdi, a Somali national born in 1975, arrived in the United Kingdom on 7 May 1995 and claimed asylum. Although his asylum claim was refused, he was granted exceptional leave to remain until February 2000. On 23 July 1998, the applicant was convicted of rape and indecency with a child and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. On 20 May 2002, the Secretary of State for the Home Department issued a decision to make a deportation order and authorised his detention pending that order. The applicant appealed and made a fresh asylum claim, but his appeal rights were exhausted on 4 December 2003. While in prison, he received fourteen disciplinary charges, including six for fighting, and was assessed as presenting a high risk of sexual offending and a medium risk of general offending.

On 3 September 2003, the applicant’s release from his criminal sentence became automatic, but he remained in immigration detention under the authority issued in May 2002. A deportation order was issued on 5 April 2004 and served on 19 April 2004. The applicant claimed membership of the Isaaq tribe from Somaliland and stated his parents were born in Hargeisa, though he was born in Mogadishu. Initially, authorities sought to return him to Somaliland, but this required clan-history bio-data that the applicant did not cooperate in providing. In August 2004, the last carrier willing to take enforced returns to Somalia withdrew, making removal impossible without consent. Carriers would only transport those who signed a disclaimer confirming voluntary return; the applicant refused a formal request to sign such a disclaimer in November 2004.

The applicant made further asylum representations in March 2005, which were refused as a fresh claim in September 2005. In October 2005, an immigration judge was wrongly informed that enforced removals to Somalia would be possible in the foreseeable future. In July 2006, the Government concluded an agreement with African Express Airlines, making enforced removals possible; the first such removal occurred on 30 November 2006. Removal directions were issued for the applicant for 29 November 2006, but were cancelled pending judicial review.

Judicial review of the detention decision was heard by Mr. Justice Calvert-Smith, who held that detention up to August 2004 was lawful, but that the period from 3 December 2004 to 30 June 2006 was unlawful due to its length, the impossibility of removal during that period, and misleading statements. Detention after 30 June 2006 was deemed lawful as removal prospects existed. The Court of Appeal subsequently allowed the Secretary of State’s appeal, holding the entire period lawful because the applicant could have returned voluntarily, and his high reoffending risk outweighed concerns about returning. Permission to appeal to the House of Lords was refused on 13 December 2007.

Separately, the applicant challenged the deportation order. After various tribunal and court decisions, the Court of Appeal found in April 2010 that removal to Mogadishu would breach Article 3, but the Supreme Court allowed the Secretary of State’s appeal in November 2010. Removal directions were issued for 8 December 2010, and on 7 December 2010, the European Court of Human Rights granted interim measures under Rule 39 to prevent removal. The applicant remained in immigration detention, having been released on bail in April 2007 but re-detained in April 2008 after breaching bail conditions.

The present application concerns only the first period of detention, ending shortly after 13 April 2007. During this detention (3 September 2003 to 13 April 2007), monthly reviews were conducted. From April 2006, a secret Home Office policy created a presumption in favour of detaining Foreign National Prisoners pending deportation, contrary to the published policy favouring release. This unpublished “near blanket ban” on release was not disclosed until mid-2008 and was later found unlawful by the Supreme Court in *Lumba and Mighty v. Secretary of State for the Home Department* [2011] UKSC 12.

**Case Summary: Rozhenko and Others v. Ukraine (Application no. 2644/04 and 23 other applications)**

This case, adjudicated by the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) on 11 April 2013, consolidates 24 applications lodged against Ukraine by Ukrainian nationals under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The central issue in all applications is the prolonged failure by Ukrainian state authorities to enforce final domestic court decisions issued in the applicants’ favor.

The core facts are consistent across the applications. On various dates between 2001 and 2009, domestic courts throughout Ukraine (including those in Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Odesa, and others) delivered judgments according to which the applicants were entitled to various pecuniary amounts or to have specific actions taken in their favor. These judgments became final and enforceable under Ukrainian law. However, the applicants were unable to obtain timely enforcement of these decisions due to the State's failure to comply. This non-enforcement allegedly violated their rights under Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) of the Convention. Some applicants also raised submissions on unrelated factual and legal matters, but the primary complaint concerns the systemic non-enforcement of domestic judicial decisions.

The applications were lodged with the Court on dates ranging from 2003 to 2011. The applicants include individuals such as Ruslan Yevgenovych Rozhenko (born 1965), Stanislav Grigoryevich Kirichenko (born 1964), and Anatoliy Aleksandrovich Bazelyuk (born 1949), among many others. Notably, the applicants in two applications (nos. 17176/07 and 48229/07) died during the proceedings; their applications were pursued by their relatives or heirs. Details of the domestic decisions relevant to each applicant are provided in appended tables, showing the dates of judgments and the dates they were introduced to the ECtHR. For instance, Rozhenko’s application referenced a Kyiv Regional Court of Appeal decision from 12 March 2003; Kirichenko’s involved two Dnipropetrovsk district court judgments from 2003; and Bazelyuk’s concerned an Odesa court decision from 28 February 2003. Similar patterns are evident for all applicants, with judgments spanning from 2001 to 2009 and applications introduced between 2003 and 2011.

The Ukrainian Government, represented by Agent Nazar Kulchytskyy, submitted unilateral declarations on various dates, requesting that the Court strike out the applications under Article 37 § 1 (c) of the Convention. However, the Court examined these declarations and rejected the Government’s request, indicating that the declarations did not provide sufficient basis for striking out. This decision aligns with the Court’s well-established case-law on non-enforcement of domestic decisions, as referenced in *Yuriy Nikolayevich Ivanov v. Ukraine* (no. 40450/04, 15 October 2009). The Court noted that the underlying legal issue—lengthy non-enforcement—is already the subject of consistent jurisprudence.

In summary, the key facts relevant to the alleged violations are: (1) domestic court decisions were issued in favor of the applicants, becoming final and enforceable; (2) these decisions remained unenforced for extended periods due to State failure; (3) the applicants lodged applications with the ECtHR, alleging violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1; and (4) the Government’s attempts to resolve the cases through unilateral declarations were rejected by the Court. The case underscores a systemic problem in Ukraine regarding the enforcement of judicial decisions, leading to repeated findings of Convention violations. The Court’s judgment likely addressed these issues in line with its prior case-law, potentially awarding just satisfaction to the applicants. This summary is based solely on the provided text, focusing on facts directly related to the alleged non-enforcement violations.

The case *Moskalenko and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 1270/12 and 249 other applications) is a European Court of Human Rights judgment delivered on 18 July 2013 by a Fifth Section Committee. It originated in 250 applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention by Ukrainian nationals. The applicants’ core complaint concerned the Ukrainian authorities’ failure to enforce final and enforceable domestic court decisions that had awarded them various pecuniary amounts or required certain actions to be taken in their favour.

The facts, set out in appended tables, show that domestic courts across Ukraine—including in Chernihiv, Nizhyn, Zhytomyr, Korosten, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, Lviv, Poltava, Donetsk, Luhansk and elsewhere—issued decisions in the applicants’ favour on dates ranging from the late 1990s to 2011. For example, the lead applicant, Oleksandr Moskalenko, obtained a decision from the Desnyanskyy District Court of Chernihiv on 29 January 2010. Other applicants had one or more decisions, some dating back to 1997, 1998 or 1999. In each case, the decisions became final and enforceable. However, the applicants were unable to obtain enforcement in due time. These delays and the continuing non-execution of the judgments formed the basis of their alleged violations.

Some applicants also made submissions concerning factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issues. The central problem, however, remained the failure to execute final domestic decisions. The Government was represented before the Court by its Agent, Nazar Kulchytskyy. The applications were communicated to the Government of Ukraine on 11 December 2012.

The Court also addressed several procedural developments. Mr Vasiliy Spiridonovich Grunskiy and Mr Petro Andriyovych Plyaka died; their spouses respectively expressed the wish to pursue the applications on their behalf. The Government informed the Court that two other applicants, Mr Viktor Mykolayovych Motuzkov and Ms Olga Mykhaylivna Moroz, had died. The Court forwarded that information to the deceased applicants’ addresses and warned that, absent any response, it would assume no one was entitled or wished to pursue those applications. No replies were received.

The key issue was whether Ukraine’s failure to enforce final domestic decisions violated the applicants’ Convention rights. The applicants alleged violations under Article 6 §1 of the Convention, concerning the right to a fair trial and the execution of final judgments; Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, concerning protection of property; and Article 13, concerning the right to an effective remedy. The essential facts relevant to these alleged violations were that binding judgments in the applicants’ favour remained unexecuted, leaving them without the awards or actions they had been granted by domestic courts. The case therefore concerned a systemic problem of non-enforcement of final court decisions in Ukraine rather than isolated disputes over the underlying entitlements.

In *M.L. v. North Macedonia* (Application no. 30206/23), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint under Article 8 of the Convention concerning a barring order that prohibited the applicant from approaching his daughter within 100 metres and from visiting her home and school. The applicant also alleged that the domestic court failed to reassess the need for that order every two months, as required by domestic law.

The applicant married D.B.L. in July 2013, and their daughter D. was born in December 2013. In December 2021 he filed for divorce and sought custody. In March 2022 the Social Care Centre recommended that he be granted custody. After moving out in June 2022, he initially stayed with D. every other week, but he later stated that he had not seen her since 2 October 2022. In January 2023 the Centre established contact rights allowing him to see D. every other weekend and on Wednesdays. He repeatedly complained that the mother did not comply and that D. refused contact due to the mother’s and her family’s influence. His appeal against the contact-rights decision was dismissed in April 2023.

Separately, criminal proceedings arose. In October 2022 the mother reported that the applicant had sent threatening messages. In March 2023 she reported that he had physically and psychologically abused D. between October 2022 and March 2023, including hitting, kicking, insulting and threatening her. On 1 March 2023, police interviewed D., who said she had not seen the applicant since October 2022 because she did not want to, and alleged that he had hit her in the face and body and had threatened and insulted her when they previously spent time together. Police also interviewed her teacher, school psychologist, pedagogical expert and maternal grandmother. The teacher described D. becoming withdrawn and upset and refusing to leave school with the applicant.

On 6 March 2023 the police temporarily detained and interviewed the applicant. He denied the accusations and maintained that he had not seen D. since 2 October 2022. The police filed a criminal complaint against him for bodily injury through domestic violence and violence against a child. The public prosecutor requested protective measures under the Criminal Proceedings Act. The same day, a pre-trial judge issued the barring order, prohibiting the applicant from approaching D. and the mother within 100 metres and from visiting D.’s school or their apartment. The order was to last until a final criminal judgment, with reassessment every two months. The judge cited the seriousness of the offences, the possible sentence, the need to prevent influence over the victims, and D.’s psychological and physical health.

The applicant appealed on 9 March 2023, arguing that he could not have abused D. during the alleged period because he had barely seen her. He submitted evidence of the contact-rights decision and his complaints about non-enforcement, and an expert report disputing the threatening messages. On 15 March 2023 a three-judge panel dismissed the appeal, finding a reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offences and confirming the barring order.

In parallel civil proceedings, protective measures were ordered against both parents in November 2022 and again in June 2023, including prohibitions on arguing or threatening in D.’s presence and a requirement to attend counselling. The case therefore concerned whether the barring order and its prolonged validity interfered disproportionately with the applicant’s family life under Article 8, particularly given the alleged failure to reassess it every two months.

In *Á.F.L. v. Iceland*, the applicant is an Icelandic man born in 1990 who was diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder, ADHD, and mild intellectual disability. He had a history of alcohol and drug abuse but had been sober since 2012. In February 2019, he and his girlfriend had a daughter, V.F. They initially shared custody, but the relationship was marked by conflict, mental health problems, and domestic violence. After separation, the mother mainly cared for V.F., though the child later stayed with her maternal grandmother. In September 2019, following an incident, the Child Protection Services (CPS) decided the applicant should care for V.F. with support from his mother.

CPS placed V.F. and her parents at Mánaberg, a residential diagnostic and guidance facility. The mother left in October 2019, and the applicant stayed with V.F. Staff knew of his disability and provided extensive guidance on parenting, routines, hygiene, and child development. A December 2019 parenting assessment found he had cognitive difficulties affecting his parenting, needed extensive assistance, and could not care for his daughter alone. Mánaberg staff reported progress but noted difficulties recognizing V.F.’s needs and transferring skills. They recommended further targeted support, counselling, and a support family.

After discharge in January 2020, the applicant and V.F. moved to the paternal grandmother’s home. CPS arranged follow-up visits four times a week, YLFA counselling twice a week, a support family, and psychological counselling. Reports in March, May, and June 2020 noted the applicant lacked insight into V.F.’s physical, social, and emotional needs and had little initiative in stimulating her development. The child showed poor motor skills and possible attachment problems. Support was increased, but concerns persisted. In June 2020, YLFA reported V.F. showed signs of an attachment disorder and urgently needed a primary caregiver who could provide security. CPS recommended temporary foster care while reassessing the applicant’s parenting capacity.

In July 2020, the Child Protection Committee ruled V.F. be removed for two months and placed in foster care. A second parenting assessment in August 2020 confirmed the applicant’s attachment to his daughter but found autism and intellectual challenges restricted his insight and ability to acquire parenting skills. Despite extensive support, he struggled to meet her basic needs. V.F. improved significantly in foster care. The District Court upheld the removal. In September 2020, the CPC decided to seek custody deprivation; the applicant refused to relinquish custody.

A court-appointed expert assessment in April 2021 validated earlier findings and considered the CRPD and Icelandic disability support legislation. The expert found the applicant lacked basic parenting skills, needed daily guidance, and that returning V.F. to his care would risk her well-being. In September 2021, the District Court deprived him of custody, finding all reasonable support measures had been tried and exhausted and the child’s best interests justified the decision. The Court of Appeal upheld this in February 2022, and the Supreme Court denied leave to appeal in March 2022.

The alleged violation concerns complaints under Articles 8 and 14 of the European Convention. The applicant argues Iceland failed to provide reasonable accommodation—necessary child-rearing support measures—due to his disability, resulting in his loss of custody. He contends further support under disability legislation could have enabled him to parent V.F. The authorities concluded extensive tailored measures had been provided but were insufficient to meet the child’s needs, and her best interests required permanent foster care and custody deprivation. The case therefore raises whether the failure to provide additional disability-related support amounted to discrimination and unjustified interference with family life.

In *Qama v. Albania and Italy* (Application no. 4604/09), the European Court of Human Rights examined an Albanian national’s complaints under Articles 6 § 1 and 8 of the Convention that the Albanian and Italian authorities failed to secure his right of contact with his child, who was living in Italy. The applicant, Flamur Qama, was born in 1960 and lived in Durrës. His son was born on 25 August 1994.

In September 1999, the applicant’s late spouse, who was suffering from a serious disease, entered Italy irregularly with their son in order to obtain medical treatment. The applicant later joined them in Italy. In August or September 2002, following disagreements with his in-laws, the applicant was expelled from Italy because he did not have a residence permit. His wife and son remained in Italy, their immigration status not yet regularised. The wife died on 7 October 2002.

On 17 October 2002, the applicant’s sister-in-law, Z., filed an action with the Ancona Youth Court seeking custody of the child. On 30 December 2002, a local social health centre reported that the child feared returning to live with his father because of the father’s alleged ill-treatment of the deceased mother. The report also stated that the father had abandoned the child and spouse without notice when they needed him most.

On 4 June 2003, the Italian Youth Court granted Z.’s request. It entrusted Z. with custody of the child under the supervision of the Social Service of Senigallia and appointed the Mayor of Senigallia as temporary guardian. The court suspended the parents’ parental rights, reasoning that they had allowed the child to leave Albania without addressing the serious difficulties he would face. It also prohibited the child’s removal from Italian territory and assigned the International Social Service (ISS) to investigate the applicant’s family situation. Crucially, the court made no provision for the applicant’s visiting or contact rights with his son. This omission, together with his expulsion from Italy, formed the central factual basis for his later complaint that he could not maintain family life with his child.

On 25 September 2003, the ISS, after attempting to contact the applicant, informed the Italian court that he refused to speak to them and simply requested that the child be returned to him. Following contacts with neighbours, the ISS reported that the applicant had remarried, that his new wife was expecting a child, and that he was unemployed and living on his spouse’s income. On 22 March 2004, the Italian social services updated the court: the child’s status in Italy had been regularised and his situation appeared balanced.

The applicant lodged his application with the European Court on 23 December 2008. He alleged that both Albania and Italy had breached Articles 6 § 1 and 8 by failing to secure his right of contact with his child in Italy. On 21 September 2009, the application was communicated to the respondent Governments, and the Court decided to rule on admissibility and merits at the same time.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore the Italian custody order placing the child with the maternal aunt, the suspension of parental rights, the absence of any contact arrangement for the father, the applicant’s expulsion from Italy, and the resulting cross-border situation in which he could not exercise contact. The Court’s examination concerned whether the respondent states had failed to comply with their positive obligations to protect the applicant’s family life and his access to his child.

**Case M.L. v. North Macedonia** (Application no. 30206/23), judgment of 24 June 2025, concerns an Article 8 complaint about a barring order preventing the applicant from approaching his daughter and from visiting her home and school, and the alleged failure of the domestic court to reassess the order every two months as required by domestic law.

The applicant, born in 1984, married D.B.L. in 2013; their daughter D. was born in December 2013. In December 2021 the applicant filed for divorce and sought custody. In March 2022 the Social Care Centre recommended that he be granted custody. He moved out in June 2022, and until October 2022 D. stayed with him every other week. In October 2022 the mother initiated criminal proceedings against him; the applicant told the Centre he had not seen D. since 2 October 2022. In January 2023 the Centre established contact rights, allowing him to see D. every other weekend and every Wednesday. The applicant later complained that the mother did not comply and that he had barely seen D. since October 2022.

In November 2022, in concurrent civil proceedings, the Civil Court imposed protective measures on both parents under the domestic violence law: they were prohibited from arguing or threatening each other in D.’s presence and from involving her in their disputes; the applicant was specifically prohibited from domestic violence against the mother in D.’s presence; both were ordered to attend counselling. These measures were later reissued and upheld.

In the criminal proceedings, the mother alleged in October 2022 that the applicant had sent threatening messages. In December 2022 police filed a criminal complaint for threatening her. In March 2023 the mother alleged that between October 2022 and March 2023 the applicant had physically and psychologically abused D. The same day, police interviewed D., who said she had not seen the applicant since October 2022 because she did not want to; she alleged he had hit, threatened and insulted her and stated she did not wish to see him. A teacher, school psychologist, pedagogical expert and maternal grandmother were also interviewed. Psychiatric reports and notes from February–March 2023 recorded that D. was upset, anxious, angry and afraid and recommended psychological support.

On 6 March 2023 police detained and interviewed the applicant. He denied the accusations and stated he had not seen D. since 2 October 2022. The prosecutor requested protective measures, and the same day a pre-trial judge issued a barring order under the Criminal Proceedings Act. The applicant was barred from approaching D. and the mother within 100 metres and from visiting D.’s school or the apartment where she and the mother lived. The order was to remain in force until a final criminal judgment and was to be reassessed every two months. The judge cited the seriousness of the charges, the possibility that the applicant might influence the victims, D.’s psychological and physical health, and the need for unhindered criminal proceedings.

On 9 March 2023 the applicant appealed, arguing that the alleged violence was impossible because he had had almost no contact with D. since October 2022. He submitted the contact-rights decision, his complaints to the Centre, and an expert report contesting the threatening messages. On 15 March 2023 a three-judge panel dismissed the appeal, finding reasonable suspicion and that the investigation stage justified the measures.

Later, the Centre set aside its January 2023 contact decision because of the criminal measures, recommended in September 2023 that the mother have custody, and in December 2023 limited the applicant’s contact to one hour twice monthly on the Centre’s premises. In March 2024 the Civil Court dissolved the marriage, granted custody to the mother and determined contact rights.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained about the issuing and prolonged validity of the barring order and the domestic court’s alleged failure to reassess it every two months. The Court gave notice of the Article 8 complaints concerning the issuing and prolonged validity of the order; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

**Monteiro and Trinta Santos v. Portugal** (Applications Nos. 40620/22 and 44221/22) is a case before the European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, sitting as a Committee composed of Anne Louise Bormann (President), Sebastian Răduleţu, and András Jakab, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The judgment was delivered in Strasbourg on 6 March 2025, after private deliberations on 6 February 2025. It is final but subject to editorial revision.

The applications were lodged against Portugal under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights on 12 August 2022 (No. 40620/22) and 6 September 2022 (No. 44221/22). The applicants were represented by lawyers R. Mendes Martins of Lisbon and V. Carreto of Torres Vedras. The Portuguese Government were given notice of the applications.

The first applicant, António Augusto Monteiro, born in 1986, complained under Article 3 of the Convention about inadequate conditions of detention in Coimbra Prison. According to the appended table, he was detained there from 27 December 2021 to 3 December 2022, a period of 11 months and 7 days, and again from 30 June 2023, pending, for more than 1 year and 6 months. In both periods he was held in a two-inmate cell with approximately 3.10 m² per inmate and one toilet. His specific grievances included overcrowding, lack of privacy for the toilet, lack of fresh air, inadequate temperature, passive smoking, poor-quality food, infestation of the cell with insects or rodents, and a mouldy or dirty cell.

The second applicant, Hugo David Trinta Santos, born in 1984, also complained under Article 3 about conditions in Coimbra Prison. He was detained there from 15 July 2022, pending, for more than 1 year and 6 months. He was held in a two-inmate cell with approximately 2.25 m² per inmate and one toilet. His specific grievances were overcrowding, inadequate temperature, lack of requisite medical assistance, a mouldy or dirty cell, lack of fresh air, and lack or insufficient quantity of food. In application no. 44221/22, he further complained under Article 13 that there was no effective domestic remedy in Portugal regarding the alleged inadequate detention conditions.

The key alleged violations therefore concern Article 3 ECHR, the prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment, based on overcrowding and materially poor prison conditions. These include limited personal space, sanitation and privacy problems, environmental discomfort, hygiene issues, food deficiencies, and, for Trinta Santos, inadequate medical assistance. The Article 13 complaint, raised only by Trinta Santos, concerns the absence of an effective domestic remedy for those detention-condition complaints. The applicants’ claims rely on the factual details in the appended table, which specifies the facilities, periods, durations, cell occupancy, square metres per inmate, toilet access, and particular grievances forming the basis of the alleged violations.

**Jeznik v. Slovenia (Application no. 32238/08)** concerned civil proceedings brought by Ms Marija Jeznik, a Slovenian national born in 1940 and living in Vuzenica. The case is relevant principally to the alleged excessive length of domestic court proceedings under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which guarantees a fair hearing within a reasonable time.

In 1994 the applicant began investing in commercial papers of the company Kompas Consulting d.d. through Kompas Maribor D.O.O. At the end of 1994, trading in such commercial papers was prohibited by the Securities Market Act, but the applicant continued the activity until 1996. In 1996 she instituted enforcement proceedings before the Maribor District Court against Kompas Maribor D.O.O., seeking payment for lost investments. She claimed that the company had failed to inform her of the legislative amendments and had continued trading in commercial papers. She also complained that, because Kompas Consulting d.d. was bankrupt, she could recover only a small proportion of her investments through bankruptcy proceedings.

On 14 October 1996 the Maribor District Court issued a writ of execution. However, following an objection, the case was referred to contentious proceedings on 12 November 1996. On 4 February 1998 the Maribor District Court rejected the applicant’s request. She appealed. On 24 November 1998 the Maribor Higher Court upheld the appeal and remitted the case for re-examination. The Higher Court noted that the applicant had clarified during the appeal phase that she was seeking compensation for damages only; this was treated as a new fact requiring consideration by the first-instance court.

The proceedings then continued before the Maribor District Court, which delivered a judgment on 24 October 2001. It found that, given the contractual arrangements, Kompas Maribor D.O.O. could not be held responsible for the damages sustained. The applicant appealed again. On 15 September 2004 the Maribor Higher Court upheld the first-instance judgment and rejected her appeal. The applicant then lodged an appeal on points of law. On 25 January 2007 the Supreme Court rejected that appeal. She subsequently lodged a constitutional appeal, which the Constitutional Court rejected on 10 December 2007.

The applicant lodged her application with the European Court of Human Rights on 1 July 2008. She was represented by a Slovenian law firm, while the Government were represented by their Agent. On 27 April 2012 the application was communicated to the Government, and under Protocol No. 14 it was assigned to a Committee of three judges.

The key facts for the alleged violation are therefore the chronology of the domestic proceedings. The applicant’s civil claim began in 1996 and was not finally resolved at domestic level until December 2007, a period of approximately eleven and a half years. The proceedings involved a first-instance judgment in 1998, a remittal by the Higher Court later that year, a second first-instance judgment in 2001, an appeal decision in 2004, a Supreme Court decision in 2007, and a Constitutional Court decision in 2007. These delays and procedural stages formed the factual basis for the complaint that Slovenia had violated the applicant’s right to a hearing within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1. The judgment also referred to the relevant domestic law as set out in Tomažič v. Slovenia, which concerned similar issues of procedural delay and effective remedies.

**Case: Kashbullina and Others v. Russia**  
**Court:** European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, sitting as a Committee  
**Judgment date:** 13 November 2025  
**Applications nos.:** 1964/22 and four others  

This case originated in five applications lodged against Russia under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights on various dates. The Russian Government were given notice of the applications. The applicants complained of disproportionate measures taken against them as organisers or participants of public assemblies in St Petersburg, in connection with various public events held in breach of regional COVID-19-related restrictions. They also raised other complaints under the Convention. The Court deliberated privately on 23 October 2025 and delivered judgment on 13 November 2025; the judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The applicants and relevant facts, as set out in the appended table, are as follows:

1. **Alena Valeriyevna Kashbullina**, born 1998, application no. 1964/22, lodged on 3 December 2021. She was represented by Natalya Andreyevna Baranova of Moscow. The event was a rally titled “Free Navalnyy” in St Petersburg on 2 February 2021. She was charged under Article 20.2.2 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences (CAO) and fined RUB 10,000. The final domestic decision was given by the St Petersburg City Court on 3 June 2021.

2. **Aleksandra Vadimovna Eller**, born 1990, application no. 37658/22, lodged on 19 July 2022. She was represented by Baranova. The event was an anti-war protest in St Petersburg on 24 February 2022. She was charged under Article 20.2.2 § 1 CAO and sentenced to detention for five days. The final domestic decision was given by the St Petersburg City Court on 22 March 2022.

3. **Sergey Aleksandrovich Fedorov**, born 1997, application no. 37671/22, lodged on 16 July 2022. He was represented by Baranova.
