**Summary of *Grupa Zastava Vozila, A.D. v. Slovenia***

The case of *Grupa Zastava Vozila, A.D. v. Slovenia* (Application no. 67793/10) originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 11 November 2010 by Grupa Zastava Vozila, A.D., a Serbian company. The applicant alleged a violation of its right to a fair trial under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, specifically concerning the excessive length of civil proceedings before Slovenian courts.

The underlying facts date back to 1996, when the applicant company entered into a contract with the Slovenian company PS ZA AVTO p.o. before a notary, establishing terms for joint investments. On 1 December 1997, PS ZA AVTO initiated proceedings before the Ljubljana District Court seeking annulment of the contract and the notarial protocol.

The proceedings were marked by significant delays, particularly in the early stages. On 14 July 1998, the court ordered the claim to be served on the applicant company in Serbia through diplomatic channels via the Ministry of Justice. Subsequent inquiries by the court in October and November 1998 revealed that the Ministry was still awaiting a response from Serbian authorities. It was not until 29 June 2000 that the applicant company's representative submitted an authority form and a request for joinder. The first scheduled hearing on 11 October 2001 was postponed.

Further procedural complications arose with requests for third-party intervention by ZASTAVA AVTO d.o.o. and the State Attorney's Office. These were granted on 10 June 2002. The applicant filed a counterclaim on 12 September 2002, prompting another postponement. A settlement hearing on 3 February 2003 failed, and the first actual hearing was held on 14 April 2003—more than five years after the claim was initially filed.

The case continued with the appointment of a financial expert in November 2003, whose report was submitted in May 2004 after an extension. A hearing took place on 6 October 2004, and the Ljubljana District Court delivered its judgment on 13 December 2004, ruling in favor of the applicant company and upholding the contract and notarial protocol.

The plaintiff appealed, and on 7 November 2006, the Ljubljana Higher Court reversed the first-instance judgment, ruling against the applicant. The applicant then lodged an appeal on points of law with the Supreme Court, which upheld the appellate decision on 12 May 2008. Subsequently, the applicant filed a constitutional appeal, which the Constitutional Court rejected as unfounded on 13 May 2010.

The domestic proceedings thus spanned nearly thirteen years from initiation to final resolution. The central factual issue relevant to the alleged violation is the length of these proceedings and the apparent delays attributable to the service of documents through diplomatic channels, the management of third-party interventions, and the scheduling of hearings. The applicant contended that this duration violated the "reasonable time" requirement under Article 6 § 1. The Slovenian Government was represented, while the Serbian Government declined to participate. The application was communicated to the respondent Government on 24 May 2012 and assigned to a Committee of three judges.

**Case Summary: Röman v. Finland (Application no. 13072/05)**

**Parties and Procedural History**

The applicant, Ms Mirja Anneli Röman, a Finnish national born in 1954, lodged an application against the Republic of Finland on 6 April 2005. She alleged violations under Articles 8 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically that she was unable to have her biological father's paternity legally established due to a five-year time-limit in Finnish legislation, and that this constituted discrimination. The case was communicated to the Government in April 2008, with merits examined alongside admissibility.

**Key Facts**

The applicant was born out of wedlock and initially bore her mother's maiden name. In the year of her birth, her mother and biological father concluded a child support agreement verified by social services. In 1956, her mother married another man, and in 1961 the applicant's surname was changed to that of her mother's husband. The spouses agreed that the biological father would never be mentioned, and the applicant grew up unaware of her true origins. She had two siblings from her mother's subsequent marriage.

The Paternity Act entered into force on 1 October 1976. Its transitional provisions required that paternity proceedings for children born before the Act's entry into force be initiated within five years—by 1 October 1981. Additionally, no claim could be examined after the putative father's death. No such restrictions applied to children born after the Act came into force.

In 2001, the applicant began investigating her biological background. She discovered that in the church registry (the official population registry until 1993), her mother's husband was listed as her stepfather, while the State population registry listed him as her father. She located the child support agreement in social services archives, enabling her to identify her biological father. The population register information was corrected in September 2002.

**Domestic Proceedings**

On 6 February 2003, the applicant initiated paternity proceedings, claiming she had only learned in December 2001 that her registered father was not her biological father. The Vantaa District Court dismissed her claim on 18 June 2003, finding the action time-barred. The court held that during the five-year period she had been an adult capable of initiating proceedings, questioning her mother, or verifying the church register (which had always been correct). The Helsinki Court of Appeal upheld this decision on 15 March 2004. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 12 October 2004. The Deputy Parliamentary Ombudsman subsequently found the courts had acted within their margin of appreciation.

In 2007, a private DNA test confirmed with 99.99% certainty that the identified man was her biological father. He died on 3 July 2008.

**Relevant Legal Framework**

The Finnish Constitution guarantees equality before the law (Article 6), protection of private life (Article 10), and access to court (Article 21). Article 106 permits courts to give primacy to the Constitution over conflicting legislation. The drafting history of the Paternity Act indicates that legal certainty for putative fathers motivated the five-year restriction, while the prohibition on posthumous proceedings reflected evidentiary concerns. However, in precedent KKO 2012:11, the Supreme Court later held that applying the time-limit where legal or factual reasons prevented timely proceedings could conflict with the Constitution, given that DNA testing now permits reliable paternity determination and that knowing one's biological origin falls within protected private life.

In *Gavula v. Ukraine*, the applicant, Mr Vitaliy Gavula, a Ukrainian national born in 1977, complained under Article 3 and Article 5 § 3 of the Convention that his arrest was unlawful, that his pre-trial detention was excessively lengthy, and that the conditions of his detention in Kyiv Pre-Trial Detention Centre No. 13 (“the SIZO”) amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment.

The applicant was arrested at 3 p.m. on 6 February 2003 in an apartment rented by his acquaintance and alleged accomplice, D., and taken to a police station. He alleged that he was handcuffed, beaten and had his nose broken. That evening he was questioned and admitted to robbing an apartment. The robbery concerned threats with a knife against K. and the taking of USD 12,800. It was unclear whether criminal proceedings were instituted before or after his arrest. The Government claimed he was actually arrested on 7 February 2003.

On 10 February 2003 the Dniprovskiy District Court of Kyiv ordered his pre-trial detention because he was accused of a serious crime and could abscond or obstruct the investigation. On 1 April 2003 the detention was extended until 7 June 2003. Between May 2003 and September 2007 the case was referred back for further investigation five times, but each time the court maintained his detention. In December 2006 and January 2007 the court refused release on generic grounds, finding he could continue criminal activity, abscond or hinder the investigation. In May 2008 the case was again sent back; in September 2008 the Kyiv City Court of Appeal quashed that decision and remitted the case, again maintaining detention. On 1 March 2010 the applicant was sentenced to eight and a half years’ imprisonment for robbery. The sentence was upheld in 2010 and 2011, and he was released on probation on 26 March 2011.

As to ill-treatment, the applicant said that between August 2003 and April 2004 he complained that police officers had physically and psychologically abused him and misappropriated his gold ring, mobile telephone and clothes. Prosecutors repeatedly refused to institute criminal proceedings against the police; several refusals were overturned and remitted for further examination. Ultimately the complaints were rejected as unsubstantiated, partly because there was no medical evidence, and the police denied ill-treatment. The applicant later submitted photographs showing his nose straight in some images and bent in another, and a 2011 medical certificate diagnosing post-traumatic nasal deformation that impeded breathing; in April 2011 his nasal bones were repositioned.

Regarding detention conditions, the applicant was held in SIZO No. 13 from 26 February 2003 to August 2010. He alleged a cold, damp cell infested with cockroaches, dirty torn bedding, and filthy toilets and sink. He submitted photographs showing dirt and dark stains. The authorities stated that cell No. 10 measured 52.06 m² and held eighteen others, had a toilet separated by a one-metre partition, was disinfected weekly, had reasonable bedding, and had been refurbished. Later, cell No. 40 measured 9.9 m² and held three others, with weekly showers. The SIZO’s maximum capacity was 2,850 but sometimes held nearly 3,200 detainees. Medical examinations found chronic pyelonephritis and crystalluria but generally satisfactory health and no need for specialist treatment.

A 2009 CPT visit to Kyiv SIZO found official capacity of 2,950 but 3,440 inmates; severe overcrowding, poor ventilation, heat and stuffiness, cockroaches, mice and rats, decrepit sanitary installations, and inadequate hygiene. The CPT considered the combination capable of being inhuman and degrading and recommended at least 4 m² per prisoner, natural light and ventilation, renovation, and hygiene improvements.
**N.M.Y. and Others v. Sweden** (Application no. 72686/10) concerned three Iraqi Christian siblings—two women and one man, born in 1963, 1966,

In *Abdi v. the United Kingdom*, the applicant was a Somali national who arrived in the UK in May 1995 and claimed asylum. Although his asylum claim was refused, he was granted exceptional leave to remain until February 2000. In July 1998 he was convicted of rape and indecency with a child and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. In May 2002 the Secretary of State decided to deport him and authorised his detention. His appeal and fresh asylum claim failed, and his appeal rights were exhausted in December 2003. Although his prison sentence ended automatically in September 2003, he remained in immigration detention pending deportation. A deportation order was issued in April 2004. The application to the European Court of Human Rights concerned only the first period of detention, which ended shortly after 13 April 2007.

The applicant claimed to be a member of the Isaaq tribe from Somaliland and said his parents were born in Hargeisa, although he was born in Mogadishu. The authorities initially sought to return him to Somaliland, which required clan bio-data that he did not provide. They then sought to remove him to Somalia. In August 2004 the last carrier willing to take enforced returns to Somalia withdrew, meaning only voluntary returns with a signed disclaimer were possible. In November 2004 the applicant refused to sign such a disclaimer. Enforced removals became possible again after July 2006 under an agreement with African Express Airlines, and the first enforced removal occurred in November 2006. Removal directions were later cancelled pending judicial review.

Domestically, the Administrative Court applied the *Hardial Singh* principles: detention pending deportation is lawful only for a reasonable period, only while removal can realistically be effected, and only if the Secretary of State acts with reasonable diligence. It held that detention from September 2003 to August 2004 was lawful, but that detention from 3 December 2004 to 30 June 2006 was unlawful because removal was impossible during that period and misleading statements had affected decisions. It found detention after 30 June 2006 lawful because removal had again become realistically possible. The Court of Appeal reversed, holding that the 2004–2006 period was lawful because the applicant could have returned voluntarily and because of his high risk of reoffending. The House of Lords refused permission to appeal.

Two broader detention issues also arose. From April 2006, the Home Office operated an unpublished policy creating a presumption in favour of detaining Foreign National Prisoners, contrary to its published policy favouring release. This “secret” policy, disclosed only in 2008, was later held unlawful in *Lumba and Mighty*, although only nominal damages were awarded because detention would have continued anyway. Separately, domestic law required regular monthly reviews of detention; in *Kambadzi* the Supreme Court held that failure to conduct such reviews could render detention unlawful.

The applicant’s core alleged violation was under Article 5 § 1 of the Convention: that his immigration detention pending deportation was unlawful or arbitrary, particularly because removal was not realistically possible for long periods, because his refusal to return voluntarily could not justify detention when enforced removal was impossible, and because of the unpublished detention policy and/or inadequate review. The case also engaged Article 5 §§ 4 and 5 in so far as he sought effective judicial review of the lawfulness of his detention and compensation. The Court therefore had to assess whether the domestic courts’ reversal of the Administrative Court’s finding was compatible with Article 5.

In *N.M.Y. and Others v. Sweden* (Application no. 72686/10), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) examined the case of three Iraqi nationals—two women and one man, born in 1963, 1966 and 1971—who originated from Baghdad. Their names were not disclosed. They arrived in Sweden on 17 September 2008 and applied for asylum two days later. They alleged that their deportation to Iraq would violate Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention.

The applicants are Christians and had lived together in Baghdad. They claimed they had been regularly harassed and insulted because of their faith. The two female applicants had been forced to wear a veil to avoid trouble. In 2006, armed men stopped a car carrying the two female applicants and their mother. When the men saw a hanging cross in the car, they forced the passengers out and took the vehicle. On 17 August 2008, armed men came to the applicants’ house and told another brother that the applicants should convert to Islam before 1 September 2008, the start of Ramadan, or be killed. The men also wrote a message with the same content on the wall of the house. The applicants left Iraq on 20 August 2008.

On 30 December 2008, the Migration Board rejected their asylum applications. It accepted that there was a threat against the applicants based on their religious beliefs and the difficult situation in Baghdad at the time. However, it found the threat limited to Baghdad because the applicants had not held prominent professional or religious positions; nothing suggested they would be of particular interest outside Baghdad. They could relocate to central or northern Iraq. This applied regardless of whether they had a social network there. As they had shared a household in Iraq, the female applicants would not lack a male relative upon return.

On appeal, the applicants maintained that Iraqi authorities would not protect them. They emphasized that their case did not rest only on the general situation for Christians; they had experienced several specific incidents because of their Christian beliefs. They further argued that the risk was not geographically limited to Baghdad: as Christians, they risked persecution throughout Iraq, so no internal flight alternative existed. The Migration Board replied that they could relocate to the Kurdistan Region and noted direct flights from Sweden to Erbil.

On 16 September 2009, the Migration Court upheld the Board’s decision. It considered the incidents to be criminal acts related to the general security situation in Baghdad at the time. It noted that two years had passed since the incidents and that the security situation in Baghdad had improved. Thus, the circumstances did not show a concrete and individual threat against the applicants upon return. On 9 November 2009, the Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal.

On 21 November 2010, the applicants lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights, alleging that deportation to Iraq would violate Articles 2 and 3. On 22 December 2010, the President of the Section applied Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, indicating to the Swedish Government that the applicants should not be deported to Iraq during the proceedings. The application was communicated to the Government on 12 September 2011. The Court’s judgment became final on 27 September 2013. Relevant domestic law and country information about Iraq were cross-referenced to *M.Y.H. and Others v. Sweden* (no. 50859/10, 27 June 2013).

text:
In *Grupa Zastava Vozila, A.D. v. Slovenia* (Application no. 67793/10), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, Committee) delivered judgment on 25 April 2013. The applicant was a Serbian company, Grupa Zastava Vozila, A.D., represented by Ms M. Kranjčevič. The respondent was Slovenia. The Serbian Government declined to take part after being informed of its right to submit written comments.

The underlying dispute began in 1996, when the applicant concluded a contract with PS ZA AVTO p.o. before a notary concerning joint investments. On 1 December 1997, PS ZA AVTO brought proceedings before the Ljubljana District Court seeking annulment of that contract and the notarial protocol.

The procedural chronology is central to the alleged violation(s). On 14 July 1998, the District Court ordered that the claim be served on the applicant in Serbia through the Ministry of Justice and diplomatic channels. On 29 October 1998, the court inquired about service; on 12 November 1998, the Ministry said it was still awaiting a reply from Serbian authorities. The next significant step shown is 30 May 2000, when ZASTAVA AVTO d.o.o. requested third-party intervention. On 6 June 2000, the court again asked the Ministry about service. On 29 June 2000, the applicant’s representative submitted an authority form and a request for joinder. On 17 May 2001, the applicant asked for a hearing. A hearing set for 11 October 2001 was postponed. On 12 October 2001, the State Attorney’s Office requested third-party intervention. On 10 June 2002, the court allowed both third parties to participate.

On 12 September 2002, the applicant lodged a counterclaim, causing the hearing scheduled for 19 September 2002 to be postponed. On 3 February 2003, a settlement hearing failed. The first hearing was held on 14 April 2003. On 23 April 2003, the applicant sought and obtained a one-month extension to submit documents. On 10 November 2003, the court appointed a financial expert; on 23 February 2004, it extended the expert’s deadline; the expert submitted the report on 3 May 2004. A further hearing was held on 6 October 2004. On 13 December 2004, the District Court ruled in favour of the applicant, leaving the notarial protocol and contract in force. The plaintiff appealed.

On 7 November 2006, the Ljubljana Higher Court amended the first-instance judgment and ruled against the applicant. The applicant appealed on points of law. On 12 May 2008, the Supreme Court upheld the appeal court’s decision. The applicant then lodged a constitutional appeal, which the Constitutional Court rejected as unfounded on 13 May 2010.

The applicant company applied to the European Court on 11 November 2010. The application was communicated to the Slovenian Government on 24 May 2012 and assigned to a three-judge committee under Protocol No. 14. Although the extract does not set out the merits, the facts are most relevant to an alleged violation of the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time under Article 6 §1, and possibly the adequacy of domestic remedies under Article 13. The civil proceedings lasted from 1 December 1997 to 13 May 2010—over twelve years—with notable delays in service abroad, third-party participation, expert evidence, and appellate review.

**Rudnichenko v. Ukraine (Application no. 2775/07), ECtHR, 11 July 2013**

The case concerned a Ukrainian national, Mr Sergey Rudnichenko, who complained under Article 5 of the Convention that his pre-trial detention had been unlawful and unreasonably long, and under Article 6 that the trial judge had been impartial and that he had been unable to obtain the attendance of a key witness. He lodged his application on 4 December 2006, adding further complaints on 23 September 2010.

The relevant facts began on 22 October 2005, when two men attempted to break into a car belonging to K. K. caught one of them, “B.” On 6 January 2006 the applicant was caught inside N.’s car trying to dismantle equipment. N. handed him over to the police. The police report referred to the car theft, N.’s complaint, and the applicant’s arrest; it noted he was drunk and had been handcuffed. On 7 January 2006 the Leninskyy District Court ordered his administrative detention for three days for public drunkenness. On 9 January 2006, however, an investigator arrested him on suspicion of robbery. On 12 January 2006 the same court remanded him in custody for two months, citing that he had been caught in flagrante delicto, had committed the offence while drunk, had recently been released from prison, and was unemployed.

The applicant later alleged that he had in reality been detained as a criminal suspect from 6 January, not merely for an administrative offence, and that his detention from 6 to 12 January 2006 was therefore unlawful. His lawyer complained to the Leninskyy Court, relying on Article 5 §§ 1 and 5, and requested the summoning of N. and the arresting officers. On 29 March 2006 the court found that the investigation authorities had clearly known the applicant was arrested immediately after a criminal offence on 6 January, yet formally arrested him only on 9 January; it described this as a violation of criminal procedure. Nevertheless, it rejected the complaint as disclosing no significant violation. The Court of Appeal upheld that ruling on 6 June 2006.

Separately, B. had been tried and convicted on 7 February 2006 by Judge R. for the 22 October 2005 robbery. B.’s statements in that trial implicated the applicant as the instigator and accomplice, including threatening K. with scissors and hitting him with a bottle. The applicant was not a party to those proceedings. On 23 February 2006 K. and B. identified the applicant. On 7 March 2006 he was indicted for robberies concerning K. and N. His case was eventually assigned on 25 April 2007 to Judge R., the same judge who had tried B. On 12 October 2007 Judge R. sought recusal because she had already examined B.’s case and expressed an opinion about the incident involving both men. The President of the court rejected her recusal on 22 October 2007.

On 14 November 2007 Judge R. convicted the applicant of robbery following conspiracy with B. and sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment, relying on B.’s prior statements read out in court. The applicant’s requests to summon and question B. were unsuccessful. He was acquitted concerning N. on the basis that the actions amounted only to minor theft. On appeal, the Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 28 July 2009 without its own witness investigation. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 14 January 2010, with disputed notification to the applicant.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 5 §§ 1, 3, 4 and 5 concerning the lawfulness and length of detention, and Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d) concerning Judge R.’s lack of impartiality and the inability to examine B., whose untested statements were central to his conviction.

In *Belousov v. Ukraine*, the applicant, a Ukrainian national, complained that police unlawfully detained him, tortured him, unlawfully searched his home, failed to bring him promptly before a judge, and conducted an ineffective investigation into his torture complaint.

On 18 July 2005, at about 11 a.m., several plainclothes police officers came to the hostel where the applicant lived and invited him to accompany them to the police station. He went with them. At the station, police told him that two mothers had accused him of sexually abusing their minor daughters and questioned him. At about 5 p.m. he confessed and signed permission for police to inspect his home. At about 6 p.m., seven or eight officers took him back to the hostel, examined his room, seized a bed cover, a rug and personal belongings, and returned him to the station. No arrest report was drawn up at that stage. He first met a lawyer hired by relatives at about 7 p.m. on 19 July. At about 8:40 p.m. that day, an investigator finally drew up an arrest report stating that he had been arrested as a crime suspect under Article 115 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On 22 July he was brought before a judge, who remanded him in custody for ten days. He was released on 29 July subject to an undertaking not to abscond. In September 2005, one of the mothers withdrew her complaint, saying it had been lodged under police pressure.

The alleged torture was central. On the evening of 18 July, the hostel concierge and neighbours said they had seen the applicant leave at about 11 a.m. sober, neatly dressed and in good health. About seven hours later, when police brought him back for the search, he was limping, stooping, had bruises and swellings on his face, and his clothes were dirty and wrinkled. Some neighbours said he arrived handcuffed and that police prevented him from explaining what was happening. At about 10 p.m., an anonymous caller complained to the police hotline. A deputy district police chief arrived at about 10:30 p.m., interviewed the applicant, who complained of ill-treatment, and questioned officers who said he had injured himself. On 19 July at about 10 a.m., a forensic expert found minor bodily injuries, including soft tissue swelling, numerous bruises and scratches on his body, face and groin, inflicted by blunt objects within the previous one to three days. The applicant said police caused them; police said they were self-inflicted.

On 20 July, through his lawyer, the applicant formally complained to the district prosecutor about his unrecorded detention until 8:40 p.m. on 19 July and about ill-treatment. He alleged torture by officers S.B., A.O., V.M. and others. Criminal proceedings were instituted on 1 August. On 6 August, questioned as a witness, he described being urged to confess under threat of torture, then placed handcuffed on a desk, with his arms twisted, punched, and genitals squeezed; three additional officers allegedly joined and took turns beating and strangling him. Unable to withstand the torture, he confessed by 5 p.m. to a crime he had not committed. The officers later gave inconsistent accounts, claiming he became agitated and injured himself. The applicant repeatedly complained that the investigation was stalled and that officers should have been treated as suspects, not witnesses.

The investigation was repeatedly stayed, renewed and discontinued. In December 2009, the prosecutor discontinued it, acknowledging a de facto arrest on 18 July but noting documentation only on 19 July; it found no criminal offence, insufficient evidence of torture, and that the home visit was a lawful inspection with consent. Courts quashed later decisions, but the investigation remained unresolved.

Sweden** (Application no. 72686/10), three Iraqi nationals—two women and one man, born in 1963, 1966 and 1971—complained that their deportation from Sweden to Iraq would violate Articles 2 and 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants were Christians from Baghdad who had lived together. They arrived in Sweden on 17 September 2008 and applied for asylum two days

**Claes v. Belgium** (Application no. 43418/09) concerned André Claes, a Belgian national born in 1952 with severe mental disabilities and an IQ of 72. In 1978, after being found not criminally responsible for repeated rape of his under-age sisters, he was committed to psychiatric detention. Following conditional release, he was re-detained several times, including in 1982 and 1987, for sexual offences or indecent assaults involving children. In 1994, after incidents in a psychiatric hospital and reports describing him as manipulative and potentially dangerous, the Mental Health Board ordered his return to the psychiatric wing of Merksplas Prison. He remained in prison psychiatric settings for many years, despite the Board repeatedly indicating that he required placement in a suitable institution under the Flemish system for people with disabilities.

Reports from 1998 to 2008 documented his intellectual disability and the authorities’ unsuccessful search for a non-prison institution willing to accept him. Prison reports described growing suffering, frustration, tension, and limited rehabilitation prospects. A 2007 prison doctor noted his minimal understanding of his illness and unrealistic hopes. A 2008 visit report found that he spent his days in communal areas and slept in a dormitory with twenty-four other people, with unsatisfactory sanitation. Psychiatric follow-up was limited and fragmented: he saw prison psychiatrists on average about once a month, but often with different doctors over the years.

The Mental Health Board extended his detention in 2005, 2007, and 2008 until a suitable place could be found. It acknowledged that treatment was not always sufficient but stated it had no legal power to order the authorities to provide a suitable place or treatment. The Higher Mental Health Board rejected his appeals because his rehabilitation prospects were insufficient and he remained dangerous to society. The applicant applied to civil courts for injunctions ordering the Belgian State to find him a suitable institution. In 2008 and on appeal in 2009, the courts dismissed these applications for lack of jurisdiction, holding that placement fell within the exclusive remit of the Mental Health Boards and that no suitable establishment had been designated. The Court of Cassation later held that decisions concerning transfer were measures relating to the manner of detention and were not appealable before it.

In September 2009, the Mental Health Board released the applicant on a trial basis to the Martine van Camp Centre. In June 2011, after aggressive behaviour there, he was arrested and placed in the psychiatric wing of Louvain Prison. Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that his detention in a place unsuitable for someone with his disability violated Article 3 and Article 5 §§ 1 (e) and 4 of the Convention. He argued that the prison environment and inadequate care amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment, and that the domestic system failed to provide effective review because the courts could not order his transfer to a suitable institution and the Mental Health Board could not compel placement. The Government disputed these claims, relying on the exclusive authority of the mental health authorities and the ordinary courts’ lack of jurisdiction.

In *Rudnichenko v. Ukraine* (no. 2775/07, ECtHR, 11 July 2013), the applicant, a Ukrainian national, complained that his pre-trial detention was unlawful and unreasonably long. He later added complaints that the trial judge had not been impartial and that he had been unable to secure the attendance of a key witness at trial.

The detention facts arose from two incidents. On 6 January 2006, at about 6 p.m., the applicant was caught breaking into N.’s car and trying to dismantle equipment. N. handed him over to the police. A police report referred to the car theft, N.’s complaint, the applicant’s apprehension, and his drunkenness; it noted he had to be handcuffed. On 7 January 2006, the Leninskyy District Court ordered three days’ administrative detention for being drunk in public. On 9 January 2006, an investigator arrested him on suspicion of robbery. On 12 January 2006, the same court remanded him in custody for two months, relying on the fact that he had been caught in flagrante delicto, had been drunk, was unemployed, and had committed the offence within a year of release from prison. He was represented by a lawyer from 13 January 2006.

The applicant repeatedly sought release, without success. His lawyer complained that his detention from 6 to 12 January 2006 had been unlawful and asked the court to summon N. and the arresting police officers, because they could show that he had in reality been detained as a criminal suspect, not merely as an administrative offender. On 29 March 2006, the court found that the investigation authority had violated criminal procedure by arresting him only on 9 January 2006, but it rejected the complaint as disclosing no significant violation. On appeal, the Sevastopol Court of Appeal upheld that ruling on 6 June 2006, holding that the administrative detention from 6 to 9 January was outside the scope of review and that the later detention was lawful. The witness request was said to have no basis in the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The impartiality and witness-attendance complaints arose from an earlier incident on 22 October 2005 involving an attempted break-in of K.’s car. K. caught one thief, B., while the applicant allegedly escaped. B. was tried separately and, on 7 February 2006, convicted by Judge R. of robbery. The judgment relied on B.’s statements implicating the applicant as his accomplice and instigator. The applicant was not a party to those proceedings. Later, K. and B. identified the applicant. On 7 March 2006, the applicant was indicted for robberies involving K. and N., and the case was sent to trial.

On 25 April 2007, the case was assigned to Judge R., the same judge who had tried B. On 12 October 2007, Judge R. sought recusal, stating that she had already expressed an opinion about the incident involving both the applicant and B. The President of the Leninskyy Court rejected the recusal request. On 14 November 2007, Judge R. convicted the applicant of robbery following conspiracy with B. and sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment, relying on B.’s prior trial statements, which were read out at the hearing. The applicant had unsuccessfully requested B.’s attendance and questioning; the Government later said the request was made at an inappropriate stage. The applicant was acquitted regarding the N. incident, which was reclassified as attempted petty theft.

On appeal, the applicant complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d) that B. had not been summoned and that statements from a trial in which he had not participated were used against him. He also argued that Judge R. had admitted having a preconceived opinion. On 28 July 2009, the Court of Appeal upheld the conviction without its own judicial investigation, finding B.’s statements concordant with other evidence. Cassation was rejected on 14 January 2010. The alleged violations therefore concerned Article 5, regarding unlawful and lengthy detention, and Article 6, regarding an impartial tribunal and the right to examine a key witness.

In *Claes v. Belgium*, the applicant, André Claes, a Belgian national with severe mental disabilities, alleged that his prolonged detention in prison psychiatric facilities unsuitable for his condition violated Article 3 and Article 5 §§ 1(e) and 4 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The case concerned his detention, principally in the psychiatric wing of Merksplas Prison, and the Belgian authorities’ failure to transfer him to an appropriate psychiatric or disability-care institution.

In 1978, Claes was found not criminally responsible for the repeated rape of his under-age sisters between 1973 and 1977 because of severe mental disabilities. He was committed to psychiatric detention. Over the following years, he was released and detained again after further sexual offences and aggressive incidents. In 1983, the Mental Health Board ordered his transfer to a private psychiatric clinic, but he was returned to a prison psychiatric wing in 1984 after aggressive behaviour and another sexual assault. In 1987, he was arrested for indecent assault on a young girl and placed in Turnhout Prison’s psychiatric wing. In 1994, following incidents involving young girls and female staff, and reports describing him as manipulative and potentially dangerous, the Mental Health Board ordered his return to Merksplas Prison.

Psychological assessments in 1998 recorded an IQ of 72 and classified him as mentally disabled. From 1998 onwards, Belgian authorities repeatedly tried, without success, to find a non-prison psychiatric or residential institution willing to accept him. Reports between 2002 and 2008 documented the ongoing failure to secure a suitable placement. A 2004 report noted that a structured establishment was needed to reduce reoffending risk, but no place was available; he was placed on a waiting list for a private care home. Later reports described growing suffering, frustration, and the need for intensive, specific care, while noting that his behavioural problems made institutions reluctant to take him.

The Mental Health Board repeatedly extended his detention in Merksplas until he could be placed in the Flemish system for social integration of people with disabilities. In 2007 and 2008, Claes sought urgent court injunctions ordering the Belgian State to find him a suitable institution. These applications were dismissed because the urgent applications judge and Court of Appeal held that the ordinary courts lacked jurisdiction; the Mental Health Boards had exclusive power to decide the place of detention. Appeals to the Higher Mental Health Board and Court of Cassation also failed.

A 2008 visit report noted unsatisfactory conditions: Claes spent days in communal areas and at night shared a dormitory with twenty-four other people, with unsatisfactory sanitation. In 2009, the Mental Health Board acknowledged his right to treatment but said it had no power to order the authorities to provide a suitable place. It considered his detention lawful and not intended to be inhuman or degrading, though it accepted that detention without adequate treatment might raise an Article 3 issue in conjunction with Article 5. It refused release because of the danger he posed, particularly to children.

In September 2009, Claes was released on a trial basis to the Martine van Camp Centre. However, in June 2011, after aggressive behaviour, he was returned to Louvain Prison’s psychiatric wing. The key alleged violations therefore concerned his long detention in a prison environment unsuitable for his mental disability, inadequate treatment and care, the State’s failure to provide an appropriate placement, and the lack of effective judicial review of the place and conditions of his detention.

In *Claes v. Belgium* (Application no. 43418/09, judgment 10 April 2013), the applicant, André Claes, was a Belgian national born in 1952 with severe mental disabilities (IQ 72). He complained that his detention in a place unsuitable for his disability violated Article 3 and Article 5 §§ 1(e) and 4 of the Convention.

In 1978 the Louvain Criminal Court found him not criminally responsible for repeated rape of his under-age sisters between 1973 and 1977 and committed him. He was conditionally released in 1978 but re-detained in 1982 after sexually assaulting a child. From then on, the Mental Health Board repeatedly considered transfer to psychiatric institutions. However, due to aggressive behaviour and further sexual offences, including indecent assault on a young girl in 1987, he was returned to prison psychiatric wings, especially Merksplas Prison. Reports described him as manipulative, potentially dangerous, and incapable of living in society. In 1998 testing revealed IQ 72 and he was classified as mentally disabled. Attempts in 1998 and between 2002 and 2004 to find a non-prison residential institution failed. A 2004 psychologist report noted an ongoing search, a waiting list for Borgenstein, and that the situation “cannot go on much longer.”

In 2005 the Mental Health Board extended his detention in Merksplas until the Flemish social integration system could place him. A 2008 visit by the Ghent Mental Health Board recorded that he spent days in communal areas, slept in a dormitory with twenty-four others, and endured unsatisfactory sanitation. A June 2008 prison psychologist report described growing suffering, frustration, and tension caused by the failure to find an institution; no institution was willing to accept him. In 2009 the prison governor noted he had priority status and financial resources were set aside, but no placement occurred. On 2 March 2009 the Mental Health Board refused release, stating the psychiatric wing was not Article 3 ill-treatment, acknowledging his right to treatment but noting treatment was not always sufficient and that it had no legal power to order a suitable place. It found detention lawful under Article 5 § 1(e) and necessary to protect society, especially children, from sexual abuse.

The applicant sought injunctions to compel the State to find a suitable institution. In 2008 the urgent applications judge dismissed the claims, holding that the Mental Health Board had exclusive power over placement. In 2009 the Antwerp Court of Appeal upheld that lack of jurisdiction. The Court of Cassation also held that transfer decisions could not be appealed. Thus, he alleged no effective judicial remedy under Article 5 § 4.

In September 2009 the Board released him on trial to the Martine van Camp Centre. In June 2011, after aggressive behaviour, he was returned to Louvain Prison psychiatric wing.

The alleged violations therefore centred on: (1) Article 3, because detention in a prison psychiatric wing unsuitable for a mentally disabled person, with insufficient care, poor conditions, and prolonged waiting, caused suffering amounting to inhuman or degrading treatment; (2) Article 5 § 1(e), because his detention as an unsound person continued in an inappropriate non-therapeutic setting; and (3) Article 5 § 4, because domestic courts could not review or compel a suitable placement or remedy the delay. The Government relied on domestic competence rules and said he was placed in the new De Haven unit in 2009, which the applicant disputed.

In *Julius Kloiber Schlachthof GmbH and Others v. Austria* (Applications nos. 21565/07, 21572/07, 21575/07 and 21580/07), four Austrian-registered companies that slaughter cattle and pigs complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. Under the Agricultural Market Act (*Agrarmarktgesetz*), they were liable to pay agricultural marketing charges to Agrarmarkt Austria (“AMA”), the national agricultural marketing board, calculated by the number of animals slaughtered.

In 2006 AMA issued payment orders against each applicant for unpaid contributions. On 5 July 2006 it ordered the first company to pay EUR 56,573.62 for 2003 and 2004 plus a 10% surcharge. On 30 May 2006 it ordered the second company to pay EUR 12,556.43 for 2004 and 2005 plus 10%; the third to pay EUR 5,936.01 for 2005 and 2006 plus 10%; and the fourth to pay EUR 96,050.48 for 2005 and 2006 plus a 60% surcharge. These surcharges formed the core of the later complaints.

The companies appealed, arguing that the AMA contribution system breached EU State-aid rules, and requested oral hearings. The Federal Minister of Agriculture, Forestry, Environment and Water, acting as appeal authority, dismissed the appeals on 17 July 2006 without a hearing. The Minister relied on a European Commission decision of 30 June 2004, which had raised no objection to AMA’s quality assurance scheme and quality mark as compatible State aid, and on Administrative Court decision no. 2005/17/230 of 20 March 2006. The Minister said a hearing was unnecessary because it was only required when a panel decided an appeal against a tax office or regional finance directorate, not in this procedure.

The applicants then lodged complaints with the Constitutional Court and the Administrative Court. Before the Constitutional Court, they alleged that the surcharges violated their constitutional right to property. Before the Administrative Court, they argued that the appeal authority was not a “court” under Court of Justice case-law, preventing review of the Commission’s decision through Article 234 EC proceedings. They also said the authorities’ findings on the surcharges were insufficient, particularly whether objective and subjective elements of the offence were met. Relying on Article 6, they complained that there had been no public hearing and that the “criminal charge” against them had not been decided by an impartial tribunal established by law. They asked the Administrative Court for a public hearing.

On 25 September 2006 the Constitutional Court declined to deal with the complaints for lack of prospects of success. On 30 January 2007 the Administrative Court dismissed the complaints in separate decisions, referring to its earlier decision no. 2005/17/230 and dismissing the cases without further proceedings in camera. It held that Article 6 of the Convention was not relevant.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained in particular that proceedings concerning the imposition of surcharges on unpaid AMA contributions had not been decided by a tribunal within the meaning of Article 6 § 1. The applications were communicated to the Austrian Government on 23 October 2008, and the Court decided to rule on admissibility and merits together. The key alleged violation therefore concerned the absence of a tribunal/public hearing in proceedings that imposed financial surcharges for non-payment of AMA contributions.

**Summary of Budrevich v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 65303/10)**

The case of *Budrevich v. the Czech Republic* concerns a Belarusian national, Mr. Andrei Budrevich, who alleged that the Czech Republic violated his right to an effective remedy under Article 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights against his expulsion to Belarus, where he feared persecution and ill-treatment.

The applicant entered the Czech Republic in October 2006 using an assumed name and immediately applied for asylum. He claimed he fled Belarus due to state pressure after importing advertisements for opposition candidate Aliaxandr Milinkevich in the 2006 presidential elections. He alleged detention, fines, confiscation of his car and passport, and repeated police visits to his home warning his family of criminal proceedings. His first asylum request was rejected in September 2007, with the Ministry of the Interior finding his allegations contradictory and not credible. The Hradec Králové Regional Court upheld this in May 2008, and the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed his cassation appeal in June 2009 due to procedural failings by his lawyer.

The applicant’s true identity was revealed in December 2009 when Czech police shared his fingerprints with Belarus. In November 2009, Belarus requested his extradition for drug-related offences. The Plzeň Regional Court declared this request inadmissible in April 2010, citing reasonable fears that criminal proceedings in Belarus would violate Articles 3 and 6 of the Convention, based on reports documenting political persecution, lack of judicial independence, and ill-treatment in Belarus.

Meanwhile, the applicant faced criminal convictions in the Czech Republic for theft. Notably, on 5 November 2008, the Prague 10 District Court sentenced him to thirty months’ expulsion. On 9 September 2010, he requested suspension of this expulsion, citing risks under Articles 3 and 6 and referencing the extradition refusal and a new asylum request. The District Court initially stayed the expulsion pending the asylum decision but cancelled the stay on 25 October 2010 after the Ministry rejected his third asylum request as inadmissible. A removal attempt on 4 October 2010 was aborted when the applicant attempted suicide.

The applicant lodged multiple asylum requests. His second request (January 2010) was rejected as repetitive, though the Supreme Administrative Court later found the Ministry should have informed him of the pending extradition request. His third request (September 2010) was deemed inadmissible under Section 10a(e) of the Asylum Act for lacking new circumstances. His fourth request (November 2010) resulted in subsidiary protection being granted in October 2011 for one year, later extended, as the Ministry recognized a real risk of inhuman or degrading treatment in Belarus.

The core of the applicant’s complaint before the European Court was that he lacked an effective domestic remedy against his expulsion. He argued that the expulsion order remained in force despite his subsidiary protection status and the extradition refusal. Under Czech law, a sentence of expulsion is inadmissible if the person has been granted subsidiary protection, yet the applicant’s appeals against the cancellation of the expulsion stay were rejected as belated. The Court applied Rule 39, indicating to the Government not to remove the applicant until further notice.

**Summary of *Belousov v. Ukraine* (Application no. 4494/07)**

The case concerns events beginning on 18 July 2005, when several plainclothes police officers came to the hostel where Mr. Vyacheslav Belousov lived and invited him to accompany them to the Kominternivskyy District police station in Kharkiv. The applicant went with them voluntarily. At the station, he was informed that two mothers had accused him of sexually abusing their minor daughters and was questioned. By around 5 p.m., he had confessed and signed permission for police to inspect his home.

At approximately 6 p.m., police took the applicant back to his hostel, examined his room, seized items, and returned him to the station. Critically, no arrest report was drawn up at this stage—his detention was not officially documented until 8:40 p.m. on 19 July 2005, more than 33 hours after he was first taken into police custody. The applicant was not permitted to meet with a lawyer, arranged by his relatives, until about 7 p.m. on 19 July.

The applicant alleged that during his unrecorded detention on 18 July, he was tortured by police officers to coerce a confession. He claimed that officers S.B., A.O., and V.M. urged him to confess under threat of torture, then placed him handcuffed on a desk, twisted his arms, punched him, and squeezed his genitals. Additional officers allegedly joined and took turns beating and strangling him. Unable to withstand the torture, he confessed by 5 p.m.

Witness evidence supports the allegation of ill-treatment. The hostel concierge and three neighbours saw the applicant leaving with police at 11 a.m.—sober, neatly dressed, and in good health. When they saw him again around 6 p.m., he was limping, stooping, and had bruises and swellings on his face. His clothes were dirty, and he was handcuffed. A forensic examination on 19 July documented minor bodily injuries including soft tissue swelling, numerous bruises, and scratches on his face and groin area, inflicted within the past one to three days. The applicant attributed these to police; police claimed they were self-inflicted.

The applicant also complained that the search of his home was unlawful. The prosecutor later characterised it not as a search but as a lawful crime-scene inspection conducted with the applicant's consent.

On 20 July 2005, the applicant lodged a formal complaint regarding his unrecorded detention and ill-treatment. Criminal proceedings were instituted on 1 August 2005. However, the investigation was marked by repeated suspensions and resumptions. The applicant was initially questioned as a witness before being granted injured-party status on 11 November 2005. The three identified officers were questioned as witnesses, not defendants, and gave varying accounts. In December 2007, proceedings were discontinued for lack of evidence, then quashed and remitted; this pattern repeated multiple times.

On 28 December 2009, the District Prosecutor's Office discontinued proceedings, acknowledging that the applicant had been de facto arrested on 18 July but documented only on 19 July. It found this administrative delay could not qualify as a criminal offence and that there was insufficient evidence of torture. Courts quashed this decision twice more, but the investigation remained unresolved, with parties not informing the Court of further steps after November 2011.

**Belousov v. Ukraine (Application no. 4494/07)**

The case originated from an application against Ukraine by Mr. Vyacheslav Belousov, a Ukrainian national. The alleged violations stem from events beginning on 18 July 2005, when several police officers in civilian clothes came to the hostel where the applicant lived and invited him to accompany them to the Kominternivskyy District police station in Kharkiv.

According to the applicant, upon arrival at the police station around noon, he was questioned regarding complaints from two mothers implicating him in the sexual abuse of their minor daughters. The applicant alleged that three police officers—S.B., A.O., and V.M.—urged him to confess under threat of torture. When he insisted on his innocence, the officers allegedly cleared a desk, covered it with a blanket, and placed him on it with his hands handcuffed behind his back. They then painfully twisted his arms, punched him in various parts of his body, and squeezed his genitals. Subsequently, three additional officers joined and took turns applying various techniques to cause him pain, beat him, and strangle him. Unable to withstand the torture, by 5 p.m. the applicant confessed to a crime he maintained he never committed.

At approximately 6 p.m., seven or eight police officers took the applicant back to his hostel, where they examined his room, seized several items including a bed cover, a rug, and personal belongings, and returned him to the police station. Critically, no documentary record of his arrest was drawn up at that stage. The applicant was not permitted to contact his family, and it was only at approximately 7 p.m. on 19 July 2005 that he first met with a lawyer hired by his relatives.

Witnesses at the hostel provided accounts corroborating the applicant's version of events. The concierge and three neighbours had seen the applicant leaving with police officers at about 11 a.m. on 18 July; at that time, he appeared sober, neatly dressed, and in good health. When they saw him approximately seven hours later, he was limping, stooping, had bruises and swellings on his face, and his clothes were dirty and wrinkled. Some neighbours noted he arrived handcuffed and that police prevented him from explaining what was happening. That evening, an unidentified person telephoned the police hotline demanding an investigation into the applicant's arrest and detention. Following this complaint, M.K., the Deputy Chief Officer, arrived to conduct an inquiry.

On 19 July 2005 at approximately 8:40 p.m., more than 33 hours after the applicant had been taken into police custody, an investigator finally drew up an arrest report. The applicant was brought before a judge only on 22 July 2005—four days after his detention—who remanded him in custody for ten days. He was released on 29 July 2005 subject to an undertaking not to abscond. In September 2005, one of the mothers who had complained of sexual abuse against the applicant withdrew her complaint, stating it had been lodged under pressure from the police.

Regarding the investigation of the applicant's complaints, a forensic expert examined the applicant on 19 July 2005 and certified that he was suffering from minor bodily injuries, including soft tissue swelling, numerous bruises, and scratches on various parts of his body, particularly the face and groin area, inflicted by blunt objects within the past one to three days. The applicant lodged a formal complaint on 20 July 2005 alleging unrecorded detention and ill-treatment, and criminal proceedings were instituted on 1 August 2005.

The investigation that followed was marked by repeated suspensions and renewals. On 28 December 2009, the prosecutor's office discontinued the proceedings, acknowledging that the applicant had been de facto arrested on 18 July 2005, but had only been documented on 19 July 2005—a delay that could give rise to disciplinary proceedings but did not qualify as a criminal offence. The office also found insufficient evidence of torture and characterised the visit to the applicant's home as a lawful crime scene inspection conducted with the applicant's consent. This decision was subsequently quashed by courts on multiple occasions, with the investigation repeatedly remitted for further investigation before being stayed again when the perpetrator could not be identified.

The applicant alleged violations of Articles 3, 5, 6, and 13 of the Convention, complaining of torture, unlawful detention, unlawful search, failure to be brought promptly before a judge, and the ineffectiveness of the investigation into his complaints.

**Budrevich v. the Czech Republic** (Application no. 65303/10, judgment of 17 October 2013) concerned a Belarusian national, Mr Andrei Budrevich, who alleged that he had no effective remedy under Article 13 of the Convention against his expulsion to Belarus.

In October 2006 the applicant left Belarus using an assumed name and entered the Czech Republic, where he requested asylum. He claimed he had been pressured, detained, fined and searched in Belarus because he had imported advertisements supporting opposition presidential candidate Aliaxandr Milinkevich. His first asylum request was rejected in September 2007 as not credible. That decision was upheld in May 2008, and in June 2009 the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed his cassation appeal because proper grounds had not been submitted. His true identity was revealed in December 2009 when Czech police sent his fingerprints to Belarus.

Meanwhile, the applicant was convicted of several thefts in the Czech Republic. In November 2008 the Prague 10 District Court sentenced him to a thirty-month expulsion order. In March 2009 the Prague 8 District Court imposed a one-year prison sentence and a five-year expulsion order. He served prison from December 2008 until October 2010.

In November 2009 Belarus requested his extradition for drug-related offences. The applicant was informed in December 2009 and formally notified in January 2010. In April 2010 the Plzeň Regional Court found the extradition request inadmissible because there were reasonable fears that criminal proceedings in Belarus would violate Articles 3 and 6 of the Convention. It relied on reports documenting political persecution, lack of judicial independence, inhuman detention conditions, ill-treatment by police and unfair trials in Belarus.

The Article 13 complaint centred on the absence of an effective remedy against expulsion. Key facts included the applicant’s repeated asylum requests. His second request, in January 2010, was rejected as a repeated request without new circumstances. The Plzeň Regional Court upheld that rejection in September 2010, even though the Ministry of the Interior knew of the Belarusian extradition request but merely asked the applicant whether he knew of any prosecution. In February 2011 the Supreme Administrative Court quashed that decision, holding that the Ministry should have informed him of the extradition request and examined whether the new prosecution and extradition request constituted new circumstances. The case was remitted but later terminated on grounds of litispendence.

His third asylum request, in September 2010, was also rejected as inadmissible. Service of the decision was disputed, and the Supreme Administrative Court later found that it had not been validly served on his lawyer. His fourth asylum request, in November 2010, eventually led to subsidiary protection in October 2011, later extended, because of a real risk of inhuman or degrading treatment in Belarus.
