In *Zeynalov v. Azerbaijan* (Application no. 31848/07, judgment of 30 May 2013), the applicant, Ahmadshah Mammadshah oglu Zeynalov, was an Azerbaijani farmer born in 1935. He became involved in a land dispute with the Sadan Municipality in the former Davachi district over a 0.8-hectare plot. Zeynalov claimed the plot formed part of a larger 50-hectare parcel belonging to his family farming business, while the Municipality asserted ownership.

Criminal proceedings were brought against Zeynalov under Article 188 of the Criminal Code for violation of a lawful owner’s right to land by unauthorised occupation or cultivation. On 29 December 2004 the Davachi District Court convicted him and fined him 100 conventional financial units (110 AZN, about EUR 84). The court relied on witness statements and information from the State Committee of Land and Cartography (“the SCLC”) to find that he had unlawfully occupied and cultivated municipal land. On 18 March 2005 the Court of Appeal upheld the conviction.

Zeynalov appealed on points of law, arguing that the lower courts had erred in assessing the facts. On 9 August 2005 the Supreme Court, composed of a panel of three judges including Judge N.H., quashed the Court of Appeal’s judgment and remitted the case for a fresh examination, noting that the conviction was based on insufficient evidence. On remand, the Court of Appeal requested detailed information from the SCLC and the Municipality. The Municipality stated that official records showed the plot belonged to it, and the SCLC’s on-site inspection concluded that the disputed land was part of the Municipality’s estate. On 12 July 2006 the Court of Appeal again upheld the conviction.

Zeynalov appealed once more. On 10 October 2006 the Supreme Court, again composed of a panel of three judges including Judge N.H., examined his appeal. It found that the Court of Appeal had assessed all relevant evidence and had committed no substantive or procedural breaches, and it dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction.

The applicant lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 9 April 2007. He alleged in particular that the Supreme Court’s examination of his criminal case had not complied with Article 6 of the Convention. The key issue relevant to the alleged violation was the repeated participation of Judge N.H. in the cassation proceedings. Judge N.H. had sat on the Supreme Court panel on 9 August 2005, when the case was quashed and remitted, and then sat again on 10 October 2006, when the Supreme Court dismissed Zeynalov’s appeal and upheld his conviction.

This raised concerns about the impartiality of the Supreme Court and compliance with domestic disqualification rules. Under Article 109.1.6 of the Azerbaijani Code of Criminal Procedure, a judge had to be disqualified if he or she had participated in the examination of the same criminal case in a court of first instance, appeal or before the Supreme Court. Article 109.2 required self-disqualification. The Plenum of the Supreme Court’s decision no. 3 of 24 November 2005 further stated that disqualification was a judge’s legal duty, even without a party’s objection, and that a judge who had already heard a criminal case at any instance could not take part in its re-examination. The case was communicated to the Government on 10 November 2010. The alleged violation therefore centred on whether Judge N.H.’s dual participation deprived Zeynalov of a fair hearing before an impartial tribunal under Article 6. The Court ultimately found a violation of Article 6 § 1 on that basis.

**Summary of *Zeynalov v. Azerbaijan* (Application no. 31848/07)**

The case of *Zeynalov v. Azerbaijan* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr. Ahmadshah Mammadshah oglu Zeynalov, an Azerbaijani farmer born in 1935, on 9 April 2007. The applicant alleged that the Supreme Court’s examination of his criminal case violated the guarantees of Article 6 of the Convention, specifically the right to a fair trial.

The case originated from a land ownership dispute between the applicant and the Sadan Municipality regarding a 0.8-hectare plot in the Davachi district. On 29 December 2004, the Davachi District Court convicted the applicant under Article 188 of the Criminal Code for unlawfully occupying and cultivating land owned by the Municipality. He was fined 100 conventional financial units (approximately 110 new Azerbaijani manats or 84 euros). The conviction relied on witness statements and information from the State Committee of Land and Cartography (SCLC).

The applicant appealed, asserting that the land was part of a larger 50-hectare parcel belonging to his family farming business. On 18 March 2005, the Court of Appeal upheld the conviction. The applicant then lodged an appeal on points of law. On 9 August 2005, the Supreme Court, composed of a panel including Judge N.H., quashed the appellate judgment due to insufficient evidence and remitted the case for re-examination.

Following the Supreme Court’s findings, the Court of Appeal requested detailed information from the SCLC and the Municipality. The Municipality claimed ownership, and the SCLC’s on-site inspection confirmed the plot belonged to the Municipality. On 12 July 2006, the Court of Appeal again upheld the applicant’s conviction, finding that the land belonged to the Municipality and the law was correctly applied.

The applicant appealed once more. On 10 October 2006, the Supreme Court, again composed of a panel including Judge N.H., dismissed the appeal, finding no breaches of substantive or procedural law and upholding the Court of Appeal’s judgment.

The key alleged violation stemmed from Judge N.H.’s participation in both Supreme Court hearings. Under Article 109.1.6 of the Azerbaijani Code of Criminal Procedure (CCrP), a judge must be disqualified if they have previously participated in examining the same criminal case at any stage, including before the Supreme Court. Article 109.2 mandates self-disqualification in such cases. Furthermore, the Plenum of the Supreme Court’s decision no. 3 of 24 November 2005 emphasized that when legal grounds for disqualification exist, a judge must withdraw from the case of their own accord, even without a party objection, describing this as a “legal duty.” A judge who has already heard a criminal case at any instance cannot participate in its re-examination.

The applicant’s complaint centered on the fact that Judge N.H. participated in both the cassation hearing that quashed the initial appellate judgment and the subsequent cassation hearing that ultimately upheld his conviction. This dual participation, contrary to domestic law requiring disqualification, formed the basis of the alleged Article 6 violation regarding the fairness of the Supreme Court proceedings. The Court communicated the application to the Government on 10 November 2010 and decided to rule on admissibility and merits simultaneously.

**Case Summary: Tomić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina (Application no. 14284/08)**

The case of *Tomić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* concerned the non-enforcement of final and enforceable domestic judgments awarding war damages. The applicants were five citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina: Ruža Tomić, Ljeposava Kovačević, Dobrinka Jovanović, Marko Tomić and Janko Tomić. They lodged their application with the European Court of Human Rights on 18 February 2008, alleging violations arising from the failure of the authorities to enforce final domestic judgments in their favour. The case was similar to earlier cases such as *Čolić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* and *Runić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina*.

The key facts began on 13 March 2001, when the Srebrenica First Instance Court ordered the Republika Srpska, an Entity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to pay the applicants 31,500 convertible marks (BAM), within 15 days, in respect of war damage, together with default interest at the statutory rate. That judgment became final on 20 April 2001. On 1 April 2002, the Banja Luka District Court issued a writ of execution. Despite the final judgment and the execution order, the awarded sums were not paid.

The applicants then complained to the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina about the non-enforcement. On 26 June 2007, the Constitutional Court found a breach of Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. However, the applicants did not claim compensation, and the Constitutional Court’s practice at the time indicated that such a claim would most likely have been refused.

Afterward, the authorities carried out an extensive information campaign explaining the options for settling the Republika Srpska’s public debt, including debt arising from domestic judgments. On 18 January 2010, three applicants—Ms Ljeposava Kovačević, Mr Marko Tomić and Mr Janko Tomić—informed the authorities that they agreed to receive legal costs in cash and the principal debt and default interest in government bonds. On 15 June 2010, government bonds were issued to them, and they subsequently sold some or all of those bonds on the Stock Exchange. The remaining applicant, Ms Dobrinka Jovanović, was not issued government bonds. The summary of the facts states that she did not accept the issuance of bonds in lieu of cash as a means of enforcement.

The relevant domestic law included the Domestic Debt Act 2012, which entered into force on 13 January 2012 and repealed the Domestic Debt Act 2004. As regards war damage, the 2012 Act envisaged the same solution as the old Act, but changed the maturity of government bonds from 14 years to 13 years. However, the new Act was not relevant to the bonded applicants because the applicable provisions were those of the 2004 Act, which had been in force when the bonds were issued. For Ms Jovanović, the key point was that she had not accepted bonds in lieu of cash as enforcement.

The alleged violations therefore centred on the failure to enforce final domestic judgments awarding war damages, contrary to Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. On 30 August 2010, the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government and to rule on admissibility and merits at the same time under Article 29 § 1 of the Convention.

In **Röman v. Finland** (Application no. 13072/05, judgment 29 January 2013), the European Court of Human Rights examined a Finnish woman’s inability to have her biological father’s paternity legally established because of a transitional five-year time-limit in Finland’s Paternity Act.

The applicant was born in 1954 out of wedlock and initially bore her mother’s maiden name. The same year, her mother and biological father concluded a child-support agreement verified by social services. In 1956 her mother married another man, and in 1961 the applicant’s name was changed to that of her mother’s husband. The family agreed that the biological father was never to be mentioned. The applicant thus grew up with the mother’s husband registered or treated as her father, while her biological father remained hidden from her.

On 1 October 1976, Finland’s Paternity Act entered into force. Its transitional provisions required paternity proceedings for children born before the Act’s entry into force to be initiated within five years, i.e. before 1 October 1981. They also barred any claim after the alleged father’s death. No such restrictions applied to children born after the Paternity Act came into force. The original rationale was legal certainty, protection of putative fathers, and evidential concerns.

The applicant only began investigating her origins later. In 2001, she discovered that the church registry, until 1993 the official population registry, listed her mother’s husband as her stepfather, while the State population registry listed him as her father. She also located the child-support agreement and, through it, her biological father. In September 2002 the State population register was corrected. In February 2003 she began paternity proceedings, claiming she had only learned in December 2001 that her registered father was not her biological father.

The Vantaa District Court dismissed her claim on 18 June 2003 as time-barred. It reasoned that during the five-year period she had been an adult and could have initiated proceedings, questioned her mother, or checked the church register. The Helsinki Court of Appeal upheld that decision on 15 March 2004, and the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 12 October 2004. The Deputy Parliamentary Ombudsman later considered that the courts had acted within their margin of appreciation. In 2007 a private DNA test confirmed with 99.99% certainty that the man she had identified was her biological father; he died in July 2008.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged violations of Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention. Under Article 8, she argued that the rigid application of the five-year time-limit prevented her from obtaining legal confirmation of her biological father and thus interfered with her private life and identity. Under Article 14, she alleged discrimination because children born before the Paternity Act were subject to the five-year deadline and the bar after the father’s death, whereas children born later were not. She stressed that she had no real opportunity to act within the deadline because her family concealed her origins and she was unaware of her legal status.

The Court found a violation of Article 8, holding that Finland had failed to strike a fair balance and that the applicant had effectively been deprived of the opportunity to establish her biological father’s paternity. It considered that no separate issue arose under Article 14.

**Zeynalov v. Azerbaijan** (Application no. 31848/07) concerned an Azerbaijani farmer, Ahmadshah Mammadshah oglu Zeynalov, who complained under Article 6 of the Convention that the Supreme Court’s examination of his criminal case had violated his right to a fair trial, particularly the requirement of impartiality.

The case arose from a land ownership dispute between the applicant and the Sadan Municipality over a plot of land in the former Davachi district. The applicant claimed the disputed 0.8-hectare plot formed part of a larger 50-hectare parcel belonging to his family farming business. The Municipality, however, maintained that the land belonged to it. Following the dispute, criminal proceedings were instituted against the applicant under Article 188 of the Criminal Code for unlawful occupation or cultivation of a lawful owner’s land.

On 29 December 2004, the Davachi District Court convicted the applicant and imposed a fine of 100 conventional financial units, equivalent to approximately EUR 84 at the time. The court found that he had unlawfully occupied and cultivated land owned by the Municipality, relying on witness statements and information from the State Committee of Land and Cartography (“SCLC”). On 18 March 2005, the Court of Appeal upheld that conviction.

The applicant appealed on points of law. On 9 August 2005, the Supreme Court, sitting as a panel of three judges including Judge N.H., quashed the Court of Appeal’s judgment and remitted the case for fresh examination. The Supreme Court found that the conviction had been based on insufficient evidence. On remittal, the Court of Appeal requested further information from the SCLC and the Municipality. The Municipality stated that official records showed the land belonged to it, and the SCLC conducted an on-site inspection and similarly concluded that the plot formed part of the Municipality’s estate. On 12 July 2006, the Court of Appeal again upheld the applicant’s conviction.

The applicant appealed once more. On 10 October 2006, the Supreme Court, again composed of a panel including Judge N.H., examined the appeal. It found no substantive or procedural breaches and dismissed the appeal, upholding the Court of Appeal’s judgment. Thus, the same judge, N.H., participated in both Supreme Court examinations of the same criminal case—first when the case was quashed and remitted, and later when the conviction was finally upheld.

The alleged Article 6 violation centred on this repeated participation. Under Article 109.1.6 of the Azerbaijani Code of Criminal Procedure, a judge was disqualified from participating in a criminal case if he or she had already participated as a judge in the examination of the same criminal case before a first-instance, appellate or Supreme Court court. Article 109.2 required such a judge to disqualify himself or herself. Moreover, in decision no. 3 of 24 November 2005, the Plenum of the Supreme Court held that a judge must withdraw of his or her own motion where legal grounds for disqualification existed, describing this as a “legal duty.” The Plenum also stated that a judge who had already heard a criminal case at first instance, appeal or cassation could not take part in its re-examination.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation were therefore: the prolonged land dispute and criminal conviction; the first Supreme Court cassation decision of 9 August 2005 involving Judge N.H.; the fresh Court of Appeal proceedings and renewed conviction of 12 July 2006; and the second Supreme Court decision of 10 October 2006, again involving Judge N.H., which finally upheld the conviction. The applicant argued that this repeated judicial participation in the same case breached Article 6 guarantees, and the domestic legal framework expressly prohibited such participation.

In *De Luca v. Italy* (Application no. 43870/04), the European Court of Human Rights considered an application lodged by Mr Giovanni De Luca, an Italian national living in Benevento, against Italy on 10 December 2004. The applicant alleged that the insolvency declared by his debtor, the municipality of Benevento, prevented him from collecting money owed to him.

The key facts began in December 1993, when Benevento declared itself insolvent (*stato di dissesto*) under Legislative Decree no. 66 of 1989, later amended and replaced by Legislative Decree no. 267 of 2000. In January 1994, the municipality’s financial management was entrusted to an extraordinary liquidation committee (OSL), responsible for drawing up a list of admissible claims for the debt repayment procedure. Under Article 248 § 2 of Legislative Decree no. 267/2000, from the declaration of insolvency until approval of the statement of accounts, no enforcement procedure could be initiated or pursued concerning claims registered with the OSL. Paragraph 4 also suspended statutory interest and inflation compensation on those debts during that period. Domestic case-law initially held that these restrictions did not apply to claims considered certain and payable by a judicial decision issued after the declaration of insolvency, regardless of when the claim arose. Such claims could therefore be enforced.

However, Law no. 140 of 28 May 2004, in force from 13 June 2004, changed this. Section 5(2) provided that insolvency rules applied to claims arising before 31 December of the year preceding the rebalancing of the budget, even if those claims had been established by a judicial decision after that date. The Consiglio di Stato later applied this provision in 2004 and 2005.

The applicant had filed a damages claim against Benevento on 28 October 1992, seeking unpaid rent and compensation for damage to his property. By judgment of 18 November 2003, deposited on 10 February 2004, the Benevento District Court allowed his claim and ordered the municipality to pay him EUR 17,604.46 in damages, plus statutory interest and inflation compensation. The judgment was served on the municipality on 9 April 2004 and became final on 9 May 2004. In resolution no. 4088 of 21 June 2005, the OSL acknowledged a debt of EUR 42,028.58 owed to the applicant. On 7 February 2006, the OSL offered a friendly settlement of 80% of the sum claimed. The applicant refused.

The domestic insolvency scheme aimed to satisfy creditors proportionately (*par condicio creditorum*) and to rebalance the municipality’s accounts. The municipality continued to exist and perform public functions. The OSL’s competence was limited to debts predating the insolvency, and enforcement was barred for registered past debts, with interest and inflation compensation suspended. Creditors could lodge appeals against OSL decisions, and the Constitutional Court had upheld the system in 1994, citing public interests and the need to prevent further financial deterioration.

The applicant’s complaint was that the insolvency of Benevento prevented him from collecting the sum owed. The central facts relevant to the alleged violation were that he held a final judicial judgment against the municipality, but the 2004 law subjected his judicially certified claim to the insolvency procedure, blocking enforcement and suspending interest and inflation compensation. Although the OSL acknowledged the debt and offered a reduced settlement, the applicant declined it, and the debt remained unpaid through ordinary enforcement. The application was communicated to the Government on 29 August 2006, with the Chamber deciding to rule on admissibility and merits together under Article 29 § 1 of the Convention.

**Summary of Röman v. Finland (Application no. 13072/05)**

**Parties and Core Complaint**
The applicant, Ms Mirja Anneli Röman, a Finnish national born in 1954, lodged an application against Finland on 6 April 2005. She alleged violations under Articles 8 (right to respect for private life) and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. Her central complaint was that she was legally barred from establishing her biological father’s paternity due to a rigid five-year time-limit in Finnish law that applied only to children born before the Paternity Act’s entry into force in 1976. She argued this prevented her from clarifying her biological identity and discriminated against her compared to children born after that date, who face no such restriction.

**Key Facts**
The applicant was born out of wedlock in 1954. Her mother and biological father signed a child support agreement that year, verified by social services. In 1956, her mother married another man, and in 1961, the applicant’s surname was changed to that of her mother’s husband. The family agreed never to mention her biological father. In official records, including the church registry (the primary population register until 1993), her mother’s husband was initially listed as her stepfather; later, state population records incorrectly listed him as her father.

The Paternity Act, which came into force on 1 October 1976, aimed to equalize the legal status of children born out of wedlock. However, its transitional provisions imposed a five-year deadline—expiring on 1 October 1981—for initiating paternity proceedings for children born before the Act. Additionally, no claim could be examined after the putative father’s death. No such limits applied to children born after 1976.

The applicant remained unaware of her true biological background for decades. In 2001, she discovered the discrepancy in the church registry, which listed her mother’s husband as stepfather, while state records named him as father. She also located the 1954 child support agreement, which enabled her to identify her biological father. The state population register was corrected on 25 September 2002. The following year, on 6 February 2003, she initiated paternity proceedings in the Vantaa District Court, claiming she had only learned the truth in December 2001.

**Legal Proceedings and Outcome**
The District Court dismissed her claim on 18 June 2003, ruling it time-barred under the five-year limit. It found she could have questioned her mother or checked the church register during the time-limit, even though she was unaware of the need to do so. The Helsinki Court of Appeal upheld this decision on 15 March 2004. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 12 October 2004. A petition to the Parliamentary Ombudsman was also unsuccessful, as the Deputy Ombudsman found the courts had acted within their margin of appreciation. In 2007, a private DNA test confirmed with 99.99% certainty the identity of her biological father, who died on 3 July 2008.

**Relevant Legal Context**
The five-year time-limit was originally justified by legal certainty and evidentiary concerns. However, by the time of this case, DNA testing had rendered such concerns largely obsolete, as later acknowledged by the Finnish Supreme Court in precedent KKO 2012:11. That ruling held that applying the time-limit to individuals who, for reasons beyond their control, could not act within the deadline, could lead to an evident conflict with the Finnish Constitution. The Supreme Court stated that the right to know one’s biological parentage falls within the core of private life protection and that children generally have a right, except in special circumstances, to have paternity confirmed by a court at least once.

**Case of Vilnes and Others v. Norway** (ECtHR, 5 December 2013) concerned seven former North Sea divers—Dag Vilnes, Magn Muledal, Anders Lindahl, Sigurdur Hafsteinsson, Knut Nygård, Bjørn Nesdal, and Per Jakobsen—who worked during the “pioneer era” of Norwegian oil exploration (1965–1990). They alleged that Norway violated Articles 2 and 8 of the Convention, with the first four also invoking Article 3, because state regulation and supervision of diving failed to protect their life, health, and physical/mental integrity, causing serious permanent injuries.

The applicants performed bounce and saturation diving at depths often between 70 and 180 metres, sometimes in experimental dives to 300–500 metres. They suffered decompression sickness, neurological damage, chronic obstructive lung disease, hearing loss, encephalopathy, and PTSD. Many experienced near-fatal incidents: gas cut-offs, rapid or uncontrolled decompression, equipment failures, trapped umbilicals, falling diving bells, explosions, and witnessing fatal accidents. Vilnes suffered spinal bends in 1977 and later PTSD; Muledal had repeated bends, gas cuts, and recovered bodies from the Alexander Kielland disaster; Lindahl had over twenty bends and convulsions; Hafsteinsson nearly suffered explosive decompression and had hearing loss; Nygård was nearly hit by a crane ball and an oxy-arc exploded in his hand; Nesdal was trapped in a shaft and his umbilical hooked by an ROV; Jakobsen had 15–20 bends and helped recover bodies.
